Editor: Śāstrī Gaṇapati.
Description: This e-text contains the *Mahārthamañjarī* together with its commentary, the *Parimala*, both composed by Maheśvarānanda. It was transcribed from the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series, No. 66.
The photographic facsimile is derived from volume 11 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.
Notes: This electronic text was transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: 02/08/2006. Publisher: Trivandrum Sanskrit Series.
Year of publication: 1919.
Place of publication: Trivandrum;
Country of publication: India; Title: Mahārthamañjarī.
Accompanied by its own commentary titled *Parimala*,
composed by Maheśvarānanda:
"Salutation to the one whose trunk does not touch the lotus-stalk with its tusk."
To him whose lotus-stalk is direct perception, who possesses leaves in the form of his two ears.
Victorious is the rootless, unfading, supreme non-dual reality—
the great lotus whose nectar consists of the vibration, the absence of vibration, and the pervasive movement of all things.
Victorious is the form of Gaurī, who wears an earring made of pearls, appearing like a whirlpool risen from the ocean of the nectar of compassion at the corner of her eye.

Salutations to the luster that is stainless, whose constant opening and closing constitutes the manifestation and withdrawal of the universe, and which is the embodiment of Śrī Śivānanda for the sake of the creative impulse of the cosmic architect.
Since it is through this that I have immersed myself in the unsurpassed great lake, and since it is through this that I have experienced the bliss of Śambhu’s auspiciousness,
therefore, [I offer praise] to the Gurus, who consist of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the succession of one's own conscious self.
I praise the pair of feet of Mova, whose vigor has arisen and increased through joy. || 5 ||
Homage to the atom of pollen from the lotus feet of Mahāprakāśa, which is most capable of dispelling every impurity.
Following the worldly understanding of Gorakṣa and the vision of the Teacher Maheśvarānanda,
I shall unfold the inner fragrance within the *Mahārthamañjarī*.
We ourselves provide an explanation even for our own activity; we remain eager to repeatedly indulge in our own self-exaltation even above this. (8)
Alternatively, let this effort be undertaken for the sake of delighting the minds of those to be trained; as for that, let it be so—
its beauty being distinguished by the analysis of both brevity and detail.
May this verbal offering of a handful of flowers be for Śambhu. || 9 ||
I am one who has realized the essential truth of the *Śivadṛṣṭi* and *Pratyabhijñā*,
who knows the secret essence of the unfolding of the sequence of its path,
and whose consciousness is dense with the skill in serving the feet of my guru.
I shall explain that dense forest which is the sky within the heart.
In this matter, for the auspicious unfolding of the great secret, my consciousness is empowered by the grace of the Yoginīs;
moreover, it is rendered fruitful by its connection to the reflection of the worship of the Kula.
Let the wise not open this even once.
May that goddess, the fair-faced Siddhayoginī, whom I encountered during the time of a dream,
be well-pleased by these seventy verses composed in the language of Svāpita.
May the illustrious Teacher flourish, and may the path of pure consciousness flourish;
may the devotees of Maheśvara flourish, and may Maheśvara himself flourish. (13)

Now, this great work entitled *Mahārthamañjarī*, which proceeds to expound the means for the reflective awareness of the Supreme Lord who is non-different from the very nature of the Self, consists— according to the position of the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (presumptive tenet)— essentially of five members beginning with the proposition (*pratijñā*).

This is the Tantra; herein there are seventy verses that function as aphorisms (*sūtra*). Among them, in the first [verse], the introduction to the opening statement is presented following the practice of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācāra*). In the second, there is the indication of the subject matter (*vastu*) to be expounded by the tantra. Then, in the [following] three [verses], regarding the reality of one's own self (*svātmatattva*)...
The elaboration on the non-utility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in the sixth [chapter], the exclusion of the distinction between qualified candidates;

in the seventh, the determination of injunctions and prohibitions; in the eighth, the description of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*); in the ninth, [the description] of one's own self...

The instruction on the propriety of the non-manifestness of even that which is manifest; the establishment of the contemplation of the nature of the contemplator as the supreme human goal in the tenth [chapter];
then, the contemplation of the nature of the two types of contemplation; and then, in thirteen [chapters], the discernment of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
In the twenty-sixth [verse], there is a profound reflection upon the ultimate reality regarding the meaning already stated;
in the twenty-seventh, the manifestation of the inclusion of the entire universe within light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*);
and in the twenty-eighth, the determination of the division between Śiva and Śakti with respect to a single and identical reality.

In the twenty-ninth [verse], the excellence of Śakti is established through the Supreme Lord’s being the body of the universe. In the thirtieth, it is demonstrated that the manifold variety of the universe exists within His own self without deficiency. In the thirty-first...
The unfolding of how the triad beginning with the knower culminates in non-duality;

from that, the exclusion of the distinction between the real and the unreal regarding those two; and from that as well, the manifestation of the superiority of the worship of the Supreme Lord over those two. And thus, among the six [categories], by virtue of being worthy of worship—

The Investigation into the Sequence of the Five Meanings (*Śrīpañcārthakramāvamarśa*). Therein, the extraction of the essential nature of worship within the five [categories] is presented. Following that, the determination of the intrinsic nature of the two deities is given. In the forty-ninth [chapter], the extraction of the reality of mantra is taught. In the fiftieth, there is an inquiry into the functions of speech.

In the fifty-first [chapter], there is the unveiling of the true nature of the mudrās. In the fifty-second, there is the identification of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) as the bestower of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. In the fifty-third, there is the establishment of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). In the fifty-fourth, there is the refutation of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*).
In the fifty-fifth [chapter], there is a description of the vibration of bliss (*ānandaspandatā*) which is the very nature of one's own self.

Following that, in four [chapters], there is a clear instruction on the means for the realization of reality (*tattvāvabodha*). Then, in six [chapters], there is the determination of freedom from anxiety for those who have entered into reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). In the sixty-sixth...

The sixty-seventh [chapter] establishes that self-reflection (*svātmavimarśa*) bestows immediate perfection (*siddhi*). The sixty-eighth proclaims that the attainment of such reflection depends upon the glance of the Guru. The sixty-ninth proves that the aforementioned subject matter constitutes the essence of all philosophical systems (*sarvadarśana*).

In the sixty-ninth [chapter], there is a presentation by way of summary of the extensive tantra; in the seventieth, the revelation that even yogins such as Vyāsa and others have the unsurpassed goal as their sole refuge; and in the final one, the application of the causes and methods for the teacher of the tantra to instruct the tantra. Such is the essential meaning and the intended purport of the tantra.

Now the text is being explained. The author of the Tantra, while contemplating the sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) of the venerable Lord of Teachers— which is capable of removing the obstacles to realizing the true nature of the manifestation of duality for the sake of attaining the glorious non-dual supreme realization— proceeds with the presentation of the Tantra.
He introduces the preliminary topic:
Having bowed to the eternally pure feet of the Guru, the Great Light, Maheśvarānanda weaves this fragrant *Mahārthamañjarī*. 1.

In this matter, there is indeed no disagreement that there exists some deity who is to be worshipped by all people; the difference lies solely in the designation of its name, form, and so forth. And when that [deity] is examined through the application of reasoning—

It follows that the deity to be worshipped by the universe is indeed Light itself, whose essential nature is the mere radiance of self-awareness. And its greatness is as follows: "That radiance is the Great Being, undifferentiated by space or time."
This very [syllable] is said to be the heart of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) by virtue of its essential nature.

Thus, according to the principle of the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā*, its sole essential nature is that of a radiant flash, having transcended all contraction. And that Guru—by the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) that he "teaches" (*gṛṇāti*) or "illuminates" (*prakāśayati*) the worldly transaction of the universe—is the benefactor of all. In the absence of such an illuminator...

Otherwise, the entire world would fall into a state resembling blindness and deafness. Ultimately, that [Lord] is the Great Subject (*mahā-pramātṛ*), whose nature is one's own Self (*svātmarūpa*) and who is synonymous with the venerable Paramaśiva Bhaṭṭāraka.
As it is stated in the *Śrīśivasūtras*: "The Guru is the means. His feet...

The term *caraṇau* (the two feet) is used because by means of these two— the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*)— the universe is moved (*caryate*), traversed (*gamyate*), attained (*prāpyate*), awakened to (*budhyate*), and consumed (*bhakṣyate*). As it is said in the venerable *Kubjikāmata*:
While the states of being— the objects of enjoyment and the enjoyers— whether with eyes or without eyes,
as well as those designated by space, time, and direction, and whether gross, subtle, or supreme, were all looking on;
"Pervaded by the expansion of existence, it is called 'caraṇa' (foot) due to its connection with movement and consumption, but not because of being a physical foot, O Dear One!
Thus, the third "caraṇa" is the Guru himself in his own essential nature; this is indicated by the use of the dual number.
Commentary: As it is stated in that very same place:
"The Guru is white on the left and reddish on the right, with hands in the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*);
he stands upon a corpse-lotus, possesses three eyes, and has his red *Śakti* seated in his lap."
"One wearing five skulls, garlanded, with a smiling face, should be meditated upon in the heart.

This very one, being both manifest (sakala) and unmanifest (niṣkala), is the fourth state (turya-pāda) whose nature is liberation (nirvāṇa) in the condition of the shaking off of all things; such is the Upaniṣad. As for worldly activity, however, it is by means of the manifest.
And by means of two feet alone, though partless, [the universe] is fashioned; as they say:
"The white foot enters the white, and the red foot rests upon the red;
by these two feet of the Parents, this entire world is born."

And those two are eternally pure, capable of reflecting other objects by means of the exclusion of the distinction between opening and closing; for this indeed is the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, which exists both internally and externally.
It is the state of being the playful manifestation of the entire universe, animated by the reflection of knowledge and action.
And this is proclaimed in the scriptures by such terms as "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*), "vibration" (*spanda*), "radiance" (*sphurattā*), and "exertion" (*udyama*).
Furthermore, by its eternal purity, it is made known that these two are animated by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is about to be described.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Since pure knowledge and action belong to the Lord precisely because they are reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
Having bowed to those two [knowledge and action] and having reflected upon them as having ascended to the highest level of excellence, [one should offer] of speech, mind, and body...

For "bowing" (*namanam*) is indeed the state of being bowed down, characterized by making that [Supreme Lord] one's sole object. Furthermore, the "greatness" (*mahān utkarṣaḥ*) of the Supreme Lord consists in His being the Great Light; and the "state of being bowed down" on the part of His worshiper toward Him—both of these have been explicitly stated.

However, if there is merely the presentation of the sacrifice, the salutation, and so forth, it is not possible for both [the subject and the predicate] to be easily understood by the audience— such that one is the explicit subject and the other is implied by the sense. And this is a great [defect].

The practice of auspiciousness (*maṅgalācāra*) consists in the recollection of the excellence of the Supreme Lord, which is an indispensable prerequisite for the commencement of this treatise. As it has been stated in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:
"It is a thunderbolt against all doubts and a fire of time for all misfortune."
"We praise the path of Maheśvara, which brings an end to all inauspiciousness at the dissolution of the eon," and also:
"All activities that are preceded by your worship bestow success.
By this it is shown that scriptures begin with auspiciousness, have auspiciousness in their middle, and conclude with auspiciousness.
"They spread; they become possessed of heroic men and long-lived men"—
according to this principle from the Mahābhāṣya, even treatises that contain only two or three auspicious verses in specific places must be accepted as authoritative, let alone those containing more.

The introduction to this Great Tantra (*Mahātantra*) is thus set forth: it causes a supreme, exalted, and auspicious radiance to blossom everywhere—like the fragrance of a fragment of *dhana-sāra* (camphor)—by means of the festive splendor of the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord being experienced in every verse. And this...

This was directly composed as an introduction to the treatise solely for the purpose of instructing the expounder and the listener; otherwise, since the removal of obstacles would be accomplished even by a mere act [of salutation], the prostration to the Supreme Lord [would not have been necessary]. And it has been stated that its form is as follows:
The contemplation of the excellence of the Supreme Lord’s sovereignty brings about for the contemplator a state of identity with Him. As it is said in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
"When, through the Self that has entered into our own form, one wards off [the notion of] a separate self..."

"May Śiva, who is the pervasive Self, act through His own power of adoration (namaḥ-śakti). For this very reason, after the act of prostration to the Supreme Lord with the words "having bowed," Maheśvarānanda stated [this]. Indeed, Maheśvarānanda is the name for the entirety [of reality] extending up to the venerable Sadāśiva.

It is indeed the venerable Lord Paramaśiva, whose characteristic is supreme sovereignty— the ultimate reality of eternal, unconditioned light and bliss— which overpowers the entire power of the succession of subjects who have entered into the states of purity and impurity. It is he, having assumed that state, who is the author of this Tantra.

...until: and his attainment of that state occurs because, through the auspicious descent of power (*śaktipāta*) from the glance of the Teacher, he has undergone the purification by the ascent of the consecrations (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the wealth of the auspicious great initiation (*mahābhiṣeka*) upon entering the *samaya*; and because [he possesses] the meaning of the entirety of the scriptures, such as the Northern Tradition (*auttarāmnāya*).

This is to be understood as being due to his possession of the training in awakening (*vabodha-śikṣā*), and because his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been exhausted through the continuous contemplation of the excellence of his own supreme lordly sovereignty. As it is said in the *Śrīniśāṭana*:
"This knowledge is based on three authorities. And that has been stated in the *Śrīkiraṇā*: [from] the Guru...
"From scripture and from oneself. Consequently, for one who is established in the state beyond duality (*avipastha*) and is the cause of knowledge—

according to the principle of the *Śrī Śivasūtra* that "giving is self-knowledge"— for such a person, there is the manifestation of their own supreme sovereignty which has been directly realized by themselves.

The author of this treatise is impelled toward the revelation of this tantra by the power of being overwhelmed with the desire to favor others; otherwise, it would result in nothing more than mere deception, like the authors of external (non-Śaiva) scriptures. As it is said in the *Śrīhaṃsabhedha*:
Many gurus, radiant with theoretical and practical knowledge, are served;
yet rare, O Goddess, is this guru who brings about the destruction of egoism.
"By him [the Veda] has been studied, by him it has been heard, and by him everything has been performed,
who has known the Absolute (kevala) itself as liberated from egoism.
As for external scriptures:
The divine wisdom is one thing, the wisdom of the scriptures is another;
that peaceful state is yet another, while people perceive it in yet another way.
Thus, by remaining in this state, it is not possible for [the means] to serve as a direct instrument for the reflective awareness of one's own self. As stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Even those who seek to penetrate that nature through an indirect means..."
"Surely those dull-witted ones who desire a firefly for the sake of perceiving the sun [are like fools]. And as it is said in the *Śrīkulakama*:
"Those who worship the path that is void of the power (*śākta*) of radiant energy..."
"They perform the *homa* in a vessel within a fireless pit.
In this regard, some degree of gradation (*tāratamya*) must be considered. As it has been said:
"That which is uttered by humans, sages, gods, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others..."
"Because each subsequent state is more distinguished, it sublates each preceding one.
And that Maheśvarānanda composes the *Maheśvarānandamahārthamañjarī* [the Cluster of the Great Meaning],
concerning the reality whose nature is the full sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), by virtue of its being the vibration (*spanda*) of both the universe and that which transcends it.

By the etymological derivation *arthyate* ("it is sought"), he demonstrates— through the composition of this work— that the reality of the manifestation of ultimate non-duality (*pāramārthikādvaitaprathāsatattva*) persists even when the sprout of the manifestation of distinctions such as Śiva and Śakti arises within that which is the object of all seeking.
This he shows by means of the textual structure.
The meaning is that it causes the world to experience [it]. For even a cluster (*mañjarī*), despite the appearance of various distinct flowers, is experienced as having a single form.
Furthermore, the stringing together of flowers and such is well known as a means for obtaining the resulting object (*upeya*) without effort. And that [cluster] is fragrant.

Because it is the locus of fragrance, whose nature is the manifestation of all that is desirable; and by this, through the establishment of the universe as an object of enjoyment, the appropriateness of the means of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) to be described hereafter is revealed. For:
This tantra is traditionally taught as "to be enjoyed without fear. As it is stated in the *Śrīsiddhāmata*:
"The six categories of meaning (*artha-ṣaṭka*), initiation (*dīkṣā*), and the Śiva-scripture—these are remembered [as its contents].
In the scripture known as Bhairava, which teaches enjoyment (*bhoga-śāstra*), the path of initiation (*dīkṣā-adhvan*) is free from fear."

"Imām" (this) means that it is not to be denied due to its excellence of manifestation, possesses an exceedingly easy taste, and has never been revealed before. As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Thus has this new path, which is indeed easy to practice, been revealed by me, just as it was taught by the Great Teachers in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* treatise.
And herein, that very play of the manifold variety of the universe, which is synonymous with the *Mahārthamañjarī*, is [described].
The subject matter to be expounded in this Tantra is the means for the act of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is synonymous with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as will be described hereafter;
for the experience of sound, touch, and so forth, by way of its experiencer, [is resolved] within that which is termed the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*).
In some cases, it culminates in a person of great spiritual power (*mahānubhāvī*).

And the purpose of that is thorough knowledge (*parijñāna*). The purpose of that, in turn, is the establishment of the true nature of inquiry (*vimarśa*). The purpose of that, moreover, is characterized by worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*).

There is the manifestation of one's own Maheśvarī-power; furthermore, there is no dependence on any other purpose, because that [power] alone is desired as the goal to be attained, and because it would otherwise lead to the fallacy of infinite regress. As the Śruti says: "Nothing exists higher than the attainment of the Self. And the relationship of the tantra with its subject matter is as follows:

There exists the relationship between the signifier and the signified; furthermore, there is the relationship of means and end between the treatise and the reflective awareness of consciousness (*cidvimarśa*) to be realized, because these two stand in a mutual relation of cause and effect.
The connection between the tantra and its practitioners is clearly perceived as consisting of the succession of the lineage of gurus.

This is because it begins with "Having bowed to the eternally pure feet of the Guru," and will conclude with "O Desi, at your glance. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), this entire relationship is in fact the nature of one's own self (*svātmarūpa*). As it is said in the *Śrī-svacchanda*:
"Abiding in the roles of both teacher and disciple, the Lord Sadāśiva himself brought down the Tantra through sentences consisting of preceding and succeeding words.
And as it has been said by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptanātha:
"That which is eternally Abhinavagupta, ancient and renowned—that heart, through the supreme manifestations, itself flashes forth as the unsurpassed. Thus [it is said].
And by the author of the Tantra, who has himself realized the truth of the matter, acting out of an excellence of compassion...

"I bind [this work] through a state of detachment characterized by the identity of all people"— by thus excluding the Supreme Person (uttama-puruṣa) whose nature is the uninterrupted sense of "I," the author employs the verb "binds" (*grathnāti*) in order to establish the context and to rouse the enthusiasm of the assembly of disciples.
The inclination toward engaging with the tantra is established by implication through its being enjoined.

By this, it is also indicated that the mention of the name [of the author] is for the sake of motivating the audience, by generating a conviction in the possibility of the author—who possesses well-known power—having composed the tantra. For the practitioners...
Regarding the qualification for the aforementioned subject matter, there is no fixed restriction whatsoever. As it is said in the *Śrīspanda*:

"Even having obtained this wealth of knowledge—which is difficult to attain—once it has been deposited within the cave of the heart, it leads to the welfare of all people forever, just as it did for Vasugupta."* *Note: This verse is cited from the *Spandakārikā*, 1.20.*

Furthermore, by the phrase "having bowed at the feet of the Guru," the secret convention (*vidyā-saṅketa*) regarding the venerable feet is also slightly unveiled here. Upon further reflection, that [convention] is as follows:
"Vidyā" refers to the seat of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā-pīṭha*), which is declared to be earthly (*pārthiva*).
The mandala is the seat of Kuṇḍalinī; that is proclaimed as the object to be attained.
The seat of action (kriyāpīṭha), known as mantra, is proclaimed to be fiery (taijasa);
but the seat of knowledge (jñānapīṭha), called mudrā, O Goddess of the Gods, is that which belongs to air (vāyavya).
O Dear One, the sky is not regarded here as a sacred seat (pīṭha) from the perspective of others' views, because there is an absence of any external ritual application rooted therein.
Vāyu consists of motion; from that, there is bowing in the sacrifice.
The lamp is taijasa (luminous); water is desired as the caru-oblation, consisting of the essence of taste.
Just as the earth possesses fragrance, so too is a flower offered as an act of reverence at the feet.

Thus, according to the principle of the *Śrīcaraṇasūtra*, one will enter precisely into the sequence of the *Śrīpañcavāha*, for the essential purport (*tātparya*) of all those belonging to the lineage of the *Śrīrasa* lies herein alone.
However, the demonstration of skill in its detailed exposition is not of ultimate utility; and thus it is said: "But not so."

The preeminence of the *mudrā*— which consists of the reality (*tattva*) of the power of wind (*vāyu-śakti*), which animates through its own vibration even the mantras, maṇḍalas, and so forth mentioned explicitly in the *Nati*, and which accords with the exertion that constitutes the commencement of other tantras— is established.

It is made understood; enough, then, with this abundance of digressions at the very outset. This verse is essentially the subtle body of the entire meaning of the Tantra, which will be elaborated upon in detail later. Therefore, if this were to be explained too extensively, it would lead to an over-elaboration; thus, I shall conclude this in brief.
It has been explained. Furthermore, the detailed elaboration of the meaning already stated will be presented in its proper place hereafter. || 1 ||

Now, the author of the Tantra, while stating the reality of the meaning to be expounded in the Tantra and the fact that its thorough knowledge is both the purpose and the object of inquiry, establishes therein— by means of repetition— that very purpose, which is the nature of self-reflection (*ātmavimarśa*), as the goal to be attained.
"May that Great Light increase, whose steady radiance is interspersed with reflective awareness (vimarśa),
wherein the scriptures function solely for the purpose of determining specific designations.
Herein, this Great Light is dependent upon the immersion into the light of each respective subject (*pramātṛ*).
When the essential nature is extracted by means of leaving nothing but the state of being manifest, knowledge shines forth externally and internally in its various forms.
Apart from knowledge, there is no existence of objects; therefore, the world is of the nature of knowledge.
For no entities have ever been made objects of cognition by anyone apart from cognition itself;
therefore, it is determined that cognition has attained the nature of those very entities.
Thus, according to the established tradition of the Śrī Devikākrama, He whose essential nature is pure Light, who consists of the condensation of the thirty-six principles,
and whose cosmic play manifests in infinite modes even when each individual principle is examined— He, [is that].

"May it increase further and further; may it experience its own radiance. This indeed is the great means for the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is about to be described. Now, [one might ask: "Is it not by means of the manifold variety of the universe—which has as its nature mere emptiness or which is animated by mere falsity—that [this occurs]?"

Fearing that the attainment of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of one’s own true nature, which is the ultimate reality, might reach the extreme limit of impropriety— thereby crossing the boundary of the Madhyamaka doctrine of ineffability— he says: "the unswerving radiance."

The meaning is that within the luminous manifestation of the world, which consists of clear illumination, there is no room for any deceptive argument (*chala*) that would establish its falsity. Let this be so;
nevertheless, by means of worldly convention, whose proximity is established through other factors—just like threshing, steaming, and so forth—[the world is perceived as real].

Anticipating the question of how the emergence of self-reflection (*ātmavimarśa*) occurs, he says: "interpenetrated by reflection" (*vimarśavicchurita*). Indeed, the universe does not serve as a means toward self-reflection by its mere existence alone; rather, it does so only in the state of being reflected upon in such and such a manner. And in that regard, just as in the case of the one whose form is the universe (*viśvarūpa*), [it is through reflection].
In order to demonstrate that falsity and its opposite must be investigated,
the term *niśchalodyota* (the light of the stainless) is joined as a single compound with *vimarśavicchurita* (interspersed with reflective awareness). Now,
if there were indeed some degree of necessity in universal worldly transaction, then its status as a means might be tenable.

And that [distinction] is not possible; for even today, proponents of various systems (siddhāntins) continue to conceptualize them separately—as six categories such as substance and quality, as sixteen categories such as means of valid cognition and objects of cognition, and as five aggregates such as form and sensation.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the difference in designations," and so forth. Where...
Regarding the reality whose nature is the play of the universe, the treatises of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, and others—
whose function is exhausted merely by specific designations consisting of technical definitions and characteristics according to their respective conventions— are not, however, [sufficient].

The meaning of the first statement is that [the opponents] are skilled in denying the continuous flux of categories such as earth and so forth, which are apprehended by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In the second [statement], however,
there is this Great Light, the undivided subject (*pramātṛ*) characterized as described above, whose reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)...
It shall be established as the ultimate goal of human endeavor; let it flourish!

Let it shine forth until the complete eradication of the impressions of the stain of *māyīya-mala*. And that flourishing does not consist in isolation (*kaivalya*); what then? It is this: "I am some extraordinary subject."

Recognition is that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which, by its very nature, constitutes a "fusion" (*vicchuraṇa*)— that is, a specific conjunction (*upaśleṣa*) characterized by a distinctiveness from other forms of illumination and by transcending the nature of ordinary worldly relations,
culminating in identity (*tādātmya*). It is through possessing this quality that [the subject] is free from deceit (*niśchala*).

The meaning is: "May that [Light] increase in such a state, whose radiance is free from the stain of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For although lights such as those of a mirror possess the capacity to manifest reflections and the like, [they do not do so independently].

Because it depends upon the light of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), it possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); however, the meaning is that the light of the cognizer itself does not depend on anything else. This will be further elaborated later. Now, one might object: since there is no necessity of verbal designation for the nature of the Self (*ātman*) which is to be contemplated, how can there be a contemplation (*vimarśa*) of it?

Fearing that there might be some heart-warming state resulting in the realization of proximity [to the Absolute], he says: "By means of specific designations," and so forth. In that regard, with respect to the Supreme Subject (paramapramātṛ), all scriptures whatsoever are employed as Śiva, Viṣṇu, Buddha, and so on.

These [scriptural passages] are occupied merely with such designations; they are not, however, capable of establishing an absolute difference in the intrinsic nature of the object. For instance, the Cārvākas maintain that the elements themselves possess consciousness, and thus [the body] is characterized by consciousness itself.

They declare the body to be the self; and likewise, the Mādhyamikas— who hold the view that Brahman is non-existence (*abhāva*) and who are conceited about emptiness (*śūnyatā*)— maintain this in the stage of the "inexpressible" (*anākhyā*).

They say that the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is characterized by the flashing forth of one's own pure nature alone. However, the Sāṅkhyas and others accept that it is essentially like the *vijñānākala*. And those who propound the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahmavādin*), identifying it with the level of *paśyantī*, consider this [Self] to be the venerable *sadāśiva-tattva*.

The Mīmāṃsakas also, considering the self to be capable of being colored by pleasure and so forth, do not deny its nature as consciousness. The Naiyāyikas and others maintain that this [self] is the locus of a multitude of qualities such as knowledge. The Sautrāntikas...
Furthermore, they describe this as having the nature of a continuum characterized by consciousness (*jñāna*).

In the same way, this may be inferred in other cases as well; thus, among all the philosophical systems, whether based on scripture (*śrauta*) or not based on scripture (*aśrauta*), there is no absolute disagreement here. However, there is a difference in their mode of existence, characterized by being "touched" or "untouched."
And the affliction of mutual strife and clamor among disputants is based solely upon that [distinction]. Thus it was said by me myself in the *Śrīpādukodaya*, beginning with the words:
"Therefore, the Lord is the soul of the universe," and so forth.
For the Lokāyatas, the self is the body; for the proponents of emptiness, the self is empty;
for those who abide in momentariness, the self is momentary; and for those who perceive duality, the self is divided.
For the Mīmāṃsakas, it is the self of the apūrva; for the proponents of Brahman, it is the self of Brahman;
for the Advaitins, it is the self of non-duality—what more need be said?
"He is the supreme teacher for children even in their play;
he alone is the great-souled one who possesses the great purpose for those seekers of the great purpose.
And likewise, in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*: "Those who stand upon that plane..."

"the positions of all philosophical systems. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Paryantapañcāśikā*: "Indeed, even that which constitutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the Bhairava-siddhānta is composed of that [very same reality]. And thus, in accordance with the actual state of things, by the proponents of the Siddhānta...
By all [authorities], the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, whose very nature is that of the universal self, is proclaimed. As I have stated in the *Śrīsaṃvidullāsa*:
"Because they stand in a relationship of the oppressor and the oppressed, they are unable to counteract one another."
They indeed proclaim your universal nature in order to refute the divergent views of disputants.

Thus, what is meant is this: although various philosophical systems (siddhānta) may propose mutually contradictory and subverting positions regarding the manifestation of the universe, there is no disagreement whatsoever that objects such as pillars and jars are directly perceived by everyone, from the commoner to the scholar.
Furthermore, "being experienced" means being the object of the act of experiencing.

And that act, by its very nature not transcending generality, cannot be accounted for—just like the cutting of a tree trunk—without some specific instrument such as an axe; this much must at least be admitted.
Consequently, at the moment of grasping an object, the presence of the eyes and other sense organs is indispensable. This has been stated by me myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"When the auspicious lamp of the imperishable mind is ignited as a great light..."
"The three worlds are illuminated without distinction through the windows that are the spheres of the external senses. Thus,
because the circle of the eyes and other senses is the locus for the mere vibration of its own externalizing activity,
there occurs the manifestation of objects even for a cognizer whose senses are unimpaired during states such as indifference.
Furthermore, since [consciousness] arises, it must necessarily depend upon some internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
this too must be admitted. Consequently, the involvement of mental deliberation (*mano-vimarśa*) is unavoidable.
As has been stated by my teacher in the *Manonuśāsana-stotra*:
Swans always fly with their own wings fully spread during their journey; yet, it is said that the royal swan of Lake Mānasa [flies differently].
Your movement in the supreme sky is truly most marvelous.
"Having abandoned the pair of wings consisting of distraction and emptiness.
Thus, because it would be inappropriate for the instruments (karaṇas) to produce their effects if they were distinct from an agent,
and because there would follow the consequence of their own essential nature collapsing.
In the act of perceiving a pillar, a pot, or the like, some specific agent is also implied by the very nature of the object.
As it was said by our supreme gurus in the *Śrīsaubhāgyahṛdayastotra*:
"Within the vicinity of the lattice of the eyes and other senses, through the playful repose upon the lotus-seat of the heart..."
O Goddess! Time and again you indulge in the honey of beauty and other such pleasures.
And because it is colored by the conceptualization of the object of knowledge (*vedya-vikalpa*), it experiences the limitations of space, time, and so forth.
This must be [perceived] by some extraordinary subject who transcends those limitations;
otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that the very manifoldness of the universe is inverted. Such is the worldly transaction of the universe.
This is not possible except by accepting two types of subjects: the delimited and the undelimited.

Among these, the non-imagined subject, by virtue of having manifestation alone as its sole nature, brings about the state of the entire class of objects being merged into a single ocean of light. The imagined subject, however, [perceives] a pillar, a pot, and so forth...

Thus, through the proficiency of the application of the manifestation of such distinctions, one brings about the differentiation of worldly discourse regarding entities whose nature consists in the agitation of various conceptual constructions; therefore, the necessity of both [the distinction and its application] is appropriate. And so:

At the moment of grasping an object, it follows through traditional transmission that there must be some innate subject (*pramātṛ*)— the ground upon which the universe is established— who is to be inwardly contemplated via the channel of the senses and so forth. As it has been said in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*:

"The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of 'this,' which is [otherwise] fragmented, is that repose in one's own essential nature; this reflective awareness is 'I am this. Thus, the repose of the Light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness' (ahambhāva).
And: "The repose of the Light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I-ness'."
And as it has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda:

"In this system, the attainment of the ultimate subject is taught precisely through the search for the subject of [empirical] cognitions such as blue or pleasure, which appear with extreme clarity. It is indeed with this very intention that...
In the Śrīvijñānabhairava:

"For the yogi whose self is unified with the singular bliss equal to the tasting of objects such as song and the like, there arises an ascent of the mind into that state through identification with it; that is the state of being that very Self."
This is established as being by way of such means. Even the Smṛti texts and others do not contradict this to any great extent, as they say:
"One who knows the true principles of playing the lute and is proficient in the science of musical notes..."
"And one who knows the measure attains the path of liberation without effort.
Thus, by means of the imperative suffix in the word "vardhatām" (may it increase),
destroy incomplete manifestation through the firmness of immersion into complete manifestation.
Create the worlds as you desire; establish them, dissolve them, and illuminate them.
By such statements as these, which illuminate the relationship between the means and the goal,

the absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord is indicated— characterized by His capacity to accomplish that which is otherwise utterly impossible. This is because, through this [work], [the author] has refuted the views of those who propound other philosophical systems.

The agitation caused by objects such as sound and touch, which is conceived as a bond to saṃsāra, is taught as a means toward the self-reflection of one's own nature, which is the very essence of the bliss characterized as liberation while living (jīvanmukti). And so it will be stated at the end of the Tantra:
"O, the bliss of saṃsāra! O, the auspiciousness of the path to liberation is easily attained!

Thus, according to the principle that one must strive for as long as possible to manifest the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)—which is the non-deviating nature of this relationship between means and end—one should understand [the teaching] through the appearance of the unity of these two statements.

The presentation is made through a double entendre (*śleṣa*), which is another synonym for *tantra*. Thus, the subject matter (*abhidheya*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the purpose of that purpose have been clearly elucidated in detail here. However, the ultimate purpose will be explained at length in the verse beginning with "a a ṭṭhāṇaparūḍho."

Now, by the reasoning already stated, some specific agent—like a potter and so forth—is not perceived directly anywhere as an object of contemplation; yet, since he must be inferred and because the status of an entity depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such a means of valid cognition must be stated. And if it is not stated:
Anticipating the objection that this would result in the Self becoming a mere mental construction (asatkalpa), he says:
"The Self is indeed the root of the universe; no one seeks a means of knowledge for it.
Or rather, who would have thirst when submerged in the current of the Ganges? (3)

In this world, the Self alone is the basis for all worldly transaction because its very nature is luminosity; for pillars, jars, and other objects appear only through their connection with the light of the subject, as in such expressions as "this appears to me" or "it is perceived by me. In the absence of that [subjective light], they would be mere pillars.

In the case of the two [notions], "this is a jar" and "this is a pillar," when they proceed to mutually negate each other's specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is no governing authority whatsoever; thus,
there arises either a doubt as to whether the pillar exists in the form of a pillar or whether it is not a pillar, or else even that [doubt] is impossible.
In every respect, the very nature of worldly discourse would be silence itself,
if those [objects] were manifested solely in the form of pillars and so forth, and not through the grace of the subject's own light.
If there were some excellence [in one], then all things would manifest in that same way, or else nothing at all would;

thus, there would follow the consequence of the cessation of the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of cognizing subjects (*pramātṛ*). Furthermore, the universe, consisting of pillars, jars, and so forth, [would have to manifest] by its own self alone.
If one were to accept that [the self] is manifest, it would follow that every class of cognizers is either omniscient or utterly ignorant, due to the absence of any regulating factor.
Therefore, even by one who does not wish to admit it, the fact that the self is the motivator of worldly activity must be accepted.

Furthermore, the relationship of the instigated and the instigator will ultimately result in their very identity; thus, it follows that this manifestation of the entire range of objects within the world is composed of the self-luminous Light of Consciousness.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Otherwise, the object would be non-luminous, lacking the nature of luminosity;

nor could the luminosity of the object be distinct from the self. The word "khalu" indicates the absence of dispute. This being the case, [the cognition] occurs within that very self as "this is such-and-such."
With respect to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), which is characterized by the determination of an object and possesses its own specific manifestation,
no dependence whatsoever arises for anyone— whether a scholar or a commoner—
because it is not distinct from the light of the cognizer (*pramātṛprakāśa*); on the contrary, it is established by that very light.
Of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For what is called a *pramāṇa* is a particular manifestation of itself (*svābhāsa*) that arises ever anew;

for it has been stated that even this manifestation of itself is "new. And its quality of arising ever anew is due to its being delimited by the mutual distinctness of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), which are themselves differentiated by their connection with various places and times.

The meaning is this: some particularity has been superimposed [upon it], but it is not an inherent property; thus, with respect to the reality of the self—which is of a single nature, comparable to an unagitated ocean, and which has set aside all disturbances of conceptual construction—no activity whatsoever is possible. Not... [the rest of the sentence].
"Someone desires [it]," it is said. One who desires a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for oneself must either be the self or not.

If one is a non-self, belonging to the category of insentient things (*jaḍavarga*), then the very requirement of a means of valid cognition is untenable. If, on the other hand, one is indeed the self, then it would follow that the self requires a means of valid cognition for itself. As they say:
"If non-manifestation is not manifestation, then manifestation alone remains;
if it is manifestation, then because it has the nature of manifestation, manifestation alone remains.
Thus, in that locus which is the state of the subject (*pramātṛtā*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is applicable.
The superiority of the agent over the instrument is accepted by others.
Indeed, it is asserted even by grammarians that the agent is independent;
and that independence consists in being primary relative to the other factors of action (kārakas).
Since the establishment of the validity of the means of knowledge depends upon that very [reality],
why would it be a futile statement to claim that they depend on that [reality]?
Indeed, because worldly means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are unreliable,
those who rely on reasoning have declared that God is the authority even in the status of the cognizer (pramātṛ).

One who asks, "What is the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for the knower (pramātṛ)? either abandons the status of being a knower or does not; it cannot be the former, because such a question would be logically untenable.
The second alternative cannot be maintained; for what means of valid cognition could possibly manifest?
Such is the purport of the question regarding the consensus on the unity of the self therein.
This distinction of "in me" and "in you" is never tenable; for if there were a plurality of selves, each would have a cognition directed toward its own object.
To say that "the opponent is being questioned" results in a great absurdity;
for if there is an error regarding the self due to delusion, it would be like [mistaking] a rope for a snake in the mind.
To say that verbal testimony is a means of valid cognition is like the speech of a madman;
for if it is then asserted that "I have no cognition at all regarding that [object]," [the claim of its validity collapses].
In that regard, one might ask for the means of valid cognition; what answer could be given? Therefore, the Great Lord, the Self, is beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition.
As it is stated in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*: "But when the subject is the ancient one, whose form is eternally manifest,
what new manifestation could there be as a means of knowledge for that which partakes in all cognitions?"
And thus says the Upaniṣad: "O, by what means could one know the knower?
Just as when one strives to leap over the shadow of one's own head with one's own feet, the head cannot be located at the place of the feet; so too is this Bindu-kalā.
In the *Śrī Tantrāloka* as well, it is said:
"Even those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which extend life to objects— the supreme life-force of even those is that very Supreme Lord."

He establishes the stated point by means of an illustration, beginning with "Of what, indeed," and so forth. For the current of the Ganges, due to the excellence of its many qualities such as coolness and clarity, is capable of removing heat both internally and externally.

In that very state, preceded by bathing with all one's limbs, during the stages of the *aghamarṣaṇa* and other rites—who indeed could be thirsty? The meaning is that no one at all would be so. By the word "thirsty" (*pipāsa*), it is implied:
even for someone submerged in the current of the Gaṅgā, if there were a desire to drink water, who [could provide it] there to drink?
By demonstrating that [the objection] constitutes an obstacle, it is shown that even in the case of the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*),
when there is an inquiry into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the Supreme Lord— who is the basis for all worldly transactions—
all means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, are indeed possible; however, they do not [apply] here [in the sense of being the primary object].
A certain dependence is thus proposed:
"The body and so forth possess an intelligent agent as their cause, because they have a specific arrangement, like a jar;
that which does not have this [arrangement] is not thus, like an atom of space."

It should be understood that even the stain of a suspicion regarding the futility of the undertaking of this treatise—which was intended to establish the existence of God and so forth by means of such proofs as those mentioned above—has been completely removed. || 3 ||

One might object: "Surely the manifestation of the Self is never perceived with such clarity as that of a pillar or a jar; and regarding an object that is not clearly manifest, one must proceed solely by means of the operation of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Anticipating this doubt, he says:
He whom even the dull-witted know, and whom even those who carry water understand—who among them would not clearly offer salutation to that very Lord of the Kula? (4)

Indeed, even those who are insentient, such as cowherds and others, whose light is not overflowing— just like the Vīreśvaras— know Him who is well-established through His universal self-nature as the Light itself; and likewise, those who consist of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
like the Vīreśvarīs, who possess the manifestation of skillful discernment.

Even those such as Ghaṭadāsī and others understand this, because for everyone, the manifestation of one's own self in the form of "I am stout," "I am prosperous," and so forth, is clearly perceived. As the Śruti says:
"Did the cowherds see him? Did the water-carriers see him?"—by this emphasis on deliberation (*vimarśa*), the superiority of the knowledge regarding the water-carriers is stated.
He says that just as by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), this [object] is embraced by the subjects, so too is it embraced by their power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

"—of whom alone is this salutation? For it is observed that the entire multitude of living beings—including the insentient, such as water and sacrificial ladles—performs salutations here and there out of a desire for various fruits.
All such salutation occurs only through connection with Him, as the Śruti says:
"That to which there is homage is the head"—it will be explained later that for everything, one's own self alone is the deity.
For it is said:
"O Lord of the Self! You alone are the self of all, and you are everything; yet within the self, you possess attachment."

Thus it is stated in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*. Furthermore, even insentient entities such as pillars and jars, as well as the powers of the senses—which are capable of perceiving and grasping objects such as sound and touch—are said to "know" [the Supreme Lord]; in this way, the excellence of the Supreme Lord’s manifestation (*prākaṭya*) is established. For:

Even pillars, jars, and the like are determined to be the substrata of knowledge and action by virtue of being made objects for this or that perceiver. As it has been said: "The Seer alone is indeed the world"; this is also an elliptical expression for "the Agent alone. As stated in the *Śambhvaikyadīpikā*:

This entire universe consists of me (*manmaya*), because it is my effect; for whatever is such [an effect] is so [composed of its cause], just as the body is. And since this [universe] is my effect, therefore it consists of me.
Likewise, the sense organs, such as the eyes and others, also exist in their respective ways solely as the retinue of the subject (*pramātṛ*).

Thus it is said. And that Supreme Lord, being of the nature described, is the sustainer of memory and other mental functions by virtue of his ultimate identity with the *kula*—the cosmic play consisting of the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth. To whom would he not be manifest? If one asks "to whom?"— [The answer follows: To no one at all. For he is the very Self of all. Since he is the Self of all, he is manifest to everyone. Therefore, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is because the Self is self-manifesting (*svaprakāśa*). Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the very essence of the universe, he is manifest even to those who are ignorant of him. This is because even those who do not know him perceive objects through his power alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Moreover, since he is the agent of all actions, he is manifest to those engaged in action as well. This is because even those performing rituals and the like do so through his power alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Furthermore, since he is the goal of all seekers, he is manifest to those seeking liberation as well. This is because even those desiring liberation seek him alone as their ultimate goal. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the conclusion. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the source of all things, he is manifest even to those who deny him. This is because even those who deny him depend on him for their very existence. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final point. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the very nature of consciousness, he is manifest even to those who are unconscious. This is because even those in deep sleep or a state of swoon are sustained by his power alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the ultimate truth. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the witness of all, he is manifest even to those who are inert. This is because even objects such as stones and wood are pervaded by his light alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the established conclusion. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the creator of all, he is manifest even to those who are deluded. This is because even those who are deluded experience the world through his creative power alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the definitive teaching. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the enjoyer of all, he is manifest even to those who are devoid of enjoyment. This is because even those who have renounced all pleasures still subsist through his grace alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final word. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the destroyer of all, he is manifest even to those who are terrified. This is because even those who fear death find refuge in him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the absolute truth. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the support of all, he is manifest even to those who are without support. This is because even those who have fallen from their station rely on him alone for stability. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the unassailable conclusion. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the essence of all, he is manifest even to those who are insentient. This is because even the elements such as earth and water are his manifestations alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the supreme realization. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the cause of all, he is manifest even to those who are causeless. This is because even the uncaused void is pervaded by him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the ultimate certainty. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the fruit of all, he is manifest even to those who are fruitless. This is because even those who have attained the fruit of liberation remain within his light alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final word of the masters. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the light of all, he is manifest even to those who are in darkness. This is because even those in the depths of ignorance are illuminated by him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the established doctrine. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the life of all, he is manifest even to those who are dead. This is because even the dead are animated by his power alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the secret truth. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the soul of all, he is manifest even to those who are soulless. This is because even the soulless bodies are moved by him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the core of the scriptures. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the end of all, he is manifest even to those who have reached the end. This is because even those who have attained the final goal rest in him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final conclusion. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the beginning of all, he is manifest even to those who have no beginning. This is because even the beginningless cycle of birth and death is rooted in him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the absolute truth. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the middle of all, he is manifest even to those who are without a middle. This is because even the middle state of existence is his own manifestation alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the unshakable principle. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the totality of all, he is manifest even to those who are partial. This is because even those with limited vision perceive him through his partial manifestations alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final word of the tradition. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the unity of all, he is manifest even to those who are divided. This is because even those who are in conflict are united by him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the ultimate reality. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the peace of all, he is manifest even to those who are restless. This is because even those who are agitated find peace in him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final teaching. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the bliss of all, he is manifest even to those who are sorrowful. This is because even those in the midst of grief experience bliss through him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the established truth. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the light of all lights, he is manifest even to those who are blind. This is because even the blind perceive forms through his light alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the final conclusion. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. And since he is the breath of all, he is manifest even to those who are breathless. This is because even those who have ceased breathing are sustained by him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to whom he is not manifest. This is the absolute certainty. Thus, the meaning is that he is manifest to everyone. Furthermore, since he is the space of all, he is manifest even to those who are confined. This is because even those in confinement experience freedom through him alone. Therefore, he is manifest to all. Consequently, there is no one to
Someone might say: "The meaning is that he himself would not exist by virtue of his own nature. This is the intended sense:

the diverse range of objects of cognition, such as the sense-objects and the senses, as well as the class of subjects, such as cowherds and water-carriers, are experienced in their worldly activity as being either impure or pure.

Thus, according to the method of the Śrī Pratyabhijñā, it is observed that the very pair of knowledge and action— whose nature constitutes worldly and scriptural activities such as "he goes to the village" or "he performs the twilight worship"— is the direct or indirect vitalizing principle [of all things]. For example:
In the Śrīpratyabhijñā it is said:
"For thus, the foundation of insentient things rests upon the living being;
knowledge and action are considered the life-force of sentient beings."

Furthermore, since these two— knowledge and action— are not possible anywhere apart from the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) as either "mine" or "I," there is no room for any doubt regarding the lack of clarity concerning the Supreme Lord, whose very nature is the totality of all "I"-states. || 4 ||

Having thus established in general the inapplicability of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the Self, he now demonstrates a certain favor [of the tradition] by establishing it specifically as well: "Perception is limited, and inference, which is based upon it, is likewise limited."
The light of the lamp of scripture reveals some of his greatness. || 5 ||

The validity of perception consists solely in the contact with the object to be apprehended; thus, this [definition] is extremely restricted. Furthermore, inference is limited because it depends upon the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the apprehension of pervasion itself is rooted in perception.

The inclusion of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and other means of knowledge within this [category] is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; or, if they are not included, their restriction must be determined by oneself through the conceptualization of the perception of the postulating agent and so forth. And thus, there is the operation of delimited means of knowledge upon the undelimited Self.
It has already been stated that [such a position] descends into a great level of impropriety. Furthermore,

if scripture deserves authority merely because it is the word of a trustworthy person (*āpta*), then when one considers what kind of trustworthiness that entails, it must derive from another trustworthy person, and that person’s [trustworthiness] from yet another.

An infinite regress that destroys its own root constitutes a lack of validity; however, when it comes to rest after three or four stages—just as in the examination of rubies and other gems—that very process serves to limit [the inquiry]. Furthermore, scripture has as its ultimate reality the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) of Maheśvara, whose nature is uninterrupted light.

When this [object] is accepted as being composed of the power of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the supreme subject (*parapramātṛ*), according to the position stated by the teacher Abhinavagupta,
then it appears within the light that constitutes the very nature of his own self, like the manifestation of a lamp in darkness.

It produces a certain aesthetic wonder by way of manifesting pillars, jars, and so forth. In that regard as well, just as the nature of pillars and the like— such as their height and circumference— situated within darkness is revealed by the light of a lamp, so it is with this [consciousness] as well.
That majesty of one's own self— which consists of its unconditioned nature,
its capacity to vitalize all worlds, senses, and so forth that are distinct from itself,
and its being the recipient of the perfection of the equilibrium between its two defining characteristics, namely being both the universe and transcending it— [is that].
Some extraordinary reality is unveiled by means of scripture,
as it was said by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
"Having attained which, one reaches fulfillment and the state of being completely filled by the confluence of all the rivers of the scriptures."
And: "I bow to that ocean of the supreme scripture, which is the essence of the flood of jewels consisting of the contemplation of the Śāmbhava reality. Thus [it is said].

Now, if there is a curiosity regarding the application of the term "means of valid cognition" here through metaphorical usage— just as one might speak of "the orb of the moon on the tip of a branch"— then let it suffice to say that perception occurs with respect to oneself,
inference with respect to another, and scripture everywhere.
By way of setting out upon the main road frequented by travelers from other tantras. || 5 ||

Now, one might object: "If this reality of the Self transcends the path of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then either everyone would be qualified for its investigation, or no one at all would be so qualified, since there is no difference in the fact that it remains unapprehended.
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states: "In this matter, there is no trouble regarding a distinction between those who are qualified and those who are not."
Thus he says:

For those who maintain that there is some distinct state of being belonging to the self that is to be defined, and who are averse to the Self—for them, let there be the delusion regarding the distinction between qualified aspirants. (6)

In this world, for those men for whom some entity such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice appears as something distinct from the Supreme Lord who is their own essential nature— something to be defined and conceptualized— it arises precisely from a turning away from the Self, which is inseparable from an orientation toward other objects.

Let there be this delusion—the specific error that "this person is qualified for this [treatise], but not that one"—which, being of the nature of a playful whim (*vilāsa*), is unauthoritative or constitutes a mere conventional usage; we do not stand as obstacles to its existence. The suffix *loṭ* is used here in the sense of permission (*atisarga*). And thus, their state of being subject to censure is also indicated.
As it was said by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
"What can be said of that fool who, without knowing himself, desires to discern another? When asked 'Who are you?', what is he to say in response?"

Regarding the phrase "some [entity]": within our system, even though there is a mere manifestation of another state as distinct from the Self, because in the final analysis it is determined to be nothing other than identity with that [Self], the verbal expression "some entity distinct from the Self" is entirely improper. As it has been said:
In the *Saṃvitprakāśa*:
"Whatever is seen here does not differ from the act of seeing;
the act of seeing is not other than the seer, for the universe is indeed the seer himself."
Also in the *Āgama*:
"O Dear One, as long as these are not knowers, how can they be objects of knowledge?
This means that [this point] will be explained further on. However, for those for whom existence is indeed the Self...
A certain transcendent attribute, whose very nature is absolute freedom, remains as that which is to be contemplated;
for those who possess this inward orientation toward the Self, there is never any distraction caused by the differentiation of eligible candidates. This is what is meant:
For objects such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, which are to be manifested, are established as distinct from the cognizing subjects who manifest them;
therefore, a certain division of qualified persons (adhikārin) based on their desire for heaven and so forth would be appropriate in their case.

Furthermore, for those for whom the very nature of the self (*ātman*) is what must be investigated, they would lack qualification if there were a doubt regarding selflessness (*nairātmya*). And in the absence of that [doubt], how could there be any gradation of qualification? By this, [the requirement of] detachment from the enjoyment of objects here and hereafter, and so forth, is also [refuted].

It has been explained that [this is] not for the sake of a specific qualification of the candidate (*adhikārin*), because it will be demonstrated here that liberation is simply the intensification of the enjoyment of objects in this world and the next,

serving as the purpose for the self-reflection of one whose nature is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). If it is argued that "then let the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*) be the qualification," we say no.
In the actual state of things, there is no bondage; in the absence of that, there is no liberation.
Both of these are merely constructed by conceptualization and are nothing at all.

According to this principle, bondage itself does not exist; how then could there be liberation, and how much less the desire for it? Or, even if it were to exist, that very [desire] unfolds all the way up to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Thus, because there is ultimately no difference between this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and that desire, it is said that the object to be attained is indeed the domain of authority (*adhikāra*). || 6 ||

One might object: "If the distinction between the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the qualified subject (adhikārī) were of no use, then injunctions (vidhi) and prohibitions (niṣedha) themselves would be rendered useless, since there would be no sublation (bādhā) in the case of error. Anticipating this, he clarifies their essential nature:
"Where there is inclination, there is injunction; where this [inclination] is absent, there is prohibition.
Such is our discernment, for us whose scriptures consist merely of the pulsations of the heart. (7)

That which is characterized by the cognition "it exists" is affirmation (vidhi), and that whose nature is the cognition "it does not exist" is negation (niṣedha); these constitute the meaning of the injunction (codanā). In this regard, it is said that in rites such as the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsti) there is affirmation, while in acts such as the eating of *kalañja* there is negation. Here, the following must be considered:

For the function of injunctions and prohibitions consists in causing the performers to engage in action or desist from it, since it has been stated that an injunction is that which, while making known what was previously unknown, impels one who has not yet acted. In that regard, do they engage or desist merely through that knowledge, or rather by virtue of their own desire? If...

By mere knowledge alone, no one would be observed as either a practitioner of the twilight rituals (*sandhyopāsaka*) or an eater of forbidden meat (*kalañjabhakṣaka*). If, however, [it were] according to their own will, the meaning would be that injunctions and prohibitions merely follow the inclination of those who perform them; and consequently, for them—

In this manner, regarding matters such as the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*), where there is a desire, there is an injunction; and regarding matters such as the eating of *kalañja*, where there is no desire, there is a prohibition.
Thus, in the case of the twilight worship and so forth—

If there is a lack of inclination toward something, there is a prohibition regarding it; if there is an inclination toward the eating of *kalañja* and the like, there is an injunction regarding that—such would be the determination of the true nature of things. According to this stated sequence, for us who are adorned with the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) which is full and synonymous with the supreme Lord’s self-reflection (*pārameśvara-vimarśa*), discernment (*viveka*) [is established].
The essential conclusion regarding injunctions and prohibitions is as follows: and when such certainty regarding reality is attained,

that alone is our scripture which is the *spanda* (vibration) of one’s own heart, characterized by its proficiency in encompassing the entire succession of principles beginning with Earth, through the unification of all consciousness.

Marvel is the essence of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). For we have already stated previously that the supreme reflective awareness of the Lord is indeed the scripture (*āgama*). Consequently, for those who practice it, the very power of will (*icchā-śakti*)—due to its orientation toward engagement and withdrawal—experiences the distinction in designation as "injunction" and "prohibition."
As it is said in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*:
"That which can be abandoned is determined to be 'to be discarded' (heya);
and that which cannot be abandoned is likewise 'to be accepted' (upādeya)."
And I have stated in the *Saṃvidullāsa*: "If the discourse of injunctions and prohibitions were authoritative, then ultimately Śiva alone would be the authority."
"He is indeed supreme among all; he is capable of performing what is prescribed and prohibited therein, and as the All-pervasive Lord, he can even revoke what has been enjoined.
By this, the superior authority of our own Tantra over the Śruti, Smṛti, and other scriptures is explained.

As it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā: "Thus, those who follow the dharma of the three Vedas, desiring objects of desire, attain the state of going and returning"; and also: "The Vedas have the three qualities as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna."
As it is stated in the Śrī-Vijñānabhairava: "That which is considered impurity by those of limited knowledge is purity in the vision of Śambhu;
therefore, a person should become free from conceptual construction, for there is neither pure nor impure."
And as it is stated in the Śrīkālikāmata: "By whatever karma living beings certainly fall into hell,
by that very same [karma] they rise up and become knowers of the three times."
Indeed, with this very intention, it is stated in the *Śrī-Vijñānendukaumudī*:
"Wherever the mind attains fullness through rest—
what field more auspicious than that could there possibly be?"
Thus, the characteristics of the field of merit and so forth have been elucidated. By this it is meant:
for those of unawakened intellect, these are indeed terrors for children;
everything has been cited for the sake of engaging [the practitioner], like a mother’s sweetmeat.
Thus, this portion of the Śrī Vijñānabhairava has been explained. 7.

Now, is it not the case that the course of worldly life proceeds by means of injunctions, prohibitions, and so forth? And since these two [injunctions and prohibitions] would exist merely as functions of one's own will, it follows that the world has no real form at all. This very [worldly course] is called *saṃsāra*, and its transcendence is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). It is for this purpose that this *tantra* has been composed.

Fearing that [the inquiry] might become like an examination of a crow’s teeth, he says: "When the heart, which is the very nature of reality, is turned away from thorough investigation, the world is deluded by the fear of saṃsāra, as if by the force of the poison of doubt. (8)
This world, consisting of the class of perceivers who are distinct from the class of perceived objects, possesses the attribute of being a perceiver;
