for that very reason, although it shares with the Supreme Lord the sovereignty of having the universe as its body and performing the five cosmic functions, this class of subjects generally identifies itself with the state of a bound soul (paśu). This is its inherent nature.

When one seeks the reality of reasoning, even though one is non-different from the Supreme Lord, because it is by His mere will, one immerses oneself in the state of "this-ness" (idam-bhāva) just like the state of "I-ness" (ahaṃ-bhāva); thus, for oneself, there is the immersion into the Heart, which is the triad of powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action.
The internal reality, which is of the nature of non-existence (*anarūpa*), maintains an attitude of indifference toward its own self-reflection.

And this [indifference] has come about for it due to the very nature of its own consciousness (*svacitta*). For that which is called "consciousness" (*citta*)—having descended from the path of pure sentience (*caitanya*)—has acquired a contraction through its skill in the internal movement within the accumulation of objects of thought (*cetya*).
It is determined that this is the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*). Furthermore, the state of being composed of consciousness (*cittamayatva*) belongs to this limited subject;

thus, the subject of *māyā* is composed of that [consciousness], as established according to the system of the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*. For, in the *Śrī-Śivasūtras*, just as "the Self is consciousness" (*caitanya-mātmā*), it is stated that "the Self is consciousness" (*citta-mātmā*).
Thus, this indifference of his is natural, as it has been taught again and again due to the impurity of the individual soul (āṇava). For this very reason,
he [remains detached] from the cycle of birth and death in saṃsāra.

Fearing the worldly course of conduct involving duality— thinking, according to the method of the Upaniṣads, "fear indeed arises from a second"— he carries about an anxiety rooted in the manifestation of difference and becomes deluded.
Due to the loss of memory regarding his own state of supreme sovereignty, he suffers internal affliction, just as follows:

Even in the absence of an actual snakebite, one who is possessed by the suspicion of being poisoned, when neglecting the investigation into the real nature of objects such as a rope that causes the mental delusion of a snake, [is afflicted].

Just as one experiences internal agony such as fainting or death from the bite of a real snake, the reality of the matter demonstrated by this analogy is made to penetrate the heart. And when his delusion takes the form described, it is his own powers alone that operate; and these [powers] reside on the level of speech.

In speech, there are the powers beginning with Parā and Paśyantī, such as Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, and the rest; in the sequence of consciousness, there are Vāmeśvarī, Khecarī, and the others, whose essence is the radiance of one's own self; and in the junctures of the vital breath, there are the powers beginning with Prāṇa and Apāna, whose functions are exhausted in sustaining the body. Of these—

Just as there is the manifestation of the true nature of the self through the capacity to penetrate the duality of "I" and "this," so too is there appropriateness in its concealment. Although it is unavoidable that this self, which is identified with the bound soul (paśu),
is animated by the triad of powers beginning with will (icchā-śakti), nevertheless, those [powers] which...
In the state of supreme sovereignty (*pārameśvarī avasthā*), characterized by unimpeded freedom, there is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*);

the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), augmented by omniscience in accordance with the manifestation of the diversity of the universe; and likewise, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), whose essence is universal agency. These very [powers], in the state of the bound soul (*paśu-daśā*)...

Contracting gradually in the manner of a tortoise’s limbs, they assume the state of *āṇava* consisting of the non-recognition of fullness, the state of *māyīya* consisting of the manifestation of the differentiation of objects,
and the state of *kārmaṇa* consisting of the performance of auspicious and inauspicious actions.

They open up the impurity, and for that reason this one is called a "transmigrator" (saṃsārī). Indeed, it is precisely to dispel this delusion that service to the lotus-feet of a true teacher is proclaimed as a duty. When, however, that very person [realizes] the actual nature of his own heart...

When one becomes intent on investigating [this], then nothing at all is found to exist as the referent of the word "saṃsāra," because it is perceived only as a manifestation of one's own mental agitation.
As stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta:
"The independent, pure-natured Śiva, who is consciousness, shines forth eternally;
and this Supreme Power (Parāśakti) has arisen at the very limit of the path of the senses."
"Then, with its sole essence being that manifestation, this entire world flashes forth;
I know not where this resonance of cyclic existence might follow. Thus it is said.
And as it is stated in the *Advayollāsa*:
This delusion is saṃsāra; how then could liberation arise from that? Alas, such a desire spreads among those of dull intellect.
But for one who possesses the non-conceptual, non-dual realization that "there is nothing other than You," [this delusion ceases].
"Stability is liberation; the conjunction of the two is transmigratory existence.
And as it is said in the *Saṃvitprakāśa*:
"Therefore, conceptual construction is not distinct from pure consciousness."
"Therefore, this very conceptualization, though non-conceptual, abides within itself.
The intention behind the statement "all conceptualization is saṃsāra" is as follows:
the unreality of that [conceptualization] and the reality of the pure consciousness constitute the state of liberation.

And so it is said. Here too, the illustration has already been stated: namely, that when the reality of the rope and such is realized, there is no longer the delusion of a serpent and the like, and consequently, no experience of fainting or similar states. This is the meaning:
for every person, apart from external worldly activity, [there is a state] directed toward one's own heart.

A certain exertion of the form "I am" flashes forth; and since that [exertion] is logically established as having the very nature of a specific consciousness in the form of "I know," the power of knowledge cannot be denied. Furthermore, in the expression "I know," a certain activity consisting of the intensity of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is also implied by the sense of the statement.
In the state where these two are sustained, there is the designation "power of will" (*icchā-śakti*).

Thus, this undisturbed essential nature (*svabhāva*), consisting of the equilibrium of will, knowledge, and action, is what is conventionally termed the "Heart. And upon the thorough investigation of that reality, there arises *vitarka* (reflective discernment).

According to the principle of the *Śiva Sūtras*, "Self-knowledge" means: "I am indeed that very Lord Paramaśiva, because I possess the triad of powers. Thus, the power characterized by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) manifests. It is with this aim—the manifestation of power—that this *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) is taught; such is the statement of the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā*.
As it has been stated in the *Īśvarasiddhi*:

"This very Self, which is the Lord within all living beings, shines forth as both the agent and the knower; if there is anything further to be established, it is only the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of Him."
As it is said in the venerable *Vijñānabhairava*:
"The Supreme Lord is omniscient, the creator of all, and all-pervasive;
'I am He indeed, whose nature is Śiva'—through such firm conviction, one becomes Śiva."
And in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
"Now, while the Śiva-principle remains omnipresent, it is being discussed here;
whether that [principle] is known or unknown, the state of Śiva is unimpeded."
Does fire not produce light whether it is known or unknown?
Is gold not gold when unknown; would it then become a stone?
Having raised this objection, [the author replies]:
"It is true; nevertheless, in this case, gold, as soon as it is known, is employed for enjoyment through its value and so forth, or for the purpose of giving."
An unrecognised wish-fulfilling gem would clearly still be a wish-fulfilling gem;
nevertheless, for the sake of obtaining its effects and enjoyments, by whom could it be worn if it were unknown?
This has been established by such [arguments] as these, and this will also be further clarified later on. And thus,

because one's own self is recognized as being the Supreme Lord, and because the Supreme Lord is accepted as having the universe as His body due to the superior force of the means of knowledge that apprehend His attributes;

Furthermore, because the wheel of saṃsāra and so forth are perceived as included within the universe— just like the variety of heaven, hell, and other realms— and because the embodied soul, through the intensification of the cultivation of the sense of "I" toward the body, becomes the sole locus for the experience of non-difference [between them].
O Supreme Lord! May I indeed be present even when those various hardships should befall me—
not merely one whose fear has departed, but one who has attained even greater rapture from the touch of Your limbs.
Thus, according to the established tradition of the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*,

this results solely in the skill of savoring the wonder of plunging into the great lake of the nectar of bliss arising from the non-dual consciousness of Maheśvara; it does not, however, involve the agitation of dualistic constructs such as bondage and liberation.
Even the suspicion of a stain upon that [Self] is dispelled here, since the Śruti says: "The knower of the Self transcends sorrow.
And as it is said in the *Śrīmadanubhavastotra*: "O Lord! when you remain within the consciousness of the Self alone, free from the agitation of external diversity..."
"When the roots have been severed, how can there be movement by means of qualities that lack substantiality and are merely illusory?
Even this being the case—
just as a sovereign emperor is augmented by the fragrance of his majesty.
Playing, he performs the activities of foot-soldiers through the nature of those very activities.

Thus the Lord, whose nature is joy, sports in such and such ways. According to the perspective of the *Śrī Śivadṛṣṭi*, due to the manifestation of the sovereignty of one's own Self, there may arise for some a state of voidness regarding the awareness of their own heart, by which the conventional distinction of transmigratory existence and so forth occurs.
As the Śruti says: "From the non-god, the god [arose], and he went into those secret places," and so forth. And here, the *Śrī-Cidgaganacandrikā* states:

"Desiring the cave of the heart through the state of non-duality, I approach Śiva— who is present, who bestows equanimity, whose body is vision and action, yet who is beyond both non-vision and non-action— since there can be no loss of friendship with him for the sake of procreation.
And as it is said in the *Samādhipañcadaśī*:
"That which is the non-recognition of this [reality] is imagined through autonomy;
indeed, that very thing is the terrifying cycle of existence (saṃsāra) for the insentient.
Thus it is said in the *Śrīsarvavīrabhaṭṭāraka* as well:
"Out of ignorance the world fears; from that [fear] come creation and dissolution.
All mantras have Śiva as their essence; all phonemes have Śiva as their essence. And in the *Mokṣopāya*:
"How great is this offense, which is merely one's own lack of self-reflection?
By that alone has been produced that which simply cannot be described.
Thus, liberation is precisely the thorough knowledge of the reality as it has been described, and its opposite is bondage.
Thus, enough of this excessive elaboration. || 8 ||

Indeed, there is a certain particularity of the Self consisting of self-reflection (*vimarśa*), which has been manifested by its possession of the capacity to pacify all afflictions such as transmigratory existence; and that [particularity] is determined to be the very nature of making manifest the [Self's] otherwise unmanifest essence. Nor is it...
In this regard, even the suspicion that [the object] is not clearly manifest might arise, because [the object] has been established as being extremely clear.
Therefore, anticipating the objection that the conceptualization of the linguistic conventions of means and objects of knowledge is useless here, he says:
Like a preeminent ruby enveloped by its own streaks of luster,
the self appears to worldly people as if obscure, even though it is extremely clear.
For the Supreme Lord, being of the nature of the Self,

due to His excellence of luminosity and His capacity to pervade the entirety of the worlds, unfolds an ever-ascending succession of sprouting flames consisting of the conceptual constructions of the universe.

Having created that, He entered into it; according to this method of the Upaniṣads, [the Self] remains eternally enveloped in that very way, as if clad in a garment. In that regard, within the universe perceived by worldly people as an object of knowledge (*prameya*), [He remains].
For those who engage in worldly transaction— the cognizing subjects—
there is an absolute transparency, which is the non-manifestation of their own form;
this is according to the position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, by virtue of having ascended to the stage of the intensification of manifestation (*prākaṭya*).

Even this [object] to be reflected upon remains in a state of non-manifestation due to the profusion of the radiance of successive series of rays— according to the analogy of the orb of the sun at midday— because of the inability to perceive the possessor of the rays. Just as:
Just as a fragment of a ruby stone, though utterly praiseworthy due to its freedom from flaws such as internal tremors,

cannot be definitively determined to be this "superior ruby" solely on the basis of its periphery being suffused with clusters of shimmering, great rays of light— in the same way, it is with the Self as well.
The suspicion of indistinctness arises precisely because [the object] is concealed by the expansion of one's own power (*svaśakti*).

Thus, it is only within this state of possessing a dual nature that the appropriateness of the world’s empirical transactions (*viśvavyavahāra*) is established. This has been stated by me myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"When the sprout of light from the Great Source is not yet fully manifest,
my external manifestation requires the rising of the sun— the mirror for self-perception— and the world requires that interval.
Thus [it is said].
And this [recognition] occurs only with respect to worldly mothers. Thus it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"But due to the power of delusion, although this [Self] is seen, it is not perceived."
"This recognition is taught through the manifestation of one's own power.
Just as a lover, though standing nearby, remains like any other person to a slender maiden because he is unrecognized despite her various entreaties, so too [is this world].

"Thus, this world-lord, whose own qualities are not perceived even by himself, is not at all capable of his own majesty; therefore, this *Pratyabhijñā* (Recognition) has been proclaimed. And furthermore, regarding those who are extraordinary and inward-looking:
Neither for one who meditates nor for one who recites mantras should there be [a result] contrary to the prescribed rule;
we bow to that devotee who possesses such devotion and appears as Śiva himself.
Thus, it is precisely the statement found in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī* that conforms to the path of reason. || 9 ||
Now, one might object: "How can these two mutually contradictory attributes—clarity and lack of clarity—possibly coexist in the Self?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that the Self possesses a certain such sovereignty (*svātantrya*) which, through its reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),...
Thus it is described; and he demonstrates that its contemplation as the goal of human life must be accomplished by all means:
"The light blazes upward, the auspicious lamp of the world and the non-world."
A gushing stream of oil from the burning impurities brought forth by the state of discernment.

This object, which is of the nature of luminosity and permeates all worldly transactions— such as "I who am this, I know," or "this throbs in me"— is indeed common to both the mass of entities that are being perceived and the class of non-entities such as a sky-flower, which are not being perceived.

It is experienced as an illuminator like a lamp. Thus, by its primary function, the world (*loka*) is the cognizer (*pramātā*) because its nature is light; the non-world (*aloka*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*) because its illumination is dependent upon that [light]; and the "world-and-non-world" (*lokāloka*) is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), due to its contact with both poles of the grasped and the grasper.
He becomes the illuminator of the universe, which is the ultimate reality of the triad beginning with the knower (*pramātṛ*).
We have already stated previously that in the absence of such illumination, the universe would fall into blinding darkness;
for this very reason, he is presented as the auspicious one (*maṅgala*). Indeed, this alone is that most great auspiciousness, namely:
Having dispelled the suspicion that pillars, pots, and so forth might mutually negate one another's intrinsic nature, as well as the possibility of their being devoid of intrinsic nature,
they are established in their suchness; and that [pillar] is upright by virtue of its self-luminosity.
Transcending the category of the manifest, it shines and manifests itself through universal consensus.

Furthermore, a certain excellence called "reflective awareness" (*vimarśa*) must be accepted as its very nature; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it falling into the realm of insentience, like the light of a mirror or similar objects. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*:
"Even though light is colored by objects, it is like an insentient thing such as a crystal.
And that [light], by virtue of its distinction from the category of effects, is the attribute of light known as agency (*kartṛtva*).
This will be established immediately hereafter.
Indeed, in this vast expanse of worldly activity,
many entities such as the earth and mountains are conventionally designated.
Their rules of legal procedure are observed to be unmixed;
therefore, let the wise consider what might be the cause for this.
Nothing other than consciousness itself is perceived;
if one were to doubt that consciousness, then even the earth would not be the earth within its own nature.
Nor was she non-existent, for how could there be a separation between her and the mountain?
And if their mutual forms were to be sublated, who would have the skill to even utter a cry?
Thus, when the object of knowledge, such as the earth and so forth, is manifested without confusion—
In both its general and particular aspects, it is consciousness alone that prevails.
If that [light] were to proceed as something to be manifested by another, just like an object of knowledge,
then it would not consist of light itself, because there would be no distinction from insentience.
If consciousness were to be illumined by something other than itself, would its nature as consciousness be lost or not?
If it is not lost, then that "other" by which it is illumined would be redundant.

If it is lost, what form would it have? Let it be illuminated by that [consciousness]. But when one considers how there could be illumination of that [object] and of another [subject], [the problem remains].
If it were argued that "one [cognition] is different from another," then clearly an infinite regress would result;
therefore, its self-luminosity is established by its very nature.
And although light, by the manner just described, is self-luminous,
it would not abandon its insentience— were it to consist merely of the nature of an object— just like that which is an object of cognition.
Even though this [consciousness] is self-luminous, it does not attain any degree of agency unless [it does so];
otherwise, its nature would not be illumination, just like that of external objects.
Consequently, his agency, characterized by repose within his own self, must be accepted even by one who does not wish it; that which the wise know as "I-ness" (ahantā).
The state of being self-established is proclaimed as the "I-sense" (ahambhāva) of that all-pervasive Lord who is the ultimate ground of establishment for the entire category of objects of knowledge.
And this very power of discernment (vimarśa) constitutes the primary sovereignty of the Lord;
therefore, it is established that the Blessed One is independent and all-enduring.
And by means of that state of that very deliberation—

the condition of its manifestation— the series of impurities, consisting of the individual (āṇava), the karmic (kārmika), and the māyic (māyīya), which is a succession or accumulation, [is dissolved] by the Light through the application of its orientation toward it.

By becoming the agent, it is burned and accepted through its entry into one's own self. In that context, *māyā* is the manifestation of a distinct object of cognition; the impurity dependent upon that is the *māyīya-mala*. That which arises from *karman*—consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of merit and demerit—is the *kārmaṇa-mala*. [The term] *aṇu* means...
Because it is devoid of the reflective awareness of the fullness of "I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva-parāmarśa*), the individual soul (*jīva*) is contracted in its thinking.
That very state is the *āṇava* [impurity]. And that consists in the cognition of the non-self as self and the cognition of the self as non-self.
It is precisely with this intention that, in the *Śrī Śivasūtras*, there is the elision of the letter 'a' (*akāra-praśleṣa*).
It has been stated that consciousness, the self, ignorance, and bondage [are related] through two types of conjunction. As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Regarding the two aphorisms: 'consciousness,' 'knowledge of the self,' 'bondage'..."
"This meaning is illuminated through the two [modes of] conjunction and its opposite.

For the Supreme Lord has as His essential nature light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), consisting of knowledge and action. And when either one of these—His state as knower or His state as reflector—is not being reflected upon, [the other remains unmanifest].
The intended meaning is that the impure individual (malamāṇava) arises.
As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"The loss of sovereignty of consciousness, and the lack of consciousness within sovereignty..."
"This impurity consists of two kinds of atoms due to the loss of one's own true nature. Thus,
they maintain that every manifestation of impurity is ignorance (*ajñāna*), the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence.
Thus, according to the principle established in the *Śrīmālinīvijayottara*, [the Self] has as its essential nature solely the act of self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*).
And that—
just as heat exists in fire and coolness in the moon— [is inherent].
Just as there is softness in beds and hardness in stones,
and as there is delusion among outsiders and awakening among yogis, so too do I possess the great sovereignty to exercise control.
Thus, the discernment is that through the state of the manifestation of consciousness, it is indeed the sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of the Supreme Lord. By this [it is meant]:

"Though one, the impurity (mala) of persons possesses manifold powers; it is the concealer of vision and action, to be known as being like the husk and the chaff, or like the rust adhering to copper."

By these and other such statements, those who assert that "impurity" (mala) is some kind of substance inherent to the self are refuted. And it has been stated therein that the "entirety" (sakala), colored by the three impurities,
as well as the gods and others residing within the interval of the *māyā-tattva*, [are so characterized].

The *pralayākalas* are bound by the two impurities (*mala*), namely the individual (*āṇava*) and the karmic (*kārmaṇa*). It should be understood that among them, the *āṇava-mala* is the cause of their being devoid of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of self-knowledge and agency. And among those [pralayākalas], in some...

Even the impurity pertaining to Māyā (māyīya-mala) occurs when conditioned by the manifestation of a distinction between the object of knowledge (vedya-bheda-prathā). However, for others who have entered into the non-manifestation of objects of knowledge (apavedya-prathā), this [impurity] does not exist; such is the distinction. Those with a single impurity are the Vijñānakalas. Even there, that impurity [belongs] to their own self...

Because they are devoid of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that constitutes the state of being a reflector; for even the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s) possess only a single impurity (*mala*), due to their connection with the mere vestige of *māyā*. The Mantras and others are characterized by the exhaustion of that impurity. Even among them, those who are merely oriented toward its exhaustion are the Mantras, while [those at] the commencement of that [exhaustion] are the [Mantra-mahāmantras].
The Mantreśvaras and Vidyeśvaras are those for whom [Sadāśiva] is the presiding lord and thinker;
the Mantramaheshvaras are those whose impurities are being attenuated, and for whom Sadāśiva is the governing authority;
while the Anāśrita Śivatattva pertains to the state where impurity is colored only by residual impressions (vāsanā).
The Lord, the venerable Paramaśiva himself, is indeed the radiance of the stainless state that is unarisen in every respect;

such is the diversity of subjects (*pramātṛvaicitryam*). Regarding the word "brought" (*ānītā*): this is the means for the burning away of the three impurities (*malatraya*), namely, their internal attainment by way of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And for those who have entered into one's own self—
For just as fuel licked by fire becomes identical with it,
so too the shrine embraced by consciousness attains the state of being composed of consciousness.

By this principle and others such as these, since the state of being "endowed with that" (tadvadbhāva) necessarily follows, their very nature as impurity (malasvabhāvatva) is overturned; this is the sense. As it is said in the venerable *Bhagavadgītā*:
"O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes."
And as I have said myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*: "Deluded by the power of the coloring of the object of knowledge, it becomes manifestly blackened, as if through contact with another metal."
"The fire of discernment, having heated [it] on all sides with garlands of flames, renders my heart pure like gold.
This means that the very abandonment of the suspicion of impurity is the means for the destruction of impurity. As it is said in the *Śrīniśākula*:
"O beloved, what can a speck of dust do to a crystal stone?
For just as a blue stain in the sky is merely a suspicion of impurity, one should therefore abandon the suspicion of impurity.
Thus it is said; for example, regarding the multitude of individual souls such as Caitra, Maitra, and others.
The lamp, which illuminates the collection of objects such as pillars and jars and is auspicious by virtue of its metaphorical designation as a "house-deity," burns upwards;
for, being a specific form of fire, it burns upward according to the principle that "the upward flaming of fire is its nature."

And just as the flow of oil brought in through the opening of its wick is consumed—this constitutes both metaphor (*rūpaka*) and paronomasia (*śleṣa*). It has already been stated that the variety of sentence-structure through figures such as simile (*upamā*) serves to make the meaning of that [sentence] touch the heart. || 10 ||
Now, he himself establishes the nature of the previously introduced *vimarśa* as the very essence of the Self:
"The existent light of the Heart becomes the agent in the act of manifestation."
That very activity is self-abiding awareness (vimarśa), which, when agitated, is the expansion of the universe. || 11 ||
It must be stated that the manifestation of one's own heart exists for everyone, because if it were non-existent, it would entail the contradiction of its own negation. As the Upaniṣad says:
"He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent."
"If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing.

Therefore, the light of the heart is of the nature of one's own self. Regarding the word "sann" (existing), there is complete agreement. In this context, the term "san" must be examined both from the perspective of its verbal root (*prakṛti*) and its suffix (*pratyaya*). [It is derived] from the root *as* with the suffix *śatṛ*.

Thus it arises in this way: one must accept that in this context, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) portion is the action called "becoming" (*bhāvanā*), while the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) portion is the agent. Consequently, the word *sann* has the meaning "the agent of the action characterized by becoming. That very action of becoming is [what is meant].

The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consisting of agency is thus described. Furthermore, by the introduction of the term "action" (*kriyā*), it is shown that "becoming" (*bhavana*) is existence (*sattva*), and that [existence] is of a general nature (*sāmānyarūpa*). Consequently, those who claim that it does not possess the nature of action (*kriyātva*) are refuted; for, according to the principle that "being" (*bhāva*) is action, it applies to the meaning of every verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
It is made known that action-ness (kriyātva) must be accepted; and that action consists here of a pair of states designated as "object" and "agency."
For it is thus: this very consciousness, existing through its own sovereignty as both internal and external, is of the nature of self-reflective awareness.
Thus, according to the established doctrine of the *Śrī Spandakārikā-Āloka*, when one abides within oneself in the very nature of the light of the heart (*hṛdayaprakāśa*),

then reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is designated as "pure reflective awareness. But when one experiences the agitation characterized by the attachment of conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*), then there is the expansion of the universe.
In that case, a certain additional qualifying element arises, namely that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consists of the manifold manifestation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Thus, it must be admitted that reflective awareness is the very nature of light (*prakāśa*); and its absence [from light] would follow otherwise.
Because it is a synonym for the destruction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it entails precisely its non-manifestation.

Consequently, it follows that this [object] would either be of slight manifestation, like a crystal or a mirror, or else be entirely non-manifest, like a pillar or a jar. Furthermore, regarding the term "existent" (*sann*) here:

That which is called *sattā* (Being) is itself called *cittva* (Consciousness); and the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Being and Consciousness is Bliss (*ānanda*). As it is said in the *Śrīrasānvaya*:
"That which is Consciousness is declared to be Being itself, and that which is Being is called Consciousness."
In this regard, where there is the pervasion of consciousness and existence, bliss shines forth.

"Wherever there may be bliss in an object, there resides the triad of consciousness and existence. Thus, one should understand that the Supreme Lord, whose own nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, is the Self within one's own heart. As they say:
"Śambhu, who consists of truth, consciousness, and bliss, is threefold within all things. Thus,
even as the manifold variety of internal and external existence unfolds, he maintains his own state, which consists of simultaneity and the nature of being the observer.
By cultivating [this state], a person attains the pure, sovereign glory;
likewise, through neglecting it, one becomes deluded by the nature of a beast.
To the extent that the wondrous power of one's own creative impulse unfolds,
to that same extent the agitation of conceptual constructions reaches its end.
"Even by a mere fraction of discernment, the wise man possesses power;
for even a slender, poison-spotted kākīṇī insect makes a snake difficult to overcome. (11)

Now, one might object: "How can the universal worldly transaction (*viśvavyavahāra*), which proceeds as if directed toward external objects of perception, be of the nature of the self-reflexive awareness (*vimarśa*) that is the Self? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) of the earth and Supreme Śiva, which has light as its ultimate reality..."
That very mutual distinction is the unfolding of the heart's reflective awareness.

For here, every relationship connected with all worldly transactions ultimately resolves into nothing but the relation of cause and effect. And it must be accepted that, in the final analysis, the agent is the Supreme Śiva himself, since both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) [are reducible to this].

Other relations connected with that, such as conjunction and so forth, even though there exist intermediate agents who bring them about, are experienced ultimately as the effects of that very agent— the Supreme Lord— since they follow His will.
Otherwise, if it were stated that there is a single relation consisting of the mutual reaching of two entities,

how could this [relation], having exhausted its entire burden of its own body in one place, be capable of even touching another object? Furthermore, if it were to subsist in both equally, how could it be called a "relation" at all?

Because it exists in two ways, there would be no possibility of a lack of connection. Furthermore, in cases such as inherence (*samavāya*), where an ordinary agent is not perceived, it must be accepted that the Supreme Lord alone is the agent.
Even though inherence is eternal, it does not transcend having the Supreme Lord as its agent.

Since it has been stated by those very [authors] that substances remain devoid of qualities for even a single moment due to their duration (*sthiti*), it is established that his skill in joining and separating them belongs to him alone. Furthermore,
these [categories], such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), do not exist elsewhere apart from their own respective appropriate objects.

It must be admitted that they function in some way or other, for otherwise there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And when one reflects upon what the nature of that "appropriateness" (*aucitya*) is, one must accept that it is a reality entirely distinct from the inherent natures of substances, qualities, and so forth, which we call the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara*).

One might cry out "independence," yet there is no disagreement that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is its effect; for even universals (*sāmānya*) and other categories, though eternal according to worldly convention,
are indeed effects in relation to the Supreme Lord, such that even space (*ākāśa*), which is considered eternal, [is likewise].

Therefore, by the scriptural text, "From this very Self, space was produced," its being an effect is indicated; and this is merely an illustration. Consequently, by this manner of presentation, the Supreme Lord is the agent of this effect characterized as the universe, and thus this relationship of cause and effect is established.

Thus, it is stated that the ultimate reality consists in the identity of the action and the agent. Furthermore, when causality is thoroughly examined, it is not logically possible for an insentient entity;
for even when the collection of causes such as clay, staff, and wheel is present, [the effect does not arise] if the potter and others remain indifferent.

Because [an effect] such as a jar does not arise [from itself]. In cases such as "a sprout arises from a seed," although no specific agent is observed, it is nonetheless impossible for the sprout to possess such capacity [at that time], because it does not exist then. If it is argued that "the seed possesses that capacity," [we reply: no. How [could there be a capacity] for the sprout?

The statement "it arises" expresses the capacity of the seed through a grammatical relation of different loci (vaiyadhikaraṇya). Furthermore, does that seed produce a sprout that already exists or one that does not exist? If it produces one that already exists, what is the meaning here of this act of production, since its existence has already been stated? If it produces one that does not exist—

How could existence and non-existence not be contradictory in that regard? Or, if they were admitted, how would there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Therefore, some non-inert entity alone must be the cause of the entire class of effects. And this non-inertness of it is nothing other than its agency (*kartṛtva*). As for the agency observed in certain cases, such as that of potters and the like—
In that case as well—
it is thus: for this potter, by his very nature as a sovereign agent,
produces a jar through a specific sequence of processing various clays and other materials.

Thus, according to the system of the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā*, it is that very [Supreme Lord] who, by virtue of His sovereignty (*svātantrya*), follows the established order such that "this jar is made of clay alone" and "this cloth is made of threads alone," and cannot act otherwise; therefore, He Himself is the agent (*kartṛ*) in relation to the potter and so forth with respect to the jar and other effects.
Even though there is some degree of non-inertness, it is indeed inertness when compared to the Supreme Lord;

thus it has been well said that all relations are simply the relation of cause and effect, and the cause is the agent alone. This being so, there is no manifestation of another agent above Paramaśiva, nor [is there any other] above the earth.

And there is the arising of another effect. That object which consists of a collection of principles situated between those two, being apprehended sequentially for each individual thing, drawn forth by the intellect, and grasped by means of valid cognitions such as perception; [of that object...]

By means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that, ultimately, light alone is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) by virtue of being the animating principle; otherwise, even when the causal complex of the eyes and other organs is present, those [objects] would necessarily fail to manifest. As it has been said in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
"That which is non-expansive does not expand, just as that which is not white does not become white.
And as it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"For that which is not of the nature of light cannot be manifested, nor can it possess the status of a real entity."

Therefore, one must first admit that the internal light of one's own self alone manifests externally as the manifold of objects to be illuminated. Consequently, since all thirty-six principles are indistinguishable in their essential nature as light, the distinction between earth, water, and so forth arises only from their mutual differences.

Conventional usage is not possible; yet, the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is indeed perceived directly by the world. Otherwise, there would result an absence of determination regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) with respect to the distinction between water and land and so forth.
And that particularity arises solely through the existence of reflective awareness (*vimarśasattā*) residing within one's own heart. Furthermore, this arising occurs in identity (*tādātmya*).
It culminates in this: because it has been stated that "whatever has arisen is indeed that very [reality] itself. By the word *unmeṣa* (unfolding), he says this:

the manifestation of the manifold variety of the universe is essentially the sprouts, flowers, and so forth of the tree of self-reflection (*svātmavimarśa*). By this, [the nature] of both the supreme and the non-supreme subjects...

It has been explained that [the Lord] is animated by *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), and that ultimately these two are identical with him. Regarding the term "Supreme Śiva" (*paramaśiva*):
his sovereignty, as previously described, rests solely in his state of being transcendent to the universe, and not...
Furthermore, regarding the sovereign empire of supreme autonomy, characterized by being both immanent in the universe and transcendent of it,
since it is inappropriate to withdraw such a nature, on the contrary, its very nature is that of the withdrawer. || 12 ||

Now, in order to further strengthen this very reflection, he examines the *śivatattva* first, establishing the mutual distinction among the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) in accordance with the sequence of emanation:
"The single convergence of thousands of powers (*śakti*) appearing in such and such ways."
He who consists of the exertion of his own heart becomes Śiva, the supreme autonomous one. || 13 ||

This mode of the manifestation of the universe, beginning with earth and ending with *śakti*, whose [powers] are will, knowledge, and action; knowledge, memory, and exclusion; creation, maintenance, withdrawal, the inexpressible, and appearance—and which is otherwise worshipped in various other currents (*srotas*).

The "yoginīs and yogins" refer to the radiance of the agitation of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). Since these powers (*śaktis*), which consist of that [radiance], are experienced in various ways in various places, they are infinite even when considering each individual manifestation; how much more so when considering them in their entirety! To illustrate this, [there is] the power of Will (*icchā*).

To that extent, [the desire to know] is of many kinds due to the distinctions between the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and so forth. Knowledge, moreover, is of infinite kinds due to the variety of recollection (*smṛti*), experience (*anubhava*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*), creative intuition (*utprekṣā*), and so on.
Action, too, is infinite due to the distinctions between going, sitting, lying down, eating, speaking, and so forth. Of these as well—

It is stated—with the intention of showing the excellence of its infinity—that there is a "disturbance of conceptualization regarding each individual division and sub-division," expressed as "of thousands of powers. And that which is their single *saṃghaṭṭa* (conjunction), while experiencing unity itself, becomes the ground for the simultaneity of mutually contradictory activities such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). And that which...
In accordance with the *Śivasūtra* principle that "exertion (*udyama*) is Bhairava," it is experienced as the very nature of the exertion of one's own heart;

and because of its union with the state of being the object of the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arising from the integration (*sāmarasya*) of the two aforementioned types of meanings, it is distinct [from them].

It is determined that [the Lord] experiences absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which is characterized by independence from looking toward any other source and is supremely exalted due to its distinctness from the categories (*tattva*). For other categories,
such as *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, exist in a hierarchy of successive lower levels.

They attain either sovereignty with respect to each successive higher reality or dependence [with respect to the lower]. "Supremely Independent" (*paramasvacchanda*) is described, as before, as being transcendent to the universe; however, the other is both transcendent to the universe and identical with it.

The venerable Paramaśiva will be revealed hereafter; such is the nature of that which is called Śiva. The intended meaning is this: by means of his sovereignty—which consists of expansion and contraction (*unmeṣa-nimeṣa*) and is difficult to find among other principles—he embraces the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) alone within the two powers characterized by the bliss of consciousness.

In accordance with the *Śrīśivasūtra*’s principle that "the universe is the accumulation of one's own powers due to the inclination toward assuming a succession of ever-higher powers such as will, knowledge,
and action," [this arises] from the unfolding of the manifold variety of the infinite external wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which consists of the agitation of the universe.

The specific subject (*pramātṛviśe�ṣa*) whose essence consists in the vibration of the rising self-consciousness, which is bold in manifesting the elements, is the venerable Lord Śiva (*śivabhaṭṭāraka*). As it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"The Self alone, the all-pervasive, blissful consciousness, shines forth within all things."
"Śiva is one whose expansion of will is unobstructed and whose vision and action are ever-expanding. Thus it is said.
As stated in the *Śrī-Vijñānendukaumudī*: "The ground of all-pervasiveness is recognized as consisting of knowledge and agency."
"The state of Śiva is said to consist of the wonder of one's own manifestation. Thus it is.

"It comes to be": all this sovereignty that has been established culminates precisely in the existence of one's own essential nature (*svarūpasattā*). And it has already been stated previously that this [existence] does not deviate from consciousness (*cittva*).

For it has been stated: "That which is existence (sattā) is called consciousness (cit), and that which is consciousness is called existence. And since that which is this "vibration" (sphurattā) is recognized as the "Great Existence" (mahāsattā), the use of the present tense (laṭ) is employed because of its state of being eternally active. || 13 ||
Now, he reflects upon the principle of Power (śaktitattva), which follows in due order:

"That very [Self], becoming intent upon seeking, knowing, and acting toward the universe, is described as having the nature of Power, the lush and overflowing radiance within the triangle of the Heart. (14)

That which has been described as Śiva by nature is said to be Śakti by nature; the meaning is that the designation "Śakti" applies to that very [Śiva] when it is in a state of slight swelling (*ucchūnatā*). And its nature is this: that, in the form of its own heart, it consists of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

By means of the honey— which is characterized by the aesthetic savoring (*sāmarasya*) of the three corners (*koṇatraya*) that are the synonyms for all conceptual constructions (*viśvavikalpa*), and which is capable of kindling the vibration of the bliss of consciousness submerged within, due to its being a festival of perpetual tasting— ...

"May I become many, may I be born"— according to the established principle of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), [the Self], through its own exertion and emission from its own heart, [becomes] abundant, exceedingly nourished, fit for the activity of carrying forth [the world], and like the water of a great lake being withdrawn.
"One experiences an intense joy, an expansion of one's own self. As it is said in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:
"Vibrating as the Self, you expand the entire universe; perceiving your own form, you perceive the universe."
"That which you yourself reel with your own innate essence—that is what causes the circle of aesthetic emotions (*bhāva*) to flash forth.
And thus follows this:
"The extreme rippling of water that was previously moving without waves..."
For by directing one's gaze toward the beginning, one indeed attains an orientation toward that [goal].

According to the perspective of the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*, when one becomes intent on projecting outward the reality of the object—which exists within one's own heart and possesses the aforementioned nature—it is then designated as "power" (*śakti*).
This state of intentness arises through that [Supreme] Will, as well as through knowledge and action. Thus it has been said.
Thus, he has been proclaimed as being of such a nature by many scriptures. As stated in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
"In this way, Śiva consists of pure consciousness; he alone is supreme bliss.
That very [bliss] attains the state of being oriented toward [the world], consisting of his own will, knowledge, and action."
"That very state of being (bhūtatā) extends from the body of power (śākta-śarīra) down to the hellish realms," and so forth. As it is said in the *Śrīkulamūlāvatāra*:
"From Śiva, the supreme cause, who is without beginning or end and is quiescent..."
From that, the power of will (icchā-śakti) emerged; from that, knowledge (jñāna); and from that, action (kriyā).
Beginning thus:
"The fourteen worlds and the elements produced by those two,
and whatever consists of speech— all that originates from Mātṛkā."

Thus far. And as it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-vṛtti*: "The very desire of the one whose body is consciousness (*cidvapus*) and who is autonomous to exist as the self of the universe is itself the causality toward the world, in the form of agency," and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Śrī-Tantrāloka*:
"Of this non-kula deity, she is the supreme Kaulikī Śakti, characterized by the expansion of kula; the Lord is never separated from her.
And as it is said in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
That power of the Creator of the world which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī) becomes the Goddess Will (icchā) when He desires to emit the universe.
"It is to be known as thus, and not otherwise"— making this known with perfect certainty in this world is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
Furthermore, when they know, "May this object become thus," and at that very moment bring that object into being, it is called "action" (kriyā) in this context.
"Thus, although she possesses these three forms, the Sovereign Lady attains infinity through further divisions by virtue of the limiting adjuncts of objects, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
And likewise, it is stated in the *Śrīparāsūkta*:
O Goddess, regarding Your constant and innate inclination toward the unfolding of Your creations at the beginning of every cycle—
those who know the scriptures have indeed defined that as "Will" (icchā).
"You know that by which you accomplish each respective purpose.
And in the *Pūjārahasya*:
"The fourfold [set] consists of orientation, will, knowledge, and action."
The vibration of the God of gods, who takes the form of Bodhabhairava.
"When the Great Lord turns His face toward [creation] by abandoning indifference, all this becomes the world; what need is there for arguments in this matter? (14)
Then Sadāśiva and Īśvara deliberate:
"In both [the categories of] knowledge and action, during the first emergence, the deity is Sadāśiva;
upon the manifestation of the second, he becomes the second, known as Īśvara. (15)

For that which is called "knowledge" (jñāna) is indeed the very nature of all living beings, established through self-awareness, whose essence consists in the manifestation of the sense of "I. And action (kriyā), connected with the hands, feet, and so forth, flashes forth as capable of manifesting everything directly. In this regard, [the thought] "I know"—

Just as in expressions such as "I do," so too in expressions such as "you know," the referent of the word *asmad* (the "I") appears as the referent of the word *yuṣmad* (the "you") through the logic of looking into a mirror; thus,
even when Caitra speaks, it is the very sense of "I" that appears, just as in the expression "Caitra bows."
Through the mediation of adjuncts, [the Self] is perceived as the first person and so forth;
thus, the "I" alone is the reality of the self everywhere. As it has been said:
"All action has 'is' as its remainder, and all grammatical factors have the agent as their remainder."

"And the singular form [of the word] is a remainder, and the person (puruṣa) is the ultimate limit. Thus, the meaning of the word "knowledge" (jñāna) consists in the manifestation of the "I" (ahantā). In this way, even in cases such as "you do" (karoṣi) or "he does" (karoti), since "I do" (karomi) alone is ultimately real, action (kriyā) is also [the self].
It is determined that she has entered into the state of egoity (*ahaṃbhāva*) just like knowledge;

however, because she is experienced primarily through the state of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*), there is the conventional usage of duality. And thus, between these two states—knowledge and action—when the first, knowledge, predominates...
And when, by implication, there is a state of subordination (*nyagbhāva*) characterized by a lack of clarity in the second [power], it is designated as the principle (*tattva*) called Sadāśiva;

and it is as its presiding deity that one who is commonly worshipped under the name Sadāśiva—being shared in common with Viṣṇu, Rudra, and others—is known. And that deity [is so called] due to the predominance of the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*).
And because there is no absolute deficiency in action,
he is capable of pursuing various purposes such as play and worldly transaction. Furthermore,
from the very beginning, this [consciousness] exists by virtue of its own essential nature as reality.
The term "Lord" (*deva*) is stated in order to indicate that this is an illumination of the Supreme Lord, who is inseparable from His own power characterized by the desire to emit the universe.
As it was said by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptanātha:
"We praise that Śiva, within whom shines the wheel of principles (tattva-cakra), beginning with the noble Śrīmat-Sadāśiva and ending with the earth.
Now, however, the designation of "principle" (tattva) for Śiva and Śakti is not in its primary sense; what then?

The designation of these two as "tattvas" is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), arising simply from their contact with the conceptualization of the form that carries forth the multitude of higher *tattvas* beginning with Sadāśiva. Since the application of the term "tattva" to these two exists even in a figurative sense, there is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the fact that the *tattvas* number thirty-six. And as for the second activity therein—

When there is an abundance of knowledge—whose synonyms include "illumination" (*ullekha*) and "vibration" (*sphuraṇa*)—and which, by its very nature, possesses a state of stillness (*staimitya*), one becomes what is called Īśvara. This is traditionally taught as the reality (*tattva*) known as Īśvara.
And the subject (*pramātṛ*) who presides over that is indeed Īśvara. This is what is meant:

From the initial predominance of the two powers of knowledge and action, characterized by "I-ness" (ahantā) and "this-ness" (idantā), there arises— by way of the analogy of a partially opened painting— the reality known as Sadāśiva, whose nature is that of the universal subject consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest. Conversely, when the power of action (kriyāśakti) is preeminent, it takes the form of one who synthesizes the universe of manifest forms.

Regarding the phrase "the principle of the Lord" (*mīśvaratattvam*) and "the first unfolding" (*prathamonmeṣa*): the so-called unfolding (*unmeṣa*) and closing (*nimeṣa*) constitute the *spanda*-principle, which is characterized by the supreme sovereignty of the Supreme Lord. In that regard, when there is the unfolding of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), there is the closing of "this-ness" (*idantā*); and when there is the unfolding of "this-ness," there is the closing of "I-ness."
By this term "nimeṣa" (closing), it is meant that Īśvara is the external unfolding (*unmeṣa*), while Sadāśiva is the internal closing (*nimeṣa*).

Thus, according to the system of the *Śrī Pratyabhijñā*, even the two other designations for these [two] that are well-known from various other scriptures are indicated; by the word "the second," while showing the lack of intervention despite the difference between Īśvara and the Sadāśiva-tattva, [this applies] everywhere.

Even when presenting a continuous series of distinctions among the various categories of reality (*tattva*), one must keep in mind the progressive gradation of the intensity of the persistence of the "I-sense" (*ahantā*); this is what is being elucidated here. As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"But when there is a predominance of external objects, the state of the Supreme Lord [is realized] through another."

Since *ahantā* (the sense of "I-ness") consists of the dual nature of Śiva and Śakti, it is appropriate that its manifestation occurs precisely here. By this, the complete citation of the verse is explained. || 15 ||

Now he illuminates Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā): "The Knower is that Self, and the nature of the knowable is worldly transaction; that state where these two have attained a unified fusion into a single essence is indeed Pure Knowledge, free from all dross. (16)
The Supreme Lord, the Self, is the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃbhāva) which, though possessing the attribute of being a knower, is yet undivided;

it is His own true nature that is embraced by His power of consciousness (cicchakti), and it is this very nature that constitutes worldly transaction (lokavyavahāra), which is the expansion of the phenomenal world animated by the reflective awareness of its manifestation.

The meaning is that both of these—namely, the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) consisting of abandonment (*hāna*), attainment (*upāya*), and so forth—have reached a state of fusion (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) characterized by the perfect harmony of their mutual cognition; that is stainless and pure *vidyā*. And that fusion is of a single flavor (*ekarasa*); it is one, its form being non-differentiated.
Because it is the substratum for the wondrous experience that is difficult to attain in reality, this [consciousness] is tasted as its locus.
And therefore:
"The identity-in-locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cognition of 'Being-Knowledge' (*sadvidyā*) and the cognition of 'this' (*idam*)."
This is what has been stated. As was said by our venerable teachers in the *Śrīmātaṅgīstotra*:
"O Mistress! I rejoice in Your two breasts, which are firm, full of nectar, and beautiful, appearing as one with each other;
O Suvidyā! They stand equally established, and I am likewise identical to them, both being manifestations of You alone."
Thus:

in the case of the group of subjects within Māyā, it is universally accepted that there is a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between these two—namely, "I" with respect to the subject and "this" with respect to the object; however, here [in the state of Śuddhavidyā], it is not so.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is expressed by the term "single essence" (*ekarasa*). Furthermore, its purity consists in the innate and naturally fitting form of the entire range of objects of knowledge—which, although appearing as external—manifesting solely as "I"; whereas for worldly people, that same range manifests as "this" (*idam*).
It is so designated. By the exclusion of that [duality], there is excellence consisting in the manifestation of things as they truly are.
As it is said in the *Paryantapañcāśikā*:
"Purity is the immersion of externalized objects into one's own 'I-ness' (*svāhantā*)."

And in the *Śrītantrāloka*: "Even regarding these [entities] which are essentially consciousness, that cognition which perceives them as distinct is declared to be the supreme impurity; purity is the dissolution of that cognition."

Others, however, conceive of its purity in this way: although there exists in [the levels of] Sadāśiva and the rest a consciousness characterized by the aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) of "I" and "this," and although there is a state of unison through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), nevertheless,
because the manifestation of the "this-ness" (*idantā*) aspect belonging to *māyā* cannot be avoided even for Sadāśiva and the others.
Because he is unacquainted with the discourse on *māyā*, this aspect of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—

having dispelled the defect of being subject to *māyā*— is established as being perceived through this [consciousness] in the same manner as the portion consisting of the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*). However, in the absence of that perception...
"Otherwise, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be compromised. This is the intended meaning:

for the Lord, the venerable Paramaśiva, there arises—due to the excellence of His desire to graciously favor even certain bound souls (*paśu*) as subjects (*pramātṛ*) by making them indistinguishable from Sadāśiva and the other levels—a stain of impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*).

Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) is the power of the sovereignty of consciousness, whose nature consists in the recognition of one's own essential being (*svasvabhāva*) as inseparable from its cleansing; by relying upon this, there arises the diversity of subjects, namely the *vijñānakevala* and Rudra as Agni. By the word "that" (*saḥ*), [the text refers to] the object that is pervaded by the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

In order to illuminate the fact that it is a distinct alternative from the whole [of ordinary experience], the state of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*)—perceived through the mental process of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpoddhāra*) regarding the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*)—is now disclosed. Indeed, by establishing its excellence through such renown, this is brought to light: that [the powers] such as the *ḍākinīs* and *rākinyas*...
The deities of the elements, the means to human goals such as conduct and ritual action, the specific types of initiation such as the Śāmbhava and Śākta,
and the distinctions between the states of waking and dreaming— all these arise in their respective ways as the vibratory manifestations of her very sovereignty.
"They are conventionally designated" (*vyavahriyante*); the word *yatra* is a particle (*nipāta*) that resembles a case ending. || 16 ||
Then he opens his eyes regarding Māyā:
"Māyā is the deluding power of the Supreme Lord, who is absolutely independent; she manifests the crafts of conceptual construction within the single-flavored nature. (17)

For the unique nature of the Supreme Lord— consisting of the manifestation of great existence (*mahāsattā*) which is the very essence of the radiance of the universe— remains, upon rational investigation, as a single flavor, having as its sole core the beauty of the vibration of the bliss of one's own self-consciousness; it does not [exist otherwise].
Furthermore, because of the propriety of embracing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as a doubt, and because the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*) is about to be refuted;
even though this is the case, there are conceptual constructions such as "Caitra," "Maitra," "pillar," and "jar" in that very [reality],
which— like the craftsmanship of ornaments such as bracelets and crowns— involve a multiplicity of dualistic appearances.
Being heart-captivating due to their capacity to produce the wonder of beauty,
these playful manifestations of the object of knowledge unfold further and further. For this very reason,
they cause one to perceive the liberated as bound by the terror of bondage, and the bound as liberated through the conceit of liberation— thus effecting a complete reversal.

Power (*śakti*) is called *māyā*, because this Lord is supremely autonomous. Indeed, this alone is the pinnacle of the excellence of His autonomy: His mastery in producing the manifold variety of distinctions and sub-distinctions within the world that exists as a non-dual manifestation of His own Self; by means of which He is the performer of the most difficult feats.

He is proclaimed as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). For this very reason, He is the Lord of the World (Lokapati), the sovereign of the phenomenal universe consisting of the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth. In the absence of Māyā, there would be no existence of the phenomenal world, since its ultimate reality consists in the manifestation of duality. And in the absence of that [world], there could be no [reality] standing in opposition to it.
Otherwise, the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord would be untenable, and nothing at all could manifest.
Therefore, this so-called *māyā* is His supreme freedom (*svātantrya*). As has been stated by our venerable teachers in the *Śrīmanonuśāsana-stotra*:

"We worship the bliss of the universe, which has dissolved and become the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*) through the dissolution of the dullness of *māyā*— the very synonym for absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
And as it is said in the *Paramārthasaṃgraha*:
"That which is the supreme sovereignty of Maheśa, the accomplishment of the impossible—
this is the Goddess Māyā-śakti, the self-concealment of Śiva.
And in the *Śacīmata*:

"O Goddess, you are my power of sovereignty (*svātantrya-śakti*), the performer of the most difficult feats; you are celebrated as *māyā*, O Goddess, bestowing upon my Lord his universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*). Thus it is said in the *Śrīmat-stotrāvalī*.

"Nothing distinct was ever created, nor is there anything here fashioned that is other than happiness; yet you are the source of suffering and of division in every way—salutations to You, the abode of incomparable wonder! Thus it is said.
Also in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"What could He not manifest therein, by virtue of this His state of absolute freedom?
It is by relying on this very [freedom] that subjects such as the Pralayakevalin, Viṣṇu, and the Sun become manifest.
Although, according to the system of the venerable *Triṃśikā-śāstra*, there is a tetrad of concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) consisting of air, fire, water, and earth, [this pertains] to Māyā.
Although there is the propriety of [the sequence] unfolding through the inclusion of the arts (*kalā*), the sciences (*vidyā*), and so forth, nevertheless,

this is solely for the purpose of manifesting the first portion of the venerable *Parā-bīja*, which was extracted as "beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Māyā, residing within the body of Brahman."
It is stated by way of distinction:

"But how can there be a refutation of the doctrine of difference, such that the nature of the universe might possess oneness? To this it is replied: What is this so-called "difference"? Is it mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), or...

Is it dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), or rather the very nature (*svarūpa*) itself? Not the first, for that pillar does not become a jar, nor does the jar become a pillar; such a form arises only in dependence upon a limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting of the mutual exclusion between the two. And that...
When these two are investigated, their distinctness (*anyatva*) manifests precisely as that which is to be distributed (*vīpsyamāna*).
Now, this distinctness of entities must be either their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) or some adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) based on difference.
If it were the former, then even those things pervaded by unity would necessarily entail difference. If it were the latter, [then...]

Difference from that [other] is only possible when difference itself exists; yet since the nature of difference is not yet established, there would be either the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*) or mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). The second [alternative] is not [the case]. For "dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*) refers to an object consisting of the specific properties of pillars and so forth, such as pillar-ness (*stambhatva*) and pot-ness (*kumbhatva*). In that regard:
If there were some fixed necessity such that pillar-ness resides only in pillars and pot-ness only in pots, then difference would be established; however, no such regulating factor is observed.
[Objection: But surely there is the quality of being made of wood and the shape of having a broad base and belly, which serve as the determinants for that distinction.

If you say this, it is not so; for that [property] is not perceived as being unique to them. And such a perception would only be consistent if there were a difference between the pillar and the others. Since that difference is included within the category of the probandum (*sādhyakoṭi*), there arises—as before—the fallacy of circular reasoning (*ātmāśraya*) and so forth. Furthermore, [this applies] even to properties such as being made of wood.

If difference consists in the nature of various mutual exclusions (vaidharmya), then upon investigating down to the level of atoms, there would be a rootless, overturning infinite regress. Nor is it the third [option],
for the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of a pillar or the like is its own form, which is not connected to any other nature.

This must be stated, for otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities. Furthermore, when investigating what the basis is for a pillar or the like not being affected by the intrinsic nature of another, the only statement that holds to reason is that "difference exists even there. And that [difference] remains even now...
The claim that its nature is merely a mental construction (manoratha) entails the very same defects as previously mentioned.

Furthermore, if the difference between entities were their own essential nature (svarūpa), then the manifestation of errors such as "this is silver" would be dismissed with folded hands; for in that case, the essential nature of the mother-of-pearl [would itself be the silver].
It is clearly perceived and determined as being silver.

Even when one adopts the position of the theory of non-apprehension (akhyāti-vāda), it must be admitted that while the erroneous cognition itself is denied, the corresponding practical activity is not. Furthermore, this...
When difference (*bheda*) appears only among entities (*bhāva*), is it itself distinct from those various entities or not?

If it is not, then it follows that there is simply non-difference (*abheda*). If it is distinct, then how is that difference itself [established]? When investigated further and further in this manner, there arises an abundance of accepting an infinite succession of differences (*bhedaparamparā*).

It establishes the very state [of the entity]. And this distinction must belong either to an entity that is distinct by nature, or even to one that is non-distinct. If it belongs to one that is distinct, what is the use of this adventitious distinction?
Furthermore, the production of something already produced is a great fault. If, on the other hand, it belongs to one that is non-distinct, there would clearly be a contradiction.
Furthermore, this must be considered:

the conventional usage of difference, such as "the jar is distinct from the pillar," requires that both of these [referents] be embraced within a single mental state for the purpose of indicating the object of that difference. And if they exist in such a manner, [then...]
"This is separate from that here"—this is the manner of the external gesture of pointing with a finger;
however, the internal nature declares the actual non-difference between these two.
By such a mode of existence, because the nature of things is non-differentiation (*abhedasvabhāva*), non-duality alone is established.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: that which manifests is of the nature of a single manifestation, because it is manifesting, like the self-reflective awareness of "I" (*ahampratyavamarśa*). And in this context, the presentation of the removal of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) and so forth [is intended].
This effort to indulge in the craving for the taste of the doctrine of difference is fruitless, as it would result in excessive prolixity.
If it is asked, "How is it that everyday usage—such as 'pillar' and 'jar'—is mutually distinct and non-confused?", we reply:
it is by way of the principle of difference-in-identity (*bhedābheda*). For the supreme Lord’s Light (*prakāśa*) is indeed present everywhere.

When the world of manifestation (*prapañca*) unfolds without distinction, it is solely due to its own sovereignty. Furthermore, the justification for distinct conventional designations such as "pillar" and "pot" occurs through the manner of the waves and ripples of the ocean.

If it is argued that, in this case as well, the critique of the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*) would consequently apply because [the manifestation] is not a part [of the whole], we say no; for [the Absolute] is pure (*śuddha*).

A distinction undergoes such censure; however, here, due to the excellence of its association with non-difference, even that distinction remains as something to be sublated, just like all beauty submerged in a salt-mine according to the maxim of the "salt-mine" (lāvaṇyākaranyāya). As for what we have stated regarding the basis of differentiation—

Thus, the difference of the universe is accepted [as being intrinsic], and not as conditioned by the quality of separateness (*pṛthaktva*), because non-difference is contradicted precisely by that second [quality]. Now, one might ask: why is there not the opposite view—that non-difference is also defective due to the misfortune of its association with difference?

If it is argued that this may be so, we say no; for the material cause (prakṛti) favors its modification (vikṛti). In that case, it must be admitted that non-difference is the material cause and the other is the modification. For even among distinct entities, their unity in their respective individual forms is unavoidable, and that very [unity] is what constitutes non-difference.

There is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that the true nature of this manifold play (*viśvavilāsa*) is precisely non-duality (*abheda*). For regarding this very reality, infinite Upaniṣadic texts such as "Brahman is one only, without a second" and "There is not even the slightest diversity here" manifest themselves. Now, [one might object]:

If you argue that this matter—both difference and non-difference—is contradictory, then alas, your venerable self has forgotten what was previously introduced! For it is accepted that the Blessed One possesses a certain exceedingly great power called *māyā*, which is the cause for accomplishing even such extremely difficult tasks. By this, non-duality alone [is established].

The Siddhānta is the essence of all; that is the ultimate foundation, the state of Parā. However, the nature of the relationship between the universe and that which transcends the universe—which sustains the entire realm of worldly transaction as both difference and non-difference—unfolds as the state of Parāparā. And as for difference...

The state of non-duality (*aparāvasthā*) unfolds, characterized by a succession of sprouts of boldness in the self-reflection of the light of the Supreme Lord who transcends the universe; its delusive play serves as a variegated pavilion for the artistic conception of the manifold diversity of the world. Within these states, there exist respectively the well-awakened (*suprabuddha*), the awakened (*prabuddha*), and the unawakened (*aprabuddha*).

Such is the gradation among yogis. And since the light of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-prakāśa) is woven through all of these states, there is no distinction whatsoever; thus, this position of ours is to be learned by those who are truly discerning. As it has been said in the *Paryantapañcāśikā*:
"Even while assuming infinite such forms, one should enter that single-characterized self-awareness and not conceptualize through mental constructs.
These very [energies] are worshipped as various deities from the perspective of those who practice devotion (*upāsaka*). As it has been said:
In the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"The Supreme Goddess (Parā) has a luster like the moon; the Intermediate Goddess (Parāparā) is red;
and the Lower Goddess (Aparā) is that supreme Kālī, the terrifying and fierce Yoginī. Thus it is said.
Thus, the very realization of the true nature of illusion is liberation while living; this is the secret teaching of the Upaniṣad. || 17 ||
Now, he examines the pentad beginning with *kalā*, which consists of the power of illusory manifestation (*māyāvibhūti*), by way of its objects:
"The Great Lord is the doer of all, the knower of all, complete, eternal, and uncontracted; those [powers] by which He appears as if contrary [to His true nature] are the five powers. (18)
For the Supreme Lord is by nature the creator and the knower of the universe; therefore, due to that very sovereignty, He is full and self-satisfied, as there is nothing to be prayed for.
Because no entity exists apart from Himself that could serve as a limitation, He is eternal.

He transcends both antecedent and subsequent non-existence; for that very reason, He is devoid of the constraints characterized by contraction. Even while being such, through those powers which act as His bonds, He appears as if contrary [to His true nature], endowed with attributes such as limited agency.
These shine forth as the five powers (*śakti*). As it is stated in the *Śrīkramodaya*:
"Passion (*rāga*), Māyā, Kalā, Ignorance (*avidyā*), Necessity (*niyati*), and Time (*kāla*)—all these, which rest upon the fivefold function, are proclaimed to be the fetters (*pāśa*)."

And these *kalās* are called ignorance (*avidyā*), attachment (*rāga*), time (*kāla*), and necessity (*niyati*). *Kalā* is the cause of its limited agency; ignorance is the cause of its limited knowledge; attachment is the clinging to sense objects; and time consists in the manifestation and non-manifestation of entities.

The sequence [of categories] follows. *Niyati* (restriction) is the cause of regulations such as "this is mine" and "this is not mine. These five [categories] are called *kañcukas* (sheaths) in the scriptures because they conceal the essential nature [of the Self]. For in their absence, the *puruṣa* would possess a power of consciousness as manifest as that of the Supreme Lord, or his sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) would be utterly submerged like that of a stone.

Or it may be so: therein, through the sequence of passion (rāga), illusion (māyā), ignorance (avidyā), limited agency (kalā), and time (kāla), there occurs the avoidance of the soul’s (puruṣa) entry into the upper and lower joints; thus, like Triśaṅku, its abiding in the middle position is achieved through the employment of those [elements] in the form of earth, water, fire, air, and ether.
By this, their nature as *dhāraṇās* (concentrations) is explained; as it is stated in the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*:
"There is a fourfold set of *dhāraṇās* for air, fire, water, and earth. (18)
Now, he reveals the essential nature of the Person (puruṣa):
