"He who is this Śambhu, the actor in the universal drama, whose nature is pure consciousness—his certain state, consisting of the assumption of various roles, becomes the Person. (19)

For I am indeed the Supreme Lord; by virtue of the excellence of the wonder consisting in the expansion of the experience of the manifestation of universal selfhood (*vaiśvātmya*), He experiences His own consciousness— which is pure, free from even the suspicion of the stain of limitation, and composed of the *vidyā* whose nature is His own sovereignty— for this very reason.
According to the *Śrīśivasūtra*, "the Self is the dancer," whereby it is designated as the actor, the stage-manager of the drama of the universe. As it is said in the *Śrīnaiśvāsa*:
"In one aspect, You are the inner Self, the dancer, the protector of the sheath."

And I am that Great Actor, Śiva, who— even while enacting the drama of human existence through all its junctures consisting of birth, childhood, youth, old age, and death— remains Śiva at the final consummation; for the universe, from the earth up to the principle of Śiva, is essentially a collection of these very principles.

According to this principle, because it is inseparable from the five stages beginning with emanation (sṛṣṭi) and maintenance (sthiti), it imitates the drama characterized by the five stages beginning with the prologue (ārambha). As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa:
"O Hara! Who else besides you is capable of being the poet to compose and then destroy this drama of the three worlds, which contains within its womb many excellent seeds that have been sown?
And that Śambhu [is the one] who provides the occasion for the relishing of aesthetic flavors (rasas) such as the erotic and the pathetic.
It is called *śam* because it is the bliss (*sukha*) consisting of the experience of sound, touch, and so forth, which arises for the perceiving senses from this [source]. And for that [bliss],
which is intent upon the performance of the cosmic drama (*viśvanāṭya*), there is the purpose characterized by the assumption of various roles (*bhūmikā*).
That very state which is primordial nature (*prakṛti*) becomes the person (*puruṣa*); it experiences the fitness for the designation "person. As it is said in the *Śrīsāraśāstra*:
"The Lord of Gods binds himself and by himself alone he is deluded."
"He himself is the enjoyer, he himself is the knower, and he himself should perceive. Thus, according to their respective states: *prāṇa* is that which initiates inhalation, exhalation, and so forth;
*vyāna* is that which is useful for rejection, acquisition, and the like; and *samāna* is that which nourishes the body and other organs.
The upward movement of the elements and so forth is *udāna*, while the expulsion of feces, urine, and so forth is *apāna*;

thus, the various modes of exertion are made known. Although even for a potter, in the act of making a jar, there exists the nature of Śiva who possesses all powers due to the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and other factors, yet this is not realized because of a lack of understanding thereof.

Even if one is devoid of the reflective awareness of the state of the Supreme Goddess within one's own heart through the process of connecting words— meaning "in the potter's workshop"— nevertheless, from the perspective of ultimate reality (tattvadṛṣṭyā), for him...
The status of being the Supreme Lord (parameśvaratva), proclaimed by the sacred tradition (āmnāya), is unavoidable. For this is indeed the unique nature of the Supreme Lord:
that He eternally performs the fivefold cosmic acts (pañcakṛtya) beginning with creation. This will be clearly examined further on.
For by not accepting this, it follows that the Self as determined by Māyāvādins, Vedāntins, and others,

falls into a state of unreality characterized by a dullness of its own self-luminous joy. And this Puruṣa, however, because he is capable of accomplishing the impossible, acts out of his own absolute freedom and stainlessness.
The Supreme Lord is skilled in the play of concealing His own nature.

Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, even though he has descended onto the path of *māyā*, he performs all five cosmic acts at all times like the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). For there is no state whatsoever in which his consciousness is devoid of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*). Even in states such as deep sleep, [there is] the subsequent...

By the power of the continuous application of awakening (*bodhānusandhāna*), one should perceive a certain subtle manifestation of worldly activity submerged within; indeed, the only difference between the various states is a mere gradation of consciousness. As it is said in the *Śrī Spanda*:
"Even though it expands through the various states such as waking and so forth, it never departs from its own innate nature as the perceiver, which remains undivided.
This will be clarified later in the passage beginning with "jo ī jā a rasiviṇa a. And therefore:
In this state of the pillar and so forth, which is the essence of the sovereignty of consciousness, when there is an orientation toward the perception of the pillar, then its emission occurs.
Since it is by this very [consciousness] that the emission takes place through being perceived as distinct from a jar or other objects, it occurs right there.

When it remains for only two or three moments, that is its persistence (*sthiti*), because the maintenance of things in their respective forms is said to be persistence. When there is an inclination toward entering into another state, such as a jar, then that is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the pillar.

And there is the emanation of the Kumbha state. Furthermore, when there is the intermediate state between the abandonment of the Stambha and the entry into the Kumbha, that is the existence of the Turya (the Fourth), because it consists of pure consciousness due to being free from the coloring of objects of knowledge. As it has been said by me:
In the *Śrīkomalavallīstava*:
"O Mother, for one who desires to abandon one state of mind and plunge into another, they declare that Your non-dual reality is the intermediate ground hanging between them."

The power of consciousness (*saṃvit-śakti*), inherent within one's own self, which permeates all the aforementioned stages and is capable of transcending them, brings [the object] into manifestation. Alternatively, when there is a synthesis with a pillar or the like, and at that time there is the ascertainment of "pillar-ness" with respect to it, [it is manifested].

At that time, its being made of wood and so forth becomes subordinate (*nyagbhavati*). And when there is the ascertainment of its being made of wood and so forth, there is the subordination (*nyakkāra*) of its being a pillar; thus, it is clearly observed that the manifestation of one entails the withdrawal of the other. However, when there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the synthesis of "pillar-ness," "being made of wood," and so forth, there is stability (*sthiti*).

Because there is neither subordination nor non-existence of even the two types of cognition; when all conceptual constructions such as "pillar-ness" have subsided, it is the "Inexpressible" (*anākhyā*). When there is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the flashing forth of one's own self, it is the "Manifestation" (*bhāsā*);
in this way, the process of emanation and so forth is to be understood. And in that very state, when [one perceives] a pillar...

When he perceives [an object] as having a restricted space, time, and form, then by the aspect of its manifestation as such, he possesses the power of creation (*sraṣṭṛtā*). By the aspect of its manifestation as not being restricted to that particular space, time, and so forth, he possesses the power of withdrawal (*saṃhartṛtā*).

But by the aspect of the universal commonality (*sāmānya*) of the pillar and other objects, he possesses the power of maintenance (*sthāpakatā*). This occurs during non-conceptual perception (*avikalpāvalokana*).

It is established that his sovereignty— characterized by the simultaneous performance of the fivefold cosmic acts such as emanation and so forth— is realized even without [the need for] the state of being experienced as the fourth (*turīya*), and furthermore, by being the gracer through manifestation as one with Light. For this very reason:
Although its nature is contracted, it is designated as "puruṣa" because it is expanded in its true essence (*tattvavṛttyā*).
As the Śruti says: "By that Puruṣa, all this is filled.
And in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*: "Because of filling, it has attained the state of being Puruṣa."

Furthermore, regarding the fivefold set of duties, the Supreme Lord exhibits no partiality whatsoever in the three acts of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal. Moreover, concerning the two subsequent acts [of concealment and grace], when there is this agitation of the mind— consisting of causing the violation of sacred commitments (*samaya-bhraṃśa*) and so forth— with respect to the deluded *paśu* beings, and when...

Due to the excellence of his compassion, by removing these defects, he grants the soul the recovery of its true nature; thus, his two functions are designated as concealment (*tirodhāna*) and grace (*anugraha*). Furthermore, when—
Just as variegated colors appear simultaneously on a wide cloth,
even so does the earth appear to yogis through the totality of its phenomena.

Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, when the entire universe is contemplated as the effect by means of removing the limitations of the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*) and so forth, then that which is called the "Inexplicable" (*anākhyā*) shines forth; this is the designation for its two functions. Enough with these intermediate details. And as for that which appears as Rāma and others to the actor in the form of a role (*bhūmikā*): that...

However, it is experienced by the audience as an object of another consciousness, distinguished from correctness, falsity, doubt, similarity, and so forth; whereas by bystanders such as Vedic scholars, it is experienced solely as a performance. The phrase "this which" refers to that which is well-known from the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other sources.
Illuminating the fact that the Supreme Lord is to be contemplated as one's own self through extreme proximity,

[the author] suggests that this duality— which manifests to the individual from the perspective of the Supreme Lord upon the emergence of such contemplation— experiences a play of flickering like cotton in the wind.
By the phrase "some such state," it is illuminated that even for a person who has attained the status of the Supreme Lord,

there exists a profound excess of delusion— indeed, a state worthy of lamentation— due to his lack of self-reflection (*svaparāmarśa*) and his consequent identification as an agent who enters into the realm of objects of knowledge (*vedyavarga*). As it has been said:

In the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*: "The principles beginning with Earth and ending with Puruṣa are [placed] in the five classes of consonants beginning with Ka and ending with Ma, respectively, O lady of excellent vows."

And as it has been explained by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda: "For the person (*puruṣa*), who is limited and consists solely of the nature of the object of cognition, is counted among the mass of objects of knowledge. And of that [person]:
"I am fulfilled, I am emaciated, I am full of affection, I am rejoicing."
"I breathe" and "I am empty"—indeed, such a sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā) is observed within these six states.

Thus, according to the method of the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*, multiplicity is also established by virtue of the proximity (*upaśleṣa*) of the body, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth; for, by taking this as a support, the differentiation of subjects (*pramātṛbheda*)—such as Brahmā, Candra, and Sakala—manifests. By this, his fitness for the enjoyment of heaven, hell, and other states is [established].

This has been explained. As it is stated in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*: "Just as through play, those who perform actions that result in the experience of suffering are destined for the depths of the ocean of hell by means of their fruits."
"The Supreme Lord assumes bodies as his dwellings.

And he, at times, due to the power of delusion, identifies his own self-manifestation as the vibration of the body, senses, and so forth. Yet this is not the ultimate, real vision. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīsvacchanda*:
"Just as a flame is not seen in the sky when a fire is well-blazing,
so too the Self, though residing in the body and the vital breath, dissolves into that state."
However, the true perspective is that even this manifestation of the world ultimately culminates in the Supreme Lord alone.
As it has been said in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*:
"Even though the stability of objects resides in [the subject] who is constrained by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*),"
"In the individual soul, and even when [the breath] has ceased there, it remains in that Supreme Self.
Furthermore:
"Shining forth from the Supreme Lord down to the level of an insect..."
Assuming many limiting adjuncts, that one alone shines forth.
Even when bodies are divided, the embodied soul is not divided,
just as a person seeing his face remains one even when mirrors are divided.
Just as there is only one oil even in a large heap of sesame seeds,
so too in this manifold display of the universe, there is but one transcendent Lord.
Just as there is no actual difference in the sky situated within each of the windows, so too should it be seen in the case of the Self.
For indeed, a single universal such as "existence" or "cowness" is postulated;
why then is it not tolerated when one says that this Self is likewise one?
Since the maintenance of worldly affairs is accomplished by a single self alone,
would the postulation of multiplicity therein not lead to unnecessary complexity?
Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that difference has no object whatsoever;
therefore, in this doctrine of non-duality, how could there be multiplicity for the Self?
Even if that difference is merely adventitious (aupādhika), Vedic passages such as "Two birds...
establish that the distinctions of pleasure, pain, and so forth are logically consistent.
Because it follows each respective individual through the single cause of identity,
its pervasiveness is established, as is also demonstrated by others.
Therefore, let this doctrine of the Arhats— that the self resides within the body according to the dimensions of each respective body, such as that of an elephant or an insect— be abandoned.
As for what they say: "If that [consciousness] were all-pervading, then consciousness would exist even in stones, just as it does in bodies."
In this regard, the reply is that even in stone and the like, there exists a latent impression of consciousness;
its lack of manifestation, however, is due to the non-arising of assistance from the vital breaths and other factors.

Furthermore, those who claim that this [consciousness] is indeed identical to the body are utterly ignorant. For instance: it could not be composed of the body and yet be the sole locus for the expansion of consciousness; otherwise, movement would be observed even in a corpse, just as before.

For those who assert that consciousness belongs to the elements, what could serve as the basis for the gradations [of intelligence] found in a pillar, a jar, a river, a stone, a deer, a bird, and a human?
Thus, this [consciousness] does not consist of the sense organs for embodied beings during states such as deep sleep,
because consciousness is not perceived even when there is contact with the sense organs.
If the body, the senses, and so forth were the self, agency would ultimately reside in them;
what other effect could then be desired apart from the agency of the phenomenal world itself?
If it is asserted that agency and being an effect exist only partially,
then by what means is the determination made as to which part belongs to whom and who is the agent of which?
Or by whom can the suspicion that the nature [of reality] is the opposite of what has been stated be prevented?
Therefore, let it be accepted that the very reality ascertained by us is the Self.
Now, he who asserts that [the world] is empty is also questioned:
is this [world] empty because it is included within the universe, or is it empty by its very nature?
Even in his own treatise, he does not record the position that [things] are empty by themselves;
for if the class of objects of cognition were empty, worldly convention would be destroyed.
While establishing emptiness, one indeed engages in all conventional discourse;
another speaks of the universe as real, while someone else speaks of it as empty.
If the status of both is identical at times such as when using vehicles or seats,
and their conduct is of one and the same form, what is the purpose of a discrepancy in speech?
Furthermore, the wise person establishing the meaning that "the entire world is empty" never encounters an opponent anywhere,
nor even a conversation with one.

Enough with this excessive elaboration; let us return to the subject at hand. And thus, for all the manifold variety of the phenomenal world, there is no state in the contemplation of word and meaning that is not Śiva.

Thus, the essential meaning is this: since it is accepted through the method of the *Śrī Spanda* that [the Self] consists of the light of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvara-prakāśa-maya*), how could there be any rejection of partiality toward this very person?
As it has been said in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
"All these subjects, because they are luminosity, are of the nature of Śiva;
they are all-knowing, all-doing, and entirely non-differentiated.
It is for the sake of illuminating this meaning that even the *puruṣa* is called *puruṣa*, because he dwells (*vasati*) in their city (*pura*).
The term *puruṣa* (person) is derived from the sense that he "steals" (*oṣati*) or "burns" (*dahati*) the city; this refers to a specific distinction in his essential nature.

Because the Self dwells within these three cities—known as the intellect (*buddhi*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the body (*śarīra*)—through the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), he is therefore remembered as *puruṣa*.
He by whom these three cities were burnt is Tripurāntaka;
he alone is declared to be Puruṣa, and he is also remembered as Smarāri (the enemy of Smara).

Thus, although this is elucidated according to the propriety of the *Śrīhaṃsabhedasthiti*, nevertheless, when considering the ultimate, ontological meaning, there is indeed an absolute identity between those two.
And within such a limitation, there is the nurturing of that threefold impurity which consists of one's own sovereignty.

Regarding the term "cause": Now, if— even when the manifestation of difference reaches its peak— there is identity (*tādātmya*) between these two, and on that basis the lord’s (*pati*) exaltation of sovereignty is established just like that of the bound soul (*paśu*), then by that very same identity, the lord too must have his heart bound by the affliction of delusion through *māyā*, just like the bound soul.
If it is argued that [the Lord] must have a subsistence (vṛtti), this is not so; for the analogy of the magician is pertinent here.
Indeed, while he himself deludes the entire world, he is not deluded by anyone.
It is precisely for this reason that the Supreme Lord is designated as a "stage-player" (śailūṣa). || 19 ||

Now he reveals the primordial nature (prakṛti): "In the state of non-differentiation of the qualities—knowledge, action, and illusion—which have the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas, that reality is Prakṛti; she is the power of Śambhu. (20)

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is illumination (*prakāśa*); action (*kriyā*) is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Māyā, however, is the power (*śakti*) which—though there is the sprouting of a slight manifestation of duality in the form of "I am this" and "this is I"—nevertheless culminates in the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), just as in the states of Sadāśiva and Īśvara. Of these...

Even those who have become the powers (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord possess the status of being qualities (*guṇa*) from the perspective of the deluded *paśu* beings. As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"The knowledge and the action which belong to the Lord with respect to the objects that constitute His own limbs..."
"In the third [category], Māyā, those two are indeed the sattva, rajas, and tamas of the bound soul (paśu).

Thus, these [powers] exist in the bound soul as sattva, rajas, and tamas; by means of them, this worldly transaction consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion occurs. And they are composed of those [qualities].
That state which is devoid of differentiation, characterized by absolute evenness like that of a balanced scale,

when thoroughly investigated, constitutes the reality known as *prakṛti*. Within it, there occurs the manifestation of thousands of qualities and defects, whose natures are both auspicious and inauspicious.

On this plane, the five forms of "I-ness" (ahantā)—delimited by the void, the intellect, the vital breath, the body, and the objects—as well as the five kalās—nivṛtti, pratiṣṭhā, vidyā, śānti, and śāntyatītā—are conceptualized by the wise as manifestations of power; and that [power] is indeed the Śāmbhavī energy itself. By this [it is shown].
The tenets of the Sāṃkhya and other systems will be ridiculed. For they indeed [assert]:
"Root-prakṛti is not a modification; the seven beginning with Mahat are both prakṛti and modifications;
the group of sixteen is only a modification; and the Puruṣa is neither prakṛti nor a modification."

By such statements as these, they declare that there is no other principle (tattva) above the Puruṣa; that the Puruṣa is indifferent (udāsīna), while Prakṛti is dependent upon him; and that she is eternal and not a modification (avikṛti), whereas the group of sixteen is eternally of the nature of modification (vikāra). Our system is not thus. For, above the Puruṣa—

There are many principles (tattvas) extending up to Paramaśiva. And the Puruṣa, though eternally omniscient and omnipotent, appears as if contracted due to the non-manifestation of its own nature (svātmākhyāti). Furthermore, Prakṛti is not impelled by the Puruṣa alone; [this occurs] only in the absence of the sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of the Supreme Lord.
Because such a capacity for instigation is absent. As it is said in the *Śrīspanda*:
"This [will] does not function as an instigator by means of an impulse;
rather, through contact with its own power, the person becomes equal to it."

And she is always transformed, though sometimes she is untransformed; the group of sixteen as well is sometimes untransformed and sometimes transformed. Now, those who call him the indifferent one say that his exertion is eternally manifest.
They should be answered as follows: "If there were always no exertion," [and so forth].
What purpose would the world have for that [Self] which is like a lump of clay?
Why would it be accepted, and what could its measure possibly be?
Whatever is said— that very state of indifference on the part of the conscious self impels primordial nature toward all that is subject to modification within the universe.
Otherwise, not even the slightest boldness would proceed from Prakṛti;
for that reason, there is the acceptance of Him whose splendor transcends the universe.
And by that very same means of valid cognition, its establishment would occur.
To this it is replied: if that [establishment] were merely a conceptualization of indifference toward it...
The intended meaning culminates in the fact that he is indeed not indifferent;
having undertaken subtle exertion, he is distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and the other categories.
Thus, this [Prakṛti] would not be devoid of activity, since that activity, though subtle,
gives rise to grosser activities both in the primary causes (prakṛtis) and in the evolutes (vikṛtis).
Since even insentient things such as the body, the senses, and the worlds proceed by His power due to their own nature, how could He be inactive?
And on this point, my own well-spoken verse is as follows: "When horses are moving, the statement arises that 'the chariot moves';
but what indeed did the man seated comfortably within the chariot do to reach another location?"
"O Śambhu! Thus it is said.
Here, this must be understood by those who know the inner truth: namely, that the multitude of principles (*tattvaugha*) beginning with Śiva and ending with *prakṛti* has been established.
In that regard, [this belongs] to this Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who transcends the universe.
All-encompassing action, omniscience, perpetual arising,
all-pervasiveness, and fulfillment— these five powers are proclaimed.
Then, when there is power and that [divine] will,
Unmanā, Samanā, Vyāpinī, Nāda, and Bindu— these five rays awaken.
Grace, concealment, withdrawal, maintenance, and emanation—
these five activities of the world are the manifestations arising from the principle of Śakti.
Furthermore, in the principle of Sadāśiva, Īśāna and Tatpuruṣa [are the faces],
while Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta are the Śaktis.
Above that, in the principle of Īśvara, there is the Great One (Mahat) which transcends form;
and the sequence is: the form-transcending, the form, the plane (pada), and the body (piṇḍa).
The states beyond the fourth (turyātīta), the fourth (turya), deep sleep (suṣupti), dreaming (svapna), and waking (jāgara)—
these five are the manifestation of the power of pure Consciousness.
This very initiation, which is Śāmbhavī, Āṇavī, and also purifying and awakening,
brings forth a radiant manifestation.

The conceptualization of means for attaining the goals of human existence consists of what is called "illumination without means," as well as knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct— all of which arise from that very [reality].
From that very [source], the great power named Hākinī arises;
likewise Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, and Kākinī as well.
That which manifests as the manifold variety within this body is called a *sākinī*; furthermore, these are the powers (*śakti*) of that reality which is termed *māyā*.
The arts (kalā), knowledge (vidyā), passion (rāga), time (kāla), and destiny (niyati) as the fifth;
as well as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—
this collection of powers within the person is entirely consumed in the maintenance of the body.
In Prakṛti, however, there are also the qualities (guṇas): sattva, rajas, and tamas.
In the same way, the five lights are said to be both modified and unmodified;
now, through the activity of the vibration of these two—the Spirit (puruṣa) and Primordial Matter (prakṛti)—it comes to be.
The conceptualization of the manifold variety of the universe, which will be explained in its entirety, and its specific modes as well, shall be set forth in detail according to the rules.
From the union of the male and the primordial nature (puruṣa and prakṛti), the element called the self (ātman) arises;
this [self] consists of what are known as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
It unfolds through what are called wind, bile, and phlegm, which illuminate their own respective portions;
and from the very friction of these two arises the mind, the intellect, and egoity.
Thus, the radiance of the internal organ is experienced in three ways;
therein, from the exertion of the intellect, there arise virtue, knowledge, and dispassion.
Sovereignty and the power of bestowing boons—such is the unfolding of diversity;
the reversal of these, occurring in succession, is held to be the craftsmanship of the mind.
The notions of "mine" and "not mine," miserliness, pride, and envy—
these are the manifestations of egoism that serve as the causes for the appearance of saṃsāra.
In the same way, by the very manifestation of those two, the three qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas—
are perceived as arising both modified and unmodified.
In that regard, the radiance and playfulness [of the mind] manifest as the beauty, good fortune, virtuous conduct, cheerfulness, and kindness of a sentient being.
Subjugation, attraction, pacification, nourishment, and protection—
these they call the undertakings of the quality of passion (rajas).
Now, as for those rites which are called incantations for causing hatred, and that which is termed eradication,
as well as the acts of paralyzing, bewildering, and killing—
All this is the agitation and play of that darkness (tamas),
insofar as the ego (ahaṅkāra) undergoes embellishment through these qualities (guṇas).
Through the distinctions of being characterized by *sattva* and so forth, it then attains a threefold nature;
therein, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell follow in sequence.
The *sāttvika* [type of mind] manifests in its own form among objects of enjoyment;
the *rājasa*, however, expands through speaking, grasping, and running.
Through emission and bliss, he possesses his own fivefold nature;
even as the tamasic aspect, he is characterized by the specific qualities of ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
He manifests as embodied through the elements, which are the material causes of the universe;
moreover, within this state called the ego (ahaṅkāra), there exists a threefold nature.
Due to the excellence of the various manifestations of power, a threefold expansion is intended:
the desire for merit, the inquiry into reality, and the longing for supramundane goals.

The determination regarding objects, prosperity, intelligence, and the faculty of conceptualization and discrimination— these are the manifestations of the sattvic person whose friends are tranquility, self-restraint, and the like.
They say that the state consisting of the senses of hearing, touch, sight, taste,
and smell is the sovereignty of the rājasa [nature], which bestows joy, fear, and so forth.
Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals— these, in their respective order,
are the attendants of the tamasic self, whose friends are delusion, indolence, and the like.
Now, that great accomplishment which has been brought forth from the two subjects under discussion—
its fivefold manifestation is experienced by practitioners.
The attainment of a body according to one's desire, entry into another's body,
traveling great distances, and hearing and seeing from afar.
And let it be understood that "making invisible" is its specific mode;
there exists some meritorious action for the production and maintenance of the universe by those two.
Vigor, profundity, sovereignty, the state of being an enjoyer, and also the state of being a giver—
this is the manifold variety of its manifestation, which is to be obtained by those endowed with good fortune.
Thus, in that very place, the *cinnāḍī* is known as the "thread of knowledge" (*jñānasūtra*);
and although the [centers] called *cit*, *padma*, and *śiva* are also said to consist of *śakti*.
The five channels proceed, bringing forth this phenomenal world;
likewise, there are Hāṭaka, Kālāgni, the Immutable (Kūṭastha), and also the Tortoise (Kūrma).
Ananta, Śaktyupaśliṣṭa, and the sage Kapila— in this sequence,
the manifestation of that [power] alone should be understood as the supporter of the seven netherworlds (pātālas).
Thus it has been said: although his nature is entirely free from worldly enjoyment, he remains unperturbed, possessing a wealth of profundity like the ocean when it is without waves.
The supreme Lord Bhairava, who possesses the fivefold powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action, shall be described at the end of the [discussion on] the principles (tattva).
The Great Lord himself revealed the supreme wonder of the fivefold reality that has taken root, unfolding the ground of the manifold variety of phenomenal proliferation.
I am the radiant one, consisting of supreme discernment.

He whose ego-sense is constant, and whose prowess lies in the exertion of that very ego-sense—he alone is truly a hero; for his scripture is indeed his own power, honed upon the whetstone of critical inquiry.
Thus, enough of this reckless exuberance in unveiling what is extremely secret. || 20 ||

Now he demonstrates the reality of the ego (ahaṅkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the mind (manas) by way of their respective objects: "The three instruments, ever surging like waves in the ocean of the heart, draw in the 'this-ness' from there and project the 'I-ness' into this [world]. (21)
Indeed, one's own heart, whose nature has been explained as the locus of all principles through qualities such as expansion,
is saluted— homage to the ocean of Śiva-consciousness, whose form is that of the subject.

Thus, by way of this state of being, it is determined as the ocean. In that regard, setting aside the limitation of specific time, there exist the three instruments—the senses—which act like great waves and serve as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the agent whose nature is the subject (*pramātṛ*). And these [instruments], just as they are animated by the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—

There, they draw forth the abundance of the variety of objects from within the heart and forcibly cause them to enter; likewise, they cast even their own heart’s power of consciousness— which has the ego as its essence— onto this plane of the object of knowledge, and though it is not natural, they cause it to be experienced as if it were natural.

These are designated as *ahaṅkāra*, *buddhi*, and *manas*. Among them, the definition of each is as follows: *ahaṅkāra* is the instrument for the conceit "this is mine" or "this is not mine"; *buddhi* is the cause of determination (*adhyavasāya*);
and *manas* is the cause of conceptualization and doubt (*saṅkalpa-vikalpa*). This is the meaning.

The internal organs of the Self, such as the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the rest, do not merely experience external objects perceived outwardly; rather, by means of the power of consciousness belonging to the subject which has been transferred into them,
they [experience] that entire range of knowable objects existing externally.

They bestow grace by means of the logic of sanctification (*pāvanīkaraṇa*), which consists in producing the nature of luminosity so as to enable [the objects] to enter into the state of being objects of experience;
thus they are said to be "surging like waves," according to the analogy of consecrating desired medicinal herbs and the like with mantras.

For these are indeed the great waves in the vast ocean of the heart; the meaning is that the organs of knowledge and action follow the analogy of waves upon waves. Furthermore, the abundance of their manifestation and activity has been explained at great length immediately following this. 21.
Now he unveils the organs of knowledge:

"The perception of objects belonging to the All-pervading Lord residing in the heart becomes unimpeded when the lamps of the organs of knowledge are perpetually fixed at the tips of their respective spheres. (22)

The all-pervasive Lord, who possesses supreme sovereignty and whose entire nature—including space, time, and essence—is delimited by His own power, is the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*). He has a certain most excellent abode suited to Him, which is called the Heart (*hṛdaya*). As it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*:
"This very [consciousness] is called the heart of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) because of its essential nature.

And for one established therein, that which is the "illumination" (āloka)—the perception extending to the surrounding limits—of external objects such as sound, touch, and so forth, is the skill of internal relishing in its entirety. That...
He becomes unshackled; he transcends the constraints of the external nature of objective existence.

And in this regard, the very cause is that those senses, which are primarily characterized by cognition and are like lamps due to the excellence of their illuminating power— [The rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

Their respective, specific spheres (*golā*) are the auditory canal and so forth; these exist as a perpetual, radiant presence, fixed at their outer extremities in locations conducive to being oriented toward external objects. And these are: the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose.

They are divided into five kinds. Their defining characteristic is that they serve as the instruments for the successive apprehension of the objects of perception—namely, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. (22)
Now he unfolds the organs of action:

"Indeed, there are five instruments belonging to the Lord of the World that have action as their primary function; by means of these, a person vibrates at will, becoming distinct from the insentient. (23)
Of that Lord who is the master and sustainer of the universe— the world perceived through the division of the insentient and the sentient— he possesses faculties primarily governed by action,
even as the organs of knowledge possess an abundance of cognition despite their contact with activity.
Even when associated with knowledge, the five senses remain preeminent in their power of action; indeed,
this is well known to be the cause by which the multitude of living beings, though afflicted by the calamities of birth, death, and so forth,
[distinguish themselves] from insentient objects such as pillars and jars, which possess limited illumination.

Attaining distinction (*vyatireka*), it vibrates—that is, it moves slightly; it does not move at all beyond the object reached by each respective sense organ. It moves only that much. "At will" (*svairam*) means: in such a way that there is an impelling of its own, that is, of its own instruments. Such is indeed its sovereignty.

And its manifestation is undivided. These [faculties] are distinguished as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Their defining characteristic is, respectively, the capacity to accomplish the actions of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure. In this regard:
Viveka:
Within this group of internal organs, egoism (ahaṅkāra) is the ground of self-conceit;
it grasps the other two—the intellect (buddhi) and the mind (manas)—as its auxiliaries.
It sets in motion both external cognition and action for the agents;
through the successive mastery over these two, there arises the manifestation of the organs of knowledge and action.
In that regard, the eye and the other [senses], which are primarily characterized by cognition,
have been established as capable of grasping objects even in the absence of bodily activity.
Among those very subsequent actions, a distinction is proclaimed:
for action is experienced in two ways—as relinquishing and as taking up.
Both of these are twofold, by way of being external and internal.
Regarding their externality, the anus would be that which primarily functions as the organ of excretion.
The hand is inclined toward grasping, and the foot performs both those actions;
that which extends all this internally is the vital breath, the wind.
That is declared to be the organ of speech, expert in the creation of sound;
it is that through which the self finds rest by calming the agitation of what has been spoken.
"Therefore, it should be known that the organ which conveys bliss is the *upastha* (genital organ).
Even though these [organs] function collectively, in certain instances, one among them holds predominance. || 23 ||
Now, he distinguishes the fivefold objects beginning with sound:
smelling all five fragrant flowers—beginning with scent—that have grown in the garden of the universe, the God, the rogue of the three worlds, plays. (24)
In the triple world— within the entire universe consisting of the means of knowledge (*māna*), the objects of knowledge (*meya*), and the knower (*mātṛ*)— he who is the rogue,
having set aside the entire collection of other worldly transactions through his cleverness,
becomes the Great Knower (*mahā-pramātā*) by virtue of his nature as luminosity.

He was inhaling all five flowers— arisen from the Viśvalakṣaṇa garden, possessing fragrances that proceeded from the unique collection of qualities of the earth and other elements, and intense with the radiance and diffusion of their scents.
Even when there is some degree of crookedness regarding the act of grasping, he connects [the senses] with straightforwardness;
he plays, vibrates in accordance with joy—meaning, he manifests his own sovereignty. And those objects are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

Thus they exist. Furthermore, their respective individual characteristics—namely, being qualities of space and so forth, or being perceptible by the ear and so forth—should be inferred in their proper order. The statement that they "begin with smell" is made according to the sequence of dissolution (saṃhāra-krama) in order to demonstrate the predominance of smell among the subtle elements (tanmātras).
As it has been stated by the learned:
"The deities of the self are to be propitiated by their very nature through the fragrances and other objects perceivable through the doors of the senses; this is the great sacrifice for the knower."
Even when analyzed, fragrance is nothing but earth; there is no other element whatsoever beyond earth—this is the secret regarding its excellence. || 24 ||
Now he elucidates the five elements:

"Just as molasses-lumps do not lose their sweetness, so too all five elements, arising from the light of Śiva—which is like sugarcane juice through a gradual process of thickening—do not abandon their inherent sweetness. (25)
Indeed, the luminosity whose essence is Śiva becomes solidified, following the sequence of Śakti, Sadāśiva, and so forth, down to the five gross elements under discussion;
this consists in the preeminence of the object of knowledge, which depends upon the subordination of the nature of the knower.

It experiences solidity. As it is stated in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*: "Bearing the nature of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) as described in such passages, He assumes as many forms for the sake of worldly transaction."
"As long as there is that which is gross, insentient in appearance, composite, earthly, and dense"— of such a thing,
its sweetness is characterized by the great bliss consisting of the radiance of the Supreme Śiva, who is to be experienced as the essential nature of the self of all subjects.

Samarasya (the state of equilibrium): even the five elements, beginning with space, do not abandon this state; rather, they proceed by internalizing everything within themselves. Their only distinction from Śiva, whose nature is pure clarity, is an excess of density (styānatā). It is just as [the difference between] sugarcane juice and its products through the process of its own maturation.
The sweetness of that which has become solidified is not abandoned by lumps of molasses; as it is said in the *Paramārthasāra*:
"Just as juice, thickened syrup, granulated sugar, molasses, candied sugar, and so forth, are all nothing but sugarcane juice."
In the same way, all the various states belong to Śambhu, the Supreme Self.
Thus it is said; and as stated in the Lakṣmītantra:
"Consciousness alone is indeed my form, filled with absolute purity and absolute freedom."
"Through union, like sugarcane juice, it attains a state of solidification;
therefore, when examined, that *caitanya* (consciousness) will attain the nature of *cit* (the conscious principle).
And thus, upon the earth, there are thirty-five principles beginning with Anāśrita-Śiva.
By this method— that they manifest through the persistence of causal impressions—
all principles beginning with earth abide within that Śiva-tattva according to the framework of the doctrine of pre-existent effects (satkāryavāda).
Likewise, even among the intermediate principles such as Prakṛti and Puruṣa, [they abide] by means of the aforementioned twofold process.
The essential conclusion is that all higher and lower principles interpenetrate one another, such that everything is of the nature of everything else. As it is stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"And within each single principle, there is the nature of all thirty-six principles."
Thus it is stated that this entire manifold diversity of the universe is, in every respect, of the nature of the vibration of the Supreme Lord’s Light. As it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"In this way, the state of Śiva resides equally in all things."
"The distinction between the higher and the lower has been described here by those who possess faith.
The elements (bhūtas) are well known as ether (ākāśa), air (vāyu), fire (tejas), water (āpas), and earth (pṛthivī).
Furthermore, their characteristics—namely, having sound and so forth as their qualities—are clear. Or alternatively:
The characteristics of these [elements] are, respectively: providing space and producing sound, mobility and vitality, cooking and burning, liquefying and floating, and maintaining hardness.
Furthermore, in this sequence of letters, the letters of touch extend from earth up to the Puruṣa.

This has already been demonstrated according to the method of the *Śrītriṃśikā-śāstra*. However, within the pentad of sheaths (*pañcakañcukī*), these [principles] reside internally. Among them, since Niyati (the principle of necessity) is all-pervasive, it does not merit separate enumeration. As for Kāla (time), because its nature is that of the power of space (*ākāśaśakti*) and because it functions solely to establish the unity of the conscious self (*cinmaya*), it belongs to the person (*puruṣa*).
Because there is no appropriateness regarding the assumption of the subjectivity of Māyā, the four internal [elements] have arisen. As it is stated in that very same place:
"The tetrad of the concentrations (dhāraṇā) on wind, fire, water, and earth."

And as it has been explained by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda: "But here, by means of the power of space (ākāśa-śakti), there is no need for the assumption of the subjectivity of Māyā. Furthermore, from Śuddhavidyā up to Śiva, these are the *ūṣmans*. Among them, the letter *ha* exists through repetition as both Śakti and Śiva.
This is because it consists of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the supreme *visarjanīya*. The very nature of Śiva and Śakti is indeed their essential unity;
for it has been established that their differentiation is merely conceptual. As it has been said:
"Above that, the group beginning with *śa* is renowned as the five Brahmans mentioned previously."
Within these thirty-six principles, the elements such as earth, water, air, and so forth—
those various categories of objects— are joined together and intermingled in many branches.
By existing as pillars, jars, and so forth, they perform purposeful action for human beings;
therein, those external objects such as jars are said to be [perceived] by the previously mentioned organs of action.
These [objects] are presented to the people engaged in worldly activity through proximity;
they are likewise perceived by the sense organs, which consist of consciousness, in their various respective ways.
These [objects], which are conceptualized and mentally constructed by the group of internal organs,
and which are determined and desired, are discerned through knowledge.
Colored by states such as the arts and time through the condition of being cognizable,
they find rest in the subject, whose nature is one's own self and who is enriched by reflective awareness (vimarśa).
And that cognizer, even in this body where both the vital breath and the intellect are absent,
binds the sense of "I" through those factors, beginning with true knowledge (sadvidyā), in their respective order.

Thus, the authorities declare that the supreme Śambhu’s establishment consists of this very [state] characterized by reflective awareness (parāmarśa). By virtue of the reversal of this, one becomes a bound soul (paśu); in this matter, the authoritative source is the teaching of the Guru.
Not so. || 25 ||
He states the essential reality of the aforementioned expansion of principles in its condensed form:
"The Great Power of Śambhu, consisting of the intensity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), unfolds like a silken thread for the entire manifestation of the wheel of the worlds' diversities. (26)

This very delusion, display, and expansion of the forms of the worlds and the principles— which consists of the production of various shapes— is itself the manifestation and transformation, such as twisting and turning, of mechanical devices like wooden dolls produced through the assembly of wood and other materials.
For all of that, [there is] a thread-like garland woven through every single joint and bond, belonging to Śambhu— who,

being both immanent in and transcendent of the universe, consists of the density of the manifestation of supreme bliss, and possesses the skill in joining and separating the manifold variety of the universe from Anāśrita down to Kālāgnirudra.

The power (*śakti*) of the venerable Paramaśiva, characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), is great; it is capable and manifests as the ultimate universal impeller (*sāmānyaprayojaka*) in the mutual relationship of the impelled and the impeller among the categories (*tattva*s), beginning with earth (*pṛthivī*).

The meaning is that even though the venerable Lord Śiva is not dependent upon the category of objective existence (*bhāvavarga*), He embraces it and expands, manifesting as its very form. As it is said in the *Paryantapañcāśikā*:
"By virtue of His nature as consciousness, this Lord, the Sovereign, reflects upon Himself through His own self..."
"One attains the stages beginning with Anāśrita and ending with Bhūmi.

This [stage] consists of the intensity (*saṃrambha*) of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); the meaning is that it is characterized by that intensity called "reflective awareness," which takes the form of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) vibrating within oneself. That...

It is designated as having the nature of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the five powers (*śakti*) whose forms are consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*). Consequently, this entire manifestation of the succession of principles (*tattva-paramparā*) has as its ultimate reality the proficiency in the unfolding process of the Supreme Lord’s self-reflection (*parameśvara-parāmarśa*).
The essential meaning is that the manifold variety of the universe’s manifestation is radiant with abundance.

As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-hṛdaya*: "Consciousness is autonomous, the cause of the establishment of the universe. This very [consciousness] is the Great One, who has assimilated the entire collection of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) into its own self.
The subject known as the venerable Paramaśiva is accepted as being thirty-seven-fold.

Even that nature of his ultimately enters the sphere of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Since one must exist as the non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), which transcends the universe, here too the non-conceptual state is the thirty-eighth.

Someone is accepted in the scriptures. As it is said in the *Śrītantravaṭadhānikā*: "The supreme Śiva, who is non-different from that [reality] consisting of the thirty-six principles, may also become an object of instruction by virtue of undergoing limitation."
"The thirty-eighth is the supreme abode, wherein this entire universe shines forth. Furthermore,

Śambhu here is of the nature of the Absolute (anuttara), and his power is likewise of such a nature— its essence being non-different from him, consisting of the natural outpouring (svarasamudāya), and known by the synonym *visarga*.

The explanation follows the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇakrama*). That [explanation] consists of the instability of *icchā* (will) and *īśana* (sovereignty), occurring respectively through the non-emergence (*anonmeṣa*) and emergence (*unmeṣa*) of the supreme bliss (*anuttarānanda*).

Furthermore, through fourfold divisions— consisting of the two [states] ascended by the union with both the Unsurpassed (Anuttara) and Bliss (Ānanda), along with the two [states] of the unfolding of Will (Icchā) and the opening of Gaze (Unmeṣa), which are not subordinate to Īśana— and the two [states] conjoined with those [latter two],
there is the nature of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the entire category of objects of knowledge previously mentioned.
Becoming manifest through the *bindu*, it rests right there within the unsurpassed reality (*anuttara-tattva*).

Consequently, through the process of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), together with the two letters *a* and *u* of the unsurpassed (*anuttara*) and the venerable *bindu* recited at the end of that sequence, there arises a certain "I" characterized by immersion into all consciousness.

A reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) arises, which is taught in the *Śiva Sūtras* as "the experience of the potency of mantra through the contemplation of the Great Lake" and as "the awakening of the wheel of the Mātṛkās. As it is said in the *Śrīkaṇṭhīya Saṃhitā*:
Mantras devoid of both beginning and end are like autumn clouds;
such is the characteristic of a Guru—that he should reveal the beginning and the end.

And as it has been stated by our own teachers in the *Śrīsaṃvitstotra*: "O Mother, you are that Guru who consists of that very [reality]—the self-evident manifestation 'I' whose nature is the collection of phonemes grasped from beginning to end; you are established by those who have mastered the scriptures as the 'potency of mantra' (*mantravīrya*)."

Indeed, the dharma associated with the Hero (vīra) is called "valor" (vīrya). In this context, the one named "Hero" is the Blessed Lord, the venerable Śabdarāśi-Bhaṭṭāraka, because he impels (īrayati) the manifold variety of the universe in various ways (vividham). As it is stated in the *Śrī-Cidgaganacandrikā*:
"This group of syllables, which attains heroism through various movements," as it is said;
and in the *Śrīprabhākula*: "The heroes are declared to be on the left."
And this,
O illustrious one, is declared in all tantras at all times to be the source of all mantras and vidyās.
Thus has it been elucidated in the illustrious Triṃśikāśāstra. || 26 ||

"Now, it is well known in the scriptures that there are six paths (adhvan). Among those, [the path of time] consists of a certain portion whose nature is the collection of principles (tattva). However, how can the stated meaning be logically established in other cases?"—anticipating this inquiry, he states the intended meaning of the present verse:

Of the six paths, one half therein is characterized by the object of illumination (prakāśa), and the other half has the nature of the word of reflective awareness (vimarśa); this is the unfolding of Śiva’s union (yāmala). || 27 ||

For it is well known in the scriptures that there are six paths (*adhvan*); and these are designated as phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), mantras, aspects (*kalā*), principles (*tattva*), and worlds (*bhuvana*). Among these, the phonemes are the fifty [letters] well known in the world. As for the words, although they are infinite—

According to the sequence of mantras beginning with *vyomavyāpin*, there are eighty-one mantras. Similarly, although they are infinite, from the perspective of contraction (*saṃkoca*), there are eleven: the five Brahmans and the six limbs (*aṅga*).
There are five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti. There are thirty-six principles (*tattva*) of the aforementioned nature. And as for the worlds (*bhuvana*):
From Kālāgnirudra up to Anāśrita, there are two hundred and twenty-four [deities].
All of this is encompassed by the five *kalās*. To explain: in the *kalā* of Nivṛtti, there is one phoneme, the letter *kṣa*; twenty-eight words; and the two mantras, Hṛdaya and Sadyojāta.

The earth principle is one. There are one hundred and eight worlds, beginning with Kālāgnirudra and ending with Bhadrakālī. In the level of *Pratiṣṭhā*, there are twenty-three phonemes from *ha* to *ṣṭa*.
There are twenty-one words. The two mantras are Śiras and Vāmadeva. [These extend] from the water principle up to *prakṛti*.

There are twenty-three principles (*tattvas*). There are fifty-six worlds (*bhuvanas*), beginning with Amareśa and ending with Śrīkaṇṭha. In the *vidyā-tattva*, there are seven phonemes from *ā* to *gha*. There are twenty words.
There are two mantras, namely the *śikhā* and the *ghora*. There are seven [principles] beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*.
The principles (*tattva*) are [the following]; the worlds (*bhuvana*) are twenty-seven, beginning with Bhīma and ending with Aṅguṣṭhamātra.

In the *Śānti* [kalā], however, there are three phonemes (*varṇa*), namely *ga*, *kha*, and *ka*; eleven words (*pada*); and the two mantras are Kavaca and Tatpuruṣa. The principles are three: Śuddhavidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.

There are eighteen worlds, beginning with Vāmā and ending with Sadāśiva. In the Śāntyatītā [Kalā], there are sixteen vowels as phonemes (*varṇas*), one word (*pada*), and three mantras: "Śiva," "Īśāna," and "Netra" (the Weapon). Śiva is the single principle (*tattva*) which is traditionally taught to have the nature of Śakti.

The distinction is that there are fifteen worlds, beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with Anāśrita. This has been established in great detail in the Siddhānta and other Tantras, and is therefore stated here in brief. Such being the case, regarding this group of six paths (adhvan) in their aforementioned forms, that which constitutes one half—

[The first] has the nature of the worlds (*bhuvana*), the principles (*tattva*), and the limited powers (*kalā*); the other, however, consists of the words and phonemes of mantra. Each of these is threefold according to the gross, subtle, and supreme methods. Therein, the distinction is that the first is the object denoted (*abhidheya*) and the second is the instrument of denotation (*abhidhāna*).

And this being so, the entire range of the denotable (vācya) has as its ultimate reality light (prakāśa), whereas the manifestation of the denoter (vācaka) consists of reflective awareness (vimarśa); thus, the "yāmala" (couple) of Śiva,
the Supreme Lord whose nature is light and reflective awareness, [is established].

The "outburst" (ullāsa) has the nature of being the friction-stick for the emission of both; the meaning is the wonder of experiencing the simultaneity of the two powers of expansion and contraction. As it says in the *Paryantapañcāśikā*:
"In that regard, for the Lord, who consists of both the signifier and the signified,
there is a sixfold nature of the paths (*adhvan*) within the sequences of gross, subtle, and supreme manifestation, occurring one by one.
And as it is said in the *Śrī Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:
"The atom of that reflective awareness (vimarśa) is threefold sound, consisting of words, mantras, and phonemes;
its object consists of the worlds, the principles (tattvas), and the limited powers (kalās)—thus [is the nature] of the subject, which is light.
And in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:

I take refuge in those two auspicious Śivas, the progenitors of the six paths, who are mutually united and intent upon one another: the Supreme Designation, whose speech has arisen as "I am," and the Light, whose manifested form is the objective world.
Thus it is said.
With this very intention, our supreme gurus have stated in the *Śrīsaubhāgyahṛdayastotra*:
"The phoneme, the digit, the word, the principle, the mantra, and even the world..."
Thus, O Goddess, the sixfold path shines within you, the conscious self.

Thus, the summary of these paths has been revealed through their respective union (*yāmala*). By this, the statements of great poets such as "word and meaning are joined together like [the body and soul]" are explained.
Therefore, we also maintain our commitment to *sāhitya*, which consists in the aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) of word and meaning.
It is indeed the supreme Lord’s grace that these compositions— animated by His very breath,
such as the *Kuṇḍalābharaṇa*, the *Mukundakeli*, the *Parimala*, the *Guhā*, the *Komalavallī*, the *Stavana*, and the *Nakhapralāpa*— are made known to the world.

This is because it has been established in the *Pratyabhijñā* that their nature consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and light (*prakāśa*), according to the principles: "Consciousness (*cit*) is the essence of reflective awareness, the supreme speech (*parā vāk*) arising from its own inherent savor," and "The light of the object belongs to the Self.
And thus, in the ancient verse concerning Śambhu, whose essential nature is light...

It has also been explained that power (*śakti*) consists of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Because phonemes, *kalās*, and so forth serve as the means for this self-reflection, they are designated by the term "path" (*adhvan*). As it is said in the *Śrī-Svacchanda*:
"Indeed, the entire universe is the cause for the manifestation of the state of Śiva in those who are liberated."
Because they constitute the path to the manifestation of Śiva-nature, all of them, beginning with Kalā, [are so designated].
"All those bonds as well are described by the word 'path' (adhvan).
And in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:
"One should contemplate everything in its entirety, sequentially, in the form of the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and so forth."
"Through the persistence of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, until finally there is the dissolution of the mind. (27)

Having established, according to the principle thus stated, that all the manifold variety of the universe is included within the dyad of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), he states that even the distinction between these two is ultimately merely figurative:
Just as in a particular painting there is the appearance of both an elephant and a bull, we conceive of the division between Śiva and Śakti within that very same single reality. (28)

For just as painters, in order to manifest their own skill, bring about the appearance of one thing and the manifestation of another through the application of a particular arrangement— even for objects such as elephants or bulls that possess distinct natures— so too [does it occur here].
"They delineate"— this is an infallible rule. This being the case,

just as in a particular painting that imparts the forms of both an elephant and a bull, there occurs a distinction due to the ascent of the stream of synthesis by the observing cognizing subjects regarding both the elephant and the bull.

Just as a specific manifestation or illumination occurs through the conjunction of the jar, the mandala, the trunk, the coiling, and so forth, and through the sequence of the hump, the peak, the snout, the cavity,
and the excellence [of form], in the same way, for all paths (adhvan) within a single object—

When the reality to be attained is reached in its ultimate limit, there is Śiva and Śakti; that is to say, whatever division there may be— such as Light (*prakāśa*) and Reflection (*vimarśa*)— which, though not transcending the nature of manifoldness, appears as if it has transcended it, the conceptualization of that [division] is inherently incapable of being so [independently].

The manifestation [of that power] occurs through the performance of actions capable of bringing it about; we perform it, we know it, we speak of it, and we practice it. As they say: "Power is the essence of a thing, whose distinctions are superimposed by the difference in its effects. And here, in the compound *gajavṛṣabhayoḥ*, there are two elephants (*gajau*) and...

The compound *vṛṣabhau* is analyzed according to the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*). The author of the Bhāṣya has likewise analyzed it as "the two dhava trees and the two khadira trees. Consequently, it follows that the word *gaja* denotes both the elephant and the bull, and similarly, the word *vṛṣabha* denotes both the bull and the elephant.
But that [freedom] does not shine for others, because they fear the transgression [of sin] that would arise from abandoning the fixed nature of things; whereas for us,
who possess the sovereignty of the tradition of independent non-dual consciousness, it is quite different.
"Pot," "earth," "substance"—in this way, my dear, it exists;
indeed, manifestation is existence, provided there is no obstruction.
If reasoning shines forth, then this pot stands before you.
Tell me, how is it that the one whose form is the universe does not shine forth?
Thus, by this principle, it is accepted that even a single entity consists of the nature of all entities other than itself; therefore, enough with this attempt to point out the faults of others.

By this, it has been stated that the theory of the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) possesses greater appropriateness than the theory of the expression of the already-stated (abhihitānvaya).

It occurs as follows: for in such cases as "Look at the pillar" (*stambhaṃ paśya*), the act of seeing, already associated with the meaning of the word "pillar," is expressed by the verbal root; likewise, the pillar, associated with the meaning of the root "to see," is [expressed] by the object-case (*karmakāraka*).
Thus, the connection [of meanings] accords with the sense established immediately prior.
Thus it is established. And in this way, even for the two primary principles of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflection (*vimarśa*):
"Heaven is *bhūḥ*, the ocean is a river, O Lord! A tree is a creeper, meaning is sound, resonance is hearing, and [the world] is both internal and external."
O Three-eyed One! [The pairs] such as white and red, light and darkness, knowledge and action—all these are the expansion of the two: Vidyā and Vimṛṣṭi.

According to this principle, although there is necessarily a dual designation— both as the ultimate locus for the manifestation of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and as the unfolding of various *yāmala* (coupled) states— nevertheless, therein:
"There is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti."

According to this principle, light (*prakāśa*) never deviates from the activity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), nor does reflective awareness ever deviate from being the agent of light; thus, the essential nature of these two is a sublime beauty consisting of their identity—this is the intended meaning. As I have stated myself:
In the *Śrīkomalavallīstava*:
"Just as you are composed of Śiva, so too is Śiva composed of you; for there is no difference between the two, Śiva and Śivā."
"The single reality, which is not the locus of outward-turning [consciousness], wherein the transformations of the universe appear as if divided. (28)
Surely there are many cognizing subjects well-known from the Purāṇas, Āgamas, and other sources,
and even more are currently perceived through direct observation; yet among them, not even one possesses such power as that which is proclaimed in what is accepted by the Supreme Lord.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Behold, even in a body the size of a sesame seed, such is the power of a worm; how much greater, then, must be that of the one whose glory is absolute freedom and whose body is the universe! (29)
For the Supreme Lord is declared in the Āgamas to have the universe as his body;
as it is said in the venerable *Śivasūtras*: "The visible world is the body. And likewise in the venerable *Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*:

"O limb of doubt! This entire body of mine, whose nature is consciousness, is established as a solid mass (piṇḍa) because it is perceived as extending from the void down to the blue [object], like a physical object.
And that is so because it is "governed by its own will" (svacchanda); that is, by its own inherent will, which is the power of desire (icchā-śakti).

"Śrī" is so called because he possesses sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) according to his desire. Furthermore, by virtue of having the universe as his body, a certain power (*śakti*) that transcends all else is attributed to him. That a being possesses a power corresponding to the dimensions of its own body is observed elsewhere as well; for example, a louse or similar creature has a body the size of a sesame seed.

A particular kind of insect is characterized by its power through the suitability of its body or through its abundance. As for the construction of the text: let alone the arrangements of atoms, dyads, and so forth, as well as specific living beings; because these are imperceptible, the illustrative example would fail to strike the heart [of the listener].

By way of an incidental remark: as for that insect such as a louse (*yūkā*) and so forth, its body is indeed of a size similar to a sesame seed; yet observe how great its power is even within that [tiny] space! For it is experienced as having many forms through various activities such as quivering and wandering about. This is indicated by the suffix *loṭ*.
And the plural number is used there to clearly manifest the authority of that meaning. (Regarding "therefore"?)—if this illustration is accepted:
"In this abode of yours, which is worshipped by the universe, while the play of destiny proceeds..."
O Lord! How vast must be the flood of the essence of bliss belonging to you!

Thus, according to the established tradition of the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*, how could that power of His be measured— whether it be so great or of such a kind? In this way, having established through inference the Lord’s nature as the body of the universe for the sake of those who hold contrary views, then this...

The excellence of His sovereignty has been established; however, in the case of full realization, on the contrary, by that very power, He possesses the state of having the universe as His body. As it is said in the *Śrī Śivasūtras*: "Upon the conjunction with Power, the arising of the body occurs," and "The universe is the accumulation of one's own powers."

And thus, this state of the Self having the universe as its body is a state of insensibility regarding the festival of experiencing the outward vibration of manifestations, caused solely by a lack of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). Otherwise, one's own power of freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) would be directly perceived everywhere, even within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), just as it is within the physical body (*piṇḍa*).
As it is said in the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*:

"Just as there is a mutual clashing of the arms of two inert beings in the body due to the sense of 'I' (asmitā), so too, by the mere power of will, such a thing occurs even between two mountains in this world. (29)

Now, one might object: "If the manifestation of the Supreme Lord's power is conceived on the basis of his having the universe as his body, then at the time of the dissolution of the universe, it would follow that he is devoid of power. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the state of the unfolding of the universe, however great is the expansion of the Lord of Teachers..."
Even while remaining in the state of the *kalala*, he becomes as vast as the entire universe in the blink of an eye. || 30 ||

In the Supreme Lord—who, as the Teacher and the benefactor of all, is prayed to—there exists a certain power characterized by the simultaneity of manifestation (*unmeṣa*). In that regard, there is a twofold process: the withdrawal (*nimeṣa*) of the universe occurs upon the manifestation of His own nature, and the withdrawal of His own nature occurs upon the manifestation of the universe. Both of these [occur simultaneously].

It arises like that which is held on a scale; and thus, the appropriateness of the symbolic designation *avaṭāṭaṅka*—meaning the Supreme Lord is both the soul of the universe and transcendent of the universe—is established. Since these two are eternally mutually dependent, when there is a doubt regarding the exclusion of one, [the other...]
Since there is the consequence of [the doctrine's] collapse, it is appropriate to accept both [the internal and external processes] as being of equal importance.
As I have stated myself in the *Śrīparāstotra*: "Some [hold that] the external process is composed of the elements of earth, water, ether, air, and fire..."
Some whispered within themselves that liberation possesses a luster like that of a few tiny grains of gold;
others, enjoying the confluence of the two rivers of nectar, declared, "O Mother, you are the inseparable sprout of both, for their union is most fitting. Thus it is said.

And this being so, just as there is an expansion within the state characterized by the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the universe— which is synonymous with the closing of the eye (*nimeṣa*) of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*)— and which consists in the manifestation of the sixfold categories (*ṣaḍadhva*),
even so, when the universe closes its eyes, although there remains only the singular inclusion of all things within one's own self;
He remains in a state whose very nature is identical to the stage of non-manifestation (*anunmeṣa*).
If it is asked, "In that case, is there not the closing of the eyes of the universe (*viśvanimeṣa*)?"—it is indeed a closing of the eyes at will;
however, we say it is a state of existence in the form of the *kalala* (the embryonic stage). It is just as [the potential for manifestation exists] within the egg of a peacock.

Just as it is accepted that the entire skill of artistic conception— consisting of the variety of colored lines and patterns such as the plumage entering into every part of a peacock— is perceived through extremely subtle observation, so too is it here. As it is said in the venerable *Triṃśikāśāstra*:
"Just as the great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of the banyan tree, so too does this entire world of moving and non-moving beings exist within the seed of the heart.
Thus, the state called the *kalala* is the undifferentiated form containing all aspects. And if that...

The manifold variety of the universe would not exist even during the state of the embryo (kalala) at the moment of closing (nimeṣa); if that were so, the state of opening (unmeṣa) itself could not occur, because it is only that which already exists [prior to manifestation] that is fit for arising. For indeed, in the state of the unfolding of the universe, there is merely the concealment of the nature of the Self; it is not...

Furthermore, there is an extreme confusion; the same applies elsewhere as well. By avoiding the consideration of this very point, the Pāśupata version of Vedānta is excluded. For in that system, even though non-duality (*advaita*) is being established with insistence, it merely ascends to the level of duality (*dvaita*).

In this regard, when there is the conceptualization of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted based on the distinction between the real and the unreal, it is unavoidable that, by that very same mode, one arrives at the limit of duality. As I have stated myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"Others describe non-duality as being merely a false construction other than duality."
Thus, alas, it culminates in duality; enough with this boastful, false knowledge!
We declare that non-duality (*advaita*) of these two—which are thus equally prosperous, and whose singular flavor is free from all indolence—to belong to some [person] or other. Thus [it is said].
"What indeed is the pride of non-duality of the great knower that would be false within this phenomenal world?
And what is the 'unaided heroism' of one desiring victory over the host of adversaries in their own self-choice marriage? Thus it is said.
Now, one might object: "Is not expansion itself contraction, and contraction itself expansion, for both the universe and that which transcends the universe? This is a great contradiction.
Anticipating this, he says: "Indeed, everything consists of the threefold structure (tripuṭī), and in that regard, it is the same with respect to both the object of knowledge and the knower."
The digit of knowledge, though possessing a firm knot, makes the three worlds appear as one.

In all worldly discourse, the entire elaborate proliferation of verbal communication among disputants culminates in the reality of the object, which consists of the synthesis of the threefold sheaths of the knower, the knowledge, and the known. This is what the followers of the Guru’s doctrine [the Pratyabhijñā] maintain, on account of its clarity and excellence, as being mutually indistinguishable from one another.

They describe [these] as being entirely perceptible. And their state of being "folds" (*puṭatva*) is due to their capacity to encompass the entirety of the universe. And therein, within the threefold fold (*tripuṭī*), that digit of knowledge which is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) existing in the interval—indeed, that is...
All this is the object of knowledge, and that Lord is the knower, according to their respective specific characteristics;
O fair-faced one, who indeed, other than you, is capable of bringing them together without the instrument of consciousness?
Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrīkomalavallīstava*, [the Guru] acts toward the group of objects— which are subsumed as the "object of experience" (*viṣayatayā*)—

and toward the knower who shines forth as the "experiencer" (*bhoktṛtayā*), in such a way that they are both equally and entirely free from the suspicion of distinction; this is achieved through a firm knot [of realization] that penetrates both poles.

Through their essential identity (*tādātmya*), they become connected by an unshakable bond like adamantine glue (*vajralepa*); thus, they perceive the three worlds as one and of a single nature. And that nature consists of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the act of knowing (*vitti*), and the knower (*veditṛ*), [manifesting] as gross, subtle, and supreme, or as waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth.

It is also established by way of its threefold nature, because it is described as having "firm knots. For, if there were a doubt regarding the lack of firmness in the relationship [of the parts], then one part would be distinct from the other; and that is not possible. By the term "the three worlds" (trailokya)—
The triad of gods, the triple Veda, the three sacrificial fires, the three powers, the three vowels,
the three worlds, the three steps, the three Puṣkaras, the three Vedas, the three castes—
whatever object exists in the world that is regulated in a threefold manner and consists of the three aims of life; [all these are established in the three lines of this verse].
All that truly follows from your name, O Blessed One, as "Tripurā."
Thus, according to the system of the venerable Laghubhaṭṭāraka, everything that constitutes the three aims of human life (trivarga) is embraced.

And so, in the final analysis, there is the acceptance of the essential identity (sāmarasya) of all natures, such that the knower is indeed the knowable, the knowable is indeed the knower, and consciousness itself is the knowable, and so forth.

Because this is the secret of our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), no one at all attempts to sprout even a single thorn upon the boundaries of the path of our movement by raising objections such as "expansion (*unmeṣa*) is itself contraction (*nimeṣa*)," and so forth.
