As it has been said in the *Śrīspandasandoha*:

Thus, this single ground of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which is undivided in nature and consists of both expansion (*unmeṣa*) and contraction (*nimeṣa*), is designated by the two terms "expansion" and "contraction. By this, it is stated that reflective awareness is all-enduring.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā-vimarśinī*: "Reflective awareness..."
For indeed, the All-enduring One (Sarvasaha) encompasses even himself, makes the other his own, unifies both, and subordinates both. And in the *Śrīparāmate*:
"To encompass one's own reality, to make both one's own..."
"Is there any deliberation capable in this world of making two things one? (31)

Now, raising the objection— "If one accepts the doctrine that all things have a single essence (sarvaikarasavāda), what is this distinction between the real and the unreal?"— the author demonstrates by way of an illustration that there is none at all:
"What specific quality of existence does a sky-flower possess that a [real] flower lacks?"
The world has its life-breath in vibration, and vibration is common to all things. || 32 ||
"What is the difference between a well-known flower and a sky-flower in terms of their existence? None at all"—this is the conclusion of the statement. The word "since" (*yad*) indicates the reason;
for the world is by nature characterized by worldly transactional activity (*vyavahāra*). It is consciousness alone (*saṃvid*)—the venerable lady—that establishes the existence of objects.

We have stated more than once that, according to the tradition of the Guru, one proceeds by embracing as the very life-force— that is, as the animating principle— the manifestation itself, which is the state of being luminous, under the designation of "refuge" (śaraṇa). And that manifestation [exists] even in a sky-flower, which is the subject of disagreement, just as it does in that which is agreed upon.

Furthermore, the universal (sāmānya) manifests without partiality toward the *campaka* and other such flowers. If its manifestation were to proceed with partiality toward them, then even the "sky-flower" (*khapuṣpa*) would not appear [as a conceptual object].
For this very reason, it was stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda in the passage: "That radiance (*sphurattā*) is Great Being (*mahāsattā*)."
Regarding the explanation of this term *mahāsattā*: "For it pervades even such things as a sky-flower. As stated in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
"There may be grammatical coordination (*samanvaya*) even with such things as a hare's horn, by means of case-inflection (*vibhakti*)."

And in the *Padasaṅgati*: "Therefore, even in that case, when there is the status of a grammatical factor (*kāraka*) through connection with a case-ending, existence itself is what is called 'the state of Śiva'. By this it is shown that for entities such as pillars and jars, it is light alone that functions as the animating life-force whose nature is the universal (*sāmānya*); it is not, however, a so-called "universal" [that exists independently].

It is stated that [the universal] is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*). In this regard, individual manifestations (*vyakti*) consist of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whereas the Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), whose nature is non-conceptual, is the universal (*sāmānya*). Consequently, the Vaiśeṣikas and others, who assert that the universal is the cause of the cognition of recurrence (*anuvṛttipratyaya*), are refuted.
Because light is causeless, and on the contrary, because it alone is the cause of the manifestation of the universe,
it is the universal of all. Indeed, for such a universal, the entire universe itself [is the substrate], without distinction from inherence, particularity, and so forth.

The meaning is that the object (*viṣaya*) is not a category (*padārtha*) delimited by substance (*dravya*) and so forth. Furthermore, he must be asked: what is the distinction of a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*) from another flower? If you say it is "insubstantiality" (*tucchatva*), then what is this so-called insubstantiality? It cannot be emptiness (*śūnyatva*), for the sky and the flower are distinct [from one another].

If it is argued that because these two exist separately, and because there is no relationship of cause and effect between them, the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is likewise non-existent by way of that [relationship], we say:
no. For "mutuality" (*anyonyatva*) is not possible when considering each of these two individually. And if it were possible, it would be exactly as previously stated.

There is the persistence of this defect. Furthermore, if it is said that "it is a part of their conjunction," then there would be a contradiction with the phrase "because of the lack of connection," since conjunction has been admitted.
And is this conjunction perceived or not? Not the latter, because practical activity (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible.
Consequently, the position of common consensus alone remains;
and that consensus, by establishing the union of these two,
endeavors to render that [union] insubstantial, just as in the case of the process of flowers such as the *campaka* and *pāṭala*.

Since there is no difference in the status of conventional discourse even regarding a sky-flower, for that which is non-existent, the opponent has no recourse but silence, as the sprouting of conceptual manifestation is impossible therein. For this very reason, some yogis are seen bringing forth flowers even from space. It is not...

And it cannot be said that [the object] there is produced from its own material cause and then manifested by the yogis, because, apart from such a volition (*saṅkalpa*), it lacks any other material cause.
As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:

"For the Lord, who is indeed the very nature of consciousness, manifests the entire range of objects externally by the power of His will, even though they reside within Him, just as a yogi manifests a multitude of things without any material substrate.
Thus, in a conversation characterized by goodness, there is no one who [can claim otherwise] regarding existence, which is dependent upon the essential nature of consciousness.

The distinction of a sky-flower from other flowers lies in this: while other flowers are fit for the conventional usage of both affirmation and negation in accordance with their illusory existence (*māyīya-sattā*), a flower born in the atmosphere is fit only for expression as an object of negation. Enough of these words easily accessible to ordinary people.
By demonstrating the expertise [gained] from the shattering of the skull. 32.

Now, it may be argued that these [entities] such as sky-flowers and the like are non-existent, and in their case, whether one remains silent is neither a defect nor an ornament; however, regarding existence and non-existence, which are established through worldly convention, how can this cleverness of the doctrine of non-difference be maintained?
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The mutual fusion of their manifestations wipes away the appearance of difference between existence and non-existence, just as it does between a ruby and an emerald. (33)

For even the entire worldly transaction (*viśvavyavahāra*) consists of the manifestation of difference— the mutual apprehension of two things, such as a pillar and a jar, or a presence and its absence— as being related as counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and correlate (*anuyogin*),
and the determination of them through their mutual distinctness; it is the intermingling of their manifestation.

Thus he wipes away [the distinction] through reasoning, setting it aside; for manifestation (*prakāśamānatā*) is indeed vibration (*sphuraṇa*). That itself is the fusion (*saṃbheda*), the connection. And that is of a single essence (*ekarasa*), such that the two entities possess an identical nature, because there is no disparity in the cognition that both of them manifest. And therefore—

The meaning is: what indeed is the appearance of difference between these two once they have been reduced to the fire of consciousness? It is like the case of a ruby and an emerald—though red and dark respectively and mutually opposed—when they are placed in close proximity to one another.

Through the process of becoming variegated by the mass of mutual radiance, the undifferentiated nature of manifestation becomes of a single flavor, thereby wiping away the appearance of difference; for both [aspects] enter into a state of unity after first relinquishing their own respective natures. Since:

In this regard, there arises a perception characterized by such variety that even a ruby (māṇikya) appears reddish-black, and even an emerald (marataka) appears blackish-red. Furthermore, according to the perspective of other philosophical systems, that which is called "non-existence" (abhāva) is actually a particular kind of entity (bhāvaviśeṣa), such as the ground or the like, which possesses the absolute isolation (kaivalya) of pillars, jars, and so forth.
Thus it is accepted. As it has been said:
"Non-existence is another state of being; there is nothing else, because it cannot be defined [independently].
And for an entity such as a pillar, [non-existence] descends through the medium of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) with respect to a pot and so forth.
And since existence cannot be avoided, when one examines both existence and non-existence through logical analysis, they are found to possess an identical nature. || 33 ||
Now, one might object: "Even though this reality of the meaning has been established repeatedly, it merely flashes forth like a streak of lightning;
it does not, however, become heart-pleasing.
And since some means must be stated for it to become heart-pleasing," [the author] proceeds to dispel such a desire by means of the Supreme Goddess's...
One must practice with devotion, and demonstrating that this devotion is distinct from worldly norms, he first examines the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) and the deity:
"Within the egg-like body of one's own self, which is the sacred seat, the goddesses of the senses manifest."
And Paramaśiva, the treasury of knowledge, shines forth in their midst. || 34 ||

For the physical body (*piṇḍa*), consisting of one's own self, is determined to be the cosmic egg (*maṇḍa*)—characterized by the manifold variety of the entire universe—because it is composed of the five elements, earth and the rest.
The identity of form between the cosmic egg and the physical body is well-known in the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*). As it is said in the *Triśirobhairava*:
"The body consists of all reality; listen now to that, O beloved!
Earth is proclaimed by its solidity, and water by its fluidity," and so forth.
And as it is said in the *Paramārthasārasaṃgraha*:
"His own or another body, or even a jar and so forth, is his temple— a divine residence filled with windows of the manifold arrangement of the thirty-six principles of nectar.
And therein, upon that which has become the pedestal, the powers characterized as the senses— the goddesses of the instruments— manifest.

Even in the absence of [ritual acts] such as invocation (*āvāhana*), bringing near (*sannidhāpana*), and concealment (*tirodhāna*), they manifest clearly by themselves. And among them, Paramaśiva, whose nature is that of the Great Subject (*mahāpramātṛ*), shines forth;
and just as his status as the Possessor of Power (*śaktimat*) becomes manifest toward those powers (*śakti*), so too [does he shine].

It shines forth; for this treasury of knowledge is traditionally taught to be the ultimate ground of support for the streams of consciousness and conceptualizations—unfolding through the emergence of the powers of the various senses—just as the ocean is for the currents of rivers. And of those powers of the senses...

Sometimes there is a state of abiding without the interpenetration of sound, touch, and so forth; and since sound, touch, and the rest are themselves the five great elements, it is said that they consist of the entire universe.
As it has been stated:
"The two categories of reality are said to be power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*).
His powers are the entire universe, and the possessor of power is Maheśvara.
Thus, all powers—such as perception and the rest—are [perceived] by the mind simultaneously with respect to their respective objects of knowledge.
Having cast [all things] everywhere, he stands in the center as a pillar of gold; though one, he shines forth in the form of the universe.
Thus, according to the established principle of the *Śrīkakṣyāstotra*, the Supreme Lord himself, whose nature is one's own self (*svātmarūpa*), is the deity of the internal wheel;
the external and internal [deities] are distinct from him. The powers of the instruments (*karaṇaśakti*) occupy the position of the deities of his surrounding enclosures (*āvaraṇa*).
And their worship is appropriately performed within the Great Seat (*mahāpīṭha*) that is one's own body and self. And therein, as follows:
Just as objects such as images and books are determined to be substitutes for the primary deity who has become their own essence, so too is one's own body regarded as the primary [deity].

The meaning is that they constitute the *pīṭhas* (seats); however, the intention is that altars (*sthaṇḍila*), mandalas, and so forth are accepted as secondary (*anukalpa*) or tertiary (*upakalpa*) alternatives. || 34 ||

Now, in response to the inquiry as to by what kind of practice this extraordinary Supreme Lord is to be worshipped, he speaks with favor: "There, He is to be worshipped with [offerings] made fragrant by the perfuming of the flowers of reflective awareness (vimarśa)."
By means of the substances for the heroic drinking of the nectar of the knowable, offered into the goblet of the mind. || 35 ||

That Supreme Lord, whose nature is well-known from the Vedas, Agamas, and other sources, is to be worshipped there in the seat (pīṭha) which is the embodied self (piṇḍātman). And in that worship, the nectar consisting of the object of knowledge—
which, because it delights all the senses, is to be intensely appropriated— is, by its very nature, though one, [divided].

Due to the variety of states such as fear, sorrow, and joy, and because it is permeated by many specific flavors— predominantly sour, bitter, sweet, and so forth— this belongs to the Hero, the Supreme Bhairava, and to the Heroine,
who consists of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) and whose primary power is that [freedom]; and to the Heroes.

Because it is drunk— that is, assimilated into one's own self— the substances characterized by the wine of the universe’s play, namely the forms of the Mothers beginning with Tattvasiddhā and the Bhairava couples, which are concealed within the venerable Four Streams (catussrotas) for those who are learned; thus, [the text speaks] of their excellence.

It is employed as an integral part of the worship (*pūjā*). Therefore, the meaning is that those very *kula*-substances consisting of the nectar of the object of knowledge (*vedya-amṛta*) on the altar are the means for accomplishing the worship. And these are to be offered by some method of grasping into the cup which is one's own mind-self. Furthermore, the state of the mind being a cup is [established] here and there [in various scriptures].

Because it serves as the means for the ease of grasping the objects of knowledge— which spread forth in many currents— by the single effortless play of one’s own self as Bhairava; for all things existing in the universe,
manifesting externally in diverse forms, are apprehended by the movements of their respective sense organs.

The natures, having rested for a moment in the mind, subsequently enter into the self of Bhairava by way of that channel; thus, this path is exceedingly beautiful. As it has been said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"Objects reside in the functions; those [functions] reside in the mind; the mind resides in consciousness;
that [consciousness] resides in the Supreme; and it is in the Void where the sequence, characterized by succession, comes to an end.
Furthermore, there is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) regarding those very objects as being one's own self in relation to the Supreme Lord.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*); that alone is the "flower," because it nourishes one's own essential nature (*svabhāva*) and because it is the very form of the venerable Guru (*śrī-guru*). By means of that, which consists of the power of mantra (*mantra-śakti*), [the flowers] must be made fragrant; otherwise, as in the case of stale [flowers], there would be the undesirable consequence of a failure in the meaning of the scripture. This is what is meant:

First, having worshipped the body as the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), one should contemplate the Supreme Lord— characterized by the great light of one's own essential nature— within its center in the form of the space of the heart; then,
having visualized the powers of the senses radiating out from Him on all sides, thereafter...

Having filled one's own mind— which is characterized as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of all internal organs— with the substance for the *arghya* offering, which is characterized as the manifestation of the entire range of objects of knowledge, and having consecrated that [substance] by means of the power of mantra consisting of the supreme awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the Supreme Lord, by that very [power]...

This Supreme Lord, surrounded by the circle of the deities of His own enclosure (*nijāvaraṇadevatā*) through the nectar of the lineage (*kulāmṛta*), is to be worshipped. And He is traditionally taught in the Āgamas as being worthy of worship starting from the letter *A* up to the letter *Kṣa*, due to the connection with contraction and expansion. As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
He is the solitary hero, arisen from the *yāmala*, possessing three powers and fourfold nature;
he has five forms and six aspects, adorned with seven and eight [attributes].
The ninefold self, possessing the powers of the ten directions and consisting of eleven innate aspects,
Bhairava stands as the lord of the great twelve-spoked wheel.
"Thus, up to the thousand-spoked wheel or even the innumerable-spoked one,
the All-pervasive Lord, the Great Sovereign whose power is the universe, unfolds within the Universal Wheel.
It is with this very intent that the ritual manuals (paddhati) established by the four currents (srotas) have been composed.

The secret of worship culminates in this much alone: mere engagement (*pravṛtti*). As for the external elaboration (*prapañca*) consisting of flowers, unbroken rice grains, wine, incense, lamps, bells, and so forth, it is accepted by us according to the maxim that "it does not cause any further fault. This will be examined further below. || 35 ||
Now, since the secret of worship has been revealed, [the author] first presents the enumeration in order to disclose the secret of the wheel of deities to be worshipped in sequence:
"Meditate upon the Śrīpīṭha, the five mounts, the three eyes, and the wheels of the multitude."
And remember the lineage of the gurus and the five powers beginning with Sṛṣṭi (36).
Remember—that is, contemplate—the Śrīpīṭha, the Pañcavāha, the three eyes, and the Vṛndacakra; these are the wheels (cakras) which, by their preeminence, must be brought under control.
Reflect upon that [lineage], and remember the succession of the venerable Gurus.

It is said "remember once again" in order to highlight the preeminence of the circle of gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*). Furthermore, remember the five powers beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), which are emanation, maintenance (*sthiti*), and so forth.
They are distinguished as *saṃhāra*, *anākhyā*, and *bhāsā*. By the term "Śrīpīṭha," its greatness is illuminated through the excellence of its worshipability.

And this greatness is due to its being the primary seat (*pradhānapīṭha*), as it serves as the foundational ground for all things, even though Oḍyāṇa and the others are intermediate seats (*avāntarapīṭha*). This...
With only a few syllables, it is capable of producing manifold meanings like a seed-mantra;
it reveals the secrets of the sequence and order of the respective wheels (*cakras*);
and because it primarily summarizes the conceptual distinctions of all the deities to be described, it is characterized as a concise enumeration (*uddeśa*).
Verse: Just as this unartificial utterance of the Great Tradition (mahāmnāya) states—

that wheel which is the manifestation of the five flows worshipped in the circles of the seats (pīṭhacakras), the wheel whose form is the void of bliss (ānandakhāmūrti), and which shines forth as the eight-times-eight wheel, that is the flood of the lineage of Gurus for the sake of the fourfold aim.
Thus [ends the section]. || 36 ||
Now, intending to unveil the Śrīcakra in due order, he first contemplates it through its divisions, beginning from the abode of the Pīṭhas and ending with the three eyes:
"In the Pīṭha there are nine and five Kalās; in the path of the five currents..."
There are seventeen in the eye of the plowshare, and twelve and sixteen in the other two eyes. || 37 ||
For it has been stated that the *pīṭha* (seat) consists of one's own body as the Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*),

because therein the Supreme Lord flows in five ways. Upon reflection on this, there is the dyad of Śakti and Śiva, whose nature is inseparable from that of the Mother and Father, oriented toward the union of mutual bliss.
Because it is certain that this [reality] is the state of being commenced by the flashing forth of the virility of the male and female powers of Śiva and Śakti,
it is determined that the expansion of the succession of waves consisting of the many circles of deities who will arise hereafter is appropriate only in this very place.
As it has been said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:

"The great virility arises from the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) resulting from the simultaneous unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of both Śiva and Śakti; from that, the body itself emerges as the Great Seat (*mahāpīṭha*).
Thus, in order to establish the primacy of the contemplation of the seat (*pīṭha*), [the author] first...
The necessity of employing female messengers (*dūtī*) is proclaimed as follows in the *Śrīkramodaya*:
"Women of all castes are undoubtedly *yoginīs*. Just like the body, the womb is purified; and just like the self, the *liṅga* is cleansed."
Having placed the nine-syllable mantra on the vulva and the seventeen-syllable mantra on the linga,
one should perform the union with the Yoginī for the purpose of worshipping the circle of the Guru.
One should establish [the deity] with the nine-syllable mantra, like a liṅga upon its pedestal;
the Puruṣa is known as the churner by virtue of being the essence of Śiva and Śakti.
"One should churn one's own power (śakti), like honey, from the blood of the bride-price.

And as it says in the Upaniṣad: "Just so, for one who knows this, when he approaches his consort, his Agnihotra sacrifice becomes truly offered. In that context, there are nine powers (kalās) which are the powers (śaktis) of the Supreme Lord.

It is said that [the universe] consists of *kalā* because everything, through the exclusion of distinctions such as female and male, is composed of power (*śakti*). When these are examined, they are first of all a certain primordial vibration (*spanda*) consisting of the aspect of the subject.
Following that, there is a certain power whose nature is the tendency toward the upward expansion of that very [vibration]. Then, of that...

There is a certain vibration consisting of the senses, whose nature is the manifestation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). From that arises the luminosity of that [vibration], which consists in the establishment of the object; subsequently follows the emergence of the object of cognition (*prameya*). And when the category of the object of cognition is examined with subtle scrutiny, it is found to be...

One experiences precisely the inclusion [of all things] within the five elements (*bhūtapañcaka*). Here, the elements—space, earth, air, fire, and water—are worshipped in this sequence. Furthermore, at the very beginning, there is the reflective awareness of one's own self as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), followed by the production of stability therein.

The sequence intended here is as follows: first, the persistence of the vibration (*spanda*) in the form of that [consciousness’s] exertion; then, the intensification of that very [vibration]; and finally, the state of being nourished, characterized by resting within oneself (*svaviśrānti*). In this way, the meaning becomes that the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the fivefold object of knowledge (*prameya*) constitute the abode of the sacred seat (*pīṭhaniketana*).

Others, however, worship this [deity] in five ways, based on the distinctions of the seats (pīṭha), cremation grounds (śmaśāna), fields (kṣetra), lords (īśa), and assemblies (melāpa). Even though it consists of nine aspects,
it possesses the nature of the pentad of ether and the other elements as apprehended by the subjects and the means of knowledge.

Nothing whatsoever transcends the identity with the wheel of the five vehicles (*pañcavāhacakra*). That is to say: there is the subject (*pramātṛ*), his power which is the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as his instrument, the manifestation (*vijṛmbhā*) of that [power] consisting in the determination of objects, and that which is embraced by it.
By this formulation as well—"the fivefold class of objects of knowledge"—it is precisely the fivefold nature that is made known. And thus:
"From the two feet up to the neck, from the neck up to the region of the heart, and up to the limit of the navel."
That body which is a hexagon is the seat of consciousness (saṃvitpīṭha), equal to the triangle.

Thus, by this principle, the worship of one's own body as the *pīṭha* (seat) must first be performed; it is thereby stated that the ritual service (*upacāra*) of those [deities] to be mentioned hereafter is to be performed subsequently. And in this context, the mention of the names of deities such as Gaṇapati and Vaṭuka is for the purpose of...
Since providing etymological explanations (nirvacana) according to each specific meaning would result in excessive bulk for the work and even reveal faults by unveiling what is extremely secret,
we proceed by way of a concise path alone. As it is stated in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"Out of fear of distorting the meaning, I shall clearly explain this very triad beginning with *dhāma* slightly, using words of impartial intent. Thus it is said;
as for example, in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*:
"Names should be hidden just as wealth is hidden from thieves;
for by being hidden, the forms indeed protect one through their great significance.
For the discerning, however, *gaṇa* refers to that which is counted or enumerated—the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), which is the manifestation of the nature of enjoyment.

"He protects that," thus "Gaṇapati"—by such an etymological method (*nirukti*), this way of explaining is extremely easy to accomplish. For they themselves have said: "One should provide an etymology even based on a commonality of letters or phonemes; one must never fail to provide an etymology. "In the path of the five carriers" means *pañca-vāha-pada-vyām*. The word *vāhāḥ* refers to the carriers.

The streams of the Supreme Lord’s manifestation are five, because they are perceived as neither more nor less than that number. And the path consisting of those [streams], which is the activity serving as the locus for the coming and going of the universe—those very [streams] are the five *kalās*; such is the grammatical connection.

By the word *eva* (only/just), the etymological significance (*anvarthatā*) of the term "five vehicles" (*pañcavāha*) is expressed. And those vehicles are Vyomavāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Dikcarī, Gocarī, and Bhūcarī. Others, however, state their sequence as [the order of] cow, direction, and earth, or as earth, direction, and cow. Among these:
Its etymological derivation should be inferred in accordance with that specific tradition; however, our own sequence is precisely as it has been indicated.
As stated in the *Śrīkramasiddhi*:
"The one known as Vyomavāmeśvarī, the plane of Nāda, and Khecarī."
The stages of mantra known as Ānanda, Dikcarī, and Gocarī.
"Because the mantras are of the nature of substances, the *āvali* is likewise the *bhūcarī*.
Thus it has been said by me also in the *Śrīkomalavallīstava*:
"What is on the surface of the earth, and what is in the lineage of cows?"
"Are you in the directions, or in the sky? Are you even above that, or are you everywhere?
Even though you are seen thus, why do you not endure [this]? Thus [it was said].
In that context,

the Goddess Vāmā is so called because she presides over the "vomiting" (vamanam) of all the pentads to be described hereafter, which are animated by the specific reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the nature of the *praṇava* consisting of the syllables *va*, *ya*, *ma*, *la*, and *ra*.

She who possesses such capacity is Vyomavāmeśvarī. She is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) of the Supreme Lord that has entered the ground of non-conceptuality. She is called Khecarī because she moves (*caraṇāt*) in the "void" (*khe*), which is the subject whose nature is pure awareness. She is called Dikcarī because she moves within the directions, that is, within the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). [She is called Gocarī] because she moves among the senses (*goṣu*)...

She is called *gocarī* because she moves among the external senses; she is called *bhūcarī* because she moves upon the earth, that is, within the sphere of objects. For the power of the Sovereign Lord’s consciousness, though by nature established in the state of non-conceptuality, while manifesting in some limited subject, subsequently...

Having first entered into that internal organ (*antahkarana*) and subsequently becoming connected to its external senses, it experiences the entire manifestation of objects characterized by external perceptibility;
such is this all-pervasive mode. These very [powers] are known as consciousness (*cit*), bliss (*ananda*), will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*).

The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are experienced as having the nature of speech, namely: *parā*, *sūkṣmā*, *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*. For the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is, first of all, the defining characteristic of the Supreme Lord’s sentience (*caitanya*), consisting of supreme sovereignty (*paramasvātantrya*), which is synonymous with being the sustainer of all things.

Vyomavāmeśvarī; Ānanda is Khecarī because its essential nature is the repose within the self of the limited subject; Icchā is Dikcarī because, being of the nature of acceptance, it is to be accomplished by the internal organ; and Jñāna...

The *gocarī* [power] is so called because it is manifested through the external senses, such as the eyes and others, which are directed outward. The *bhūcarī* [power], though an activity belonging to the supreme powers of the Lord, is perceived solely as the manifold variety of the external objects of knowledge due to its extreme grossness. In this same way, the pentad of speech beginning with *parā* is also to be understood.
"Reflection (vimarśa), the point (bindu) and the resonance (nāda), the burst (sphoṭa), sound (śabda), and the sequence of speech (vāk-krama)"—
according to the procedure of the arising of the venerable Pādukā, one should oneself infer that [the Goddess] consists of these five powers, in accordance with their respective arisings.
Furthermore, everything consisting of the fivefold process beginning with emanation and maintenance is included within this very [system].

These [five] have been written and recited in books by the venerable Kṣemarāja and others; therefore, we too have explained them with some effort, having first provided their names. Now, thus [it is] fivefold.

Indicating the mode of worship through the threefold division of subject, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge belonging to the Supreme Lord who carries [all things], he first describes the *mūrticakra* (the wheel of forms) with the words:
"having seventeen [eyes] on his forehead. "Forehead" (*phāla*) refers to the brow; the eyes located there are the seventeen powers (*śakti*).

And that is traditionally taught as the "circle of forms" (*mūrticakra*). It is called "form" (*mūrti*) because of its nature as a solidification (*mūrchanāt*), which consists of delusion (*moha*) or of upward elevation (*samucchrayaṇa*).
And because it conforms to the manifestation of the dyad of "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) internally and externally, therein, as for that "I-ness":

When there is the elevation (*samucchrāya*) of "this-ness" (*idantā*), then there arises the delusion (*moha*) consisting of the subordination of "I-ness" (*ahantā*); conversely, when there is the elevation of "I-ness," then there arises the delusion of "this-ness" in the form previously described.
Thus, both [states] have the same meaning. And in this way, for that which consists of the fire of the subject (*pramātṛ*),...

The supreme power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*)— consisting of the ascent from the form of supreme light up to the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava (*parabhairava-saṃvit*), and the descent down to the insentient consciousness of stones and the like— is denoted by the term "form" (*mūrti*). Within that [power], seventeen *kalās* (aspects) are said to exist.

It is well known in the traditional scriptures (*āmnāya*) that there is a group of ten digits (*kalā*) and a group of seven crests (*śikhā*) of fire, distinguished by their external and internal divisions. As they say:
"Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Viṣphuliṅginī..."
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā are the Kalās.

"Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā, and Atiraktā—these are the seven tongues of the consumer of oblations (Agni). Thus, by that same number, there are an equal number of powers (śaktis) in the wheel of forms (mūrticakra). And these:
Upon reflection, consciousness, predominance, self-conceit, agency, determination, speech, grasping, locomotion, excretion, the state of being a feeler of pleasure,
knowledge, volition, hearing, and touch [are found].
Seeing, tasting, and smelling are themselves modes of the manifestation of the subject (*pramātṛ*),
for which the internal and external organs serve as the means (*upāya*).
And these are the powers of form (*mūrti-śaktayaḥ*) belonging to the contracted [subject].
By adhering to the distinctions in the savoring of those objects by the cognizer, they produce the state of a bound soul (paśutva); yet,
by proceeding as the instigation for the unfolding of the power of absolute sovereignty in the unconstricted [subject], they manifest the auspiciousness characterized by the state of Supreme Śiva.
And now he speaks of the two wheels of Light and Bliss: "Twelve and sixteen in the other two eyes.
This means that in the other two eyes—namely, those of the right and left forms—there are twelve and sixteen powers respectively. Among them, the right eye...

The Wheel of Manifestation (*prakāśacakram*). By the etymological derivation that "that by which the multitude of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) is manifested is manifestation," the meaning of "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). In that regard, there are twelve powers (*śaktayaḥ*). Although [powers] such as Haṃsamati and the others are of the nature of subjects (*pramātṛ*) due to their status as teachers, they are [counted] with respect to the Great Subject (*mahāpramātṛ*).

By virtue of their status as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they possess the nature of power (*śakti*). And from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), these are respectively the organs of action (*karmendriya*)— consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*), speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—
and the organs of perception (*jñānendriya*)— consisting of the mind (*manas*) as the foremost, along with the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
And the organs of knowledge (jñānendriyāṇi) also exist. Because the ego (ahaṅkāra) is woven through everything, it is not counted separately.

And thus, the Lord Mārtāṇḍa, who is the nature of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), shines forth in twelve ways; such is the Upaniṣad. Furthermore, the left eye is the wheel of bliss (ānandacakra). Bliss is indeed—

The manifestation of the entire range of objects of knowledge (*prameya-varga-ullāsa*), which is by nature a complete abundance (*samṛddhi-svabhāva*) of the Supreme Lord who is one's own self as He flashes forth through the mode of "this-ness" (*idantā*), is the gentle aspect (*saumya-aṃśa*). Within that, there are sixteen *kalās*.
In reality, however, these sixteen are of the nature of the sixteen transformations (*vikāra*); and the transformation is the mind (*manas*).

The five organs of action, the five organs of knowledge, and the five elements beginning with space—in these, the entire play of the objects of cognition, such as sound, touch, and so forth, is included. The gross state of sound and the other qualities constitutes the great elements (mahābhūtas). And by the mind...
It is the embracing of both intellect (*buddhi*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*). As the authors of the Purāṇas say:
"The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; attached to sense objects, the mind leads to bondage; free from sense objects, the mind leads to liberation."

In this manner, other [points] should also be inferred. Furthermore, these—the wheels of Form (mūrti), Manifestation (prakāśa), and Bliss (ānanda)—consist precisely of the pentad of powers beginning with Vāmeśvarī. Among them, the wheel of Form, which is the nature of the fire of the subject (pramātṛ-vahni), resides at the very summit of all.
Taking as the primary cause Vyomavāmeśvarī—who vibrates through commonality with all because her essential nature is entirely undivided—the [cognition] proceeds by means of the power Khecarī;
and it has already been stated that Khecarī is identical with the vibration of the subject (*pramātṛ*). [This cognition] takes the form of the sun of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The Wheel of Light (*prakāśacakra*), however, is initiated by the union of both the *dikcarī* and *gocarī*;
for both of these consist of the manifestation of the internal and external senses.
The distinction is that the Wheel of Bliss (*ānandacakra*), which consists of the moon of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), is the vital support of the *bhūcarī*.

By means of these very three wheels, there are the powers (*śakti*) of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*); the drops (*bindu*) of fire, sun, and moon; the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*) of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvaḥ*; the vital airs (*vāyu*) of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and *udāna*;
the locations (*sthāna*) of earth, atmosphere, and heaven; and [the quality of] *sattva*.

Rajas and tamas are the qualities (guṇas); iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā are the channels (nāḍīs); the path of the gods (devayāna), the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), and the great path (mahāyāna) are the vehicles (yānas); the gross, the subtle, and the supreme are the states (avasthās); kula, kaula, and akula are the divisions (vibhāgas); and mantra, mudrā, and nirīhā [are the means].
Thus, everything beginning with "the secrets" (rahasyāni) is encompassed as characterized by the number three; as the Śruti says:
"That which has one felly, is threefold, and has sixteen spokes," and so forth. || 37 ||
Having thus established that the gross body is to be worshipped as the *pīṭha*,
he now contemplates the circle of the *vṛnda* in order to reveal that the subtle body should likewise be so considered:
When the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are manifested, there are sixty-four in the circle of the multitude (*vṛndacakra*).
"Circle of the multitude" (*vṛndacakra*) means a wheel (*cakra*) of multitudes (*vṛnda*); and a "multitude" (*vṛnda*) is by nature a collection (*sandoha*).
Its being such [a collection] arises spontaneously from its consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*).
Because its essential nature is the totality of the fivefold group beginning with the Jñānasiddhas;
and that [group] has the five aggregates (skandhas) manifested. There are sixteen Jñānasiddhas, twenty-four Mantrasiddhas, twelve Melāpasiddhas, and [the Śāktasiddhas...]
There are eight [groups], and the four Śāmbhava-siddhas;

thus, in accordance with the sequence of the five carriers (*pañcavāha*), they manifest as five types. In total, there are sixty-four in the *Vṛndacakra*. Among them is the one known by the synonym Śrī Kālasaṅkarṣaṇī.
Rudra and Raudreśvarī, being the sixty-fifth [deity], are not counted separately because they persist throughout all [the preceding ones]. And this is stated:
"The Vṛndacakra is revealed through the nature of the abode, the mudrā, the phoneme, the kalā, consciousness, and existence, as well as by the vision of the homeless one."

Thus, according to this principle, it becomes eightfold. In that context, the *dhāmas* (abodes) are the locations of Jñānasiddha and the others, which are respectively the *kanda*, the navel, the heart, the throat, and the space between the eyebrows.
The *mudrās* are Karaṅkiṇī and the rest. As it has been said:
"Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanī, Bhairavī, Lelihānikā, and Khecarī— thus exists the fivefold nature of the mudrā.
Likewise, in the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka:

"At the moment of the gaze of Karaṅkiṇī, Krodhanā, Bhairavī, Lelihānā, and Khecarī, the supreme pervasion (parā vyāpti) shines forth. Thus it is said. Furthermore, the method for binding the mudrās is established in that very same [text], as follows:
On a soft seat, having placed the hands and feet without support by resting on one buttock, through the practice of that, the supreme,
perfect wisdom shall arise.
Sitting properly on a seat with the arms bent at the elbows and placed in the space between the armpits, one attains tranquility by fixing the mind through the absorption of consciousness.
Having fixed one's gaze steadily upon a gross object and having made the mind supportless in a short time, one shall go to Śiva.
Having placed the consciousness in the middle of the mouth with the tongue positioned centrally,
and mentally uttering the syllable "Ha," one then dissolves into the state of peace.
"Seated upon a seat or lying down, one should contemplate one's own body as being without support; when the mind has waned, one becomes, in an instant, one whose latent dispositions have waned.
According to the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvavṛtti*), however, she is named Karaṅkiṇī, who is adept at dissolving the distinctions known as "one's own body" and "the senses."

The Mudrā: As it is said in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*: "O Mother! These hands of yours, whose bodies are unbroken even externally; this very body which is your lap—since both of these are [your own], O Karaṅkiṇī, you lead us to the sky of consciousness beyond them."

She is Krodhanī because she, through her wrath characterized by the desire for internal withdrawal, leads the entire collection of principles from earth up to primordial nature (prakṛti) back into the state of her own self-nature. As it is said:
"The circle of principles beginning with the earth and ending with primordial nature..."
"Your abode is the limited grasp; you are Krodhanī, the embodiment of mantra here, manifesting as his yawning out of a desire to withdraw [the world].
Thus, Bhairavī is of the nature of full consciousness through the simultaneity of internal and external states—as for example:
"O Thou who art the two-fold six knots! She by whom these are held is the state of the sky of consciousness free from obscuration.
Bearing the majesty of differentiation through the form of vibration, You are Bhairavī, the one who merges the universe. Thus [it is said].

And this [state] is, for us, due to the propriety of the aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the two types of samādhi—closing and opening [the eyes]. It is nurtured as follows:
"With the internal focus and the external gaze, free from blinking and opening—
the Bhairavī Mudrā, this is what is hidden in all Tantras," so they say.
As it is stated in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"Possessing the nature of the Great Assembly (*mahāmelāpa*), their forms being the unfolding of the *krauṇḍalī*,
they shine eternally, established in the abode of the unobscured sky of consciousness."
Having filled [the universe] with the display of differentiation arising from the abundance of her own power,
she remains possessed of full majesty, her form entirely unobstructed.
She alone is celebrated as Bhairavī, the mudrā that is free from both being and non-being;
she is the sole protectress of the state of aesthetic identity (sāmarasya) arising from the expansion of the waveless [consciousness].
"This [mudrā] is always sealed by these goddesses who are perfected through union;
this mudrā of Bhairava-nature appears in two ways.
Thus it was said by our Guru in the *Manonuśāsana-stotra*:
"Your seat, though free from conceptual construction, has a fixed gaze and relies upon external objects;
like a parrot released from its cage, assume that noble form of Bhairava!
Thus it was said by me as well in the *Śrīparāstotra*:

That [state] which the wise occupy above all, touching only the inner space, having scorched the earth with the openings of their eyes— eyes that are free from turbidity, possessed of upturned lashes, warm, and marked by the dawning of bliss;
and which serves as a festival for the full manifestation of the "I" (aham).
"That certain one of yours, possessing inconceivable accomplishment, is called the great, immovable *mudrā*. Thus it is said.
She is the "Licking One" (*lelihānā*), eager to swallow the entire store of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as those of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). As it has been stated:
"By the multitude of rays intent upon withdrawing the latent impressions of the seeds arisen in the eight cities..."
"O Mother! You remain as the Lelihānā (the repeatedly licking one), with Your mouth slightly parted after having just tasted [the nectar].

Thus, Khecarī is that which causes the agitation of all conceptual constructions such as the signified and the signifier; She transcends the boundaries of the path of the Suṣumṇā, and Her form is non-different from the consciousness of Her own Self.
Just as you, O Goddess, intent upon dissolving the expansion of the final manifest articulation beginning with the letter *pa*,
become the sky-faring goddess (*khecarī*) who expands consciousness and dwells in the abode of Śambhu, which is free from all veils.

O Mother! Devouring the abodes of fire, sun, and moon, you rise up from the *kuṇḍalinī* like a bee; O Śāmbhavī, you are considered the *khecarī* by way of the central path (*madhyamādhvan*) leading to the *bindu*.
Thus is the classification of the mudrās.

The phonemes (varṇas) are of the nature of the venerable Śabdarāśi-Bhairava. Among them, the sixteen accomplished through knowledge (jñānasiddhas) consist of the vowels; those accomplished through mantra (mantrasiddhas) range from the letter *ka* to the letter *ma*.

Those consisting of the [consonantal] phonemes (*varṇa*) are the *melāpaka-siddhas* and have the form of the neutral vowels (*ṣaṇḍasvara*). Those whose nature consists of the letters from *ya* to *ha* are the *śākta-siddhas*. And those whose form consists of the digit of the letter *a* (*akārakalā*) are the *śāmbhava-siddhas*. Furthermore, the digits of the letter *a* are...

The bindu, the half-moon (ardhacandra), the nirodhana, and the nada are their essential natures. Among these, the bindu is the anusvāra in the form of a moon, whose nature is light inseparable from its entire range of denotable objects.
The half-moon is that which is tranquil, characterized by a slight predominance of the denotable object.
Because it is the very nature of the *maṇḍala* and because of the complete departure from crookedness, and furthermore,

because of the removal of the crookedness of the object of cognition (*vedya*), it is the *nirodhikā*, which has the form of a straight line. Just as there is the entry into the *nāda* by means of this [line] for limited yogins, so too is it for unlimited yogins.
And the immersion into the state of duality is restrained. Sound (*nāda*) is the supreme reality of self-reflection;

such is the secret of the digit of the letter *A*. The letters beginning with *A*, residing in the venerable Lord Pañcapiṇḍanātha, belong respectively to Jñānasiddha and the others. Furthermore, Jñānasiddha and the rest—
In due order, [the letters] consist of the portions (*kalā*) of the letter *A*; however, those belonging to Śambhu (*śāmbhavī*) are the collective totality (*tatsamaṣṭi*) of them.
This is because we accept the very identity between the letter *A* and the five-fold aggregate (*pañcapiṇḍa*).
As it is said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"The non-dual path consists of the five vowels, the five consonants, and the two forms [of the phonemes].
Therefore, it is said: 'The body of the Goddesses is fully contained therein.
By this, it is shown that there is no absolute distinction between the Śrī Mahārtha and Trika systems.

This has been explained. The same should be understood regarding the syllable *oṃ* as well. For this [syllable] is of the nature of the sacred seat of Oḍyāṇa, consists of the essence of *nāda*, is of the form of the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*), and is capable of withdrawing the threefold manifestation beginning with creation.
He is the one whose form consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—the presiding deities of the three states beginning with waking;
who consists of the syllables *a*, *u*, and *m*; who is animated by the half-mora (*ardhamātrā*) characterized by the expansion of the non-differentiation of all things;
and who is manifested through the power of the four phonemes already described.
It is a synonym for the seed-syllable *mahārāva*. Thus, it is said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"He is solely intent upon the swallowing of the manifestation of emission, maintenance, and withdrawal;
he is solely intent upon the constant flashing forth of the ineffable great radiance."
I bow to that very one named Praṇava, whose nature is the abundance of the four-and-a-half-fold divisions, for the sake of attaining the scriptures; I call him by the name Pīṭha.
Such is the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇakrama*).

The *kalās* are Raudrī and the others. Among them, Raudrī, Vāmā, Ambikā, and Jyeṣṭhā are respectively conjoined with Jñānasiddha and the other [Siddhas]. And those characterized by the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with these are the Śāmbhavyas.
As it is said in the *Śrī-Cidgaganacandrikā*: "In the rays of knowledge, Raudrī arises; in the rays of mantra, Vāmā has arisen;
in the rays of yoga, Ambikā expands; thus, Jyeṣṭhā presides over the rays of power."
"The Goddess, as the fourfold group of undivided *kalās*, shines as the vowel within the rays of Śambhu.

Now, regarding the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*): therein, what is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the primary, general manifestation, which they term "indeterminate perception" (*ālocanā*). This is the mantra.

Reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) consists of the intense impulse toward the emergence of objective categories. That very awareness, when resting within its own self, is *melāpa* (the union). For that which has such a nature, there is the power of Śakti (*śākta*), which consists in the pacification of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And for this [state], wherein all stains of latent impressions have dissolved, the result is the remaining over of nothing but the pure consciousness of one's own self (*svātmasaṃvinmātratā*).

Regarding the term *śāmbhava*: now, as for the nature of existence (*bhāvasvabhāva*). For the supreme Lord’s light, by its very nature, resembles an ocean that is clear, profound, and without waves; it is essentially free of conceptual construction (*avikalpātman*) within.

He experiences the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*), which consists of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). And the powers belonging to him that have entered into such a nature are those of Śambhu (*śāmbhavyaḥ*). When he assumes a slight inclination toward the activity of surging waves, then there is the manifestation of the power (*śākta-ullāsa*). Of that very [power], a slight...

In the state of becoming a great wave (*kallolībhāva*), there is the throbbing of the *melāpa* (the union of the powers). When there is the conception of ever-increasing, surging waves, there is the unfolding of the mantra. Like the rising of the moon or some other cause for increase, the tumultuous agitation that overflows its banks is the emergence of the accomplishment of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*).

Thus, those perfected through knowledge (*jñānasiddhas*) are to be considered as a portion of the object of cognition (*prameya*); those perfected through mantra (*mantrasiddhas*) as consisting of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); those perfected through the assembly (*melāpasiddhas*) as being of the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*); and those perfected through power (*śāktasiddhas*) as being the pure cognizer by virtue of having discarded that limitation.

And the Śāmbhava-siddhas [attain their state] by virtue of having the nature of the venerable Supreme Śiva, who consists of the sovereignty of perfect consciousness. Now, the sequence beginning with "the descent of Vāmeśī upon the Śāmbhava-siddhas" serves to illuminate the identity (*tādātmya*) of the Śāmbhavī-siddhas and others with Vāmeśī and the other goddesses.
The contemplation of the identity between the group of five currents and the wheel is "falling" (pāta); such is the manner of falling.

In this way, falling is also to be contemplated within the sequence of emanation and so forth. As it is said in the *Śrīkramasiddhi*: "O God! O handsome one, listen to this sequence of consciousness; I shall speak."
[He perceives] emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as the unnameable, the manifestation, and the essential nature.
"Knowledge, mantra, and melāpa, together with the Śākta and the Śāmbhava.
As it is said in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*:
"One should know that knowledge is emanation (*sṛṣṭi*); maintenance (*sthiti*) is proclaimed to be mantra."
They know the Mahākāla-melāpa to be the supreme dissolution.
"That which is called the Ineffable (anākhyam) is the nature of Power (śakti), while that which is called Manifestation (bhāsa) is the form of Śambhu.
Indeed, this fivefold [reality] should be known by those who perceive the true principles.
Thus, one who is "without abode" (aniketa) refers to those such as the Jñānasiddhas and others, due to their movement in reverse order through the stages of contemplative realization (bhāvakrama).

The eightfold division consists of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the state of ultimate establishment (*paramapratiṣṭhābhūmi*), which remains after the removal of the agitation of conceptual constructions such as "this is an object of cognition" (*prameya*) and so forth.
Among these, for those who have attained knowledge (*jñānasiddha*), there are sixteen manifestations consisting of the sixteen transformations (*vikāra*).

The mantra-perfected ones possess a nature consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the internal and external movement of the sense-faculties. And these sense-faculties are perceived as twelve, taking as their material cause the *ahaṅkāra* which is woven through all of them. And sometimes, having descended from the essential nature of the Self (*ātman*), due to the variety of their immersion in objects, at other times—
Because they turn back from the objects of the senses and are occupied solely with resting in their own self,

there exists a twofold nature due to the occurrence of these two modes. And based upon that, there arises the manifestation of the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*) in the form of these latent impressions (*vāsanās*).

It has been stated that the *melāpaka-siddhas* are the ultimate subjects (*pramātṛ-paramārtha*). In this regard, the inherent nature of these subjects is such that they cause the entire range of objects of knowledge—which consist of the accomplishment of gnosis—to rest within their own self by means of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which consist of the accomplishment of mantra. And therefore:

Because it is precisely the sense organs (*indriya*), which have become authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that predominate in their activity therein, the meaning is that the *melāpasiddhācakra* consists of the twelve sense organs. Now, as for the Śākta-siddhas: *Śakti* consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and she is...

Because it has the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city) as its object, it becomes eightfold. It is well known that the *puryaṣṭaka* consists of the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the mind (*manas*), and the five [subtle elements] beginning with sound; this expansion of the wheel is its vital support. And it is called *śāmbhavī*.
The powers (*śakti*) of the Lord Śambhubhaṭṭāraka, whose latent impressions of the entire universe have been dissolved, are non-different from his own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
And in the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), they consist of Ambā, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, and Raudrī.
Thus, like a talkative parrot, I have [uttered] this account of the conduct of the circle of Vṛnda, obtained through the oral tradition from the mouth of the Guru—
a discourse pregnant with the entire essence of the secret knowledge of the stages of the path of the five-fold meaning.
I did not say.

Thus, having contemplated one's own body as the seat (*pīṭha*)— as the gross in its nature as the abode, as the subtle in its nature as the *vṛndacakra*, and as the supreme in its nature as the five flows—
one should contemplate the ultimate reality of that threefold [nature] through the forms characterized by the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

Having contemplated [the lineage] through the wheels of light and bliss (*prakāśānandacakra*), he reveals the venerable succession of the *Gurunātha*s— who are to be honored above that— by means of their non-duality:
"Indeed, a restriction regarding the circle of gurus is not appropriate for those who have transcended all restrictions."
This alone is the distinction between the pedestal and the deity installed upon it:
that although they stand in a mutual relationship of support and supported, the former lacks inherent radiance, whereas the latter possesses an inherently radiant nature.

Regarding the phrase "the excellence of eternal radiance": therein, the rule concerning the deities of the *pīṭhas*— which consists in their being conditioned by adventitious attributes (*aupādhikatva*) with respect to their vibrancy (*sphurattā*)—
is distinct [for each] starting from the venerable goddess Śrī Maṅgalādevī and ending with Śrī Maheśvarānanda.

A circle or a row of those who are [merely] "first" teachers is not possible there, because they exist by transgressing the rule under discussion. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the lineage of the venerable Gurus is of the nature of perfect consciousness (*pūrṇasaṃvitsvabhāva*). Because these...
They transcend the restriction consisting of the delimitation of space, time, and so forth; therefore, there is a plurality of them.

This does not accord with the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvavṛtti*); it is accepted only as a figurative designation (*aupacārikatayā*) due to the influence of association with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Just as [one and the same thing...]

An object reflects in various ways according to the differences in its substrates, such as a mirror, water, oil, and so forth. Likewise, even the coloring [of consciousness] by the body and other limiting adjuncts does not establish the manifestation of actual difference. As I have stated myself in the *Śrīpādukodaya*:
In that regard, our great mandala of powers, which is to be worshipped,
is entirely contained within Śambhu, whose nature is his own essential being.
He too attains identity with the God, the Guru, and his own self;
and being one by nature, he appears as if manifold.
Having undertaken the sequence beginning with Maṅgala, Ādīpti, Śiva, Ānanda, and so forth,
one is worshipped through the lineage by virtue of abiding in the state of Ambā and Nātha.
He is known as Śakti, Śiva, Devapāṇi, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
or else he is designated by other names in the world—he is this very one who is transcendent.
In accordance with the requirements of each particular time, the Lord assumes various distinct forms for those seekers of knowledge,
just as the sun appears in diverse ways through its waves.
"And the diversity of the body and so forth is the unfolding of His very will;
through its conceptual differentiation, one should understand that multiplicity exists even in the sandals [of the Guru].
Therefore, in its true nature, it consists of the power of the state of the Unsurpassed (Anuttara), which is non-different from one's own Self.

It is said that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) itself is the venerable Guru-Nātha. As it is stated in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*: "In reality, I take refuge in that unborn Teacher who shines as the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), whose nature consists of the swelling forth of the expansion of the unstruck sound (*asvara*)."
And in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:

"This Nāda, the teacher of the universe, is the seed that flashes forth from the unstruck sound (*asvara*), whose body is the initial swelling [of consciousness], and which is devoid of sequential order; it is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within the Lord. Thus it is said.
And because it has been stated that "the mouth of Śiva is spoken of here," the venerable *pādukā* (sacred sandals) is to be accepted as the means for thoroughly knowing His such nature;
and she is indeed remembered as being just like that, as taught by those who know the inner [reality]: "Of the one whose self is both supreme and non-supreme..."
The Supreme Power (Parā Śakti), who consists of supreme bliss and is intent upon swallowing all that is distinct from her own self, is celebrated as the *pādukā*. And of her:
"In the ring at the base of the snare, the threads and other such things have been swallowed."
Likewise, the knowledge of the Kulārṇava is established in the pādukā.
Thus, by this established principle, it is unavoidable that the state of containing the sequence of all objects within itself is demonstrated. As stated in the *Śrīpūrva* (Mālinīvijayottara-tantra):
"The pill of the contraction of the sequence has as its sole root its own expansion."
"May the Pādukā, whose nature is each respective [deity] from Vīra to Divīra, protect [me].
This exposition is to be found in my *Śrīpādukodaya-tantra*, whose function is exhausted by the mere presentation of that [Pādukā]. || 38 ||

Now, in order to manifest the fivefold extraordinary activity (*pañcakṛtya*), whose nature is the unfolding of the power of autonomous consciousness (*svātantryasaṃvicchakti*), of the venerable Lord of the Doctrine (*śrīdeśikanātha*)— who has been established in this way as non-different from the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva who is one's own true self— the [text] transcends all [other categories].
Having set aside speech for separate discussion, he first clarifies the fourfold process beginning with creation:
"In creation there are ten digits (kalās); in maintenance, there are twenty-two powers (śaktis)."
There are eleven in the Saṃhāra and thirteen in the fourth parvan. || 39 ||

For it is traditionally taught that what is called "emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is the aggregate of fivefold manifestations characterized by exertion (*udyoga*), manifestation (*avabhāsa*), relish (*carvaṇa*), dissolution (*vilāpana*), and the state of being waveless (*nistaraṅgatva*). That all knowers (*pramātṛ*), including ourselves, are inseparable from this fivefold manifestation should be inferred for oneself. To illustrate:

Potters and others first exert themselves to separate from their own consciousness such entities as jars, which abide in a state of identity with it; they then manifest that very same thing externally by means of external implements such as the rod, the wheel, and the cloth. Once manifested, [it is perceived as external].

They experience it repeatedly as their own through placing it on the kiln, baking, establishing it, and so forth; subsequently, because their sole intent is its functional utility, they adopt an attitude of indifference toward it; and this very indifference is its dissolution.

And when the memory of their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is lost, they become waveless therein; for it is the jar and other objects themselves that arise as waves and dissolve back into the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, this pentad of manifestations becomes purified by the self-reflective awareness of one's own nature (*svātmaparāmarśa*); such is the extent of the distinction.

We have stated this previously as well. In that creation, there are ten powers (*śakti*) characterized by the orientation toward the first activity; these are the *yoni*s, and those who are perfected therein [are the *siddha*s].
And in the vision of their true nature (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), they consist of the pentad of *kalā*s beginning with *udyoga*, by virtue of possessing their respective *kalā*s.

In this way, the nature of the agent is established through a gradual process. These [powers] are extracted as being essentially the manifestations of action, knowledge, will, effort, intuition, emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, the unnameable, and light. And from that, the fivefold [process] beginning with emanation—
It is stated that all the manifold variety contained within the *kṛtya* (the fivefold cosmic act) flashes forth within a single creation alone. As it is said in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*:
"By her this entire universe, the three worlds with their mobile and immobile beings, is pervaded."

Thus, in other wheels as well, there is the necessary occurrence of entering into the essential nature of the wheel distinct from that [specific aspect], according to the principle that designations are made solely by way of the predominant factor. The separate arrangement of emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest occurs through the inclusion of their respective predominant portions. For example:
In the *Śrīkramasiddhi*:
"Just as milk pervades the cow and flows forth from the two udders, so too Śivā is all-pervasive, omnipresent, subtle, and yet flows forth within the One. (13)
For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*: "Those rays of light belonging to that [Sun], whose body is beyond comparison,
have arisen for the sake of bestowing a fixed planetary configuration."
These very five wombs, which lead to the supreme abode,
have been described as being entirely free from the conceptualization of fixed planetary positions and configurations.
In such passages, being engaged in the fixed positions (*saṃsthāna*) of the planets and being free from them are described.
Also, in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*:
"Listen to my supreme Kālī-vidyā, which pertains to the nature of emanation."

And so forth. This will also be indicated further below. Thus, it is stated that even regarding each individual act, the Supreme Lord possesses an orientation toward the activity of the fivefold acts (*pañcakṛtya*).
As it is said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"In this way, she alone shines forth spontaneously in the form of the fivefold self;
I take refuge in that Goddess who reveals her own true nature.
Thus, from among these goddesses, when one shines forth spontaneously...
"All those [states] shine forth at that very time, eternally and perfectly through aesthetic oneness (*sāmarasya*).
And in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"O Goddess! if, among the five functions which consist of You, any one should manifest spontaneously..."
"Constantly and instantly, all those [powers] shine forth at that very moment, having ascended to the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).
And as it is said in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:
"Since an effect never arises from the manifestation of only one [element], therefore the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of all categories is established.
Now, he states the sequence of maintenance: "In maintenance, there are twenty-two powers."
Stability (*sthiti*), indeed, is the unmuddled persistence of created entities until the emergence of the desire to withdraw them. As it has been said:
"Stability is the maintenance of one's own nature in its respective form."
Those Śaktis and the four Yuganāthas in the head-cakra, along with their four goddesses,
make eight. In the six-spoked wheel (ṣaṭkoṇa), there is a pair of twelve princes, divided according to their status as having authority or lacking authority.

In the midst of that are Kuleśvara and Kuleśvarī; thus there are twenty-two. There, having presided over the four seats—Oḍḍiyāṇa, Jālandhara, Pūrṇagiri, and Kāmarūpa—in accordance with the sequence of the ages consisting of Kali, Dvāpara, Tretā, and Kṛta;

They are the protectors of the universe—which is subject to the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turyā)—for the sake of its stabilization; their sovereignty is augmented by the mantras consisting of the four kalās of the *praṇava*, namely the syllables A, U, M, and Nāda; and they are, respectively, the agent, the knower, the determiner, and the conscious one.
The four specific agents who are vitalized by the radiance of the Supreme Agent are called the Yuganāthas. And their goddesses are as follows:
she hears sound in the crown-lock (śabdamolambe) and beholds with the two eyes (puṣkaradvaye).
He utters a cry while clinging to the mountain Karāla, and he smells the fragrance on Mount Sahya as if it were a fragrant substance.

According to the principle that "the Lord pervades everything within the great seat (mahāpīṭha) of Mātaṅga," activities, cognition, determination, and the power of consciousness— which consist of the sovereign forms residing in their respective seats— are worshipped as the actual reality (*tattva*). And the princes—
Because he delights the world, the king is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) himself;
his sons are the princes. [...]
Thus, by means of the arising and abiding of the venerable *pāduka*, those various sense organs are designated. And as it is said in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"O King, because of illumination (*rañjana*) from the Sovereign (*rājan*), I am known as *rājasa* [the quality of passion], due to the functions of awakening and action."
"O Śivā, these six have been established by you as distinct initiators, elevated to the status of sons.

In this context, "possessing authority" (*sādhikāratva*) refers to the predominance of ritual action (*karman*), since it has been stated that "authority is sovereignty over ritual action. Conversely, "lacking authority" (*niradhikāratva*) arises from the opposite case, namely the preponderance of knowledge (*jñāna*). And therefore—

The intellect (*buddhi*), speech, and the other organs of action (*karmendriya*) possess authority; the mind (*manas*), the ear, and the other organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) are without authority—these are the princes. The Lord of the Family (*kuleśvara*) is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
his power of self-conceit (*abhimāna-śakti*) is the Lady of the Family (*kuleśvarī*)—such is the reflection upon the meaning of the principles (*tattva*). Now...
He describes the manner of withdrawal: "The withdrawal is elevenfold.

Withdrawal (saṃhāra) means the subsistence of external objects, from the earth up to Rudra, within the supreme Lord’s light of consciousness in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā), according to the principle of the banyan seed and so forth, in order that they may be fit for future manifestation.

In that regard, there are eleven powers (*śakti*). The established conclusion regarding the reality is that they came to be eleven because they manifest by devouring the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of all internal organs, as well as the ten external sense organs. Among these:

Such an ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) alone is the subject (*pramātṛ*), because apart from it, that [limited subject] is not perceived. The senses are the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and their objects are the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). Thus, the *kalās* (creative powers) are those which inwardly savor this triad consisting of the subject and so forth, as well as the object of knowledge.

It is said that they are "the destroyers. Furthermore, due to the delimitation caused by the proximity of these powers (*śakti*), the Supreme Lord is well-known as the eleven Rudras. Now, he proclaims the sequence of the Inexplicable (*anākhyā*):
"Those thirteen are the fourth stage (*turya-parvan*). The fourth is the wheel of the Inexplicable (*anākhyā-cakra*).
"In that form" refers to a specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) during the festival (*parvan*). "Inexpressible" (*anākhyam*) signifies the absence of designation (*ākhyā-śūnyatvam*).
And designation consists of the threefold nature of gross speech, beginning with *paśyantī*. As it is stated in the *Śrī-cidgaganacandrikā*:
"O Beloved of the Lord, the three voices— Nāda, Bindu, and Lipi— which are the spray of the upward-moving *vimarśa*,
are active within the abodes of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and emission (*visṛṣṭi*) below you. And that,
from the perspective of ultimate reality, refers to the perceivers (*pramātṛ*) and so forth who have been withdrawn.
It is determined to have as its essential nature the state of being nothing but the fire of consciousness whose inherent character is withdrawal;
and that [state] is:
"Laziness consisting of exertion, and darkness whose sole essence is light."
The Śāmbhava reality is neither empty nor is it like something empty; it is some indescribable essence.

Thus, by the principle of the unfolding of consciousness (*saṃvid-ullāsa*), a certain level (*kakṣyā*) appears which, though not empty, consists of emptiness. For this very reason, it is called the "fourth stage" (*turīya-parvan*).
Since even within this manifestation, something must be inwardly contemplated by the undaunted yogi.
It culminates in the expansion of the wealth of bliss consisting of the experience of the light whose nature is the non-worldly radiance. As it is said in the *Śrīspanda*:
"Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved..."
"Like the state of deep sleep, the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured.

And although, in that context, the postulation of power (śakti) as a primary function, or its being defined by such a limited extent, is not logically tenable, nevertheless it is so taught in the Āgamas by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra). As it has been said:
In the *Stotrabhaṭṭāraka*:
"That which is unspeakable or beyond the triad is sung of by way of metaphor.
And therein, those powers are thirteen. Regarding the word "those": they are the creative and the sustaining [powers].
And those [powers],

though being the sole remnant of the agent of withdrawal at that immediate state, remain like a certain internal bulb in relation to the variety of objects to be experienced that will arise, existing in the form of the twelve organs and their collective totality.

Thirteen [cycles] arise. And since each one of these possesses the nature of a wheel (*cakrarūpatā*) at the beginning of every creation and so forth, according to the arrangement of the *Śrīkramakeliklṛpti*, there are:
the creation of creation (*sṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), the maintenance of creation (*sṛṣṭisthiti*), the dissolution of creation (*sṛṣṭisaṃhāra*), and the fourth state of creation (*sṛṣṭiturīya*).

The manifestation of the twelve faculties consists of: the emission of persistence, the persistence of persistence, the withdrawal of persistence, and the fourth state of persistence; the emission of withdrawal, the persistence of withdrawal, the withdrawal of withdrawal, and the fourth state of withdrawal. Thus are the twelve pulsations of the senses.

In this context, since it is established that "no separate *manu* is taught for the unmanifest (*anākhyā*) and the manifestation (*bhāsa*)," all things are determined through the vibratory movement (*parispanda*) of the venerable Goddess Bhāsā— who is the thirteenth, being permeated by all and conjoined with the fourth state (*turya*). For example:
In the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*: "I bow to the thirteenth Goddess, who is intent upon the vomiting and devouring of these twelve goddesses, for the sake of attaining identity with her."

And these [powers] are revealed through the hymns of praise (*stotrabhaṭṭāraka*) by means of designations such as Sṛṣṭikālī and so forth; thus ends the thirteenth chapter on the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*). 39.
Now, he illuminates the light that transcends all: "In that light, where the splendor of the one, throbbing, partless [reality] shines, no conceptual construction manifests;
yet, if it manifests by way of reflection, there is the Supreme Goddess, exceeding the sixteen. (40)

Speech (*bhāṣā*) is the supreme power of consciousness belonging to the Lord, which encompasses the diversity of worldly activity pervaded by creative acts such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*), and which is both transcendent of all things and the benefactor of all;
it is determined to be none other than His very sovereignty. As it is said in the *Śrīpādukodaya*:
And this speech is indeed a great inspired eloquence, containing all within its womb;
it consists of pure consciousness, which teaches that the singular essence is the auspiciousness of one's own true nature.
For upon that [consciousness], which serves as the foundational wall, the world—
consisting of the knower and the known— shines as a reflection, like a city and so forth in a mirror.
"That certain power of consciousness belonging to the Supreme Lord is of the nature of absolute freedom;
the Blessed Lord is composed of that, and the Guru is the Lord, while she is composed of the Guru.
And she is the splendor of the single, undivided, throbbing [reality], shining forth as she manifests, devoid of any distinction between self and other.
Being one who has transcended the manifestation of duality and possesses identity with her own self, she is partless (*niṣkalā*);
like creation and the other cosmic acts, she cannot tolerate the agitation of conceptual constructions such as division or designation.
She is characterized by sovereignty that corresponds to the arising of Śrī; [the state] in which this [sovereignty] resides—within that, conceptual construction...

In this way, a contradictory conceptualization (kalpanā) in the form of "this is such-and-such" does not manifest. If anything at all flashes forth, it is precisely the sixteenth [consciousness]; and that occurs solely through the principle of reflection—such is the literal meaning of the words.
