This is what is being said: the radiance of the expansion of the supreme freedom of the Parameśvara’s supreme consciousness.

In this light, which is one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), because the manifestation of universal identity (*vaiśvātmya*) remains as its sole residue, no suspicion whatsoever can arise regarding the emergence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Rather, it is precisely the wheels (*cakra*) of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the rest, introduced previously, that are reflected within this [light] by way of the principle of reflection (*pratibimba-yukti*), owing to its possession of the excellence of transparency (*svacchatā*).

By this manner of expression, "quivering forth" (*parisphurantī*), even the worship of those various powers through conceptualization (*vikalpa*) becomes somewhat consistent. As it is said in the *Śrīkramakeli*:

"Therefore, those who desire that which is beyond the fourth state (*turyātīta*) to be devoid of reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*) are indeed without instruction. The phrase "the sixteenth plus" refers to the seventeenth digit (*kalā*).

In that regard, the sixteen powers have the nature of being reflections of the universe; however, the final one is "the likeness of a level wall for the variegated painting of the manifold universe. Thus, according to the system of the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*, it consists of the totality of those [powers].

By the phrase "having that as its substrate," both the universe—which consists of sixteen [categories] plus the one beyond—and the Supreme Lord who transcends it are subsumed. Furthermore, the process of reflection must be accepted as something extraordinary, distinct from common examples such as crystal or a mirror; for:
For a crystal and the like, there is a necessary dependence upon an original object (*bimba*) for reflection;

however, because this [Consciousness] serves as the very wall (*bhitti*) for the reflection of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it is the reverse of that. This will also be explained further below.
And this [power], having entered this wheel, is the "sixteen-plus" (ṣoḍaśādhikā),
because it consists of the collective totality of the sixteen transformations and their reflections; thus, first appearing as seventeen modes of manifestation, it subsequently...

By virtue of the conjunction of the distinction between the two— illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— it is experienced as thirty-four parts through the methodological division of Bhairava and Bhairavī; and by means of the method of expansion,
it constitutes the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the reflective awareness of the universal manifestation consisting of the fifty phonemes.

When considered in brief through the mudrā of contraction, [it consists of] those forms of the Supreme Lord— which, though undivided from the venerable Guru, flow fivefold toward the abode of the *pīṭhas*—
namely, the clusters of manifestations, lights, and blisses that take the form of the wheels (*cakra*) and consist of the pentad beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
There are nine wheels (*cakras*), and thus the venerable Nine-Syllabled Mantra (*navākṣarī*) consisting of them is accomplished.

Even further, through the condensation of the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) into five streams (*pañcavāha*), it is reduced to five clusters (*pañcapiṇḍa*); these [clusters] are contained within the seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, and that [seed-syllable] likewise within the syllable Anuttara.

Even this [state] culminates in nothing but the self-reflection of one's own Self. And in the various established doctrines (siddhāntas), this is designated differently according to the gradations in the sequence of ascending through their respective levels of authority.
As they say:
In whatever form it is meditated upon, the power of the followers of Maheśvara becomes identical with that; for the Sāṃkhyas, she is the supreme Prakṛti.
And Tārā, the great queen of the Sauras who praise the Sugata,
was then proclaimed as the foremost among the Lokāyatikas for the sake of the present life.
Śāntā is the [goddess] of the Pāśupatas and others; Śrī belongs to those who know the Arhats;
Śraddhā belongs to the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha; and Gāyatrī belongs to the exponents of the Vedas.
"It is remembered as the deluder of all those blinded by the darkness of ignorance.
With this intention, the Laghubhaṭṭāraka also said:
"Lakṣmī in the royal court, Jayā at the front of battle, and Kṣemaṅkarī on the road..."

"On a mountain difficult to traverse due to wild beasts, elephants, and serpents, amidst the Śabara tribes, and in fear of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and jambhakas, by remembering Mahābhairavī, one overcomes delusion; and by remembering Tripurā, one crosses over calamity, just as one crosses a great flood of water. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Ambāstava*:
"You are the moonlight in the moon, you are the radiance in the sun; you are consciousness in the person, and you are strength in the wind."
"You are sweetness in water, you are heat in fire; if everything were devoid of essence without you.
Thus, in my *Śrīparāstotra* as well:
It rests upon the sprout-like hands of donors, upon the temples of elephants, upon the flowers of trees, upon the orb of the breasts of beautiful women, upon the shoulders of kings,
upon the tips of the throats of singers, and upon the tongues of poets and the hearts of the wise.
"And some fortunate ones conceive of Your very exertion within their own conceptualizations. Thus it is said. Also in the Āgama:
"That same Mahādevī Kālī is celebrated in both the world and the Veda."
"In the Itihāsas, the Tantras, the Siddhāntas, and the Kulas.
And likewise in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā: "Whatever being is possessed of glory, or is endowed with beauty or power..."
"Understand each of those to have arisen from a portion of my own splendor.
Thus:
"At the time of birth she is the mother, and at the time of worship she is the deity."
She is the messenger (dūtī) at the time of pleasure, and Kālikā at the time of death.

Thus, the rest should be inferred. Therein, we—who have entered the tradition of the venerable Devapāṇi—investigate the cycle beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with the manifestation of light (*bhāsā*), according to the method indicated, and not by the reverse order. As it is said in the *Śrīkramasadbhāva*:
"Among them, which one should be worshipped first in due order? Tell me that, O lady of beautiful hips! in detail and according to the prescribed rule."
Following this question:
"O Lord, regarding that Great Sequence of the Five Vehicles which was previously mentioned—
of those kings of sequences, the one whose nature is emanation is always foremost."

"Then one should worship that which is called Sthiti (Maintenance), then Saṃhāra (Dissolution), then the one called Anākhyā (The Ineffable), and after that Bhāsā (Light); thus one should worship in the sequence of non-sequence.
This very [sequence] constitutes the Supreme Lord's authorship of this pentad.

We have stated more than once that this is supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*). It consists, respectively, according to the scriptures (*āgama*), of: the manifestation of the four categories of objects when they have [otherwise] perished;
the persistence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three submerged objects of knowledge; the state of being a knower who devours both the object and the means of knowledge;
the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the object accompanied by conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*); and the manifestation of the object free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*).
This is established in brief. Furthermore, regarding this, the extraction of the mantras for each respective deity should be examined in my *Mahārthodaya*. || 40 ||
Now, regarding the manner in which each of the fivefold group beginning with emanation (sṛṣṭi), as thus taught here, manifests, one must reflect upon a certain simultaneity; thus he says:
"People reckon that the fifth digit of emanation is the manifestation [of the world]; [thus they perceive] an interval."
Creation is the root bulb of manifestation; manifestation is the sprout of creation. || 41 ||
For the Supreme Lord, manifesting the fivefold acts such as creation and so forth without interruption— like the appearance of a whirling firebrand—
demonstrates His own identity with all [attributes] such as being the creator and the sustainer.

He remains experiencing the excellence of agency, by which he is recognized as a helmsman of the great ocean of the nectar of the Kaula scriptures— one who has emerged from the muddy pond of the doctrines of those who propound an insentient Brahman (jaḍabrahmavāda), which is another term for being a mere observer. And this being so:

This world of perceivers, afflicted by birth, death, and so forth due to the lack of thorough knowledge of the reality of things, is— counting the sequence of the five wheels from emanation up to manifestation—
the fifth [wheel], separated from emanation by the triad of wheels beginning with maintenance.

One perceives a separation between "power" (śakti) and "manifestation" (bhāsa); however, in terms of the actual state of reality, manifestation is the foundational ground of emission. And because that [ground] has the nature of the first vibration and consists of a flowing form, it should be contemplated as "emission" (sṛṣṭi).

This is merely an illustration; therefore, the sequence—such as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) being the root-stalk of persistence (*sthiti*), and persistence being the sprout of emanation—should also be inferred by oneself. The underlying point here is that within each of the four activities (*kṛtya*) beginning with emanation, there is the "emanation of emanation," the "persistence of emanation," and so forth, in that order.
There is a fourfold nature, and ultimately, the state of culminating in speech (*bhāṣā*). And this speech,

although its essence consists in the wonder of the reflective awareness of the unity of consciousness upon the observation of the extraction of forms, nevertheless conforms to the nature of the manifold universe that has entered into the logic of the reflection of all things.
"Having the very nature of the pentad" means that all five activities do not transcend the state of each being essentially a pentad. And within these,
by taking hold of the fifth fraction of each preceding pentad, the first [fraction] of each subsequent pentad manifests.

Thus, there is an experience of resting within the powers that culminate in the lower group of five, starting from the first vibration of each successive group of five; although there is a sequential existence, this supreme power of the Lord is one whose sequence is imperceptible, like the swift flash of joy when a thousand lotus petals are split asunder.

The manifestation of the wheel of the fivefold activity remains as something to be contemplated by certain mature individuals through extremely deep and intense practice. Thus, this very reflective awareness of the sequence is liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), consisting in the reflective awareness of one's own self. For [from this arise] the states of being a bearer of the command (*ājñādharatva*) and so forth.
The outward manifestations of power emerge spontaneously as something unavoidable;
yet they do not come to fruition except through contact with the guru’s glance. As it is said in the *Śrīkramasiddhi*:
"The letter *kra* is of the nature of wrath, while the letter *ma* is auspicious."
In the case of anger, however, one should perform the auspicious rite; such is the sequence, the sequence of time.
"Knowledge of the Transmission (krama) is dependent upon the Guru; it is supreme and brings about the perfection of the Command (ājñā).
O Great Goddess! By means of the knowledge of the Transmission, the three worlds have been swallowed up. Thus [ends verse 41].

Having thus, through this much elaboration, reflected upon the true nature of the circle of deities to be worshipped from the perspective of ultimate reality, he now states [the following] in order to establish the essential form of this worship, even though it was introduced previously:
The contemplation of one's own true nature alone is worship, and that is difficult to attain in this world;
whereas wine, betel, fragrance, and flowers—belonging to the Lord of the Universe—are easily obtained.
Indeed, worship is traditionally taught as being fourfold: *cāra*, *rāva*, *caru*, and *mudrā*. As it is said in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"That worship of You which is distinguished by *cāra*, *rāva*, *caru*, and *mudrā*..."
"By virtue of that, the lineage descending from your feet attains [the goal], as has been made clear.
In this context, *cāra* is the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*); *rāva* is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);
*caru* is the substance consisting of the first, second, and so forth; and *mudrā* is for the purpose of establishing one's own self as the Supreme Lord.

With respect to one's own body, it refers to the specific arrangement of hands, feet, and so forth, as well as the specific manner of assuming a particular attire. However, the "Great Mudrā" (mahatī mudrā) ultimately falls within the category of sound (*rāva*) alone. Among those four sequences of worship, sound alone is primarily employed. As for the others...

Ultimately, however, it is grasped as that which impels [the ritual]. Therefore, the supreme worship is precisely the reflective awareness of one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpaparāmarśa*). The intended meaning is that everything else—such as perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps—is merely a display of ostentation (*āḍambaramātra*).
As for the literal meaning of the words: the Supreme Lord himself is of the nature of the radiance flashing forth within one's own heart.

It has been stated and will be further explained that [the deity] is the *devatā*. In this context, that which is one's own innate power (*bala*)—which has entered into identity with one's own self (*svātmatādātmya*), characterized by the capacity to endure the agitation of the universe, and consisting of the state of being a contemplator—that very act of reflecting upon it is *varivasyā* (worship). And that power is designated simply as "power" (*bala*). As it has been said:

In the *Śrīspanda*, it is said: "Mantras are indeed the power of the Self," and "Having seized that power, the mantras [act]. And in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*: "Upon attaining power, one assimilates the universe to oneself. As the Śruti says: "O Rudra, there is nothing more powerful than you. And that...

When the class of subjects established in the world as ordinary worshippers is considered, [the state] is difficult to attain through one's own self-deity— that Supreme Lord— because the world lacks such a vision. For only a few great yogis indeed perceive it in that way.
One must perform such worship as this, by which [the deities] become capable of deep reflection; whereas other forms consist of the offering of wine and so forth—
the offering of lamps, the providing of water for rain from the sacrificial fire, and the drawing up of water for drinking stations.
And this fanning with the hem of a garment by a whirlwind is today your offering of food.
By such reasoning, it is determined that [the Lord] is extremely easy to attain,

because this Lord of the Universe is the presiding authority who establishes the identity of all objects of worship, as well as all other entities, with His own essential nature. That [identity] is inherent...

The meaning is this: for the Blessed One, who pervades all the playful manifestations of the entire universe without exception, what purpose is there in the mockery of the ostentation of offering betel, wine, and other such things performed by another agent?
As it has been said in the venerable *Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:
"By whatever substances one worships or satisfies the Supreme and the Lower, and whoever is the worshiper and the object of worship—all that is indeed One; where, then, is the act of worship?
As it is said in the *Śrīprabhākula*:
O beautiful one, as long as they do not realize that supreme state of peace,
so long must they perform worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, the veneration of the liṅga, and other such rites.

"But when the supreme reality is known—in its every aspect and free from all affliction—where is there worship, where is recitation, where is fire-offering, and where is the formal adoption of a *liṅga*?
Thus [it is said]. However, if those very same substances are purified by such a power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), then...
Let them remain at their ease as materials for worship. As it is said in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā:
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—that offering of devotion from the self-restrained person, I accept."
I have also stated in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"Do the deities not partake of the flowers, which are made fragrant by the contemplation of their own sovereign power?
For if that [fragrance] were easily available in the forests, would there be satisfaction from mere common scent? Thus it is said.
But in the absence of such awareness—
repeatedly blocking the nose with the tip of the hand and repeatedly glancing at what stands beside them;
Some worship the gods, but we perform only the great worship of the single seal of our own bliss.

According to this principle, external ostentation results solely in the fruit of mere mockery. As it is said in the *Arcanātriṃśikā*: "That worship is like the play of a doll made of cloth fashioned by a young girl."
"Wherein the mind comes to rest, having taken refuge in the midst of the vast ocean of stainless consciousness.
And as it is said in the *Śrīpaścima*:
"Worship, fire-sacrifice, the ritual sequence, conduct, vows, and the study of the scriptures..."
"Austerity, meditation, recitation, and purity are fruitless for one who is devoid of the [supreme] reality.
And as it is said in the *Śrīgītāniṣyanda*:
"Falling at the feet is not devotion to the all-pervading Supreme Self."
"Devotion is the contemplation of the essential nature of all things as being one with That.
And as it is said in the *Śrīmat-Stotrāvalī*:
"Neither yoga, nor austerity, nor worship, nor any ritual procedure is prescribed [as the means]."
"In this path of Śiva, which is free from illusion, single-minded devotion alone is praised.
Likewise, in the *Śrīmahānayapaddhati*:
"That firm reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) directed toward the form of the Supreme Self, which is utterly unconditioned..."
"Although it has been determined by the Lord that this is indeed worship in this manner,
as stated in the *Śrīpādukodaya*:
'And worship is the contemplation (*vimarśana*) of the supreme teacher through the nature of one's own self.'"

By this— according to the position of the venerable *Ṛjuvirmāśinī* that "worship is the resting of the entire knowable within the ground of consciousness"— worship is not that firm mental act which is performed with flowers and other such offerings.
In the non-conceptual great void, that worship is indeed absorption through reverence.

Thus, the scriptural statement beginning with these words is also explained. For what is called "the dissolution of one's own self" culminates in the self-reflection characterized by resting within oneself. As they say:
"Wherein the forest of duality is the fuel, and death itself is the great sacrificial animal."
"By that supramundane sacrifice, we worship eternally.
It is with this very intention [that it is said]:
"Her mouth filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor..."
By such statements as these, the satisfaction of one's own self-deity is declared in the scriptures as something to be practiced first. As it is said in the *Śrīpūrva*:
"From the union with liquid substances, his bathing takes place."
The perceiving of the fragrance of perfumes, flowers, and so forth is known as sacrifice (yajana).
"The tasting of the six flavors serves as his food offering;
whatever syllable one should utter, that is proclaimed to be *japa*.
And this form of worship belongs only to some person of blessed birth.
It enters the path of experience. As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"This certain sacrificial rite resides in the heart of someone;
for whomsoever the wheel of consciousness (*ciccakra*) becomes gracious, [that person] belongs to the final birth."

In this regard, liquor acts as a purifier of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); betel-leaf acts as a purifier of both the external and internal aspects of the body; fragrances such as sandalwood primarily act as an embellishment for the external limbs;
and flowers likewise [act] in that very same way.

The intention regarding the sequence [of the items] is based on the relative predominance of each preceding factor, as they serve as the substrates (*adhivāsa*) for the subsequent ones, beginning with the hair.

In the term *viśvapateḥ*, the genitive case denotes mere relationship (*sambandha-mātra*), not a restrictive connection as in the expression *māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("one should eat beans"). Therefore, even when used with the particle *khalu*, such a construction is not faulty.
As it has been said:
"For this treatise appears like the speech of an ignoramus to those whose minds are indolent in perceiving its greatness; yet, it does not forfeit its inherent excellence. (42)
Having thus reflected in general upon the nature of worship, and intending to apply its specific details in the same manner, he first proclaims the ultimate reality of breath control (prāṇāyāma):

Even when one is motionless and intent upon a task during a state of prosperity, the suspension of external activities while reflecting upon one's own inner essence should be known as the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyama). || 43 ||
For this is the nature of those subjects who are intent upon the worship of the Supreme Lord: that,
by the power of the expansion and coloring of the radiance of their own self,
they bring forth the unfolding of the phenomenal world, which is pervaded by the manifold variety of its various modes of manifestation.
Having ascended to their own supramundane plane, which is stainless and devoid of the distinction between internal and external,

they remain at their own will, with an essence consisting solely of the skill in savoring the great delight of consciousness. In that state, what is designated as "restraint of breath" (prāṇasaṃyama) is merely something fashioned by them at the commencement of their practice.

Those desiring to know must understand it thus: one's own *sattva* is the true being (*sad-bhāva*) whose nature consists of the aforementioned power; because it is always experienced only as being conjoined with the agitation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-vikṣobha*), its basis [in reality] arises from mere persistence (*anvaya-mātra*).
It is determined that there exists some extraordinary internal reality (*tattva*), and not, however, even by way of exclusion (*vyatireka*).
Furthermore, exclusion is not established through the conceptualization of absolute negation; it is merely figuratively attributed due to a simple contraction [of consciousness]. And therefore—
Only that effort which is directed toward external objects is lost here;
when that is lost, the ignorant person thinks, "I am destroyed."
But as for that inward-turned state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience,
its loss could never occur, because nothing else is perceived [to take its place].

Thus, according to the method of the *Śrī Spanda*, even while experiencing a state of inertia (*staimitya*) consisting of abiding in the embryonic stage (*kalalāvasthā*) within the sovereign power (*vibhava*) that is one's own capacity— characterized by an orientation toward the descent into the knowable—
the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which consists of the vibration of one's own Self, remains transcendent of the universe.
Śiva pervades my body, which is but the manifestation of the universe,
just as an elephant occupies its own spacious stable or gazes upon its reflection in a mirror.

According to this principle, there is a thorough contemplation that corresponds to the mental apprehension of the lordly scent-elephant (gandhagajendra) and so forth once they have entered within the circle of a mirror. As the means of establishing that [contemplation], there is the "breaking"— that is, the shattering— of the occurrences of the external manifestations of objects (*vedya*), which are characterized by their specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*).

"Stambhana is prāṇāyāma. This means that prāṇāyāma is the means for the continuous contemplation of the radiance of one's own self, even when there is an absence of the agitation caused by various conceptual constructions (vikalpa). As it is said in the *Śrī Svacchanda*:
One should exhale through the right nostril and inhale through the left;
for this is the purification of the channels, the path to the way of liberation.
Prāṇāyāma is traditionally said to be threefold: through exhaling (recaka), filling (pūraka), and retention (rodha).
These are common [to all], but there are also three internal types.
"One should exhale by means of the internal [wind], and fill by means of the internal;
having performed the motionless *kumbhaka*, the three internal [breaths] should be practiced.
For example:
"From the movement from the navel to the heart, and from the mind toward the range of the senses,
the fourth breath-control (prāṇāyāma) abides in the state of supreme tranquility. Thus,
according to the established principle that consciousness first transforms into the vital breath (prāṇa), for everyone...

The use of the singular form "of the breath" (prāṇasya) is because the wheel of winds, which is grasped through the manifold processes of exhalation, inhalation, and so forth, is essentially nothing other than the vital breath itself. || 43 ||
In connection with *prāṇāyāma*, he stimulates the understanding of the reality of the drying, burning, and flooding that are subsequently prescribed:
"Drying is the destruction of impurity; burning is the eradication of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*)."
The bathing of the bodies is a purification produced by the sprinkling of the nectar of knowledge. || 44 ||
For the officiants (*arcaka*), at the very commencement of their worship, a certain form of transcendental state (*alaukikatā*) must be produced;

and that culminates in the removal of the coating of impurities (*malopalepa*). In this regard, what is called the "drying up" of their bodies refers to the drying up of that impurity which is dependent upon them—the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that serves as the cause for the sprouting of *saṃsāra*.

Only emaciation is described. Furthermore, what is called "burning" (dāha) is the very nature of the removal of those impurities—their latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—which persist as the essence of their residual traces (*saṃskāra*).
Likewise, "bathing" (*āplāvana*) also arises through its inseparable connection with the dispelling of ignorance.

Because it bestows the joy characterized by the attainment of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*), that knowledge which is the awakening to one’s own self acts as nectar; the purification (*śuddhi*) or sanctification (*pavitrīkaraṇa*) is that which is fashioned by the continuous, flowing stream of its expansion. As has been stated by my supreme gurus in the *Śrīkramavāsanā*:
"I resort to the body of the sovereign of conceptual thought for the purpose of attaining the purity of the true nature of consciousness through processes such as drying.
This is the intended meaning: for those who worship, [the process] first occurs by way of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Through the contemplation of identity with the wind-element, which has become a living being, the capacity for both burning and flooding— which will be performed hereafter— is produced. Subsequently,
by means of the reflective awareness of supreme subjectivity (*paramapramātṛtā*), their limited subjectivity (*avacchinnapramātṛtā*) dissolves.
There is no utility for the burning of the self. As it is said in the venerable *Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka*:
"One should contemplate one's own city as scorched by the fire of time arising from the station of time; at the end, the appearance of peace arises. Thus.

Thereafter, in order to consolidate that very state, there arises the experience of being drenched by the immersion in the flood of the nectar of the great object of knowledge (*mahāprameya*), which consists of the moonlight of the bliss of extraordinary egoity (*alaukikāhantā*). As it has been said in that very same work:
"One should contemplate the entire world or one's own body as filled with one's own bliss;
simultaneously, by means of that very nectar of one's own, one becomes composed of supreme bliss.
Thus, ultimately, through valid authority, there is the experience of the state of equilibrium between light and bliss (*prakāśānanda-sāmarasya*).
The *Bhūtaśuddhi* is thus the Upaniṣad. It is indeed called the "unworldly creation. As it is said in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:
"Even within this very world, for those possessed of devotion..."
"The world exists as something entirely different, abundant with the manifestation of joy.
And as it is said in the *Stotrabhaṭṭāraka*:
"The supreme state is one in which light and bliss have become merged within."
And as it was said by me myself in the *Śrīkomalavallīstava*:

"O Caṇḍī! You shine in the heart of some initiate as a wonder consisting of consciousness—overflowing with floods of nectar in a state of equal flavor, like a rain of fire directed toward every side. (44)
Now he presents the essential nature of the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the water offering (*arghya*), purification, the flowers, and so forth:
"The reflective awareness of the entire range of conceptual constructions through non-conceptuality is the armor of the limbs;
the water offering is the play of the object of knowledge; the flowers are the states that nourish one's own true nature. (45)

For, regarding the limbs— which consist of parts such as hands and feet— appearing as distinct effects, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) by means of a single Self that has entered into the body as their cause, through the method of shattering all conceptual constructions.
This is called the deposition of the limbs (*bhavāṅganyāsa*). Thus, it culminates in this:

by means of a certain non-conceptual state, whose nature is the cultivation of the full sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), [one sublates] the manifold proliferation (*prapañca*) of conceptual agitation characterized by hands, feet, and so forth.

Regarding "contemplation" (*vimarśana*): as stated by our supreme gurus in the *Śrīkramavāsanā*: "I perform a purification of the two hands consisting of consciousness, which effects the state of the fingers as the effect contemplated within the causal Self."
"I contemplate the emergence of the existing powers of omniscience and so forth within the Self, the Lord, through the application of the ritual of the six limbs.
And that [contemplation] is called the "armoring" (*sannāha*) of the limbs, by which the blow from the weapon of the manifestation of duality is warded off.
It is thus refuted. Now, he describes the purity of the *arghya* (offering water), which is uniquely suited to his own established doctrine:
"The *arghya* is the play of the altar" (*vedyavilāsa*). Indeed, worship (*pūjā*) as previously established is called *arghya*.
That which is worthy of it—a certain extraordinary liquid substance—is the *arghya*.
That which bestows maturity upon the loving words of the innocent, which shakes off all trepidation during the act of love-making,
and in which all the deities moving in their celestial chariots take delight— [that is the sound of the flute].
There, that honeyed nectar instantly brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, [the deity] is installed as having the sole purpose of satisfying the deity within one's own heart, through the threefold division of external, internal, and both; and that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), should be understood as the play (*vilāsa*) of the object of knowledge (*vedya*). Of this object of knowledge, which is characterized by the expansion of all conceptual constructions (*viśvavikalpa*), that which...

The term "play" (*vilāsa*) is a figurative expression for the fact that even in a state of contraction, there is no transcendence of the totality of one's respective inherent nature; in reality, however, it results in the conclusion that the object of knowledge itself, possessing such play, is the substance of the offering (*arghyadravya*). Of that...

Since the pentad of gross elements, beginning with earth, is inseparable from the pentad of qualities characterized by sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, and because it is merely sustained by entering into the gross state of these qualities,
it follows that the entire agitation of the universe flashes forth within that very [ground].

Furthermore, this [consciousness] is earth because it is the locus established within one's own heart; it is water because it provides internal nourishment to that very [heart]; it is fire because of its boldness in burning away the fetters of past latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
and it is air by virtue of imparting the movement of the reality of self-awareness.
Wind, because it culminates in pure consciousness alone, is determined to be "space" (vyoman);

and because it is the collective nature of the five elements beginning with earth, it is understood to be the very play of the universe. Its refinement and its application will be set forth immediately hereafter.

Having thus explained that particular substance which is skilled in offering its own essence for the satisfaction of the Self among external objects, he states the nature of the flowers and so forth, which are to be accepted as its adjuncts:
"Flowers are entities that nourish one's own nature. That which is one's own nature (*svasya yo bhāvaḥ*)...

The aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) is defined as having the nature of the deity to be worshipped; the flowers have the purpose of nourishing that [wonder] through the establishment of such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).
The intended meaning is that they are called "flowers" (*puṣpa*) based on the etymological derivation: "those which nourish the essential nature" (*svabhāvam puṣyanti*).

This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Consequently, by the word "flower" (*puṣpa*), there is the inclusion of all substances—both external and internal—that nourish one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
As it was stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda in the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstravimarśinī*:

"By means of flowers" refers to all substances, both external and internal, which nourish the heart precisely because they offer their own essential nature within the heart. For fragrance is a quality that is said to consist of the very manifestation of the entire phenomenal world. As it was stated by me myself:
In the *Śrīpādukodaya*:
"The abiding of all causes within their respective functions occurs through non-destruction, by virtue of their not abandoning their own nature."
The relationship between cause and effect, which pertains to Śiva, Śakti, and the rest,
having been attained through the successive lineage, all comes to rest in the earth.

"Therefore, the earth consists of the universe, and its fragrance is likewise composed of that [universe]. Furthermore, the organ that perceives it must be the perceiver of the entire universe. Thus, by being animated by such qualities as fragrance, the term "flower" (puṣpa) implies the inclusion of all ritual implements.
This has been well said. Likewise, in the venerable *Triṃśikāśāstra*:
"Then one should worship with fragrant flowers according to one's capacity. (45)

Thus, having set aside from among the substances taken in common both worldly and transcendental that specific substance which, according to the second position, is the object of all the senses, he says the following in order to examine it by means of its refinement and application:

We proclaim the complete libation of the *kula-bindu*, purified by the manifestation of the mantra, which stirs the agitation of the sprouts of all dualistic constructions at the mouth of full egoity. (46)

Indeed, what is called *kula* is the Blessed Lord, the most venerable Master himself, whose nature is the manifestation of the group of knowables (*vedya*). In that context, his "drops" (*bindu*) are the vibrations of power (*śakti-parispanda*) which manifest sequentially as parts and wholes. By means of these—
We say—and by this we mean we reflect—that the propitiation of the deity is being performed in this manner.

The use of the plural number is intended to proclaim the excellence of the extraordinary ego-sense (*alaukikāhaṅkāra*) of those who contemplate in this way. And the manner of this recitation is as follows:
There is no other Supreme Person distinguished by being a remnant of you;
you alone are the Great Person, the sole refuge of all beings.

Thus, according to the principle of the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*, having established even the subjects (*pramātṛs*)— who are delimited by the categories of the manifold of objects (*prameya-prapañca*)— within the class of the knowable (*vedya-varga*), that reality which is "I" (*aham*), transcending all contraction, and that which is—
I am the vital breath and the mind; I am also considered the ego-sense.
I am the intellect, I am power, and I am that Lord Śiva.
What is the use of much talk regarding this world of moving and non-moving beings?
Whatever object is established by valid means of knowledge, that is I, abiding as the Self of all.

Thus, according to the system of the *Śrī Haṃsabhedatantra*, [the Self] is contemplated as the form in which the entire phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) manifests; and according to the system of the *Śrī Śivasūtras*, with the sole aim of extracting its essential nature— that "consciousness is the Self" and "exertion (*udyama*) is Bhairava"— it is so understood.
The great radiance being conveyed by means of that [body]—

the "face" of that [radiance], which is synonymous with one's own self-deity, refers to one's own body as the locus, being the point of commencement for the expansion of consciousness through the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth.

When this is reflected upon, according to the method of the Upaniṣads, there is indeed nothing whatsoever that is not food for one who knows thus; for [the Self] exists as the subtle cause of the entire range of effects, acting as the sprout from which all the conceptual constructions existing within the universe arise.

The meaning is that those specific artistic capacities (*kalā*) which are emerging should nourish the universe— which consists of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and is of the nature of the play of His vibration— by means of worshipping the Supreme Lord, who is one's own self consisting of consciousness.
According to the principle of the *Śrīśāmbhavadīpikā*, the object characterized by distraction (*vikṣepa*) is indeed the nature of the internal oblation (*antarhoma*).
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows:
we call such a form of libation (*tarpaṇa*) "distraction. And that libation—

"Purified by the delineation of mantra" (mantrollekhaviśuddham): Mantra is indeed a certain particular form of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose nature will be described later. By means of that "delineation"—which is characterized as an intensification consisting of the penetration into identity with one's own self—[the reality is purified] through the refinement of the sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*).

It is pure, meaning it has reached the excellence of a supramundane experience established through the complete elimination of all prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For this very reason, it is called "perfect merit" (*pūrṇapuṇya*). Indeed, that is the ultimate pinnacle of purification, [unattainable] by those bound souls (*paśu*) who are stained by the impurity of the blemish of duality.
Not only is it impossible even to touch it, but on the contrary,

those who are incapable of reaching that state engage in its censure; according to the maxim that "those who are unable to reach a place revile it," this [state] is even censured for the fact that it dares to purify even that which is otherwise impure.
What doubt can there be regarding its inherent purity? As it is stated in the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*:

"Then, one should sprinkle with water consecrated by reciting the name of Śiva an infinite number of times all the offerings, such as flowers and so forth, in their proper order, as well as the liṅga or the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*)."
Also in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"Everything touched by droplets of water from the *arghya* vessel becomes purified;
what other purification could there be than that which comes from contact with the rays of the sun that is Śiva? Thus it is said.
And therefore:
Whatever comes forth in whatever manner attains fullness by virtue of its heart-pleasing quality;
in that very way it is fit for the worship of the Supreme Lord—there is no other characteristic here.

Thus, according to the principle of the *Śrījñānendukaumudī*, the essential meaning is this: the supreme gratification of the Supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*) consists precisely in the enjoyment of wine, meat, women, and so forth, which is traditionally taught as liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). As it is said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
For attachment to sexual intercourse, intoxicants, and meat is generally observed in all living beings, though it appears more intensely in some individuals at certain times.
If that instruction is imparted to them preceded by a display of renunciation and zeal, it does not take root in their minds even in the slightest degree.
Beginning with these words:
"With this very intention, for the sake of perceiving the Supreme Brahman here,
women, wine, and meat are especially the foremost objects of worship."
Thus far. || 46 ||
Now, one might object: "Just as the nature of the worship under discussion has been extracted and described, so too should the form of the deity be established.
In response to this expectation, he speaks in order to manifest that very nature:
Whatever meditative state one cultivates, that indeed becomes one's deity;
for images, when permeated by that very state of being, bear fruit accordingly according to one's desire. 47.
For those who worship, the so-called deity who is the object of worship is not something other than the cognizing subjects themselves; rather,
among them,
for each individual, that very state which is characterized by the vibration of their own heart is the deity.
It must be so, and not of the nature of images made of clay, stone, copper, iron, cloth, wood, and the like;

for between the insentient and the sentient, it is observed that independence— characterized by being the motivator of purposeful action such as rejection or acquisition— belongs solely to the non-insentient Self, while objects such as pillars and jars are insentient.

Indeed, the very nature of deities consists in this much: being the accomplishers of what is desired and the preventers of what is undesired. If that [nature] does not exist in them by their own right, then on what basis is this prideful arrogance of images—this ceremonial enthronement with the title of "deity"—founded?
And that sovereignty, of the nature described above, does not transcend the essential nature of consciousness.
And as for its being that very nature— O Amareśa, though you are worshipped incessantly by the great ones, you remain essentially of the same form as the worshipper.
Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*, this [realization] is consistent with those very subjects (*pramātṛ*);

we have stated more than once that our conviction is that the deity is none other than the manifestation of one's own glorious self (*śrīsvātmaprakāśa*). As it has been said in the *Śrījñānendukaumudī*:
"For what could they worship as insentient, having abandoned this sentient self?
As it has been said in the *Nayasamgati*:
"There is no mantra higher than the Nāda; there is no deity higher than one's own self."
"There is no worship higher than *anusandhi*, nor is there any fruit greater than satisfaction.
And as it says in the *Gītā-niṣyanda*:
"Those who, having abandoned self-concentration (*ātma-samādhāna*), meditate upon other deities..."
"They beg for abundant wealth, yet even after begging, they remain hungry. Thus,

because the perceivers (pramātṛs), by means of the limiting condition (upādhi) consisting of the state of being a worshiper, maintain the manifestation of distinct duality, [the Lord] says "of whomsoever" and so forth regarding entities (bhāva).

Divinity is manifested by way of establishing its abundance, as they say: "Whatever form one desires, that very form becomes the form of the deity. For this very reason, the Bahvṛcas declare: "The Bountiful One (Maghavan) becomes every single form. But in the primary sense...

The essential meaning is this: because every distinction of state ultimately results in nothing but identity with the Light (prakāśa), the single nature of the Heart’s manifestation is the sole deity to be worshipped as such throughout the entire phenomenal world (prapañca). It is not, however, an insentient object such as an image or a book. By this, [the author establishes] the yoga of contemplation (bhāvayoga).
Thus, the word *yoga* has been explained here. For *yoga* is such a power (*śakti*). As it is said in the *Śrīśacīmata*:
"O Goddess of gods, you are *yoga*; and I am the eternal *yogin*."
"By yoga, this entire universe is pervaded by you, Śambhu, and by me.
Also, in the *Śrī Bhagavad Gītā*: "Behold my divine yoga. Therefore, the deity is none other than the Great Light itself, which is introduced by the words "having bowed" (*ṇami ūṇa*) and so forth.

It is thus stated that the insentient phenomenal world is the unfolding of one's own self-manifestation, which is dependent on the impetuous outburst of this very freedom (*svātantrya*). Accordingly, in the *Śrīpūrva* [Mālinīvijayottara-tantra]:
"Having abandoned everything else, one should fix the mind upon this."
One should not worship a *liṅga* made of clay, stone, gems, or similar materials.
"One should worship the Liṅga consisting of consciousness, wherein the moving and the non-moving are dissolved.
And as it is said in the Śrīprabhākula:
"Behold the power of delusion, even though Śaṅkara resides within one's own heart!"
"In the linga, on the sacrificial ground, in fire, and in water, they behold Śiva as he truly is.
And therefore:
"Indeed, with his mind turned away from women, Maheśvara, out of anger, burned the god of love (Puṣpaketu)."
Even then, surely that same wisdom was his; truly, O Mother, you are called "the Fortunate One."

Thus, according to the established tradition of the *Śrīkomalavallīstava*, because the illumination of one's own heart is far more praiseworthy than the illumination of the universe, there is no disagreement on this point: that the deity is of the nature of one’s own self, consisting of the consciousness of auspiciousness (*saubhāgyasaṃvit*). As it has been said:
"One's own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose form is the universe.
This should be reflected upon in works such as the *Śrīmad-Ṛjuvimarśinī* composed by our supreme guru.
And thus, when there is a firm rooting in such reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), of that [self] which has been established as the deity—

The "being" (bhāva) of an entity refers to its existence (sattā), which is synonymous with its manifestation; by that [existence], those images— which possess the forms of Skanda, Gaṇapati, Vaṭuka, and so forth, and consist of specific arrangements of clay, stone, and other materials— are "infused," meaning they are colored [by consciousness] until their own hearts are made manifest.
They bestow upon those worshippers whatever desired object they seek, foremost among which are sons and wealth.
As it is stated in the *Śrīpūrva*:
"Since the status of being a *liṅga* for the external *liṅga* is presided over by this [internal one]."
"Therefore, one who has taken refuge in supreme non-duality (paramādvaita) should worship this.
Likewise, in the Siddhānta as well:
"Having firmly bound the internal liṅga, one should then worship the external liṅga."
With this in mind, it is said in the *Śrīmat-Stotrāvalī*:

"Even while worshipping with the words 'Salutation to me, who am Śiva,' one whose eyes are closed in the savoring of the wonder of internal devotion would [regard] even blades of grass as [the deity]."
Thus it has been said. And in that regard, there is no difference whatsoever between these images and the principal deity of one's own heart, such that—
by the principle of a metal transmuted by an alchemical elixir— the firmness of attaining its very nature would not arise here.

And as it is said in the *Śrī-Virūpākṣapañcāśikā*: "Whatever purpose a deity accomplishes, for one who seeks that purpose and firmly maintains the ego-identification with her, that purpose is attained in an instant. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the fact that meditation (bhāvanā) yields its fruit as if it were primary is stated in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"Even a mere mental construction is not false, for even a fruit residing in Śiva arises from such things as the meditation on Garuḍa."
Thus [ends the verse]. 47.
Now, in order to provide an illustration for the sake of making it easy for people who understand to grasp this extraction of the deity's form as thus presented, he says:
"The painter does not paint the picture; look, he paints that which is the picture."
Therefore, tell me where it is appropriate for both of you to direct your perception toward them as deities. (48)

A person who doubts whether an object is insentient or sentient, and wonders if it is a deity, should be enlightened in this way: namely, that with respect to an insentient entity such as a man or woman depicted in a painting, there is no [recognition] of another belonging to that same class.
The capacity for such an act of carving is not observed in anything else;

on the contrary, it is possible only for a conscious being who possesses a distinct nature and excels in the skill of crafting such art—this process is beyond dispute. To make this stated point resonate with the heart:

"Behold! it is said. The repetition of the word "picture" (*citram*), apart from the reference to its behavior and so forth, is intended to clearly demonstrate the capacity and incapacity of the sentient and the insentient. Therefore—because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)... [the conclusion follows].
It is volition alone that possesses the agency for the aforementioned action, and not anything else distinct from it;
for that reason, consider and reflect: between these two—the painting and the painter—which one is rightly understood to be the deity?
Even children undoubtedly perceive this aspect,

namely that from the diversity of effects such as paintings, there exists a certain excellence characterized by sovereignty— according to the principle that among makers such as painters, there is a "sovereign maker"— because this meaning is extremely clear.

Even though a position has been determined, it is not presented in its final, definitive form. By this it is stated that the status of being a deity belongs primarily to the conscious [Self] alone, whereas for objects of consciousness, it is attributed through metaphorical transference (*upacāra*) because they are the locus of its penetration. For this very reason, they are called "other deities."
As it is said in the Śrī Gītā:
"Even those who are devotees of other deities and worship them, endowed with faith— they too, O Kaunteya, worship me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule."

Regarding the Supreme Lord, who is being established as the Divine, the fact that the manifold variety of the universe is like a painting is explained by the very word "painting" (*citra*). Thus it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Like the even surface of a wall for the painting of the manifold variety of the universe.
And as it is said in the *Padasaṃgati*:
"In its own limb consisting of the space of consciousness, which brings about the painting of the universe..."
"Salutation to the one who is the source of the arising of all wonders, the one with the uneven eye.
Likewise, there is the saying of the learned:
"Having painted the variegated world within himself by means of the brush of his own self..."

"Having beheld that himself, the Supreme Lord rejoices. By this manner of expression beginning with "He does not paint a picture," it is meant that the mind—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—does not paint [itself] as if it were an object of knowledge (*prameya*); rather, the "picture" is the aforementioned mind, which is a distinct internal organ.

This should also be understood in accordance with the path of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, *cit* means the conscious; its state is *cittva*, which is consciousness (*caitanya*). That *cittva* is not a distinct entity of a similar nature—either as a mind (*citta*) in the form of an object of knowledge (*prameya*), or as *cittva* in the form of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—which has the nature of cognition (*jñapti*).
The meaning is consistent with the category of phenomena characterized by valid cognition, such as "he writes" or "he does not open [his eyes]," and so forth.
Thus, when these three meanings are considered, since the state of consciousness alone reaches the pinnacle of praiseworthiness, this is also for the purpose of experiencing wonder and amazement.

The word *citra* (variegated/marvelous) should be understood as being used in its ultimate sense (*pāryantika*), since its referent has already been expressed by the pronoun itself. Furthermore, the root *likh* (to write/draw) is used not only in the sense of producing something but also in the sense of bringing something to a conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), as in the expression "the royal [seal] is to be engraved with iron. A meaning consistent with that should also be introduced as threefold. And this threefold nature is as follows:

This is because of the simultaneous utterance (*tantra*) of the synonyms for the consciousness of the internal organ within that painting—the various mental states and the nature of consciousness itself. || 48 ||

Now, if there is such insistence that one's own self alone is the deity, then what benefit does this [deity] receive from the elaboration of mantras, tantras, and so forth? For indeed, those [mantras and tantras] are accepted for the purpose of being directed toward a deity distinct from oneself.
Anticipating this objection, [the author states that] the mantra, first of all, conforms precisely to the deity of the aforementioned nature.

He states the conclusion: "The meaning of the word 'mantra' is a certain ineffable experience (*anubhūti*): in its own expansive power, it consists of reflection (*manana*); in its own contraction, it consists of protection from fear; and it has swallowed all conceptual constructions of the universe. (49)

"Mantras are so called because their nature is to protect through reflection"—such is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*). In that regard, for one who investigates the mantra, there are two states: expansion (*vibhava*) and contraction (*saṅkoca*), which arise through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of mere will.
Of these two, "expansion" is as follows:

Expansion is the cultivation of the state of full selfhood (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*) through the method of the aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) of all things with that which transcends them; this is what is called supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*). Contraction, on the other hand, is its opposite—the conceit of incompleteness—which is designated as the state of bondage (*pāśava*). And in this regard:

The distinction is that the former is innate (*svābhāvika*) while the latter is superimposed (*āropita*). This being the case, when such an expansion of the Self unfolds, the repeated contemplation (*manana*) of it, as well as the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) whose nature consists in a continuous thread of reflective awareness (*parāmarśānusyūti*), arises by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*). It is the same in the aforementioned form.
When one's own contraction is presented, that which protects from it is as follows:
when this contraction is investigated, because it shines forth as identical with consciousness (*cidaikātmyena*), it is composed of consciousness alone; otherwise, it would be nothing at all.
Thus, according to the principle of the *Śrīpratyabhijñāhṛdaya*, even that contraction [is ultimately consciousness].

It is characterized by the removal of the cognitive distress (cākitya) consisting in the contingency of the destruction of one's own essential nature, through the production of a contemplation that penetrates the manifestation of universal selfhood (vaiśvātmya). And becoming identical with that [universal self], by those same two causes, it possesses an unimpeded unfolding that devours the entire essence of the agitation of the object of knowledge (vedya).

That very power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), which is an experience to be known solely within one's own heart, is experienced as the denotable meaning of the word "mantra. As it is said in the *Śrīrājarājabhaṭṭāraka*:
"Mantra is not composed of phonemes; it is neither the body of the ten-armed [Lord] nor even the five-faced [Lord]."
"At the prior limit of conceptualization (saṅkalpa), the resonance of sound (nāda) becomes mantra.
And as it is said in the *Śrī-Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka*: "That meditation which is cultivated again and again within the supreme reality..."
"Recitation, praise, the spontaneous resonance (nāda), and the essence of mantra—such is the nature of that which is to be recited.
And as it is stated in the *Śiva-sūtras*: "The mind is mantra. Also, in the venerable *Stotra-bhaṭṭāraka*:
"The mantra, which is the ray of the withdrawal of the fire of consciousness, arises while dissolving the mental constructs of awareness."
And in the *Śrīkramakela*: "This very Goddess, the deity of consciousness (*saṃviddevī*) who is of such a nature, is the mantra.
Bhaṭṭa Śrī Bhūtirāja has also said: "Because she exists by encompassing everything, the Goddess alone is the mantra. And thus:
A mantra separate from the mantrin never attains success;
all this has its root in knowledge, for otherwise it does not succeed.

According to this principle, it is stated that the primary meaning of the word "mantra" is the very nature of one's own self-awareness (*svātmasaṃvitsvarūpa*); as for the arrangements of syllables, however, it is spoken of only figuratively. As they say:
"Those mantras which are being uttered—do not know them to be mantras."
"Deluded by false knowledge, the gods and Gandharvas are filled with pride.
And as I have said myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"Like the sugar-cane of Puṇḍra, when the mantra possesses a sweetness that touches the heart..."
"The *ṛjīṣa* remains in the mouth, characterized by the utterance of the syllable.
With this very intention, the disciple, contemplating through his intellect the identity of the Guru, the Deity, and the mantra, [should proceed].
Thus the learned declare. By this, *japa* (recitation) is explained. For it is called *japa* because its nature consists in generating and protecting. As it has been stated by our supreme gurus:
"By means of *japa*, which has the quality of generating and protecting, one whose self is turned inward [attains liberation]."
And that [recitation] culminates in the contemplation of one's own manifestation and in the mere withdrawal of oneself.

Recitation is said to be the reflective awareness of the essential nature of the mantra as it has been established. And because the mantra consists of the experience of universal identity, everyone [is engaged in it].
Verbal discourse arises precisely as the nature of reflection upon that [reality].
As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa: "And what speech is not expressed by which? For this very reason, it is stated in the Śrīśivasūtras: "Discourse is japa. (49)

Now, one might ask: "If it is thus established that mantras consist of a supramundane experience, then what is the nature of that collection of sounds—which is their common form, universally undisputed, and perceptible by the sense of hearing?
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] speaks in order to reveal the true nature of the principle of speech (vāktattva) itself:

The activity known as *vaikharī* consists of knowledge; *madhyamā* speech is likewise [knowledge-based]. *Paśyantī*, however, is the subtle *icchā* (will), the state in which all [levels of speech] are of one identical flavor.

The principle of speech (*vāktattva*) is divided, in order, into four types: the subtle (*sūkṣmā*), the visionary (*paśyantī*), the intermediate (*madhyamā*), and the articulated (*vaikharī*). As it is stated in the *Sāmbapañcāśikā*:
"That [power] which, emerging from the abode of Mitra and Varuṇa, [consists of] sixty-three..."
"Through the manifestation of phonemes here due to contact with the vital breath, she gives birth first to Paśyantī; then, abiding in the intellect, she becomes Madhyamā;
and finally, made clear by the organs in the mouth, she attains the state of Vaikharī speech—thus I take refuge. Thus [it is said].

In this context, speech known as *vaikharī* is determined to be the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), because it consists of a manifestation mounted upon the operation of the organs such as the palate. *Madhyamā*, on the other hand, is the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), because it is set in motion solely by the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhi*). *Paśyantī*, moreover, is the power of will (*icchā*).

Because that [parā-vāk] consists in the acceptance of an outward expansion, the etymology of *paśyantī* is derived from the root *paś* (to see), as in "the supreme speech sees. The subtle (*sūkṣmā*) speech, however,
by virtue of the analogy of the fluid within a peacock's egg, has as its nature the state of being a variegated mixture of the three aforementioned types of speech.

The activity characterized by the exertion of the Supreme Lord, who is the inward-looking witness, is called *parā* (the supreme). Furthermore, *parā vāk* (supreme speech) shines forth as it enters into the very nature of that same Supreme Lord.
As has been stated by our supreme gurus in the venerable *Ṛjuvimarśinī*: "Mātṛkā..."

The meaning is that it is consciousness (*saṃvit*), whose nature is the Supreme Lord Anāhata-Bhaṭṭāraka, the essence of the supreme Śiva who is the self of the speech of others, and which is the cause for the emanation of the thirty-six ontological principles (*tattvas*).

And its status as "speech" (*vāk*) arises from the etymological derivation [of the word *vāk*] as the agent in the sense of "it speaks," and not, however, in accordance with its being the object in the sense of "it is spoken."
As it was said by our supreme gurus in the *Śrīsaṃvitstotra*:
"Those who have served you, the highest of gurus, call you the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*), whose manifold nature is undivided from the universe;
they, relying on the etymological derivation that 'speech' (*vāk*) is so called because its essence is self-luminous and ever-new awareness (*vimarśana*)," thus they speak.
Therefore, it is stated that every manifestation of speech is essentially the expansion of the triad of powers beginning with Will (icchā).
As it is said in the *Yoginīhṛdaya*:
"That very power of Will exists in the form of Paśyantī."
The power of knowledge is said to be threefold; it is proclaimed as the middle speech (madhyamā-vāk).
"But this power of action is Raudrī, the Vaikharī, whose body is the universe.
And likewise in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"First Paśyantī, then Madhyamā, and another, Vaikharī—these are they."
The Goddess is both supreme and non-supreme; she is the final one, yet her nature is that of the non-supreme.
"This very triad of powers, beginning with will (icchā), is thus described; it is only when animated by this that worldly activity (vyavahāra) unfolds.
And the radiance of one's own Self (svātmasphurattā) has precisely will and the other powers as its essential nature; it consists of those [powers].

That a certain experience is the meaning of the word "mantra"—all this is consistent. Furthermore, by the transposition of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) in the term *paśyantī*, another meaning is also illuminated:
"There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words."

According to this principle, every nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) ultimately does not transcend the state of being composed of speech (*vāṅmayatā*). Consequently, the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) alone is the vitalizing breath of the Self, whose nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*). And that [power] consists of manifold [acts] such as the recitation of mantras (*mantra-japa*) and worship (*pūjā*).
It becomes expressible by words; the distinction consists solely in the respective means [of expression]. || 50 ||
Now, because it accompanies the mantra, one should understand that there is also a certain extraordinary mudrā; thus he says:

"The glorious radiance of bliss, which has eclipsed the fortune of the eight great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhis)—that very state in which it is perceived is itself all the mudrās of the Lord. (51)

In that state, there is an outpouring toward the bliss characterized by self-rest for the Supreme Lord— who possesses the essential nature of manifold forms of sovereignty such as play and the desire for victory, and who is endowed with the equilibrium of the dual nature of both the worshiped and the worshiper; and likewise...
The splendor (*śrī*) of that [consciousness]— characterized by its manifestation through being perceived and its continuous upward threading— is seen as a fully developed state;
it is undoubtedly made directly manifest, and that very [splendor] is all the *karaṅkiṇī*s and so forth.
It should be understood that those various mudrās, such as Saṃkṣobhiṇī and others, are well-known in other ways as well.
And by means of that splendor of the outburst of bliss, one should become possessed of the fortune of the eight great siddhis in their most subtle form.
For even in the world, the manifestations of power (vibhūti-spandas) are seen in things such as the sword, gorocana, and the designated underworld (pātāla).
These are called *siddhis*. In relation to them, because they are free from even slight contraction, the powers such as *aṇimā* possess the status of "great *siddhis*" (*mahāsiddhi*).
And their number is eight, consisting of those forms that cause the heart of each respective practitioner to rejoice.

This is because the attributes of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, action, experience, memory, and exclusion possess an external manifestation through the medium of the eightfold substrates beginning with Brahmā,
as it is said in the Āgama:
"I bow to her, the Mistress of the eight great Siddhis arising from the eight groups (aṣṭavarga), in whom the eight measures (mātrā) abide through the application of the sequence of the groups.
Although this entry into the group of eight occurs everywhere due to the state of universal identity (sāmarasya), nevertheless, in some places...
Because the predominance of certain [qualities] necessarily occurs in some individuals, there is a well-known tradition regarding the eight great supernatural powers (*aṣṭamahāsiddhi*).
Among these, *aṇimā* is the capacity to make one's own body minute;
*mahimā* is the skill in pervading space and so forth; and [the power to walk] on the waters of the ocean with one's feet...

Lightness (*laghimā*) is the absence of contact with the body during movement. Attainment (*prāpti*) is the acquisition of desired objects. Irresistible power (*prākāmya*) is the state of having unimpeded motion everywhere by mere will. Sovereignty (*īśitṛtva*) is universal lordship. [The power of] enjoyment (*vaśitva*) is the capacity for the enjoyment of sense-objects...

*Vaśitva* (mastery) is the state of being able to take up or discard [objects] according to one's own mere will. *Kāmāvasāyitva* (the power of determining desires) is the distinction wherein there is the immediate experience of heaven, hell, and so forth, by the mere force of one's own longing.
Furthermore, their *saubhāgya* (good fortune) is characterized by the excellence of captivating the hearts of those who practice spiritual realization.

The literal meaning is that by means of the abundance of bliss (*ānanda-sampad*) thus acquired, [everything] is made small, that is, rendered insignificant. This is the underlying sense: by transcending the contractions such as the bending and stretching of hands and feet, one reaches a state comparable to that of a waveless ocean; for that very reason...

It is a certain extraordinary experience—a wealth of bliss—bestowing joy, according to the etymological derivation that it "gives delight" (*mudaṃ rāti*). This experience consists of the activity of reflective awareness, which is synonymous with the wonder of resting in oneself; it is the state wherein all external vibrations of bliss have subsided into its own interior like foam, bubbles, and droplets.
The ground for the arising and dissolution of the manifold expansion of other mudrās, such as Karaṅkiṇī and so forth, should be contemplated as the Mudrā itself. As it is said in the Śrī Paścima:
"That is the accomplishment (siddhi) which is proclaimed as the very essence of accomplishment among all accomplishments."
For gnosis is indeed one and undivided, and the mudrā is one, consisting of the nature of the planets.
"He in whom these two are born is a true follower in the established teaching. Thus, with respect to bliss (*ānanda*),

she is of the nature of the entirety of bliss, consisting of supreme bliss (*parānanda*), joyless bliss (*nirānanda*), great bliss (*mahānanda*), bliss of the object (*viṣayānanda*), and bliss itself (*ānanda-svabhāva*).
The presentation of both "Ullāsa" (Elation) and "Śrī" (Gloriousness) is for the purpose of manifesting *sāmarasya* (the state of aesthetic or spiritual equilibrium).
As it is said in the *Śrīstotrabhaṭṭāraka*: "She whose form consists of waves of bliss from the ocean of the Kaula.
And as it is said in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"That which is beyond, free from afflictions, supreme, great, and absolute in Śiva;
and that which is higher than the sphere of objects—that is your bliss, for you shine forth as its very density.
And in that regard, when those accomplishments (*siddhis*) exist in the form of manifestation...

*Āṇimā* is the capacity for the inclusion of all objects within oneself; likewise, *mahimā* is omnipresence; *laghimā* is the removal of the weightiness of differentiated forms; *prāpti* is the attainment of repose in one's own self; and *prākāmya* is the playful enjoyment of the manifestations of the knowable.
Sovereignty (*īśitṛtva*) consists in possessing unconditioned majesty; mastery (*vaśitva*) is the capacity to sustain all things through the state of being the contemplator;
and the power of determining objects at will (*yatra-kāmāvasāyitva*) is the cultivation of the full sense of "I-ness" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*).
When these are reflected upon as being appropriate to the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmayatva*), then our previously stated sequence of the *mudrās* [is established].
"Entry" (praveśa) does not imply making these [elements] insignificant, as there is no purpose for doing so.

Like mantras, mudrās, and the like, other practices of the practitioner—such as meditation, fire-offerings (homa), and so forth—should also be inferred by oneself in accordance with the non-duality of consciousness (saṃvidadvaita). As it is said in the *Śrīvijñānabhairava*:
Meditation is that steady contemplation which is formless and without support;
meditation is not the conceptualization of the body, face, hands, and so forth.

"In the fire that is the abode of the Great Void, the elements, the senses, the objects of the senses, and so forth, are offered together with the mind by means of the ladle of consciousness; this is the *homa*.
It should be understood that the acceptance of the *kulārghya* is essentially equivalent to the internal *homa*.

As it was said by our supreme gurus in the *Śrīsubhagodaya*: "One who is not oriented toward the external should offer as an oblation into the fire of consciousness— which consists of the supreme I-consciousness and is satiated by the object of cognition— the sacrificial offering characterized by 'this-ness' (*idantā*)."
And as it was said by me myself in the *Mahārthodaya*: "Then, repeatedly offering this [oblation] called 'this-ness' (*idantā*) into the mouth of one's own consciousness,
one should remain at ease like Mount Meru, having transcended the impurity of *māyā*."
Thus, enough of this elaborate exposition for the purpose of revealing the secret. || 51 ||
To establish the purpose of this nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa), which has been demonstrated through such extensive elaboration, he says:
"The great tree of reflective awareness, with its massive branches, is rooted in the station of the Heart."
It blossoms with the glory of enjoyments and bears fruit as the vision of the festival of stainless bliss. || 52 ||
For the "heart" (*hṛdaya*) is indeed a most vast locus because it is the ground upon which the universe is established.
As the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta has stated: "The heart, indeed, is said to be the place of establishment."
And as it is said in the Upaniṣad:
"One should know that heart, the great abode of the universe.
Therein, [the Self] is pre-eminently established, having attained a state of being relished for its own sake.

The cause possesses an infinite variety beginning with the manifestation of differentiation; its excellence consists in its "simultaneous manifestation" (*sakṛdvibhātatva*), which, according to the stated principle, transcends the process of gradual production. For if it were otherwise, even for those endowed with such reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), there would be no attainment of the enjoyment of heaven and the like.
Even when one has attained the mere removal of latent impressions (vāsanā), if one does not remain vigilant,
the obstructing spirits (vināyakas) will join such a person to impermanent enjoyments;
therefore, one should not form attachment to them out of a desire for the highest goal.

By the removal of such terrors as these, a state of total freedom from anxiety arises everywhere; for the consciousness of the Self is by nature the wonder of the aesthetic relish (*camatkāra*) of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of consciousness and bliss.
Upon its expansion, there arise in succession the powers of will, knowledge, and action. And as for action—
For this time is essentially action; action depends upon a grammatical factor (kāraka), and the collection of grammatical factors, being sixfold, resides within the Self as power.

By such reasoning, being of the nature of the factors of action (kāraka) such as the instrument (karaṇa) and the locus (adhikaraṇa), she manifests sequentially as the effect. As it is said in the *Śrītantravaṭadhānikā*:
"The vibration of her own self is the will (*krayā*); from that arises the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and then that which is produced by it."
"This diversity of time is not, indeed, anything beyond the vibration of consciousness.
And the effect, being manifold through its status as the object of injunctions and prohibitions,
is variegated by the agitation of thousands of conceptual distinctions, such as various substances and qualities divided by their respective internal differences.

It culminates as the entirety of all remaining worldly transactions; thus, this is merely the expansive manifestation of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*). And such is this [power], which, by virtue of sustaining the totality of thousands of paths of external and internal cognition, [is the source of all].

The aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose essence consists in the self-recognition of the subject characterized as the reflector; it is that which is determined to be like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpaśākhī*), possessing the skill of bestowing every single desired object without exception. And that...
For those persons who know their own true nature, [this state] flourishes with the glory of enjoyment; that is, it brings forth the splendor of enjoyment, which stands in the place of a flower.

For enjoyment is the experience of external opulence, such as embracing a beloved woman and so forth. And its very glory is this: that one who transgresses injunctions and prohibitions [is thus empowered].

Through the auspiciousness of savoring the non-duality of consciousness, one becomes proficient in the means for awakening to the unfolding of one's own self, which arises precisely from the perception of the curiosity toward the grasped and the grasper; such is the very nature of the attainment of liberation.

By this, it is experienced. Furthermore, that tree of conceptualization known as *vimarśa* [is that] bliss which is devoid of the stain of *kalā*—characterized by the division, interruption, or limitation of the stainless distinction between "I" (*ahaṃ*) and "this" (*idam*)—which has the nature of resting in itself and is the joy of one's own heart. That...
Thus, while Indra enjoys this festival upon the slope of Śacī’s breast, he becomes a worm wallowing in hell;
both possess an identical mental state— how strange is the delusion of latent impressions!

According to this principle (*ityādinyāyāt*), in order to exclude that superimposition of happiness which is merely imagined by the mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*) of the hearts of particular individuals who experience it, [this was taught] by many lords of yogins (*yogīndra*), such as Śrī Śivānanda and Mahāprakāśa Maheśvarānanda.

Because it is experienced through collective consensus (*saṃbhūyasaṃvāda*), it brings forth such a form of festivity as light (*āloka*) and inward radiance (*pratyakprakāśa*). Furthermore, regarding the term *niṣkala* (partless), the word *kalā*—
derived from the etymology "it measures" (*kalayati*) or "it delimits externally by means of limitation" (*pārimityena paricchinatti*)— refers either to the power of *māyā*.

It is manifoldly described as either the pentad of sheaths (pañcakañcukī) characterized by the reinforcement of limited agency; or the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of the presiding deities of the classes [of letters], such as Brāhmī and the others; or the Mātṛkā who is presided over by them;
or its own contraction, characterized by the non-recognition of its own fullness.
