It should be explained as follows:

"I am the Supreme Lord, possessing supreme sovereignty, whose essential nature is the contemplation of the manifold variety of the universe"— this [realization] must reach the point of becoming fully integrated within one's heart.

This reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is being cultivated and is expert at encompassing the manifestation of all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca-vikalpa*), accomplishes even the two-fold human goal characterized by enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) for yogins who have realized the nature of the self as it has been explained. And therein—
For that autonomous enjoyer, this very unification with the object of enjoyment is itself enjoyment; it is itself liberation; it is itself the supreme state.

Thus, according to the method of the *Śrīprabodhapañcadaśikā*, even enjoyment (*bhoga*) is of the nature of liberation (*mokṣa*), and liberation is also of the nature of enjoyment; the fruit of this [teaching] is *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living), which consists in the mutual fusion of these two and is achievable solely through the doctrine of the non-duality of the venerable supreme consciousness (*adanuttarasaṃvidadvaita*). As it has been said by the venerable Tadeva:

"O Goddess! For one by whose will the liberation while living (jīvanmukti) of the virtuous may occur in an instant, I shall declare to him the Divine Current (divyaugha) for the further increase of that liberation while living.
Even a tree, having grown from some excellent seed-bed and flourishing with many branches...

It produces both flower and fruit. Even there, by way of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), the existence of the fruit resides in the flower; and even in the fruit, because it does not abandon the nature of its cause, the connection with the flower persists—thus the flower is the fruit, and the fruit is also [the flower].

The phrase "it is indeed a flower" is the manner in which discerning people reflect upon it; and its status as a tree is stated based on its renown in the scriptures, as it is said in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:
"It bestows various fruits that transcend the stage of mere prayer."

"Victorious is Śiva, the wish-fulfilling tree, whose unprecedented history is such as has been described. And thus, disregarding the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of this very nature, the doctrine of external non-duality lies prostrate upon the bed of the scriptures of the bound (*pāśava*). For instance:
The establishment of the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda) is also found within the Vedāntas;
therein, there exists a certain transcendent Self characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).
He alone shines as reality— pure, free from egoism,
without beginning or end, peaceful, and the ground of the universe’s creation and dissolution.
By virtue of its nature consisting of pure consciousness, it is devoid of the states of existence and non-existence;
bearing self-luminosity, it is described as eternally liberated.
All this is consistent; however, it is not tenable that the non-agency of that Self, the Lord, is equivalent to its lack of deliberation.
And that power of his to act, which does not transcend its own nature,
functions as common to both the roots "to know" (jānāti) and "to do" (karoti).
Even that action would be knowledge, which is said to be a property of the knower;
thus, because it has the nature of an agent, its knowledge is also an action.
The desire for these two is their orientation toward manifestation; this entire universe is their unfolding.
Therefore, we declare that reflective awareness (vimarśa) is the very nature of the Lord.

These are indeed its synonyms: power (*śakti*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), exertion (*udyama*), vibration (*spanda*), autonomy (*svatantratā*), manifestation (*sphūrti*), wave (*ūrmi*), vigor (*ojas*), and digit (*kalā*).
Thus, enough of this fickle indulgence in chewing over what has already been chewed.
Now, an objection might be raised: "Surely the state of being a Great Lord (māheśvarya), characterized as liberation while living (jīvanmukti), has been established as his fruit;

yet that is not possible, because others maintain the dogmatic view that the attainment of liberation for persons occurs only at a time distinct from the limitation of the body. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
If he is a gradualist and not a god, how could there be for him any contact with the impurity of death?
And even for one who is eternally unobscured, what obstacle to liberation can there be while living? (53)

For the one called "Deva" (the Shining One) is the Supreme Lord whose essence is the universe, because he possesses the skill to bring about various meanings such as illumination by means of fashioning the offering of the consciousness of his own nature toward the manifold play of space, time, and so forth.
Thus it is determined. Therefore, this [reality] is not sequential;

it is not traversed by a sequence consisting of the conceptual construction of distinctions such as priority and posteriority. For, in the Blessed One, there prevails the intense outpouring of the single expansion of universal selfhood.

"Having moved, where will you go, since everything is composed of Śiva? By this reasoning, when one reflects upon logic, the only answer for an opponent is silence—silence regarding whose distinctness from whom could exist, and the sequence caused thereby. Thus it is.
"Succession belongs to my cognizer and so forth, which are sequential, but consciousness itself is both with and without succession.
According to this principle from the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*, for one who is unacquainted with the discourse on succession, contact with the stain known as "time" is impossible in any way whatsoever.
Because time, in its ultimate reality, culminates precisely in succession; as it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"Time is the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, or the birth of various flowers and other phenomena."

"Whether it be cold or heat, that very sequence is its true nature. By the word *kalmaṣa* (impurity/affliction), this is revealed: that time (*kāla*) is also a certain power of the Supreme Lord, by which He Himself is not delimited; on the contrary, it is by this [power] that the universe is delimited.

There is no impurity in Him characterized by the limitation of time; rather, this [Self] is traditionally taught to be eternal because He encompasses that very time within His own nature. Likewise, His pervasiveness is to be inferred from His lack of spatial limitation. Thus, of His own self—
By the logic of being an all-encompassing veil, even though [the Self] is at all times unobstructed by anything else,
that specific state consisting of contact with the vital breath, the body, and so forth is established as a defect;
it constitutes an obstacle to liberation, which consists in the attainment of the bliss of consciousness known as self-reflection.
A certain obstacle in the form of a counter-argument, whose nature is otherwise considered impossible, is raised by others;

what is it? Nothing at all would be tenable if one were to investigate the reality of reasoning. However, if "livingness" (*jīvatva*) is indeed a specific conceptual construct (*vikalpa*) of the self, while [the goal] is non-conceptual experience (*nirvikalpānubhūti*), [then no such obstacle arises].

If it is argued that these two [definitions] are mutually non-contradictory because they constitute the meaning of the word "liberation" (mokṣa), then the same resolution applies to the case of the separation of the vital breath from the body; for this is what is meant:
upon the attainment of consciousness-bliss, even while the body and other such things are still being perceived.
"Jīvanmukti is the firm realization of identity with Consciousness alone"—
according to the principle of the *Śrī Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya*,
this liberation while living, characterized by the direct experience of the state of aesthetic-spiritual equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between enjoyment and liberation, is entirely mine.

"Vibhava" (manifestation) is the very nature of subjects whose sovereign powers are kindled by the contemplation of their own universal selfhood; it is not some adventitious excellence. As I have stated myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"The universe is His form; the Vaikharī [speech] is the garland of His names; His sovereignty transcends space and time;
for His devotees, there is freedom of movement, worship according to one's own will, scripture as one desires, and one's own innate nature is liberation. Thus it is said.
Therefore, what is the basis for this distressing insistence on a restriction of time regarding him?

For this alone is its distinction from other philosophical systems, namely, that which is called the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) in the simultaneous experience of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). As it is said by the venerable Ratnadeva:
"Enjoyment as well as liberation do not exist apart from the single reality;
both enjoyment and liberation, O Goddess, are proclaimed to be specific aspects [of that one].
And as it is said in the *Śrīsiddhāmata*:
The six paths and initiation are known as the Śiva-scripture;
in the scripture named Bhairava, initiation is the path, and enjoyment is fearlessness.
Thus [ends section] 53.

Now, one might object: "Liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is the experience of the festival of one's own bliss, occurring without distinction across all states of the self that is permeated by birth, death, and so forth. How could this be consistent with the position that such [experience] lacks stability? Anticipating this doubt, [the author addresses] precisely the doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅga).
To refute this, he says:
Is there anything whatsoever that does not exist in some form, somewhere, or by some means?
Therefore, the Self is eternally stable; it is only momentary destruction that is unstable. || 54 ||

In this context, indeed, the established rule is that the universe is the object of illumination and the Self is the illuminator. Therein, its status as an object of illumination exists solely through the power of its contact with illumination. And that contact—

Therefore, the fusion of multiple forms is indeed their identity (*aikātmya*). Thus, through the establishment of the relationship [between them], the process unfolds until it reaches the identity of the manifestor and the manifested. And if one were to accept that light (*prakāśa*) possesses merely the status of being a property of the object—

The apprehension of an object would be contradicted by the claim that it depends upon a subject; consequently, everything would manifest to everyone, or else nothing at all would manifest, and thus the entire worldly transaction (*viśvavyavahāra*) would collapse.
Therefore, the statement "the object manifests" means that the object experiences the state of being a manifester.

As it has been stated in the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhivimarśinī*: "The manifestation of cognition as 'this is my knowledge' is not direct; rather, [the direct manifestation] is 'I know,' which is precisely the cognition's resting within the referent of the 'I' (*asmadartha*). And such being the case for this...
Since being contained within manifestation is necessarily so, the identity of the universe and its manifestor, the Self, is unavoidable. For by accepting this,
the Supreme Lord’s characteristic of not looking to any other face is established.

It experiences sovereignty and appropriateness; otherwise, if it were characterized by independence from other deities of the same class, the blemish of limitation would necessarily follow. In this regard, it must be asked: is that which is in question of the nature of an entity or of a non-entity?

Whether an entity exists or not—be it at any time, such as the present or the future, or in any location, such as one that is in front or not near—it exists by means of some homogeneous nature or a divisible essence; or else it does not exist. First of all, it cannot be said that it does not exist.

To say that [it does not exist] would entail the consequence of its being empty; and the position that phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is empty has already been refuted previously. Therefore, it must be said that whatever object exists indeed exists.
And since this Self manifests as having that very nature, how can its instability be asserted? This...

The state of being: even if one accepts that the Self possesses the form of the universe and acknowledges the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) of all entities existing within the universe, that which is called "momentary destruction" is nonetheless an objective reality that cannot be denied; and by that much alone, the Self is composed of that [destruction].

Stability is unagitated; how much more so when stability is being attributed to the universe as a whole? Furthermore, the course of worldly affairs is accomplished through the synthesis of multiple cognitions characterized by direct experience, its conceptualization, and recollection—as in such instances as "See the pillar! or "Bring the jar! and so forth.
This is because there is the inevitable occurrence of the experience and recollection of the conventions regarding the meanings of various words.
As it has been said in the *Apohavāda*:
"For the sake of linguistic usage, an investigation into the meaning of a word is introduced."
"For that very purpose, both the convention and the understanding thereof are maintained.

Furthermore, it is impossible for those cognitions to possess the capacity for mutual reflection, because all of them are self-luminous; and if that were the case, it would be improper for there to be a reference to another [cognition].
Since there exists no one endowed with stability who is capable of synthesizing the experiences of these [beings] who are ignorant of each other's communications, this boundary is unavoidable.
Furthermore, the self must be understood as eternal, because it transcends the sequence of time.
This reasoning, which is well-known to the entire world, is now set forth therein.
Immediately after birth, as the infant drinks from the mother’s breast,
it is postulated that he indeed remembers the causal efficacy (arthakriyā) of the milk for his own benefit.
And memory depends upon experience, yet no such experience exists here in this birth;
therefore, it must be due to some prior experience.
And the learned maintain the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of those two;
therefore, let it be understood that this Self is eternal because of its perpetual stability.

This has been stated by me myself in the *Śrīparāstotra*: "O Mother, as that infant was descending from the casket of your womb onto this earth, he gazed with his charming face, which was then intent upon the tips of your breasts."
"O supreme ones! He declares that state to be imperishable by making it his own; yet why is this body, which is merely a garment for play, never cast aside anywhere?
Thus, by proposing the eternal and stable nature of the Self, its perpetual steadfastness is established.
It is established that even pillars and the like possess stability until their destruction. For instance, if a perceived object were to perish in a single moment,
its existence would belong only to this very moment— such as that of a blue thing— and not to any subsequent moment.
If one grants that the consciousness which perceives in this manner persists for two moments,
then the doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is destroyed.
If it is argued that even that consciousness is broken into moments, then those various distinct moments—
being cognitions existing at different times— are mutually unaware of one another.
How could others know that [existence] lasts for only a single moment,
or how could the course of worldly life not perish for human beings?
As for what they assert— that the continuum performs that action—
if the continuum were as unstable as something that is not a continuum, then it would indeed be so.
The teacher Śrī Somānanda stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* that the stability of the world is understood as occurring through the succession [of moments] when that [consciousness] is firm.

Furthermore, in the extensive treatise beginning with "Thus there is unity in the world," and by the reasoning stated therein, momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) itself is unstable and impossible to maintain. When that [flux] is unstable, the stability of the universe is established by implication. By this, [the stability] of the Supreme Lord...

The state of being the agent of universal worldly activity has been explained as consisting in the possession of the triad of powers: knowledge (*jñāna*), memory (*smṛti*), and the power of removal (*apohana*).
As it is stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*:
"There may be one whose body is consciousness, possessing the powers of knowledge, memory, and removal."
And as it is said in the Śrī Bhagavadgītā: "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. And in that regard:
"The Great Lord (Maheśvara) has within Himself embraced the entire range of objects of knowledge."
To embellish the course of worldly life with its various manifold diversities.
That power of vision which, by its own will, pierces through certain fixed objects and causes them to emerge from within itself is called *dṛk-śakti*.
Even when engaged in outward orientation, one's own nature as the radiant form of consciousness,
not abandoning its own pure transparency, becomes ever-new knowledge.
Even though this ever-newly blossoming [consciousness], which is like a flash of lightning,
is flashing forth, people are unable to engage in worldly affairs according to their desires.

That which is the locus of inwardness for that consciousness when it is turned outward— the nature of consciousness itself— remains unchanged throughout all states, even across the vast divisions of time.
The boldness of its external conceptualization is called memory;
moreover, whether that object is a new appearance or something remembered, it is in reality [nothing other than consciousness].
One should not abandon identity with one's own conscious power, which consists of the universe;
therefore, both awareness and memory would be the two excellent [powers] of the Great Lord.
That object of cognition is known through consciousness; that consciousness, in turn, is known through another instance of consciousness;
and the object of cognition is distinguished from other objects of cognition.
Thus, a certain glory of the Lord’s sovereignty is called *apohana*;
in this way, the powers of knowledge, memory, and exclusion (*apohana*) have been clearly explained.
Being a weaver, a potter, or [a creator] through these three powers,
Śiva experiences happiness, remembers, and conceptualizes the manifold diversity of the universe.
Thus [ends the verse]. 54.
Granted that the human goal in the form of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) belongs only to a self that possesses stability;
however, its nature as bliss (*ānanda-svabhāvatva*) is contested, since some maintain that the state of liberation is like that of a stone. Anticipating this objection, he says:
Indeed, the Śruti declares that everything is dear for the sake of the Self's own pleasure;
therefore, the Self is of the nature of bliss, whether it be liberated or unliberated.
Indeed, there is the Vedic revelation (śruti) stating, "Everything is dear for the sake of the Self," which,

by its very nature as a reflection upon the Supreme Lord, possesses intrinsic authority; furthermore, unlike statements such as "Brahman is bliss" (*ānando brahma*), this [text] specifically conveys a particular reasoning.
It expresses an object that is indeed free from sublation:

namely, having made one's own pleasure— the joy consisting of the manifestation of desire for what is dear to oneself— the motive, every object such as children, friends, and so forth, which is engaged with in worldly activity, is experienced as being a source of gratification.

Thus [it is said]. The word "nanu" (surely) is intended to establish the opponent's own admission. Therefore, because the Self—characterized by the radiance within one's own heart—is full, the internal cognition "I am" is called bliss.

Thus, the bliss whose true essence consists in resting in one's own self—which is the contemplation of the fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*)—is itself the unique form [of consciousness]. And since its nature is such, there is no difference whatsoever between the two states of liberation and non-liberation. Furthermore, if...
Bliss would not be the inherent nature of that self; rather, its children, wife, and so forth, or states such as tranquility and self-restraint, would be what bring it satisfaction.
For even a thousand children and the like cannot satisfy one who is devoid of consciousness.

They are capable of drawing forth something [from consciousness]. And it has been stated that bliss is precisely the state of consciousness resting in itself. When, however, there is indifference toward the reflective awareness of this self-resting, then there occurs the designation of the experience of suffering such as burning or cutting. But in reality, [it is otherwise].

Even though such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) may be absent from the perspective of ordinary vision, there is never any lack of rest in one's own nature for this [consciousness]; thus, it is observed that there is never any suffering apart from the constant experience of bliss. [Objection: But if its essence is bliss (*ānanda*), how can there be anger and the like in men?

If it is argued that this is a readiness to experience the afflictions of being struck by weapons and so forth, we say no; rather, such exertion arises solely from the helplessness caused by the obsession of passion for fields, wives, and the like, and thus, at the commencement of such worldly activity, there is for them only a determination toward pleasure (*ānanda*).
Because even sufferings enter the stage of bliss—just as in states such as striking—their nature as bliss is established;
as it is said in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*: "Even sufferings become like happiness. And thus, of the Self...

The meaning of the Śruti has been explained as follows: whatever state of one's own—such as desire (*kāma*), longing (*icchā*), eagerness (*autsukya*), hope (*āśā*), or craving (*spṛhā*)—exists as its very nature (*svabhāvatvena*), it is precisely that which, when opened up, causes the entire manifold of objects of knowledge (*vedyaprapañca*), such as children, women, and so forth, to become a source of gratification. In this context, the particle *tu* serves for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). [The phrase] "for the sake of desire" (*kāmāya*)...

The dative case is used according to the rule *tumarthācca bhāvavacanāt* ("and after words expressing an action denoting the purpose of an infinitive"). Likewise, in such cases as "one should abandon the earth for the sake of the self" (*ātmārthe pṛthivīṃ tyajet*), the distinction [between the two types of self] should also be inferred. Since the word "for the sake of the beloved" (*priyārtham*) presents the meaning of "affection" (*prīti*) by means of the word "beloved," affection is indeed the very nature of the self.

It is experienced in many ways through the diversity of its own agents, instruments, and so forth; however, it is indicated that there is no other entity such as "pleasure" apart from this—whether one is liberated or unliberated. Indeed, according to the system of the Naiyāyikas and others, in the state of liberation...

Because the self consists primarily of stone, it is devoid of bliss; this is presented with such disregard in order to illustrate that since its very nature is thus unavoidable even in the absence of liberation, what need is there to mention the experience thereof? Furthermore,

Since one's own nature is necessarily that of bliss (*ānanda*), no disturbance caused by dualistic conceptualizations such as bondage and liberation can possibly arise here, because bliss consists of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of consciousness (*cit*), existence (*sat*), and experience (*anubhūti*). As they say:
"Where there is the pervasion of consciousness and existence, there bliss shines forth;
where bliss exists in an entity, there is the abiding of consciousness and existence. It is for the purpose of unfolding this very bliss that [the teachings] exist in our traditions.
The insistence on accepting the first, second, and subsequent substances is what is bound; such is the Upaniṣad. 55.
Now, having thus established the reflective awareness of the radiance of the true nature of the Self,
and intending to teach the extremely clear means (upāya), such as the individual means (āṇava) and others, he first introduces all three by means of a single verse:
If there is a desire to determine the radiance of one’s own heart, which is eternally partless,
then the central *tuṭi*— the junction where the moon and the sun [of the breath] are severed— must be split.

One's own heart, which is by nature capable of being illumined by direct realization and whose essential character has been explained, undergoes an "expansion" (ullāsa)— that is, its manifestation through the variety of states such as being an object of cognition or a cognizer;
that [expansion], by its very nature, is partless, as it transcends the divisions of time.
If there is a desire to make that very [reality]— which is free from the stain of all conceptual constructions regarding what is to be rejected or accepted,
and so forth— the locus of certainty characterized by the wonder of direct perception through extreme clarity.
If some desire should arise according to the principle established in the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā: "For you who have approached Me, this person consists of faith; as is one's faith, so is that person."
Thus, this is the method here; it is the mode of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) common to all the matters to be explained.

In that regard, these two—Soma and Sūrya—consist of the phonemes *sa* and *ha*, because they vitalize the class of objects of knowledge (*vedya*) and because their nature is that of the non-differentiated knower (*veditr*), being respectively *Akula* and *Mārtāṇḍa*.

The two specific phonemes (*varṇaviśeṣau*) are [the letters *r* and *l*]; their weapon (*astra*) is the *visarjanīya*; and the nasalization (*anusvāra*), characterized by the encapsulation within one's own heart, belongs to those two as they pervade [the vowels]. The *tuṭi* situated between them is that fragment of time (*kālakhaṇḍa*) characterized by the moment of abiding in a state of division. That...

It must be severed; it must be extracted like a ruby from its setting. This means that at that moment, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "I am the *haṃsa*" arises. The underlying idea is this: although in the recitation of the *mātṛkā* and other contexts, these two [phonemes] are grasped as being common to other letters—namely, *ha* and *sa*—nevertheless, even so...

The dyad "haṃ" and "saḥ," which reside within one's own heart and are inseparable from the Absolute (Anuttara), should be contemplated as the essence of the Great Mantra through their union as "haṃ saḥ," serving as the means for the recognition of one's own Self; thus, it is extracted in reverse order.
A practitioner of mantra, concealing worldly external activities that fall within the scope of deliberation,
and moving along a path of guile, should lead them toward the left-hand way (vāmamārga).

Thus, according to the principle of the *Śrīlaghubṛṃhaṇī*, this is for the purpose of indicating the necessity of secrecy and for the purpose of bringing to mind another mantra, namely "So 'ham" (That am I). And this is a certain *āṇava* means (*upāya*), because it consists of the reflective awareness of specific phonemes that constitute a mantra.
As it is stated in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*:
"That immersion (*samāveśa*) which occurs through the mental formulations of utterance, the instruments, meditation, phonemes, and locations, is correctly called the individual means (*āṇava*)."

The same should be inferred for *uccāra* (articulation) and the others as well. Among these, *uccāra* in the form of the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is as follows: "When [the breath] is in the state of retention (*kumbhita*), exhalation (*recita*), or inhalation (*pūrita*), at its conclusion that which is named 'Tranquil' (*śānta*) shines forth, tranquilized by peace. Thus it is said.
An example of an action consisting of the stabilization of the body is as follows:

"O Mother! Some, with their tongues—whose tips are coiled around the base of the palate—seize that digit [of the moon] which rests upon the tip of the sprout of the *lambikā* and consists of the nectar-water."
Dhyāna has the nature of mental elevation, as follows: the beauty of the pale-red sprouts, arising gracefully from within the basin of the tree-trunk which is constantly moistened by nectar;
"By firmly grasping the pillar, a certain tender creeper, shining with light, bears forth some indescribable state.
Thus, the conceptualization of the postures (*sthāna*) consisting of the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the *mūlādhāra* and other centers is as follows:
"In the *yoni* [cakra], Your light has the luster of a mass of gold; in the heart, it blazes with flashes of lightning;
in the *ājñā* [cakra], O Maheśvarī, it is a great splendor resembling the moon.
Thus, although there is some mutual intermingling among these [descriptions], one should consider the predominance of each respective [aspect]; enough said.

By means of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). Furthermore, *Soma* is the manifestation of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), whose nature consists of that which is to be sought, that which is to be known, and that which is to be accomplished.

*Sūrya* is the flashing forth of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), consisting of will, knowledge, and action. The locative case here is used to characterize a state (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*), meaning "while these two are attaining their respective purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*)"; thus it is said. Likewise...

And the "fracture"—the defect characterized by doubt—regarding these two [objects] and my own self as the subject must be severed; the meaning is that the doubt arising toward one's own self must be cut away. This is what is being said: [this is the life-force] of the desire for attainment and so forth—
This gross manifestation of the phenomenal world cannot arise anywhere without the activity of the three powers, beginning with will (*icchā*); thus,
it dispels the affliction of doubt and suspicion, which consists in the contrary state of not having a clear and direct perception of the Self whose nature is that of the desirer and so forth.

From that, there arises the attainment of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of one's own heart in its previously described form. And this is the *śākta* means (*upāya*), because it consists solely of the conceptualization of one's own consciousness, being devoid of vocal utterance (*uccāra*) and the like. As it is said in that very same [text]: "Meditating with the mind alone upon the reality that is free from vocal utterance..."

"That immersion which one attains is here designated as Śākta. Furthermore, it is well known that Soma is apāna and Sūrya is prāṇa; [their movement extends] from the dvādaśānta to the heart, and from the heart to the dvādaśānta. The word "astam" is a past passive participle used in the sense of an abstract state (bhāve niṣṭhā).
Since the two [powers] spontaneously attain *āsana*, which is the throbbing characterized by projection (*kṣepa*),

that *tuṭi* which stands between them— perceived as both external and internal— is of the nature of the activity of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) and is characterized by wonder (*camatkāra*); it is that which must be "unstrung" (*uttruṭitavya*).
The meaning is that one must determine this for oneself until it reaches the state of being heart-felt. This is the underlying intention:

that the two vital breaths, prāṇa and apāna—which are by nature eternally emergent and common to the entire body, and which constitute the ultimate reality of the movement of one's own self—simultaneously possess the nature of the source (araṇi) for both types of emission.

Although reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is self-established, it should be personally integrated through contemplation in order to produce stability in the wonder of the joy within one's own heart; for even in its absence, there is no impairment whatsoever to its essential nature. This, moreover, is the means [to transcend] the agitation of all conceptual constructions.
It should be understood as *śāmbhava* because it functions by establishing only its own essential nature through the exclusion [of all else]. As it has been said:
"One who was previously thinking of nothing at all is awakened by the Guru."
"The possession that arises is declared to be Śāmbhava.
Furthermore:
"In this very manner, for a long time during the onset of the dark fortnight in the terrible night..."
One should meditate on a form appearing as if through cataracts; it will become the form of Bhairava.

Thus, according to the principle of the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka— that a specific fragment of time situated between the moon and the sun, which simultaneously reach either the particular western mountain or their destruction, must be extracted by the intellect—
this interpretation is extremely clear; however, it has not been set forth here out of insistence [on brevity].

And here, because of the predominance of the common vernacular, it is stated by means of a *tantra* (concise expression) as "astra," "āsthāma," "artha," "asta," "madhyam," "mama," "tuṭi," and "truṭi. Furthermore, when this triad of means is examined with subtle scrutiny, their mutual intermingling exists as something unavoidable. Only...
To teach that there is a separate designation based solely on predominance, [it is said]:
"In this matter, the wise should not conceive of a difference in the fruit of consciousness.
According to this principle, there is nothing whatsoever regarding the fruit for all the means (upāyas).

The statement is made all at once in order to demonstrate this disparity; however, if it were stated by way of sequential connection, it would be with the intent of winning over those to be trained (*vineyajana*). And in that regard:
"The means of non-differentiation is taught here as Śāmbhava, while the Śākta is said [to follow]."
The means consisting of both difference and non-difference, the means of difference, and that which is the individual (āṇava) [means].
The first [levels] are accomplished through the utterance and other [practices] belonging to the stages of *prāṇa* and so forth;
the middle ones by means of pure conceptual constructions; and the others when those [constructions] have been stilled.

Thus, according to the principle of the twenty-fold means (*upāya*) in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, the impure conceptualization consisting of the vibration and articulation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the individual means (*āṇava*). That which consists of pure conceptualization brought about by mind alone is the empowered means (*śākta*).
And that whose nature is the total dissolution of all conceptualization is the divine means (*śāmbhava*). Such is the threefold reality of the means.

The penetration of the manifestation of power (*śaktyullekha*) is present everywhere through a gradation of grossness, subtlety, and so forth; however, it should be understood that its excellence in the *Śākta* state consists merely in its intensity. As it has been said: "That power is declared to be threefold, as the *āṇava*, the *śākta*, and the *śāmbhava*."
Having manifested Śiva through the means created by Himself, He liberates these beings.
Thus [ends verse] 56.

Having thus established the three means simultaneously, and wishing to elaborate upon each of them individually for the sake of instilling them in the hearts of those to be trained, he first examines the *āṇava* [means]:
"Observe, even within the grossest elements, the partless state of space."
How could that Somanātha be anything other than one who has utterly transcended the thirty-six [tattvas]? || 57 ||
Among the principles (tattvas) thus explained, the venerable Lord Paramaśiva stands as the supreme,

being the one to be realized through all means (upāyas). Furthermore, among the others, some such as Śiva and so forth are conceived as subtle, while others such as Prakṛti and Puruṣa are considered gross.

The relative grossness of earth and the other elements is also established; for their effects, such as pillars and jars, are designated as "most gross. And even within those most gross things, [one perceives] the partless nature of space (kha) in comparison to earth and the rest.

Contemplate that state which is your very nature, devoid of the play of the subtle parts (kalās) characterized by limitation; it is through this state that its well-known status as the locus of Khecarī and the other powers is established.
"Contemplate" means that all [beings], without distinction between those who hold contrary views and those who do not, [should do so].

The meaning is: "Examine [this] in accordance with your own scholarship. Thus, if even this [reality], which is exceedingly gross, is admitted to be partless (niṣkala), then what kind of Supreme Lord (parameśvara) would He be who transcends even the thirty-six principles? What would be the excellence of His partlessness, and how great would it be?
And let this be understood, if the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (the simultaneous occurrence of two events) is mastered:

this is the method consisting of meditation upon the subtle. And thus, by the gradual elimination of the grosser levels, through the observation of increasingly subtle states, there arises the tasting of the nectar of the reflection upon one's own extremely subtle Self.
By the term "attainment" (*siddhi*), the Śākta [means] is also indicated here. As it is said in the *Upāyaviṃśati*:
"Abandoning each grosser level, one should take refuge in each subtler one;
thereafter, having abandoned even the subtle, one becomes solely composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*)."
And as it has been stated by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka: "One should contemplate everything in its entirety, sequentially, in the form of the path of the worlds and so forth,
through the states of gross, subtle, and supreme, until finally there is the dissolution of the mind."

This is an indicative illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it should be understood that in each respective reality (*tattva*), when there is the contemplation of partlessness (*niṣkalatva*), the supreme Lord’s own nature, which is partless in all its aspects, undoubtedly manifests.
As I myself have stated in the *Śrīparāstotra*:
"The earth first, then from this [earth] a forest, then from that a tree, then a branch, then a leaf, then a flower, then a fruit, and from this, sweetness"—
for one who perceives even from a single source this path of gradation leading to excellence, [how can there be any doubt regarding the superiority of the Supreme?]
"O Supreme One! That which is accomplished even from the entire universe—that we call You alone.

Having intended this very point, it was indeed stated in the *Īśvarasiddhivimarśinī*: "Like a householder among his family circle, like a king among his circle of householders, like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) among his circle of kings, like a world-protector (*lokapāla*)..."

He is the presiding lord over the group of universal monarchs (cakravartin), just as he is the presiding lord over the group of world-protectors (lokapāla) beginning with Brahmā, and even over the group beginning with Brahmā.
And thus:
grossness is the expansion of the subtle itself, while subtlety is the closing of the gross.

Thus, by virtue of this state of being the knower, this entire gross manifestation of the object of knowledge (*vedyollāsa*) is the mode of vibration of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is considered subtle. And by means of the method of counter-manifestation (*pratīkārayukti*), through the contemplative realization that "He is the Supreme Lord whose essence has been extracted [from the world]," [the world is dissolved].

The state of Śambhu is also manifested as that which is to be cultivated (*bhāvya*). As it is said in the venerable *Svacchanda*: "O Dear One, that very [reality] becomes gross due to the influence of gross limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
through the distinction between the gross and the subtle, that one [reality] is established."
And in the Āgama it is said:
"O Dear One, for him who knows water and snow through the oral tradition of the Guru,
there is indeed nothing further to be done, for he is one whose birth is his last."
By this it is meant:
"Therefore, while remaining distinct, he may make the Self an object of knowledge;
yet, because of his orientation toward that object of knowledge, his sovereignty is not fragmented."

Thus and so forth has been explained. The form *bhavatu* is the imperative (*loṭ*) used in the sense of a request (*saṃpraśna*). The form *prekṣadhvam* is used in the sense of permission (*atisarga*) and so forth. Regarding the term *somanātha*: *Umā* is the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), for it has been stated that "the maiden is the power of will.
He exists together with her, according to the Vedic tradition: "May I become many, may I procreate"—thus externally.
Because it experiences an expansion of propriety, its grossness is indicated by the word *soma*;
as for its immediate succession, they say "as it is," meaning that this [state] is not from that, nor is that from this.
Thus, by the method of the *Śrīpādukodaya*, through the transcendence of all conceptual constructs (*vikalpa*).

His subtlety, which consists in the attainment of the ultimate pinnacle of partlessness, is established by the word *nātha* (Lord). And when these two qualities are combined, his status as a vessel for the auspiciousness of possessing both forms—the manifestation of the universe and transcendence beyond it—is extended through the appropriateness of his gross and subtle aspects. He...

This means that [the reality] is being contemplated as it is proclaimed in the various successive traditions (auttarāmnāya), by virtue of being the locus for the manifestation of mutually contradictory capacities such as grossness and subtlety.
Furthermore, these three means have been established in the preceding verse through the very function of denotation (abhidhā).
In this context, however, the distinction is that while the first two [powers] exist through denotation (*abhidhā*), the other two exist by way of suggestion (*vyañjanā*).

And what is called "suggestion" is a certain function of a word that transcends the well-known modes consisting of denotation, intention (*tātparya*), and indication (*lakṣaṇā*). It is like [the power] of the self.

There exists a certain transcendent nature called "independence" (svātantrya), which is distinct from [ordinary] things such as beds, seats, and food. As stated by the author of the *Tattvāloka* in the *Kāvyāloka*:
"Furthermore, there is another very different thing to be perceived in the speech of great poets."
"That which appears as something distinct from its well-known parts, like the grace in women"—as for this, the effort expended in elaborating such a proof is irrelevant; enough of it. || 57 ||
Now he reveals the Śākta [path]:
Those connoisseurs who engage in the great festive joy of drinking the nectar-liquor from the jar of the Kula, are indeed capable of biting off the sprouts of conceptual construction. (58)

Those great souls whose minds have been purified by the falling glance of the Guide— [they perceive] that jar of the manifestation of the knowable, which belongs to the family whose nature is the expansion of the six paths;
for according to its etymology, it is called a "jar" (*kumbha*) because, by virtue of its own blissful nature, it "jars" (*kumbhayati*), that is, it holds [the world] steady and undisturbed.

The cause of establishment is a specific support; therein, that elixir (*āsava*) which is designated by the term "immortal" (*amṛta*) because it is the locus of the aesthetic relish (*sāmarasya*) of worldly and transworldly sweetness— the substance belonging to Bhairava—
its drinking consists of the prior contemplation of the predominance of one's own sovereignty.
The acceptance [of the object] without hesitation is itself the great festival in the form of a sacrifice (*makha*), whose essence is the *adhvara*,
and which is the good fortune consisting in the attainment of the direct realization of one's own bliss; with regard to that [festival],

they proceed— that is, they exert themselves— preceded by excellence characterized by the dissolving away of conceptual constructions such as the relationship between the known and the knower (*vedya-vedaka-bhāva*).

Indeed, "khalu" is used here in the sense of a reason; for that very reason, O Lord! even without drinking the nectar of devotion to You and without beholding You, living beings attain perfection through Your mere conduct alone—[perfection] consisting of various conceptualizations such as those of the Pāśupatas and Śaivas.

Thus, according to the established principle of the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*, they are capable of savoring the playful manifestations of the expansion of duality— which are animated solely by the residual traces of latent impressions— by means of the method of attaining identity with one's own Self in the form of absolute proximity, and in accordance with the fitness of the voidness of re-emergence.

They experience supreme stability; for these connoisseurs (*rasika*) experience, as their own, that *rasa* which is established by such scriptural passages as "He is indeed *rasa*" (*raso vai saḥ*). This alone is called *rasa* in its primary sense (*mukhyayā vṛttyā*), whereas [the other] is so called figuratively (*upacāreṇa*).

Sweetness, love, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), and so forth, are also designated in this manner; for it is with this intent that the Upaniṣad reveals: "This very person consists of the essence of food" (*anna-rasamaya*). Otherwise, the employment of the word *rasa* would result in meaninglessness.

By the employment of the two terms "sudhā" (nectar) and "āsava" (intoxicant), there is a distinction in their essential nature as belonging to the Pāśava and Śaiva [traditions] respectively; by "injunction" and "prohibition," there is a diversity of exhortation; by "worldly" and "unworldly," there is a gradation in conventional usage; by "to be concealed" and "not to be concealed," there is a classification of dispositions; and [by] "faith"...

The distinction between states such as "one should feel disgust," the differentiation of results as "pertaining to the next world" or "this world," and the classification of deities as "gods" or "asuras"— all such oppositions inherent in worldly conduct do not cause even a single sprout of doubt or anxiety for those who are blessed with the savoring of this [reality].
The term *mala* (impurity) is thus unveiled. For, by abandoning the distinctions between Brahmins, Caṇḍālas, and so forth—[namely] disgust, doubt, fear, shame, and fifthly, loathing;
as well as family, caste, and character—these eight are proclaimed to be the fetters (*pāśas*).
Thus, by means of this state of abiding— through the fixed order of the castes, stages of life, and so forth— all the sprouts of bondage, though manifesting,
fall away of their own accord once they have been surpassed by the beauty of resonance within one's own heart.
And as for those here who seek to establish authority by means of analogies such as the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, they are surely...
They regard that Brahminhood as crooked, even though it has been dissolved by the very look of violence.
But for us, who have leaped over all the mountain peaks of doubt— blessed are those few who, like wealth hidden by the Lord through His scriptures, [perceive] it...

They honor in their minds as a great divinity the mantra-power— the first path of sweetness and the foundation of all auspicious things— which reveals the world in a different way through the heroic stride of the Hero.

Thus, according to the principle of the manifestation of consciousness (*saṃvidullāsa*), for those who take refuge in the One, there can never be any suspicion of invalidity nor any need to establish validity; so enough of this distraction from examining the hearts of those desiring to ascend. For it is with reference to such a non-worldly reality (*alaukika-artha*) of the aforementioned nature that [the scripture says]:
In the *Śivadharmas* and other such texts: "Even though the status of being an *āgama* is common [to all], why is there such hostility toward the *Śiva-āgama*,
wherein liberation is said to be attained with ease in a single birth?"

This and more is established. Furthermore, this introduction has been examined in detail in the *Agghavejjavilāsa*, under the verse beginning "puṇṇāhantāṇa muhe. And this is the method for accepting this specific substance.

Because he has been established as having the nature of the playful manifestation of the All-Knowing One (*viśvavedya*), and because it is determined that his powers constitute the entire universe through the state of equilibrium among all powers (*sarvaśaktisāmarasya*),
there is the savoring of the Unsurpassed Conduct (*anuttarācāra*) in contrast to the conduct of other systems.

And because it is experienced as having the nature of power (*śakti*), which is another synonym for "vibration" (*sphurattā*), it is called *śākta*. Furthermore, from the perspective of the ultimate view, it is the wonder of the experience of the excellence of bliss, which is accomplished by the acceptance of the substance as established [by the preceding stages].

It should be understood that this is indeed the Śāmbhava [state], because it is experienced as being of the nature of one's own essential being (svasvabhāva). For, according to the principle established in the *Rājabhairava-sūtra*—namely, "the activity of common folk is the authority"—this is perceived as the object of spontaneous human activity. And because it is stated in the *Śrī-Vijñānodyota*:

Through the expansion of the bliss of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arising from the delight in the essence of eating and drinking, one should contemplate the state of fullness; thus, one becomes composed of great bliss (*mahānanda*).

In this regard, the illustrious Kṣemarāja has explained that "this is the Śāmbhavī manifestation" within the section concerning the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka. This is also an illustrative indication;
therefore, this same principle applies everywhere regarding the bliss of savoring the five objects of sense. For example:
In the *Viṣayapañcikā*: "The joy produced by hearing sweet sounds such as the music of the lute (*vīṇā*), the flute (*veṇu*), and singing, has sound alone remaining."
Thereafter, one whose form is awakening flashing forth as the cessation of worldly existence, being liberated from the power of worldly existence, attains perfect liberation.
And so forth. As it is stated in my *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"Abounding in flower offerings, thick sandalwood, flutes, cymbals, and the performance of dance, with young women as charming as honey..."
"Even if thousands of phenomena were to awaken, the one digit of the supreme consciousness, which brings delight within each of them, remains victorious. Furthermore,
whether these [states] belong to the Śākta, Śāmbhava, or other categories should be understood from their respective specific contexts and so forth.
And as it is stated in the *Śrī-Vijñānodyota* with reference to a single object characterized by the enjoyment of a beloved person:
"It culminates in the immersion into power (*śaktyāveśa*), which is agitated by the union of powers (*śaktisaṅgama*)."
That bliss which belongs to the reality of Brahman is called the bliss of one's own self.
Thus, in this state, there is the condition of being "without protection" (*aṇavatva*),
because of the intense recollection of the bliss of woman through licking, churning, and striking; O Mistress of the Gods, even in the absence of physical power, there occurs a flood of bliss.
In this regard, the nature of Śākta [power] is as follows:
when great bliss has been attained, or when a long-lost kinsman is seen,
one should contemplate that surging bliss and, taking it as the focal point, become absorbed in it.
Thus, in this context, the nature of Śāmbhava has also been thoroughly examined. || 58 ||
Now he teaches the Śāmbhava [state]:
"Ah! Let the face reflect, let it cause reflection; likewise, the mirror [is the locus].
But that in which the mirror itself reflects must also be known. (59)

For it is a matter of common knowledge in the world that an object such as a face, shining forth by facing toward a clear substance like a mirror, appears vividly through the principle of reflection (*pratiphalana*). In this regard,
the actual nature of the mirror, the face, and so forth will be demonstrated right here immediately below.

In the gross view, the entity considered to be the face undergoes the act of reflection; and since the mirror serves as its substratum, it acts as its instrumental cause—let this be so for now. But as for this mirror itself...
Due to its purity, it is experienced as the locus for the reflection of the face and other such objects;

that very [purity] in which, within one's own extremely pure self, [the object] reflects in such a form must also be known— that of which this manifestation of the capacity for all reflections consists.

In the phrase "jñātavya" (to be known) and so forth, one should consider the various meanings of the kṛtya suffixes— such as being worthy of knowledge, being capable of being known, or being necessarily to be known— or [the senses of] command, permission, and so on, for the purpose of directing the minds of those to be trained. This applies to the passage beginning with "pratibimbatva" (the state of being a reflection).

The *loṭ* (imperative) mood is used here for the purpose of addressing oneself with the freedom to act as one wishes. By the word "hanta," compassion is expressed toward those other established philosophers (*siddhāntika*) who are devoid of the realization of the nature of the original object and its reflection; and by that [compassion], all this [work] is characterized as being like a mirror-face and so forth.

The expanse of the sacrificial altar, including its pillars, jars, and so forth— having entered into the enclosure of the garland and being characterized by a preeminent clarity due to the absence of other objects, and consisting of the Supreme Lord whose nature is non-different from one's own—
is [reflected] in that great mirror-surface by means of the principle of reflection, which is synonymous with identity with that [mirror].

The intended meaning is that it "vibrates intensely" (*parisphurati*). This is also an illustrative indication; by it, [the following is included]: "Sound in the ether, and beautiful touch in the abode of bliss;
and other touches as well, arising from firm blows, pain, cold, and so forth."
Because it exists as a reflection, that which stands outside does not cause the shaking of one's own body;
in the same way, smell is clearly present within the nose, and taste within the saliva of the teeth.
Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, sound consists of an echo in the ether;

and in practices such as the recollection of the woman (*aṅganānusmṛti*), there is touch within the bodies of those possessing delicacy, due to the contemplation of a proximate rough touch at the foundational wheel (*ādhāracakra*).

From the mental connection with a tamarind fruit or the like being tasted by another person, there arises a taste in the saliva; during the state of burning sandalwood and such, there is a fragrance within the interior of the nose; and in cases such as memory or imagination, there is the manifestation of joy, sorrow, and so forth, whose nature is experienced by other people within one's own mind.

This excellence of the perfection of reflection is universal. Thus, while in external objects such as mirrors, the perception of a reflection depends upon an original object (*bimba*), in the case of one's own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*), the reverse is true: it contains the entire manifold variety of the universe.
Because it is experienced as a reflection. As it is said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*: "A reflection is presented by means of an external original;
if that very thing is the reflection, what original could remain?"
And so it is said in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"O maiden, the state of being a reflection (*bimbatā*) is clearly [perceived] in fire, water, mirrors, and other transparent objects;
yet, because it is accompanied by its own adjuncts (*paricchada*), that original object (*bimba*) of yours is not perceived."
And this extraordinary principle of reflection culminates precisely in the Śāmbhava means (upāya).
As they say: "This [world] has arisen from me alone; it is reflected within me alone."
"The Śāmbhava means of attainment (upāya) is threefold: [the self], the world, and that which is beyond both.
As it is said in the *Śrītantravaṭadhānikā*:
"Just as the existence of jars and other objects in a mirror consists of a mixed nature [of both the object and its reflection]..."
"Thus, within my own self, there exists this variegated form of these [external] entities.
This very capacity of the Supreme Lord to reflect the universe is called His transcendent sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which should be contemplated by the wise within. And of the universe...

In the Supreme Lord, whose nature is light, no other method than this process of reflection (pratibimba) accords with propriety as a way for [objects] to manifest. If it is argued that there is instead the theory of illusory manifestation (vivarta) or transformation (pariṇāma), we say no; for what is called "illusory manifestation" is—
Error is defined as a cognition consisting in the superimposition of one thing upon another, which is synonymous with delusion (*bhrānti*).
Accordingly, it must be admitted that either the universe is superimposed upon the Self, or the Self is superimposed upon the universe.
Regarding these two positions, in the first case, just as the "serpentine-ness" perceived in a snake is superimposed upon a rope;

Thus, having thought, "Where else has this been seen?", the universe might be superimposed upon the Self. Furthermore, no subsequent sublation is experienced here, such as "This is not a snake" or "This is not the universe. If it is argued that sublation will be established there by means of reasoning (*yukti*), we say no. What indeed is this so-called "reasoning"? It is *tarka* (logical inference).

Or would it be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Not the first [alternative], because, since its root is something to be brought about (*āhārya*), it is not accepted as independently establishing an object apart from its role as an auxiliary to a means of valid cognition. Nor the second. And what would that means of valid cognition be: perception (*pratyakṣa*) or scripture (*āgama*)?

Or is it inference? Not the first, because no one perceives its sublation by direct perception; on the contrary, the entire worldly transaction proceeds unimpeded through causal efficiency and the like. Nor is it the second. For as for scripture—

"Brahman is one only, without a second; there is not even the slightest diversity here," and so forth. This is its meaning: first of all, for Brahman—which is non-different from the Supreme Lord who is the very nature of the Self—there is no propriety for the manifestation of difference in any form whatsoever. However, this much remains to be considered therein: [The text continues: ...In that regard, [the following objection is raised: "If Brahman is indeed the Self, then since the Self is directly perceived, why is it not realized? Furthermore, how can it be said that Brahman is 'without a second,' when the world of names and forms is directly perceived? Moreover, if Brahman is the Self, then since the Self is eternal, how can it be said that Brahman is 'unborn'? To this, the reply is as follows: It is true that the Self is directly perceived, yet it is not realized because it is obscured by beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*). Just as the sun is not seen when covered by clouds, so too the Self is not realized when veiled by ignorance. Furthermore, the world of names and forms is not real; it is merely a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon Brahman, like the appearance of a snake on a rope. Therefore, Brahman is rightly said to be "without a second. And although the Self is eternal, it is called "unborn" in the sense that it is not produced like a pot or other objects. Thus, there is no contradiction. As it is said: "The wise see the same Lord dwelling equally in all beings, the Imperishable within the perishing. Those who perceive Him thus become immortal. (Gītā 13.27) Therefore, Brahman is indeed one, without a second, unborn, and eternal. This concludes the explanation of the meaning of the scriptural passages.

What is the nature of the existence of this throbbing phenomenal world (*prapañca*)? To this we reply as follows: here, within Brahman—which conforms to linguistic usage and is determined as "this" through introductory context and so forth—this entire phenomenal world, consisting of ether, wind, and the rest, does not become manifold.
The locus of the manifestation of difference does not come into being. What then?
By means of the perspective of reflection—which has been established as consisting of that very sovereignty—the nature of Brahman alone is perceived as undivided. Otherwise, there is no reality here.

Otherwise, it would be heard as "something" (*kiñcana*), or the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would follow as a consequence. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because the logical mark (*liṅga*)—such as "the contested [world] is false because it is perceived, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"—is subject to the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) by the very scripture already cited. In this same way, other fallacies such as "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) should also be inferred. However, for fear of making the book too voluminous, they are not detailed here.
That shall not be elaborated here. Furthermore, by which knower (*pramātṛ*) is this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) superimposed upon Brahman?
If it is argued that it is by that very Brahman, then it follows that the error would lack a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhāna*), since Brahman has been accepted as the one who performs the superimposition.

If it is argued that [the Self] accomplishes both of those purposes in part, we say no; for even so, it would follow that it is subject to error. If it is then argued that the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is the superimposer (*adhyāropaka*) and Brahman is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), we say no.
This is because the doctrine of difference is not accepted, and because there would necessarily be a partial self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

If it is argued that a conceptual difference is freely admitted, we say no; for that very [difference] was intended to be designated by the term "illusory manifestation" (*vivarta*). Furthermore, by what kind of similarity [is it established]?
The phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is superimposed upon Brahman; and if that [superimposition] were disregarded, how could there not be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)?

Furthermore, the dissimilarity between Brahman and the phenomenal world is well-established by virtue of the distinction between reality and unreality, and so forth. As for the position that Brahman is superimposed upon the universe— [...the text continues...]

The *kṣoda* [of Brahman] is unestablished because it would entail the transgression of the boundary [of reality] and because it would result in the falsity of Brahman; therefore, it must be determined to be absolutely insignificant. Consequently, the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the universe is its existence as a reflection of the aforementioned modes through its diverse nature.
There is nothing inappropriate in this explanation. As it is stated in the *Śrīkramakeli*:
"The manifestation (*vivarta*) of that is considered to be the mass of rays, preceded by the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśin*).
Regarding this, it is explained: "Manifestation (*vivarta*) means existing in a diverse form, but not due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*)."

"But rather, [it arises] from autonomy. By this, because the worldly transaction (*viśvavyavahāra*) is necessarily determinable through the Great Being (*mahāsattā*)— which consists of the autonomy of consciousness and maintains an equanimity toward both established existence and non-existence— it follows that its opposite is [the state of being] indeterminate (*nirvacanīya*).

Thus, even its position that [the world] is indeterminable (anirvacanīya) would be cast aside. The same should be said regarding transformation (pariṇāma). For transformation is the assumption by milk and the like of another form similar to itself, such as curd, through the destruction of its previous form. In that case too, is it Brahman...?

It must be asked: does the universe transform into Brahman, or does the universe become Brahman? Not the first, because it would entail the destruction of Brahman’s own nature. Nor the second, because it would result in the universe possessing the very nature of existence, consciousness, bliss, and so forth. If that were accepted, [the distinction] from Brahman...

Because the universe consists of all various forms of disparity, and because the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is untenable; likewise, the worldly position of identity (*tādātmya*), such as that between "tree-ness" and "śiṃśapā-ness," should also be understood as refuted. [Objection: But would this not apply equally to the theory of reflection (*pratibimba*) as well?

The doubt regarding falsity is unavoidable. For in that case, it is established by common consensus that the rays of the eye, struck by a clear substance such as a mirror, turn back and perceive themselves; thus, the cognition "a person in the mirror" is determined to be an error. That [error occurs] in the mirror...

If it is argued that the subsequent sublation, namely "the person does not exist," alone prevails, we say no. For the reflection-theory of the Supreme Lord, being extraordinary, ascends to an entirely faultless position; as has been set forth in this [theory].

In this way, the dependence upon an external object (*bimba*) does not arise. For if that [dependence] were possible, there would be room for the suspicion of falsity, based on the fact that the manifestation of the reflection follows the presence and absence of the original object. Furthermore, even in the case of worldly mirrors and the like, it is not so.

We say that there is indeed a sublation (bādha) conducive to falsity; moreover, it is non-worldly (alaukika). If it is argued, "But has it not already been stated that the sublation 'there is no person in the mirror' is actually experienced? No, [it is not so]. If a person were superimposed upon the mirror, then there would indeed be a sublation such as "he is not there. However, it is not experienced in that way. In that case...

Since what is actually perceived is merely its shadow, and not the person possessing that [shadow], this is experienced as such; therefore, because there is no cognition among the rational that "the person exists in the mirror," there would be no sublation of this [cognition]—this is the intended meaning. It is not so.

Furthermore, even when there is the actual presence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), falsity (*mithyātva*) is still appropriate. For indeed, various types of causal efficiency, such as cleaning the teeth and so forth, are observed in those looking into a mirror and the like;
however, no causal efficiency whatsoever—such as that of silver—is ever produced by mother-of-pearl and similar objects. Now, [one might object]:
If it is argued that this type of reflection indeed transcends the established boundaries of truth, we say no;
for one could equally say that it transcends the boundaries of both the well-known and the unknown.
If it is then asked whether this results in a third category distinct from both the true and the false, the answer is: true; there is a third.
The "peak" (*koṭi*) is that which is called the extraordinary, supreme, and great sovereignty of the Lord (*pārameśvara-svātantrya*).
In accordance with this, it is stated in the *Śrīmat-stotrāvalī*:
"The dual state of existing things—whether as being or non-being—is logically established."
"Having transcended that, salutation to the third, the wondrous Śambhu.
Now, if it is argued that the connection with a reflection is never observed apart from the original object (*bimba*), [the response is]: true.
What can be done? For this very reason, this [teaching] belongs to the Supreme Lord.
We have stated more than once that this is "autonomy" (*svātantrya*). If it is argued, "Let this then be the original object (*bimba*) itself," we say no;

for it lacks the defining characteristics of such an object. For an original object is perceived as a thing that is independent and devoid of any admixture with another, just like a face that has not come into contact with a mirror.
As it is said in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"But surely, in the absence of an original object (*bimba*), how could there be a reflection?
What can we do? For it is indeed seen; let it then be called an original object."
"It is not so, because it lacks that characteristic; for what indeed is called a 'reflected image' (*bimba*)?
It is that which appears as independent and unmixed with anything else, just like a face.
[Objection: "But in that case, the definition of a reflected image (*pratibimba*) would also be untenable? [Response: No, for its [definition] is as follows:
Because it is being perceived.
As it has been stated in that very same place:
"Due to the impossibility of confusion with anything else, its differentiation cannot be manifested."
They call it a reflection, just as a face [is seen] in a mirror.
"This [object] is mixed with consciousness, or else, due to its difference from consciousness, it would be impossible for it to appear;
otherwise, when there is cognition of the reality of the object and so forth, why does the reflection not appear?
[Objection: But surely, [your position] differs from the theory of reflection established in the Buddhist tenets which you have proposed...

If it is asked, "What is the difference? it is said: For in their [the Mīmāṃsakas'] view, only the object of cognition (vedya) is reflected in the cognition (vitti), but the cognition is not reflected in the object. In our view, however—even for the Buddhist—the object of cognition offers its reflection to the consciousness (saṃvid), but the consciousness does not offer its reflection to the object; thus says the *Śrīpratyabhijñāvivṛti*.

In the state of reflective awareness (*vimarśinī*), consciousness produces a reflection both in the object of knowledge as if it were the knower, and in the knower as if it were the object of knowledge.
Since both of these are modes of the vibration of the Supreme Lord, the Knower, they do not experience any disparity regarding the excellence of their transparency. As he will say: "avi..."
In passages such as "āroha apāse," that which is reflected in both [spheres] is designated as the manifold variety of the universe (*viśvavaicitrya*). As I have stated myself in the *Saṃvidullāsa*:
"Like two mirrors that have received reflections from one another..."
"There may be infinite internal interconnections between Śiva and Śakti.
Furthermore, in that regard:
"This [universe] is mixed with the object of cognition; or, when there is a distinction from the object of cognition, it is the manifestation of the possible."
Why is wisdom, mindfulness, and so forth not called a reflection with respect to enlightenment?

Thus, the principle is the same. In that regard, there is the reflection of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) within the knower whose nature is consciousness (*vitti*), whereas there is the reflection of consciousness within the object of knowledge. In every respect, the universal agitation of the world is dependent upon the impetuous outpouring of His very sovereignty. Thus, [this differs from] the theories of reflection held by the Sāṃkhya and others.
"It is to be inferred" means that, apart from theories such as illusory transformation (*vivarta*), the theory of reflection (*pratibimba*) proposed by us alone attains maturity.
As they say:

"Therefore, O Supreme Lord Śambhu! Those who assert that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is illusory, those who assert it is an effect, those who assert it is a reflection, and those who assert it is unreal—none of these touch upon Your state even in the slightest degree.
By the term "being a reflection" (pratibimbatva), this is indicated: just as a face or the like [is seen] in a mirror, what [exists] within oneself?
A person who is confused by the view of the analogy that "the universe reflects [in it]" is thus corrected: by disregarding the coarse instruction,
one's own primary manifestation is superimposed upon the universe.
Is it not as if the bank of a river seems to move for one who has boarded a boat?
Thus, by this established principle, the primary capacity for the act of reflecting the universe— which resides within one's own self—

is metaphorically attributed through similarity even to objects such as crystal or a mirror, despite their relative lack of purity. Otherwise, there would be no sense of a common object of comparison in expressions such as "the swan [is like] the moon."
Regarding the consequence that the *kvip* suffix would be rendered meaningless:
although learned scholars employ [the word] even without the comparison implied by "it reflects" (*pratibimbatīti*) and so forth, nevertheless,
in the state of extracting its refined linguistic excellence (*sauśabdya*), the aforementioned meaning necessarily follows.
Thus Maheśvarānanda, whose sole wealth was his devotion to the service of the Guru’s feet,
has declared for the sake of his own heart this good fortune consisting of the perfection of the Pratibimbavāda.

Moreover, this entire proliferation of means has been deliberated upon with reference to those people who desire to ascend to the various specific levels of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). However, in the ultimate state,
which is mounted by those who have already ascended—

In the state characterized by the exclusive remainder of one's own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), the status of being a means (*upāyatva*) reaches its ultimate conclusion; for in the absence of that [nature], the very manifestation of a means is impossible.
As it is said in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"Whatever means there may be, whether external or internal, all of that looks toward Him; how then could it possess the status of being a means [to Him]?
And in the *Śrītantravaṭadhānikā*:
Śiva does not appear through means; rather, these [means] appear by His grace.
He alone am I, self-luminous, shining as the very nature of the universe.
Thus [ends verse] 59.

Now, in order to describe the extraordinary state of those yogins whose intense joy is nourished by the self-realization attained through the manifold means taught herein, [the author] first describes their freedom from anxiety (*naiścintya*), which is unrestrained because it eliminates the distinctions between the internal and external natures.
To determine this, he says:
"When the object on both sides of the changeless state is like the color of a blue jay's wing, how can there be the conceptualization that 'the yogi is inward-facing' or 'outward-facing'? (60)
That which is sought by all and attained is the *artha*. It is a certain extraordinary reality whose nature is one's own self (*svātmarūpa*).

Indeed, unlike the plumage of a peacock, that [reality] is maintained as being of a single form in both parts, like the feathers of a blue jay and a peacock. As for the process regarding the wings of the blue jay and the peacock:

This is well-known in the world. And for an object of the nature described above, its two sides are precisely this: its appearing in two ways through the internal-external distinction, according to the propriety of "I" and "this. Furthermore, there is no other manifestation of spatial extension apart from that.
For even this [consciousness], which takes the form of being either "eastern" or "western," is perceived as being included within this [central state].

And regarding those two sides, that experience of disparity— which is based on the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower, and which is constructed by relying on a gross perception— is [a modification].

In the contemplation of the actual state of things, [the Self] follows a path of impropriety; thus, there is no modification. Indeed, for both "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*), there exists no other principle of animation apart from the vibration of the sovereignty of consciousness (*saṃvitsvātantrya*); otherwise, such a transformation would be possible. Regarding the word "object" (*artha*):

The locative case in *kartari* (in the agent) and *jñātari* (in the knower), as in such expressions, indicates a state of established existence (*siddhasvabhāvatā*). With that meaning established in this context:
"The consciousness of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings."
But for yogins, this is the distinction: vigilance regarding the connection.

Thus, according to the position of the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka, for one who accepts yoga— whose nature consists of the reflective awareness of the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower— as the very life-breath of the self, and who, for that very reason, possesses identity with the supreme reality;

For what reason could there be this artificial conceptualization—the inward-turned state of the knower consisting in abiding within one's own self, and the outward activity characterized by distraction toward objects of knowledge? It does not cohere at all. This is so even in the case of the two types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which consist of closing and opening [the eyes].
The sense is that such [entities] necessarily exist as being accomplished through mere conceptualization (*kalpanāmātra*).

This is what is meant: this knower and the known, the possessor of power and power itself, the Lord (*pati*) and the bond (*pāśa*), the world and its constituent entities (*bhāva*), are all brought to completion solely through the conceptualizations of various eminent persons.
