The opposition of dualistic constructs such as the seer and the seen, the Puruṣa and Prakṛti, the self and the body, the internal and the external, the inward-turned and the outward-directed, and the real and the unreal— all of this is Śiva; Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire universe.
Therefore, in the investigations into words and their meanings, that state which is not Śiva does not exist.
In reality, within the heart that consists of Śiva, everything shines forth clearly as being composed of Śiva;
for since everything is pervaded by Śiva, where could one go even if one were to move?

Thus, for that Great Being who— by means of the many traditional injunctions such as these— perceives this entire phenomenal world as the supreme reality of the Supreme Lord’s light, and who has directly attained the state of the Supreme Lord himself,
what proof could there be, and who else could exist, apart from the nature of his own Self?
"May it flash forth! As it is said in the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:

"O Lord! For one who perceives this entire manifold of objects as your own form, free from conceptual construction, and for whom the world is filled with his own self—how could there be fear for that eternally blissful one?"

And as it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*: "For one who recognizes, 'All this is my own manifestation,' there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of mental constructs, since he is the self of the universe."
As it has been said by the learned: "Within is the stainless light, and without are the eight forms;
everywhere, everywhere is the couch, with swan-feathers for its downy mattress."
Thus [ends verse] 60.

Now, in order to reveal that there is no stain of limitation whatsoever for this [consciousness] even through the temporal path, as was the case with the spatial path, he says: "The yogi [perceives] the sequence of the stages of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth."
It bears [this work] like a variegated garland of jewels, strung together upon the single thread of critical inquiry. || 61 ||
Regarding these stages— waking and so forth— which are sustained by the sequence of time and constitute specific states: therein, according to worldly reasoning and as a common experience for all,
waking is that which is produced by both external and internal sense organs with respect to objects.
Dream is a mental construction (*vikalpa*) whose nature consists in the creation of uncommon objects, caused solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Deep sleep (*sauṣuptam*) is the absence of the manifestation of objects in any form whatsoever.
As it is stated in the *Śrī Śivasūtras*: "Knowledge is waking; dream is mental construction; non-discrimination is *māyā*."

Regarding the term "deep sleep" (*sauṣupta*): as it has been stated in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*: "That common creation which, through the range of all the senses, exists as external and stable—that is waking (*jāgara*)."

"Even that which is the path of the mind alone is considered the state of dream, because of the delusion that objects appear clearly as sensory objects; and when one remains in that much alone, it is called the state of deep sleep, comparable to cosmic dissolution. Thus [it is said].
From the perspective of the yogi, however, these take the form of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*.

In the scriptures, they are defined as follows: *dhāraṇā* is the binding of the mind to a particular place; *dhyāna* is the continuous flow of cognitions regarding that object; and *samādhi* is the dissolution of the state of subject and object, and so forth. This is the fourth [state].

Furthermore, even the non-yoginī remains as a single form with all yoginīs; the distinction of the yogin lies solely in his capacity for such reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). And regarding the "fourth" (*turīya*), according to the principle established in the *Śivasūtra*, it is the fourth among the three, to be poured like oil.
The great radiance that persists through the three states beginning with waking is an illustration;

for it is necessarily the case that there is a second within one, a third within two, a fourth within three, and a fifth within four. Furthermore, this is [stated] in the aphorism by way of instruction.

It has been stated in summary: the yogi, whose nature has been explained, perceives that sequence of these phases— which, despite their mutual distinctness, possesses a single form due to its inherent structural stability—
as being like a string of pearls or rubies set with various other gems, by means of what is called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness).

Weaving together all things with a single thread that is bold in its universal penetration, he carries them forward; by means of a certain excellence that transcends worldly ways, he brings them to their respective essential natures through reflective awareness and establishes them within his own self. And therein—

Even for worldly people, that which transcends the three common states and is ascertained as having the nature of the fourth state (turya) beyond the supreme subject is here designated as "reflective awareness" (vimarśa), by means of which—
By the logic of the "garland-thread" (*sraksūtra*), the three preceding states are encompassed. Even therein, because the constituent parts (*aṅga*)—

which are themselves pervaded by association with waking and the other states— are being integrated through their aspect that has entered into the very nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), they are to be encompassed.
Thus, both [the notions of] "embracing" and [the others] are consistent. For instance, within the four states beginning with waking—
namely, waking-waking, waking-dreaming, waking-deep sleep, and waking-turiya— a mutual interpenetration is perceived in such a manner.
In that regard, for one who is awake, there are four distinctions: unawakened, awakened, fully awakened, and perfectly awakened.
[The states of] going and returning, being well-dispersed, being gathered, and being well-composed.

Thus [is described] the state of dreaming; "arisen, vast, peaceful, and perfectly serene" refers to deep sleep. But as for the fourth state (turiya): "Indeed, this boundless state of turiya cannot be conceived within this [sleep]."
Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, there are three divisions: *manonmana*, *ananta*, and *sarvatobhadra*;
and within the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*), there is this single division known as *satatodita*.

According to this principle, because it manifests as the eternal subject of awareness (*nityavimraṣṭṛtā*), it is metaphorically designated by the single term "constantly arisen" (*satatodita*). Furthermore, due to the distinctions in manifestation—namely, clear, clear-unclear, and unclear—it exists as a continuous thread throughout all states. They describe its characteristics in successive order, as it has been said:
In the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Whatever form appears clearly to someone, let that be considered waking;
whatever form appears unstable, such is the nature of dream."
That which appears indistinct is deep sleep, as is that which exists prior [to it];
and by virtue of which the synthesis of these three arises.
"Let that musical instrument, like a garland-string, be grasped in all its varieties.

Thus, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is experienced everywhere as undisturbed due to its uniform nature, having the essential character of the supreme Bhairava, which is one's own true self. As it is said in that very same [text]:
"That which has all distinctions melted away by the radiance of the fullness of non-duality is called the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta); one should apply this [definition] everywhere.
Thus, it is well said that the fourth state possesses the capacity to establish both meanings.
With this very intention, it was stated that the simile is "variegated" (*citrā*). Consequently, just as a string of pearls woven with many gems such as rubies, pearls, sapphires, and emeralds—
due to its excellence in the intermingling of the variegation of colors such as red, white, and dark blue— is in some places...

Even though something may be unique to a particular individual, its invariable concomitance with the association of all other distinct phonemes is experienced and directly perceived; likewise, within the succession of stages such as waking and so forth,
the variety of their mutual interpenetration is synthesized according to the method already explained.

Thus it is aphorized. This is what is meant: the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka, who transcends the fourth state (turyātīta), whose nature is the power of consciousness (cicchakti), who is named the Great Light (mahāprakāśa), whose form is that of the supreme subject (paramapramātṛ), and whose essence is the vibration of eternal emergence—[he is] the subjectivity delimited by the name "Accumulation" (pracaya), which consists of his own bliss.

By means of the fourth state (*turya*), which has the nature of indifference toward form and the other [objects] and serves as the instrument, there occurs the animation of all triads—such as the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*); the aggregate (*piṇḍa*), the word (*pada*), and the form (*rūpa*);
and action (*kriyā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and will (*icchā*)—namely, the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep states.

Having ascended the power of yoga, which is characterized by the reflective awareness of supramundane sovereignty—the threefold characteristic already explained—one pursues the ultimate reality, which consists solely in the vibration of the radiance of one’s own freedom. As it is said in the *Śrī Śivasūtras*: "The Lord of Heroes is the enjoyer of the triad."
And it is said: "It is the vitalizing breath of the three steps and so forth. As stated in the venerable *Spanda*:
"Even though it flows through the various distinctions of waking and the other states, it does not deviate from its own innate nature as the perceiver; it remains non-different from that [nature]."
Thus [ends the verse]. 61.

Surely this has been described: the yogin’s sovereign freedom (*svācchandyam*), which is characterized by the absolute nature of the unique state of pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvitkalākaivalya-svabhāva*)— exalted by its freedom from the conceptual constructions of space, time, and so forth—
and which possesses an aversion to being tainted by any conceptual construction of a body, vital breath, or other factors distinct from himself.
This [state] would indeed arise for him; however, that is not possible because any attachment to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is eternally unavoidable.
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"With a heart agitated by the wine of the nectar of the bliss of the vault of heaven..."
The yogi desires a different flavor from the chewing of tamarind that constitutes the worldly course of life. 62.

This which is the "ulloka" (the world beyond) is the singular bliss of Brahman; according to the method of the Upaniṣads, it is that which transcends the bliss of the hearts of limited subjects such as human beings and gandharvas, and whose essence is the wonder of the contemplation of the full sense of "I-ness."

It is a certain excellence of bliss, whose own vibration consists solely in the beauty of the perfection of resting within itself; indeed, by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency— which can be conceived as the union of the two flavors whose nature is the nectar of immortality—
it is the experience of the supreme sweetness of one's own essential nature, which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and self-reflection (*vimarśa*).

Due to its proficiency, it agitates the heart of the yogin and, having extracted it, directs it elsewhere toward an object that is its own counter-correlative. And such is this "journey"— the constant flow of activity— of the world, including the body, the senses, and the worlds, by means of the heart serving as its instrument.

Just like the taste of a tamarind fruit, another flavor—such as sourness or the like—arises in relation to the excellence of sweetness previously experienced; this occurs where the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) unfolds for the yogin whose heart has been repelled [by that previous taste]. Furthermore, the power of the yogin’s will extends until the attainment of its result.

This is a misconception, as stated in the *Śrīśivasūtras*: "Just as with the stability of the mind, [it occurs] regarding the body, the organs, and external objects. Furthermore, it is well known in the world that for those whose minds are repelled by the excessive consumption of extremely sweet things such as milk and sugar, there arises a longing for other sour substances like tamarind. This...

Bhāva is the state of exaltation (ullāsa) attained by relying on the bliss characterized by the direct realization of one's own self alone, through the removal of the agitation caused by objects of knowledge such as the body and the senses; it is a form of spiritual confidence for the limited yogin whose mind is otherwise distressed by the terrors of external objects.

However, for that which is immeasurable— whose nature consists of the relish of the vibration of unconditioned bliss characterized by the reflective awareness of full selfhood— there necessarily arises the experience of "thisness" (*idantā*), since the entire external manifold has been cast into the side of one's own Self. And from that, [arises] the totality of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Even the descent into the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*), which follows the variety of experienced disturbances, ultimately culminates in the great stage of the subject (*pramātṛ*) alone, which shines with the uninterrupted sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*). As it is said in the *Śrīkramasūtras*: "The entry from the external into the internal, or from the internal [into the external]..."

"Entry into the external nature" means: as explained by the venerable Kṣemarāja—therein, from the collection of objects being grasped externally, entry into the supreme ground of consciousness within occurs precisely through the process of devouring; this is immersion (*samāveśa*).

From the direct realization of the internal power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) in its own nature, through the very capacity of immersion (*samāveśa*), there arises an immersion characterized by the solidification of the essence of consciousness (*cid-rasa*) within the external world of objects— which is otherwise designated as "this" and so forth— by means of the method of vomiting [it out]. It is with this in mind that [the following was said]:
It is stated in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*:
"I am the one whose form is the universe, 'this,' expanded by undivided bliss. And as it was said by our own teachers in the *Ānandatāṇḍavavilāsa-stotra*:
But we bow to this [power] of yours, which shines forth as the universe when you are turned outward, yet remains inwardly directed;
it consists of the bliss of absolute freedom arising from the dissolution of the universe within itself.
Thus it is said.
For this indeed is the purity of the yogin’s knowledge: that it remains undisturbed even when in contact with this [phenomenal world]. As it is stated in the venerable *Candrajñāna*:
"He who, while experiencing sense objects himself, does not fall into a state of bondage by virtue of that awakened state— he is celebrated as the Moon of Knowledge.
Furthermore, when one has consumed something of such intense sweetness that there is no longer any desire for tamarind and the like;

From the very tasting of that [bliss], through the pacification of the agitation toward the object at hand, there arises once again the capacity to take up sweet substances; likewise, from the contemplation of the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness), the perception of "this-ness" (*idantā*) necessarily follows. And upon the persistence of this "this-ness," there occurs, by implication, the entry into such a state of *ahantā*.

Through the state of abiding within the wheel (cakra) of the Self, there is no room for any suspicion of failure regarding its eternal emergence; for when this-ness (idantā) is not perceived, the "I-feeling" (ahambhāva) remains like a king who has fallen from his kingdom, and likewise, the aspect of "this" (idamaṃśa), uncolored by the aspect of "I" (ahamaṃśa), [remains as such].
There is no appropriateness for wonder in that which is like a kingdom without a king;
as it is said in the *Śambhvaikyadīpikā*: "For the internal pervasion of light rests as 'this,' while the external rests as 'I'; this pair is well-known to all people and is undeniable. (62)

Anticipating the objection that "since this-ness (idantā) necessarily belongs to the realm of Māyā, how can this demonstrated non-difference between 'I-ness' (ahantā) and 'this-ness' be consistent?", he says:
"By whichever channels of the senses the yogi grasps the pleasures of objects..."
With those [energies] whose nature is to vomit forth from his own heart, he makes the three worlds consist of vibration. || 63 ||
By his very nature, although he has ascended to the station of the supreme subject,

the yogi— merely through the limiting adjunct of his own will— descends into the state of a limited subject; for this very reason, he appears as a great lake of the nectar of the essential identity of light and bliss.

By means of those very processes of the flow of methods, characterized by the internal and external faculties, through which one grasps— that is, makes one's own— the forms of pleasures consisting of objects such as sound and touch.

This triple world is the ultimate reality of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, constantly disgorging its own heart— which has already been explained— according to the analogy of the trunk of a rutting elephant whose lotus-like hand is moistened by the spray of froth emitted during the act of drinking water.

He effects [this] as the nature of the radiance characterized by his own heart. This is the meaning: for the yogi, while emitting these [faculties] from the state of the supreme subject within the limited subjectivity of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and those [external senses] into the external senses, and those into the ground of the object (*caityabhūmi*), he does so by this very [means].

Through the channel (*nāḍī*), this entire manifoldness of the world— consisting of the triad beginning with the subject (*pramātṛ*)— assumes a nature that is the solidification of one's own self-consciousness. As it is said in the *Śrīcidgaganacandrikā*:
"O Goddess, for which wise person is there not liberation through that conceptual cognition— which consists of the means of knowing the object and the knower— that arises by Your grace? And thus,
by the logic of devouring the universe, one possesses the experience of attaining one's own bliss through the swallowing of one's own consciousness."

The intended meaning is that by means of this *mudrā*, even the suspicion of the defect of its being illusory (*māyīyatā*) is wiped away. In the verse beginning with "ti u ḍima aṃ khu samattha," the fact that the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), consisting of the triad of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth, is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*) was revealed; here, however, of that...
Precisely because of the reason that [the Self] consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there is the exclusion of the denial of the form belonging to Māyā; this is the distinction. || 63 ||

Now, one might raise the objection that this state of non-conceptuality (*naiścintya*) of the yogins, because it depends upon means such as the *āṇava* and other [powers] and because it is capable of transcending the stage of conceptualization (*vikalpaka*), actually falls under the category of non-non-conceptuality; anticipating this, he says:
"Remain free from anxiety, just as you are"—this is indeed the established meaning. Even in that regard, it is discernment alone that teaches this; what else could it be?

Although the means beginning with the individual (āṇava) involve entry into the stages of conceptual construction because they are animated by the manifestation of duality, nevertheless, in the individual means there is a predominance of conceptualization;
in the empowered (śākta) means, there is merely its vibration; but in the divine (śāmbhava) means, there is freedom from conceptualization—thus it is progressively [higher].
From the repeated study of the stages (*parva*), their aforementioned state of freedom from thought (*naiścintya*) remains unimpeded.

Furthermore, even in the *Śāmbhava* stage, because of the entry into the general nature of the means (*upāya-sāmānya*), there may be—through subtle scrutiny—an unavoidable slight suspicion of conceptualization (*vikalpa*); yet even that [suspicion] [is overcome] by the proximity to the *Nirupāya* stage.
That which consists of absolutely pure consciousness, being real, ultimately culminates in a state that is ignorant of even the mention of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For it is said:
"Abide exactly as you are; do not go to what is external or internal."
Abandon the multitude of transformations through some expansion of consciousness.
Thus, by means of the manner in which the stability and activity of your instruction abide, remain transcending the thought characterized by conceptual construction; abide undisturbed—
this is the meaning characterized as the ground of the means.

Indeed, that which is established by transcending the sequence beginning with the individual soul (āṇava) and so forth, through the Śāmbhava state, is called "ultimate. Even therein, there exists a certain discernment; it must be contemplated through some form of reflection, namely, this instruction which has been demonstrated by such a method as "it is thus."
Regarding the revelation of the secret meaning: since that injunction expressed by "Come,

indeed" (*āssva*) and so forth has its very life in the distinction consisting of the differentiation between self and other, it cannot logically be either transitive or intransitive with respect to him.
Because, in reality, there is no difference between the object of instruction and the instructor, who constitute the action and the agent respectively.

If it is asked, "How then is this manifold proliferation of conceptual constructs, divided by such differences as these and occurring within their respective tantras, possible? we reply: "By way of metaphorical designation (upacāra). As for that which...
This was explained by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda at the beginning of the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*:

"In the passage beginning with 'The Venerable Goddess said,' it is the deity who is one's own Self that, in the state of awakening, incessantly questions itself through reflective awareness," and so forth. Furthermore, as it has been said:
In the Śrīsvacchanda:
"The Lord Sadāśiva himself, abiding in the roles of teacher and disciple," and so forth. Consequently, this state of being fearless from all quarters is the very nature of yogis.

The intended meaning is as follows: In this universe, which is purified by its identity with the reflective awareness of the Supreme Lord’s light shining in all its forms, every mode of conceptual construction—such as attention or inattention directed toward one's own self—is ultimately devoid of purpose. As it has been said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"Abandon all attentions; indeed, where can you possibly place your attention? Seek that [Reality] yourself.
For it is not fitting to seek the Full through attentions, nor does the state of Truth ever come through what is incomplete. Thus [it is said].

Furthermore, by the statement "who else could be teaching whom? it is indicated that this entire manner of instruction penetrates the non-real ground from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*).
For, since the Supreme Lord who is one's own Self is established as absolute fullness, the conceptualization of such modes [of teaching] is untenable. Just as...
Thus, these two [statements] are redundant. Since a distinction between an external and internal self is untenable, that which is based upon it [is also untenable]:
"Having moved, where will you go, since everything is permeated by Śiva?"

According to this principle, since the object consisting of coming and going is unreal, it is undisputed that its correlates— standing and sitting— are merely figurative. Furthermore, by the maxim "the Self (puruṣa) is the ultimate limit," the referent of the word *yuṣmad* (you/that) is as good as non-existent apart from the referent of *aham* (I).

Nor is it avoidable; for since there is no thought at all due to the principle that "in some cases there is affirmation and in others negation," its inconceivable nature—which consists in the negation of that thought—does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*).
Likewise, regarding the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) consisting of the impelling of one who has not yet acted, such as "sit thus" and so forth...
The point that there would be a lack of coherence, and so forth, should be inferred by oneself. || 64 ||

Thus, contemplating the nature of the yogins who possess such freedom from anxiety (*naiścintya*)— a state of extreme wonder— the author of the Tantra, because his own self is not distinct from them, [attains] a richness of reflective awareness regarding that very same nature.

Experiencing an extraordinary surge of bliss, his mental fluctuations rising with the weight and grandeur of his own consciousness—intensified by the helplessness born of this immersion—he uttered a cry of wonder:
"Oh, what a supreme joy of worldly existence! Oh, how easily accessible is the fortune of the path to liberation!"
Ah, the dual perfection of the Śiva-yogins, from which the stain of anxiety has been shattered! 65.

Truly wonderful is this supreme pleasure characterized by saṃsāra, which, though consisting of birth, death, and so forth, is of the nature of affliction for ordinary people; and although it is determined to be something to be abandoned, it is nevertheless relished by us as being equivalent to liberation. As it has been said:
In the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*:
"Where even sorrows turn into happiness, even poison turns into nectar,
and even worldly existence turns into liberation— that is the path of Śaṅkara."

And this is a marvel: the good fortune, the heart-captivating quality, and the accessibility of this matter characterized as liberation— which is sought after by all people and obtainable solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord.

"Even one who has not seen the maṇḍala [may attain this], provided it is devoid of oblations of sesame seeds and the like"—this is according to the principle found in the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra* and other texts. It is an experience free from exertion that arises from the enjoyment of liquor, meat, and so forth. This was stated by the venerable Mahāvana-muni:
I am one who is not distracted by the enjoyment of wine, meat, and women;
I am one honored by the undertaking of various kula-yogas;
I am one turned away from the state of the fettered (paśu); I am one who has taken refuge in Bhairavī.
"I am devoted to the feet of the Guru; I am Bhairava; I am Śiva.

Thus, even while each [aspect] holds primacy, one should cherish their fitness characterized by mutual inseparability, and [realize] their identity (aikātmya), defined by an absolute lack of disparity, like the balancing of a scale.
Strengthening [the argument] by means of the application of reasons, he says: "truṭitātaṅka... and so forth. Regarding those called Śiva-yogins:
we bow to those endowed with devotion, for whom the manifestation of Śiva occurs in this very way, even without meditation or recitation performed according to prescribed rules.
Thus, according to the tradition of the *Śrīmatstotrāvalī*, those great souls— who, through abundance, praise, and eternal union with Śiva, whose nature is light,
attain a connection characterized by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— [attain] that which belongs to them...

Siddhi is the radiance whose form is the wonder of one's own essential nature; that [radiance] is always dual (yāmalī), never transcending the state of duality consisting of the creation of the pair of the object and the subject.
It is by its opening and closing that the dissolution and emergence of the universe occur.
Within that, by the union of time (*kālayoga*), the Moon and Sun are proclaimed;
they consist of the fusion of the rays of Śambhu, whose nature is knowledge and action.
Thus, according to the method of various traditions (*āmnāya*), [there exists] the state of being a knower and an agent, characterized by contraction and expansion.

In the scriptures, it is traditionally taught that the nature of the manifestation of the *yāmala* (the couple) consists of the state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) between the light (*prakāśa*) and the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the other's modality. This has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptanātha:
"In that regard, the knower [is characterized] by opening and closing, which consist of contraction and expansion..."

By its very nature, characterized by knowledge and action, it consists essentially in its own vibration; and of this *yāmala*, one pole radiates as far as the absolute freedom of the consciousness of Supreme Bhairava, while the other extends to the manifestation of utterly insentient objects such as jars. That which...

The nature of the arising and resting of one’s own Self, the Supreme Lord, is "a," which is Brahman; that which has arrived there as "I" is, according to the method of the *Aitareya Upaniṣad*, called the *Rudrayāmala*—the nature of which is eternally risen exertion, consisting of the union of Śiva and Śakti. As it has been said:

In the *Śrītriṃśikāśāstra*, it is stated: "This is the Rudrayāmala. The reason for this is its state of being free from the blemish of *ātaṅka*. For *ātaṅka* is the anxiety rooted in apprehension (*śaṅkā*).
And apprehension is that which is sustained by doubt, conflicting views, and so forth; [this text], however, possesses the nature of being once-and-for-all manifest (*sakṛdvibhātasvabhāva*).

It is experienced as an obstacle to the savoring of the singular unity of one's own self-consciousness (*svātmasaṃvid-ekarasya*). Its nature as a stain consists in this: that even within one's own pure self, a suspicion of impurity is introduced.
And such a terror shatters; it perishes along with its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). At that time—

The intended meaning is that the attainment of accomplishment has been established. As stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda: "In this case, however, nothing such as the *vidyāvrata* or other observances is useful as an auxiliary factor; rather, it is only the removal of the anxiety arising from doubt regarding one's examination that is useful here. The syllable *o* indicates wonder (*āścarya*).
From the hollow of the thorny forest of the wilderness of rival philosophical systems,
some primordial Kirāta bestows the honey of the nectar of mantra.

Thus, within this manifold world— a dense thicket of endless other scriptures that employ numerous arduous means such as vows, fasts, and other afflictions— this [teaching] of ours has been brought forth solely by the supreme compassion of the Supreme Lord, who is expert in the composition of the venerable Anuttara-krama, through the state of the radiance of consciousness.
The *yāmalī* accomplishment is that which is described in the *Śrīkulagahvara* and other texts:
"That which is the unmanifest syllable situated even upon the neck of the Beloved,
having the nature of sound, free from desire, and devoid of meditation and concentration."
"Having thus directed the mind there, one should simultaneously bring the world under control.

By such statements, it is established that [the practice] consists of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*); this is what is being explained.
As it has been said in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
On this ground, pleasure and pain, bondage and liberation, consciousness and insentience—these words have a single referent, like the terms "jar" and "pot. (65)

Now, one might object: "In this supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), which consists of the essence of experiencing the bliss of consciousness that is fearless from any quarter and free from duality, there must exist some extremely intense form of worship that accords with its excellence and is to be cultivated through the succession of time; yet such [worship] is not possible for people like us immediately."

To dispel the doubt that this unfolding of the meaning possesses the mere good fortune of being heard as "it is accomplished" (sampadyate), but does not culminate in personal experiential realization within one's own heart, he says:
"By this existence, whose nature is nectar, even when touched for only a moment..."
Transcending all, he attains everything, all for a long time, and all good fortune. || 66 ||
This very state that is being pointed out— synonymous with the vibration of one's own heart and known as Great Being (mahāsattā)—
is indeed that which occurs at the time when the Guru has spoken without conceptual construction.
At that very moment, it is said, he is liberated; only the machine remains.

Thus, according to the tradition of the *Śrīratnamālā*, although he has entered into the creation produced from a mere fraction of time— which is characterized by the falling glance of the Guru— he remains one whose essential nature consists of the state of aesthetic unification (*sāmarasya*) between the two: the nectar-nature and the bliss of consciousness.

Through that liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), there occurs a great enjoyment of the self; or rather, for this very reason, its nature is immortal (*amṛta-svabhāva*), because of its necessary connection with eternal savorability. Beginning from "When this [mantra] is uttered" and ending with "or whatever fruit is desired," [this is established] according to the system of the *Śrītriṃśikā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, through the continuous application of repeated reflection upon the successive stages of increasing temporal duration— beginning with moments, *praharas*, days, and so forth— a firm state of yoga is achieved.
And by means of such a state as the cause, all [the conditions of] animalhood, humanity, and living-beinghood...

The class of subjects (pramātṛvarga), devoid of any gradation such as death, insentience, or non-insentience, transcends everything— from the entire web of fetters (pāśajāla) ending with *samanā* up to the end of *unmanā*, according to the established principle that "the Supreme Śiva is beyond.
Thus, it has emerged from the cause of bondage, which is characterized by the manifestation of the universe (*viśvavilāsa*).
Existing as the very nature of pure consciousness for all eternity,
the lifespan of Brahmā is remembered as ten times that of Viṣṇu;
the supreme lifespan of Rudra is indeed a thousand times greater than that.
Therefore, the supreme lifespan of Īśvara is said to be a hundred thousand times that;
from that, the lifespan of Sadāśiva is declared by the wise to be ten million times greater.
Therefore, the assumption of bodies by Śiva and Śivā is multiplied by the ocean [of time]. Thus,

by means of the sequential unfolding of the progression of the lifespans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and other Puruṣas as established by the limits of the venerable *Laghuvṛṃhaṇī*, the entire reality of time— up to the very essence of time— is [revealed] through the dismantling of that chronological sequence.
The sovereignty of "thisness" (idantā) extends as far as the attainment of the nature of insentient objects such as stones;

meanwhile, the plenitude of "I-ness" (ahantā), which reaches its ultimate limit in the excellence of consciousness in the form of the state of Supreme Śiva, is the very essence of enjoyment. Thus, together, they constitute the savor of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between the universe and that which transcends it.

The excellence characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which consists in the skill of captivating the inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), attains—that is, reaches—an extraordinary degree of praise through its nature as one's own spontaneous activity.
This is the intended meaning: at the very same moment as the falling of the glance of the venerable Lord Deśika...

There is no disagreement regarding the attainment of the human goal characterized by liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which possesses the beauty of resonance with one's own heart for men. As it is said in the venerable *Triṃśikāśāstra*: "It bestows immediate Kaulika perfection; it bestows immediate liberation through yoga."

And as it has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavaguptapāda: "He who attains this is, at the very moment of that attainment, no longer a bound soul (paśu). And for such a state of being, there is an internal reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by the repeated performance of action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*), which consists of the various powers of sovereignty such as *aṇimā* and so forth.
The outward movement of manifestation is experienced. As it is said in that very same [text]:
"For one who practices this, the perfection of omniscience is attained.
This was explained by Abhinavaguptapāda as follows: "Even without practice, there is liberation while living (jīvanmuktatā)."

"The supreme Kaulika accomplishment" means "in a mere moment. For reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is indeed instantaneous; as it is said according to the perspective of the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "Once gold has been known, one need not resort to the practice of contemplation (*bhāvanā*). Thus, even regarding external objects, there is no doubt concerning their causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*).
He employs means; what need is there to mention [employing them] toward that reality called the Supreme Lord, which is one's own essential nature?
As it is said in that very same place:
"Once, by means of a valid authority—whether from scripture or from the words of a guru—"
When Śiva-nature has been known, through a firm-minded realization established therein.
"There is no purpose whatsoever served by an instrument, nor even by meditative cultivation.

Here, the detailed exposition of the manifold meanings of all words, which possess various distinct significations, is for the sake of expansion; therefore, enough with this prolixity of the text. That which, having come together, possesses the nature of universal equality—
The *Mahārthasiddhāntopaniṣad* is now being unveiled. As it is stated in the *Āgama*:
"There is equality of all states of being and of all mental fluctuations in every respect;
there is equality of all views and of all substances in every respect."
There is equality among all the stages (bhūmikās), among all the vines (ovallīs) in every respect, among all the gods, and indeed among all the castes (varṇas) in every respect.
Thus [ends the verse]. 66.

Now, one might object: "If this goal is thus easily accomplished, since all cognizers are equally capable of attaining it, how can the conventional distinction between the two states of liberation and non-liberation be maintained?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:

For those who are fortunate, when the glance of the Teacher falls upon them, this [reality] becomes more hidden than the hidden and more manifest even than the manifest; for them, the first stage does not exist. 67.

This subject matter, being considered in its primary context, brings forth two states within the Self— manifestation and non-manifestation— according to the system of the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*, which describes them as gross and subtle, manifest and unmanifest, evident and non-evident, perishable and imperishable. And therein:

That which is not hidden with respect to worldly convention consists of pillars, jars, and so forth; that which is hidden is the reality of the object as determined by the Vedānta and other scriptures. Yet this [reality] is even more hidden than that, being extremely secret.
As it is said in the venerable *Triṃśikāśāstra*:
"O Lord, tell me this secret, the great secret.

Thus [he asks]. Furthermore, compared to that manifold expansion of objects of cognition (*prameya-prapañca*) which, though appearing clearly as pillars, jars, and so forth, is yet indistinct when contrasted with the flowers of the sky and the like, [the Lord] is even clearer and possesses a superior manifestation.
It exists. And this has been explained at length in the passage: "Whose [is that] touch, O Lord of the Kula?

Thus, given its dual nature, no other limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is logically possible apart from its own sovereignty. If it is asked, "How then is the distinction between the liberated and the unliberated established?"

We reply: "Because of the differentiation of the objects [of grace]. For instance, when the glance of a spatial teacher (*deśika*) or a lineage preceptor (*kulācārya*)—which is inseparable from the descent of power (*śaktipāta*)—falls upon certain fortunate perceivers (*pramātṛ*) who are in their final birth, the first [stage of initiation] occurs.
The position previously introduced is not of the nature of a hypothesis that is more hidden than hidden; rather, it is of the form of being clearer than clear.
"The true being of Śiva is bestowed, and the accumulation of bonds is destroyed."

According to this principle, their second position alone results in being inseparable from initiation (*dīkṣā*), characterized by giving and expiation (*kṣapaṇa*). Consequently, for those men who are blessed by the falling glance of the Guru, liberation (*mokṣa*) consists in becoming Supreme Śiva; for others, however, its nature is the possession of bonds (*pāśa*).

The intended meaning is that "bandha" (bond) signifies the established order (*vyavasthā*). Here, "deśa" refers to the teaching (*deśanā*), which consists of the instruction on the secret reality in the form of the recognition of one's own Self (*svātmapratyabhijñāpana*); by this etymology—meaning "that which possesses such a nature"—the Supreme Lord has entered the body of the Guru-Natha.
Thus it is proclaimed that Śiva, out of compassion, delivers the disciple whose nature as a limited subject has been severed;
as it is stated in the Āgama:
"Presiding over the Kula-teacher, Lord Śiva is the one who bestows initiation."
And as it is stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*: "Śaṅkara, the bestower of grace, resides within the heart of the Guru.
By this—
O Dear One, a living being is liberated through initiation as well as through intuitive insight;
yet that initiation depends upon the Guru for the release from the bonds of bondage.
"Intuition (*pratibhā*), however, is one's own essential nature, which bestows the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*).

Thus, according to the method of the *Śrīkiranatantra*, even for those men whose experience of liberation is accomplished solely through their own intuition, there is ultimately some grace from a Lord who acts as a teacher.

It is stated that this is indeed a matter of necessity; for within the universe, which unfolds under the sovereignty of the Supreme Lord, such intuition simply does not arise for them without His command.
And [this applies] only to the Blessed One whose body has entered into the Supreme Lord.
The capacity of the Lord Teacher (deśikanātha) consists in his ability to initiate and perform other extraordinary rites.
By the phrase "when his glance falls," it is indicated that initiation is described here as being purely visual (*cākṣuṣī*).
This pertains to those who have entered into each respective stage—namely the *āṇava*, *śākta*, and *śāmbhava* modes—of those various locations.
All those various modes, possessing the appropriateness of any one of them according to time, nature, and circumstance,

are taken into account; for that which is called a "glance" (kaṭākṣa) is the consciousness consisting of one's own heart, intended to cause the disciple to enter into the state of being graced by the Guru.
The power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) that is permeated by all initiations beginning with the *śāmbhavī* is so designated. As it has been said:
"And that [vision] is the gaze bestowed upon the disciple by the Guru, who is non-different from the pure consciousness that fills all paths, and who acts with the intent of grace."

In this context, *āṇavī* initiation is that which bestows immersion into one's true nature (*svarūpasamāveśa*) for the disciple primarily through the act of hearing the mantra revealed by the Guru; *śāktī* initiation consists of the manifestation of the power of Kuṇḍalinī and is to be pursued through mental activity; [and *māntrī* initiation is characterized] by turning away from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).
The distinction is that *śāmbhavī* is of the nature of immersion (*samāveśa*) into Śambhu, who is non-different from one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*).
In this way, the various gradations of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), such as "intense-intense" (*tīvra-tīvratara*) and so forth, should also be inferred by oneself.
In every respect, this [process] is sustained solely by the service (*śuśrūṣā*) rendered to the feet of the Lord Guru.
The investigation of the Kaulika Siddhāntas is the secret. As I myself have stated in the *Śrīpādukodaya*:
"In our scripture, it is said that the supreme fruit is the state of being possessed by the Guru."

And as it is said in the Śrī Mahābhārata: "Those who do not honor the Guru, the giver of the unsurpassed Truth (Ṛta), the treasure-trove of treasures for the four lineages— they, being sinful, go to worlds that offer no support."
Thus ends [verse] 67.
Now, it might be objected: "Indeed, the four currents (srotas) established by the Supreme Lord are revered by those who know the inner truth;

yet here, the study of the Anuttara tradition has been presented as the primary means for achieving the goals of human life. Consequently, would this not result in the former being rendered useless, or give rise to a suspicion of lack of confidence in them?"
Anticipating the objection that there is impropriety in both cases, he says:
"Let other sciences be set aside; even as [the churning-stick churns] the four oceans, so does the Lord Manthānabhairava churn this very [Tantra] which consists of nectar. (68)
For the Supreme Lord, by virtue of being the benefactor of all—
just as fragrance is in a flower, oil in sesame, the living soul in the body, and nectar in water—
so too is the Kula established within the scriptures.

Thus, according to the established position of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, it is the Kaulikī [vidyā] alone that penetrates the external sciences such as the Śruti and Smṛti; and it is our conviction that the venerable *Srotas-catuṣṭaya* brings forth this very same meaning in order to cause people who have approached it to experience it. With this intention—
"One should not revile Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, or the Vedas"—
thus it is declared in the Āgamas. In that regard,
[the systems such as] Nyāya and Āgama, though disregarded by me, are nonetheless devoid of essence.
Some, having accepted it, carry an excessive pride; for even the discarded remains of an offering, though cast upon the earth by their master,
female servants carry about upon their heads.

According to this principle, let alone that knowledge (vidyā) whose nature is Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth—which is conceived as "other" because it appears as something external; let there simply be its non-arising. The word "knowledge" (vidyā) is used in the singular to denote the class. Enough with citing the Śruti, Smṛti, and other authorities on this point.
This means by way of the great purposeful means (*mahārthopāya*) of the external sciences (*bāhyavidyā*), through their proficiency in providing instruction.
This has been examined in detail in the verse beginning with *tac ca saṇṇāvisesaṇiṇṇa* (verse 2).

Furthermore, as for those [sciences] which are extraordinary, they are [treated] by virtue of their common characteristics such as extensiveness (*vaitatya*), profundity (*gāmbhīrya*), and imperturbability (*akṣobhyatva*).
The four streams, originating from the four faces of the Supreme Lord in the order of east, south, and so forth, are like the oceans,
for they possess an excellence of inner delight through their clarity, sweetness, coolness, and essence.

The commands (*ājñās*) consist of the flow of one's own self-awareness; [the Guru perceives] this very nectar-like [reality], whose hidden nature has ascended to the level of the innermost intention (*tātparya*) belonging to those commands, as being identical with his own self-awareness.

By means of a certain delight, the Lord whose essence is Manthānabhairava churns the intended excellence of meaning; disregarding other meanings propounded by various streams, He gathers them together separately by His own power and causes them to arise. This is what is meant: in the external sciences...

Even arts such as dance and song, by being instrumental in producing the excellence of aesthetic wonder— characterized by one-pointed concentration on the consciousness of the heart of a connoisseur during the state of contemplating their own vibration— ultimately reveal the Great Reality itself; how much more so, then, [the other arts]?

The Vedas, Śāstras, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth— since their distinction consists solely in being means [to the goal] through traditional succession, any elaborate effort at argumentation regarding this is futile. However, as for the fourfold supramundane stream (srotas):

Even though various distinct meanings have been elaborated according to the predominance of knowledge (*jñāna*), yoga (*yoga*), ritual action (*kriyā*), and conduct (*caryā*), when one reaches the ultimate conclusion,
this very meaning is established as the ground to be attained. As it is said in the Āgama:

Regarding the phrase "become the treasury of the four commands" (*caturājñākośabhūtām*): as has been explained by our supreme gurus in the venerable *Ṛjuvimarśinī*, the "four commands" (*caturājñā*) are the Great Path consisting of the four currents that proceed by taking as their support the Great Consciousness (*mahāsaṃvit*) presiding over the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*); [the scripture] is the treasury (*kośa*) of that path.
"She is the great bestower of empowerment, the treasure-trove"—thus it is said. And as stated in the *Śrīkramakeli*:
"It should be understood that even within the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other Tantras, everything proceeds as being composed of this [very essence] alone.
And thus, regarding all philosophical systems (sarvadarśana)—

Because of its essential nature, this *Śrīmahārthakrama* possesses an indescribable excellence of praiseworthiness that transcends all other streams [of teachings]. As it is stated in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"In order to realize such a reality of the Self in this world..."
And the eradication of the proliferation of false conceptualization is not possible without resorting to the correct reasoning that consists of the Great Way (Mahānaya);
for the Great Purpose is therefore the most supreme among all that is supreme. Thus it is said.

For this very reason, elsewhere it is revealed with the boldness of accomplishing the most difficult of feats that for those who have no other refuge, this alone is their sole refuge— as they say: "Those seekers of the Great Purpose (mahārtha), indeed, have all other means exhausted."
And it is said: "There is no other recourse for them than the daring act of devouring conceptual construction.

And because the Blessed One is thus bold in churning such objects [of experience], he is therefore the Lord of the Kula (*kuleśvara*), who is the very form of the foundation for all limits; for he [projects] his own power (*svaśakti*).

The connection is as follows: "I bow to such a Śrīmanthāna Bhairava, who, having churned [the source], is the agent of creation and so forth. Thus, through the composition of the *Śrīkramakeli*, it is experienced as the agitation of the universe manifested by His mere will. In the Kaula tantras, He is generally known as Bhairava.

The designation [of "Bhairava"] occurs as follows: either because he is related to those living beings who are fearful and terrified of *saṃsāra* by virtue of being the bestower of fearlessness (*abhaya*) upon them; or because he is the initiator of that "cry"—where "fear" (*bhīḥ*) is the dread of *saṃsāra* and "cry" (*ravaḥ*) is the lamentation of living beings caused by that dread.

Or rather, it exists in the mind as an object of contemplation for the sake of removing the incapacity that has been explained; or, he is the Lord (*svāmī*) of the group consisting of sovereignty (*māheśvarya*) and the other [perfections], whose nature is the sounding (*ravaṇa*)— that is, the utterance (*śabdana*)— of fear directed toward those bound as cattle (*paśu*).
Or, he is called *bhīru* because he roars with fear related to the world, apprehending that [the world] must be given away;
or, he is the terrifying one even for that group of terrifying things such as death and time which are not limited by it;
or, he is so called because he impels (*irayati*) those luminaries characterized by the stars, such as the moon and the sun.

*Bhairava* is so called because he causes *bhara*—meaning time (*kāla*)—to be blown away or dried up; thus, he is the presiding lord of those great yogins who delight in devouring time (*kālagrāsarasika*). Alternatively, he is called *Bhairava* because he is the one who impels the filling (*bharaṇa*), the delighting (*ramaṇa*), and the clothing (*vasana*) of the universe. As it has been said:
By Śrī Kṣemarāja:

He is the bestower of fearlessness to the timid; he is the cause of the wailing of those afraid of worldly existence; therefore, he is celebrated in the abode of the heart as the Lord of those who delight in fearlessness, and the ender of Death himself.
"Bhairava, the Lord of that multitude of excellent yogins who sound the drum,
Śiva, whose nature is pure consciousness and who effects the sustenance and other functions of the universe, is victorious.
And that God [is so called] because of the capacity of the root *div* to denote various meanings such as "to play," "to desire victory," and so forth.

In this context, *krīḍā* (play) is the surging forth [of consciousness] as a single mass of self-awareness, through turning away from conceptual constructions such as "what is to be abandoned" and "what is to be accepted. *Vijigīṣā* (the desire to conquer) is the orientation toward existing in a state of supreme excellence. *Vyavahāra* (worldly transaction) is the reflective awareness of the manifestation of conceptual construction even within the non-conceptual Self. [It is the awareness] of the entire manifold of phenomena to be manifested—

Self-luminosity (*svayamprakāśatā*), which is inseparable from manifestation (*bhāsanā*), is its radiance (*dyuti*). Its praise (*stuti*) consists in being the locus for everything from the attainment of its own nature (*svarūpalābha*) up to the culmination of the activity of all the scriptures (*sarvāmnāya-pravṛtti-paryavasāna*). Its recourse (*gati*) is the acceptance of the triad of powers consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*) within the activities of creation and so forth. As it has been said:
By me alone—
desiring to act as the supreme one through an intense state of freedom from anxiety,
reflecting upon the internal differentiation even within my own indivisible self while manifesting as non-distinct from my own essence.

May the Lord—who possesses the splendor of the rising and falling of all things, who is the very essence of the earth’s expanse, whose majesty is kindled in both perception and action, and who sports within all states of being—shine for you. 68.

Now, one might object: "How can there be this uniformity regarding the production of the fruit for these four streams—even though they consist of such diverse forms as different mantras, tantras, manuals (paddhati), and lineages? Thus, while challenging this expectation, [the author] introduces the present Mahātantra.
In order to reveal the extracted essence of the matter in brief, he says:
"Alas, O fools! We shall proclaim the secret; do not wander within the spheres of the womb.
Contemplate that heart which is exceedingly near, and its exertion. (69)

O fools! O subjects whose souls are defiled by the soot-like impurity of the delusion of *māyā*, and who, for that very reason, possess the persistent identification with the body and so forth as the "I"! We are these few [fortunate ones] whose loftiness of the sovereignty of the Self has been made manifest by the falling glance of the Teacher.
And with their mental dispositions overcome by the compulsion of the desire to favor others, they say:

"This supreme secret, which resides in the mouths of the Yoginīs, is a reality that must be hidden according to this established rule; yet we shall speak it until it reaches the level of articulate speech."

We reflect upon this: for the presentation of the aforementioned intensity (*saṃrambha*), which consists in directing [the mind] toward another, is not possible without imparting such a reflection into that mind; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the futility of *vaikharī* speech—thus [we address] those being addressed.
It has been stated that we shall consider a certain reality regarding the purposelessness of specific types of persons.

Having established the subject matter to be discussed therein, the excessive affliction caused by the condition of ignorance of that reality is explained in the interim with the intent of inspiring interest in its thorough knowledge— do not be deluded.

Regarding the phrase "in the wombs": the meaning is, "why [should they suffer] while experiencing the affliction of dwelling within the depths of their mother’s belly, when some effortless means for its remedy exists?
By stating the prohibition against wandering in the womb's abyss with the words "do not wander," [the author implies this].
The non-deviation of the skillful mastery regarding the obstruction of the meaning that is about to be explained is manifested.

For dwelling in the womb is the ultimate ground for the experience of calamities. And by means of wandering [through various births], according to the maxim "he has had thousands of parents," its persistence over many periods of time is implied. And that—

Birth— according to the principle of the *Bhagavadgītā*, "for one who is born, death is certain," and according to the statement of the venerable Kṣemarāja, "origination is permeated by destruction"— is inseparable from the experience of death; thus,
everything included within those two [birth and death] consists of an abundance of the experience of suffering.
All the miseries of saṃsāra are subsumed within the suffering consisting of birth.
With this intention it was said by the venerable Laghubhaṭṭāraka:
"Knowing this, men do not again experience childhood within a mother’s womb."
Now, in order to establish that this very meaning is extremely easy to express, he constructs an introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) by stating: "The heart is exceedingly near.
This [heart] exists as the vitalizing principle of one's own body, which is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the manifestation of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvollāsa*).

In the state free from conceptualization (*avikalpa*), that inner reality— which transcends [dualistic] representation and is characterized by the fusion of the dyad of being (*sat*) and light-consciousness (*prakāśa-vimarśa*)— is called the Heart (*hṛdaya*). Regarding this, no suspicion of non-proximity can ever arise, unlike [the distance between] a mountain peak and a riverbank.
Because it is non-different from its own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*), an excellence (*atiśaya*) toward this proximity is experienced;

and since the exertion (*udyoga*) of such a [nature] consists in an emergent agency whose very essence is the casting aside of indifference with respect to any form whatsoever, that is the vibration (*parispanda*) of will, knowledge, and action on all sides.

Reflect upon this with a prior consideration for the manifestation of all worldly conventions that have been set in motion, observing it from the perspective of its own conformity; for within this single goal to be accomplished, the four streams of mantra,
tantra, and so forth, have been set in motion like the manifestation of a wind.

Various means such as the wind from a fan, a window, the hem of a garment, a leather bag, or blowing with the mouth are employed; by which, even if connected for only a single moment, [the suffering of] birth, death, and so forth—
There arises the great enjoyment of the fortune of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), characterized by the removal of all remaining afflictions.
And that effort, at times associated with the movement of the senses and manifesting as the expansion of the power of action,
lies upon the bed of external objects out of a curiosity to grasp sense-objects such as form and taste.
It experiences distraction and confusion, and at times, seized by the power of knowledge,
it turns back from sense objects and enjoys the abundance of inner bliss whose nature is repose in the self alone. This duality is like [the distinction between] a staff and a shaven head—
It is taught in the scriptures as being sequential in nature. As it is said in the Āgama:
"Shaving [the head] consists of the nature of knowledge, and the staff consists of the nature of action;
therefore, the sequence of shaving and the staff are considered to consist of knowledge and action."
The state consisting of stillness and so forth is a particular mode of exertion of the heart.
As it is said in the *Lakṣmītantra*:
"I am the stillness of that Supreme Brahman which is itself still."
And when worldly transactions are pervaded by the exertion of such a heart—
therefore, whether it be reality or unreality, nothing can exist without manifestation.
That manifestation, by virtue of its own sovereign power, is equal toward both reality and unreality.

According to the principle that "in whatever way a man's manifestation occurs, that is the power of Śambhu and nothing else," there is no room whatsoever for any consideration of degrees— such as whether an object is prohibited or not prohibited— because [the reality is one].
When merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the objects of injunctions and prohibitions, are examined, [the distinction between them] does not [hold],

because of their relationship as general and particular, because of the diversity in the classification of those entitled [to perform them], and because they are animated by the establishment of various distinctions in the boundaries of many mutually non-contradictory scriptures.
Since some degree of certainty is observed, this meaning is audible to all. However, regarding that which is "not for the six senses" (*aṣaḍakṣīṇa*)—

according to the principle of the secret tradition (*rahasyāmnāya*), "one should satisfy the Goddess residing in the intellect, action, and the senses with precisely those things that are forbidden"— there are [substances] such as women, wine, meat, and so forth, which are censured by other scriptures.
"These very substances are highly esteemed as the requisites for the worship of the deities we venerate. As it is said in the *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*:
"Those things which others have rejected because they are considered obscuring..."
"For by those very knowers of reality, the supreme consciousness blazes forth intensely.
This has already been explained at length previously; therefore, enough with this persistent chewing over the matter.
By the imperative suffix (*loṭ*) in the word "bhramata" and so forth—
"Father"—a little; "son"—a little; "mine"—a little; "not mine"—a little;
"yours"—a little; "not yours"—a little.
"O Bhūta, you yourself repeatedly proclaim [this] in many ways.

Thus, by means of this statement attributed to the venerable Āla, the pitiable state of the common folk—their minds utterly deluded by *māyā*—is illuminated. By the word "alas" (*hanta*), however, the author of the Tantra expresses pity for other people who have not cleansed that [delusion].
The excellence of compassion is its very nature. || 69 ||

Now, the very reality of the ultimate goal as established by us is the deity to be meditated upon within even other great sages such as Vyāsa and others; for, when one reflects upon the intended meaning (*tātparya*) in the treatises composed by them, [it is found to be] through the Great...

This very secret of the meaning is disclosed by the throat [of the author] in such passages as "in the Bhagavadgītā Upaniṣads," which refers to the moisture from the spray of the ocean of the venerable Anuttara-Āmnāya regarding this manifold variety of the phenomenal world, both high and low.
To indicate that he remains as the very breath of life (anuprāṇana), he says:
"At the commencement of the battle of Pāṇḍu’s son, the Lord Mādhava, possessing sixteen thousand powers, taught this very great purpose. May there be auspiciousness! || 70 ||

This very meaning— which has been introduced through this great treatise— consists of the meaning of existence (*bhāvārtha*), the meaning of the tradition (*sampradāyārtha*), the innermost meaning (*nigarbhārtha*), the Kaula meaning,
as well as the meaning of all secrets and the meaning of the Great Reality (*mahātattvārtha*).

According to the established tradition of the scriptures (*āmnāya*), the "Great" (*mahān*) object— the reality to be attained— is that which, by virtue of being the foundational substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the totality of the manifold variety of all objects and their respective essences, is expert in encompassing the distinctions and subdivisions of every object; and this is as follows:
It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor is it of the nature of both;
for that state is difficult to discern—it is some indescribable, unsurpassed reality.
This is not the object of meditation because of the absence of a meditator; there is no meditator because of the abandonment of meditation.
It is not the object of worship because of the absence of a worshipper; there is no worshipper because of the absence of worship.

Thus, according to the established doctrine of the *Śrī Tantrāloka*, one experiences that very nature which is augmented by the singular density of its own sovereignty— transcending the entire essence of the discourse on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). That very [nature] is the venerable *Kālasaṃkarṣaṇī*, who possesses sixteen thousand powers, who is the sixteenth [beyond the fifteen], whose characteristic is playful manifestation (*vilāsa*), and who is unconditioned by time.

Experiencing that very state of being, the Lord Mādhava— the beloved of Mahālakṣmī, the ornament of the Madhu clan, and the Blessed One— confident in his many playful movements and activities, at the commencement of the battle,
during the stage of the initial clash between the hosts of the Kaurava and Pāṇḍava armies...
"He instructs" (upadiśati) means "he has instructed" (upādikṣat),

because in the vernacular language there is no fixed rule regarding the tenses such as the past or the present; or alternatively, because this activity of [the Lord] in the *Mahābhārata* and other works is set in motion by the Blessed One in this manner in every age.
The use of the present tense (*laṭ*) indicates ongoing existence by virtue of its continuous flow. In that context, by the phrase "at the commencement of the battle"—referring to [the verse]:
"Having observed all those kinsmen standing there, that descendant of Kuru..."
Overcome by supreme compassion and despondent, he spoke this.
Having begun thus:
"Alas! We have resolved to commit a great sin, in that we are prepared to slay our own kinsmen out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty."
If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle while I am unprepared and unarmed, that would be better for me.

Thus far, Arjuna’s hesitation regarding the sin characterized by the slaughter of his own kin— such as his father and grandfather— which is forbidden by the external traditions of the Śruti and Smṛti, and which arises from a demonic obsession permeated by numerous ancient latent impressions (*vāsanā*); and [his hesitation] concerning the attainment of sovereignty and all other [worldly gains] resulting from that [action].

The detachment from pleasure and the resulting emergence of despondency are suggested. By the word "Mādhava," having revealed some kind of matrimonial relationship between him and Arjuna—[the Lord asks:
"Whence has this dejection come upon you at such a critical moment?"
O Arjuna! It is practiced by the ignoble, it does not lead to heaven, and it brings ill repute.
Do not yield to unmanliness, O son of Kuntī! This does not befit you.
Cast off this petty weakness of heart and arise, O scorcher of the foe!
Thus, there is the Blessed One’s inclination toward making [Arjuna] recognize the reality of the secret meaning.
Immediately after this:
"My nature being afflicted by the defect of wretchedness, I ask you..."
My mind is utterly deluded regarding dharma; tell me decisively what would be for my highest good. I am your disciple; instruct me, who have taken refuge in you.
Thus, because of the disciple’s state of being a student—characterized by wretchedness and helplessness—the Lord’s heart was overcome with compassion. [As it is said:
"He who thinks of him as the slayer, and he who thinks of him as slain..."
Both of them do not understand this: that it neither kills nor is killed.

By such statements as these, through the demonstration that— because the Self, which is contained within the entire bodies of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others, is eternal, all-pervading, and so forth— it is impossible for it to be slain by other people, [the author asks]: "Why, like worldly folk, should you be terrified by the threats of external scriptures?"
The statement "you experience cowardice" reveals an outpouring of grace toward him.

By the phrase "possessing sixteen thousand powers," it is indicated that just as there is external enjoyment with sixteen thousand women, so too internally there is an ascent of the intensity of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by sixteen [powers].
By making known the immersion into thousands of various intermediate powers,
[the Lord] showed the supreme sovereign form to Pārtha;
thus is established the propriety of manifesting the universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*).
"I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown great and now engaged here in withdrawing the worlds"—such was the ferocity of his proclamation of his own majesty; yet [Arjuna said]:
"Salutations, salutations be to you a thousand times, and again, once more, salutations, salutations to you!"
Thus, because his splendor was being kindled by the thousandfold praise of Arjuna,
Vāsudeva, having spoken thus to Arjuna, again showed him his own form.
And having again assumed a gentle form, the Great-Souled One comforted this terrified man.
Thus, there is a further restoration to one's former nature;
for if you do not listen out of egoism, you will perish.
This is the demonstration that failing to carry out the meaning of what has been said regarding the Self results in the great calamity of transgression.
And other difficult and marvelous deeds are recounted.
By way of expressing many meanings such as "play" and so forth, [the Lord says]:
"O son of Kuntī, I am the taste in the waters; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun."
The syllable Om is foremost among all the Vedas; sound is foremost in the sky; and manliness is foremost among men.

Through such elaborations as these, [the Lord describes] the grand display of His external manifestations of power: "I am seated within the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
By all the Vedas I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta, and I alone am the knower of the Vedas."

Thus he describes the manner of the subsequent manifestation: although there is no difference between the Lord and Arjuna regarding the absence of external latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—as indicated by the terms "Mādhava" and "son of Pāṇḍu"—[the Lord says]:
"Many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna."
I know all of them, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.

By such statements as these, the superiority of the former’s power of omniscience and so forth, and the opposite in the case of the other, indicate the appropriateness of their relationship as the benefactor (*anugrāhaka*) and the beneficiary (*anugrāhya*).
The term "teaches" (*upadiśati*) is that which runs through all [the sections] as the primary member (*aṅgin*), with the eighteen chapters serving as its subordinate members (*aṅga*).
Through this stylistic expression of inner intent (*bhāvabhaṅgī*), which is the locus of the essential purport of both external and internal scriptural systems,
even though there is a diversity in Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Vedānta, and so forth— furthermore:
"Even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion..."
He indeed should be considered a virtuous man, for he has rightly resolved.
Thus, fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
you shall come to Me alone— this I promise you as the truth, for you are dear to Me.
And thus, [the text] reveals the primacy of the worship of one's own self as the deity alone.
By the term "mahārtha" (of great significance), it is meant:
"He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me..."
I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.
Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone.
Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve.
In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a small amount of this dharma protects one from great fear.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than all secrets, been declared by Me to you. Having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.

Thus, the skill in proclaiming the meaning established by the venerable *Anuttarasrotas* is extended during the state of the Blessed One’s awakening of Phalguna; for Mādhava instructs the son of Pāṇḍu, thereby manifesting the relationship of teacher and disciple.
I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu spoke it to Ikṣvāku.
Thus the royal sages knew this [teaching] as received through tradition;
but in the course of time, O scorcher of the foe, that yoga was lost here on earth.
This very same ancient Yoga has been declared by Me to you today;
for you are My devotee and My friend, and this is indeed the most supreme secret.
Thus, by means of the lineage of the succession of gurus, the necessity of investigating the [spiritual] connection is illuminated.
By the phrase "of the son of Pāṇḍu," the possession of qualities such as goodness— which are inseparable from the noble birth of Arjuna— is indicated.
This should never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who lacks devotion,
nor to one who is unwilling to listen, nor to one who finds fault with me.
Thus, it is established that the revelation of this meaning is not prescribed for an unfit disciple, whereas for a fit one,
it is shown that what is being expounded culminates in the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).
The son of Parāśara is a great yogin, an ocean of fortitude and profundity.
In Bhārata, he spoke this concerning the Bhagavadgītā.
Having marched upon Kurukṣetra while the archers among the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the Pāṇḍavas were readying themselves, he gathered an akṣauhiṇī in an instant.
Seeing his fathers, grandfathers, brothers, sons, grandsons, and even his teachers— all those who ought to be slain— overwhelmed by such a state of distress, he [acted] with his own hand.
Trembling at his cruel deed, having cast aside his efforts in battle,
Bībhatsu felt loathing for it, being indifferent to the prosperity of the kingdom.
Having investigated the matter, the Blessed Lord Mukunda, the husband of Rukmiṇī, his heart overcome with compassion, addressed him as he stood upon his chariot:
"Alas! What has happened to you so suddenly, that you are overwhelmed by such dejection?"
Let this despondency, which is censured in both worlds, be abandoned.
Who is your father, who is your brother, who is your teacher, and who are your kinsmen?
First of all, who indeed are you, and what is this thing called compassion to you?
Who might be the recipient for this? By whom is it struck, or what is it that is struck?
Many common expressions are conceived in both worldly usage and in the treatises.
"Lest there be fear of them due to a lack of thorough knowledge of their specific distinctions," [the author] thus gradually unveils the supramundane Seal of Meaning (arthamudrā).
Through a series of incidental digressions, [I shall describe] the conceptualization of the universal agitation,
which consists of consciousness and is composed of pure, autonomous bliss that is untouched by time.
Ascertaining that [the feat] was merely the manifestation of the intense exertion of his own steady self,
the lord of heroes, overflowing with compassion for Savyasācin, [remained unmoved].
Having entered through yoga that digit which is the consort of Time (Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī) and whose sole delight is the devouring of time, one whose splendor is adorned by the *khecarī* [mudrā].
Becoming one whose Kaula lineage is pervaded by the majesty of the onset of his own power,
he bestowed upon him that supramundane vision of unswerving radiance.
Tall in stature, he manifested his universal form out of grace,
wherein there were millions upon millions of arms adorned with shimmering armlets.
There are thousands upon thousands [of beings] whose crowns touch his head;
within him are all the oceans and all the principal mountain ranges.
All the forests and the entire earth became overwhelmed;
so too did Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Kṛpa, the son of Droṇa, Karṇa, Duryodhana, and the others.
Seeing Dhananjaya filled with both terror and wonder as he lay there, clutching the flames issuing from his mouth like moths, [Arjuna spoke].
The Blessed One, whose voice was as deep as a thundercloud, spoke:
"Behold, the entire universe, from the smallest insect up to the Grandfather Brahmā, has been swallowed by me."
