there is the unity of the triad beginning with the knower, which shatters the distinction between existence and non-existence.
The contemplation of worship along with its ritual service, the latent impression of the sequence of great purpose, the extraction of the essential nature of worship, and the definition of the deity.
The contemplation of the reality of mantra is the ascertainment of the manifestation of the activity of speech;
it is the reflective awareness of the form of the mudrā, which resides within the self of pure consciousness.
Boldness in bestowing the fruit of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) of worldly enjoyment and the glory of liberation;
the presentation of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); and the rejection of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
The nature of one's own bliss, the three stages beginning with the *āṇava* [means],
the discernment of the means, and the state of freedom from anxiety for those endowed with yoga, in due order.
The lack of delay in the deliberation regarding the attainment of the fruit,
and the dependence of the excellence of one's own self-reflection upon the compassion of the Guru.
The essence of all philosophical systems regarding the subject matter under discussion,
a summary of all points already stated, and consistency with the *Mahābhārata* and other authoritative texts.
And the application of reasoning in the sequence of entering the Tantra—
for the sake of perfecting one's own spontaneous vibration (spanda), let this compendium of Tantras be grasped.

Thus, according to the logic of the oral tradition from the mouth of his Guru, the Lord Maheśvara, as if dancing in the midst of an assembly of gold, composed this *Parimala* on the *Mahākrama-mañjarī* out of affection for his disciples— a truly wondrous work.
If Śiva, who consists of discernment, can be directly realized here with ease.

First is the recitation of the verses, followed by their shadow [the commentary], and then the exposition; such is a certain method, both profound and heart-pleasing, in the task of weaving together the words and meanings of the text—
a festival for the deliberation on the meaning of reality through the synthesis of thousands of concordant statements.
And let it be understood that good fortune consists in the perfection of discernment; this is the central point of the system.
The Cola country is a land of perpetual festivals; Madhava is praiseworthy for his virtues;
the Lord is a bestower of seed, pure-hearted like crystal, illustrious, and great;
and his sovereignty is a stream of unsurpassed, mature wisdom that is perfectly clear.
"Speech is under my control"—indeed, this author of the treatise stands as the most excellent of all.
To the venerable feet of the teacher Abhinavaguptanātha— who is a wish-fulfilling tree for the great ocean of the tradition of true consciousness—
I offer this creeper of speech, which, reaching to its very roots, bears abundant fruit through its stainless intellect.
Sprouting.
Having studied the *Kāvyāloka* and the *Locana*, I became a helmsman in the ocean of literature;
thus, like a traveler, I have attained clear understanding.
On the path of recognition.

How could the shore-eroding [wave] of that great ocean of bliss not increase— the ocean which, though remaining motionless despite its efforts at the wondrous activity of the left [the creative impulse], does not undergo any transformation from the rising of the moon of non-dual consciousness as it pervades the universe?
Through the expansion of the agitation of speech, there arises a tumultuous roar of waves from many mouths.
Like the sweetness of the Kāverī, like the fragrance of the white water-lily,
and like the dance of Naṭeśa, is the majesty of this treatise.
The Blessed Lord Śiva, the ground of the creation and destruction of the universe, is the speaker here;
I am merely a mountain cave echoing his voice, and thus I harbor no pride. Whether this results in a fault or a merit, it certainly does not depend on me—such being the case.
Let either envy arise in the great, or let compassion blossom forth.
May the sound "Śiva, Śiva," cool as a fragment of camphor, always accept the foul odor acquired from the ointment of talk concerning others upon my mouth.
Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*, the work of the illustrious Maheśvarānanda, disciple of the illustrious Mahāprakāśa and also known by the name Gorakṣa.
Homage to Śambhu, the original architect who fashioned the mechanism of the Kālacakra water-clock, and whose retinue consists solely of his own autonomous consciousness.

Victorious is the Teacher Maheśvara, who expands upon this earth the consciousness of the Great Meaning through the sequences of hymns devoted to the tender *Stavapara* and the *Pādukodaya-mahārthamañjarī*.
Victorious is the rootless, unfading, non-dual supreme reality—
the great lotus whose nectar consists of the vibration, stillness, and movement of all things.
May there be auspiciousness.
